docs.title: Kubernetes Network Engineering
docs.text: A 34-lesson course covering Linux networking foundations through Kubernetes CNI, service meshes, OpenShift, AWS, GitOps, and AI GPU cluster networking.

docs.title: Start Learning
docs.text:
• :fontawesome-solid-network-wired: Track A — Linux Foundations veth pairs · bridges · iptables · namespaces · VXLAN · BGP · bare metal

  • :fontawesome-solid-plug: Track B — CNI Plugins & eBPF CNI spec · eBPF/XDP · Calico · Cilium

  • :fontawesome-brands-kubernetes: Track C — Kubernetes Networking Services · CoreDNS · IPv6 · NetworkPolicy

  • :fontawesome-solid-route: Track D — Ingress & Load Balancing Ingress · Gateway API · MetalLB · Cloud LBs

  • :fontawesome-solid-layer-group: Track E — Advanced Topics Istio · Multi-cluster · Security · Observability

  • :fontawesome-brands-redhat: Track F — OpenShift OVN-Kubernetes · Routes · EgressIP

  • :fontawesome-brands-aws: Track G — AWS EKS · VPC design · ALB/NLB controller · Hybrid

  • :fontawesome-solid-code-branch: Track H — GitOps ArgoCD · sync waves · multi-cluster delivery

  • :fontawesome-solid-microchip: Track I — AI Platform RDMA · SR-IOV · Multus · RoCE · EFA · GPU Operator

docs.title: Practice Environment
docs.text:
Every lesson uses two terminals:

# Terminal 1 — Linux node (kernel commands)
minikube ssh

# Terminal 2 — Mac / local machine (kubectl)
kubectl get pods -A

Linux-only commands (ip netns, iptables, bpftool) run inside minikube ssh. Cluster commands (kubectl, calicoctl, cilium) run from your local terminal.

docs.title: Killercoda — Free
docs.text:
Browser-based Linux and Kubernetes environments. Spins up in 30 seconds — no local install. Use for any lesson that needs a real Linux node or Kubernetes cluster. Search "Kubernetes Networking" or "Linux" in the explore page for community scenarios.

Best for: Lessons 01–24 (any minikube ssh or kubectl commands)

docs.title: iximiuz Labs — Free
docs.text:
Interactive container and Kubernetes labs by Ivan Velichko (former Google SRE). Automated verification tells you when you've solved a challenge correctly.

Resource Lessons Container Networking from Scratch 01, 02, 04, 05 eBPF Beginner Challenge 10 Networking Challenges 24

docs.title: Isovalent Interactive Labs — Free
docs.text:
Official Cilium/eBPF labs. Browser-based, no account needed for most. Each lab runs in a real Kubernetes cluster with Cilium installed.

Lab Lessons Foundations: Kubernetes Networking and Cilium 09, 12, 13 Getting Started with Cilium 12 Build an eBPF Monitoring Tool 10 Cilium: Host Firewall 16 Gateway API + cert-manager 18 Advanced Gateway API Use Cases 18 Gateway API: External Authentication 18 Cilium Cluster Mesh 22 Zero Trust Visibility 23, 24 TLS Visibility 21

docs.title: ebpf.io Interactive Lab — Free
docs.text:
Write and load a real eBPF program in your browser. Based on the opensnoop example. No kernel setup, no install.

Best for: Lesson 10 (eBPF and XDP)

docs.title: xdp-project/xdp-tutorial — Free
docs.text:
Step-by-step C labs writing XDP programs with an automated testenv setup script. Covers every XDP return code and TC hook.

Best for: Lesson 10 (eBPF and XDP)

docs.title: NetworkPolicy Editor — Free browser tool
docs.text:
Drag-and-drop visual NetworkPolicy builder. Build policies graphically, see the selector logic, export YAML, test in-browser. No account needed.

Best for: Lessons 16, 23

docs.title: Kubernetes Network Policy Recipes — Free
docs.text:
20+ ready-to-use NetworkPolicy examples: default-deny, namespace isolation, CIDR-based, metadata API block. Apply directly with kubectl apply -f.

Best for: Lessons 16, 23

docs.title: Istio — Get Started — Free
docs.text:
Official Istio quickstart on minikube. Deploys the Bookinfo app, enables mTLS, configures VirtualService traffic splitting. Covers the full lesson 21 flow.

Best for: Lesson 21 (Service Mesh / Istio)

docs.title: Tetrate Academy — Istio Fundamentals — Free (account required)
docs.text:
Free Istio course from Tetrate (major Istio contributor) with browser-based labs. Covers PeerAuthentication, AuthorizationPolicy, DestinationRule, and Envoy filters. Free certificate on completion.

Best for: Lesson 21 (Service Mesh / Istio)

docs.title: Submariner Quickstart — Free
docs.text:
Connect two local kind clusters with Submariner. Free substitute for practicing cross-cluster pod connectivity without cloud infrastructure.

Best for: Lesson 22 (Multi-Cluster Networking)

docs.title: Red Hat Developer Sandbox — Free (30 days)
docs.text:
Real OpenShift cluster for 30 days. The only free way to run oc get egressip, HAProxy routes, ovs-vsctl show, and OVN commands.

Best for: Lessons 25–28 (OpenShift track)

Setup: 

# After signing up, download oc CLI and login
oc login --token=<your-token> --server=<sandbox-url>
oc get network.operator cluster -o yaml

docs.title: Red Hat Interactive Learning Portal — Free (Red Hat account)
docs.text:
Guided browser-based OpenShift labs. Shorter than the Sandbox but no 30-day limit.

Best for: Lessons 25–28 (OpenShift track)

Full hands-on EKS workshop covering VPC CNI, NLB/ALB, Security Groups for Pods, Transit Gateway, and more. Run the networking modules only (~2 hours, ~$3 in AWS costs if you clean up).

docs.title: Lesson 01 — Linux Networking Fundamentals
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Basic Linux command line familiarity · Time: ~2 hours

Goal: Wire two virtual pods together on a single Linux host using veth pairs, a bridge, and ip_forward — replicating exactly what every CNI plugin does on node startup.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
All commands in this lesson run on Linux. Use two terminals side by side:

# Terminal 1 — minikube Linux node
minikube ssh

# Terminal 2 — your Mac (observe differences)
ip addr   # uses iproute2mac wrapper

Inside minikube ssh you have full Linux networking: ip netns, ip link add veth, bridge, iptables, etc.

docs.title: 1. The Linux Network Stack
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Application\nsockets] --> B[Transport Layer\nTCP / UDP]
    B --> C[Network Layer\nIP]
    C --> D[Link Layer\nEthernet / drivers]
    D --> E[Physical\nNIC / vNIC]

    style A fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style D fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style E fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff

Kubernetes adds virtual layers (veth pairs, bridges, tunnels) between the Link and Network layers. The kernel enforces namespace isolation at the network layer — each pod gets its own complete stack. CNI plugins operate at this virtual layer, never touching the physical NIC directly.

docs.title: 2. Network Namespaces
docs.text:
A network namespace gives a process its own isolated network stack: interfaces, routing table, iptables rules, and sockets.

# Create a namespace
ip netns add ns-blue

# List namespaces
ip netns list

# Run a command inside the namespace
ip netns exec ns-blue ip link list

# Delete
ip netns del ns-blue

Each Kubernetes pod runs in its own network namespace. The pause (infra) container holds the namespace; app containers join it via --network=container:<id>.

See also: Lesson 04 — Network Namespaces Deep Dive covers the full pod namespace lifecycle, CNI invocation sequence, and how to debug pod namespaces from the host using nsenter.

docs.title: 3. Virtual Ethernet Pairs (veth)
docs.text:
A veth pair is a bidirectional virtual wire connecting two network namespaces. Packets written into one end emerge from the other — zero buffering, kernel-internal path.

# Create a veth pair
ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1

# Move veth1 into ns-blue
ip link set veth1 netns ns-blue

# Configure veth0 on the host
ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev veth0
ip link set veth0 up

# Configure veth1 inside the namespace
ip netns exec ns-blue ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev veth1
ip netns exec ns-blue ip link set veth1 up
ip netns exec ns-blue ip link set lo up

# Test connectivity
ping -c3 10.0.0.2
ip netns exec ns-blue ping -c3 10.0.0.1

This is exactly what a CNI plugin does when it creates a pod: one veth end goes into the pod namespace (named eth0 by convention), the other stays on the host (named cali<hash>, veth<hash>, or similar).

docs.title: 4. Linux Bridge
docs.text:
A bridge (layer 2 switch in software) connects multiple veth endpoints so pods on the same node can communicate without routing.

# Create a bridge
ip link add br0 type bridge
ip link set br0 up
ip addr add 10.244.0.1/24 dev br0

# Attach veth0 (host side of pod veth pair) to the bridge
ip link set veth0 master br0

Flannel's cbr0, Docker's docker0, and Calico's cali*-to-bridge wiring all follow this pattern.

docs.title: Architecture: Two-Pod Node
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph poda [Pod A namespace]
        PA[eth0\n10.244.0.10/24]
    end
    subgraph podb [Pod B namespace]
        PB[eth0\n10.244.0.11/24]
    end
    subgraph host [Host network namespace]
        VA[veth-a-br]
        VB[veth-b-br]
        BR[br0\n10.244.0.1/24]
        ETH[eth0 — node NIC]
    end

    PA <-->|veth pair| VA
    PB <-->|veth pair| VB
    VA --- BR
    VB --- BR
    BR --- ETH

    style poda fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
    style podb fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
    style host fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff

docs.title: Flow: Pod A to Pod B (same node)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PA as Pod A (10.244.0.10)
    participant VA as veth-a-br (host)
    participant BR as br0 bridge
    participant VB as veth-b-br (host)
    participant PB as Pod B (10.244.0.11)

    PA->>VA: Packet src=10.244.0.10 dst=10.244.0.11
    VA->>BR: Frame enters bridge port
    Note over BR: ARP or FDB lookup<br/>dst MAC maps to veth-b-br port
    BR->>VB: Frame forwarded to correct port
    VB->>PB: Packet delivered to Pod B

docs.title: 5. Routing Table
docs.text:
Linux uses routing rules to decide where to send packets.

# Show main routing table
ip route show

# Add a route: reach 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.10
ip route add 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.10 dev eth0

# Add a host route for a pod IP (Calico-style)
ip route add 10.244.0.5/32 dev veth_pod0

# Policy routing — multiple tables
ip rule list
ip route show table local

For cross-node pod routing, CNI plugins either: - Add static routes per remote pod CIDR (Calico BGP, Flannel host-gw) - Encapsulate packets in a tunnel and route the outer header (VXLAN, Geneve)

See also: Lesson 02 — IP Routing and Forwarding for longest-prefix match, ECMP, policy routing, and cloud provider differences.

docs.title: 6. ARP and Neighbor Table
docs.text:
ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses within a L2 segment. The kernel caches results in the neighbor table.

# Show ARP cache
ip neigh show

# Flush ARP for an interface
ip neigh flush dev eth0

# Static ARP entry (useful for VXLAN FDB population)
ip neigh add 10.244.0.5 lladdr aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff dev eth0

Calico uses proxy_arp on each veth so pods can reach any IP without an ARP for the gateway:

cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/cali1234abcd/proxy_arp
# → 1

docs.title: 7. Key Kernel Parameters for Kubernetes
docs.text:
# IP forwarding — required so the node can route between pod and external traffic
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1

# Allow iptables to see bridged traffic (needed by kube-proxy and many CNIs)
sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1
sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables=1

# Avoid conntrack table exhaustion
sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=1000000

These are set in /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes.conf by kubeadm.

docs.title: Sysctl Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change net.ipv4.ip_forward 0 Enables packet forwarding between interfaces Must be 1 on every Kubernetes node net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables 0 Routes bridge traffic through iptables hooks Required for kube-proxy and most CNIs net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables 0 Same for IPv6 bridged traffic Required for dual-stack clusters net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max 65536 Maximum concurrent tracked connections Raise to 524288+ on nodes with many pods net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter 1 Strict reverse path filtering Set to 0 or 2 for Calico asymmetric routing net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh3 1024 ARP table hard limit Raise to 16384+ on nodes with 100+ pods net.core.somaxconn 128 Maximum socket listen backlog Raise to 32768 for high-connection workloads

docs.title: 8. Hands-On Lab: Simulate a Two-Pod Node
docs.text:
Reproduce what a CNI plugin does on a single Linux machine.

# 1. Create two "pod" namespaces
ip netns add pod-a
ip netns add pod-b

# 2. Create a bridge to act as the node bridge
ip link add br0 type bridge
ip link set br0 up
ip addr add 10.244.0.1/24 dev br0

# 3. Create veth pairs and wire them up
ip link add veth-a type veth peer name veth-a-br
ip link add veth-b type veth peer name veth-b-br

ip link set veth-a netns pod-a
ip link set veth-b netns pod-b
ip link set veth-a-br master br0
ip link set veth-b-br master br0
ip link set veth-a-br up
ip link set veth-b-br up

# 4. Configure IPs inside pods
ip netns exec pod-a ip addr add 10.244.0.10/24 dev veth-a
ip netns exec pod-a ip link set veth-a up
ip netns exec pod-a ip link set lo up
ip netns exec pod-a ip route add default via 10.244.0.1

ip netns exec pod-b ip addr add 10.244.0.11/24 dev veth-b
ip netns exec pod-b ip link set veth-b up
ip netns exec pod-b ip link set lo up
ip netns exec pod-b ip route add default via 10.244.0.1

docs.title: Step-by-step Observation
docs.text:
# Observe bridge MAC learning — run after first ping
ip netns exec pod-a ping -c1 10.244.0.11
bridge fdb show dev veth-a-br
# → aa:bb:cc:00:01:01 dev veth-a-br master br0 (pod-a's MAC learned)

# Watch ARP resolution inside pod-a
ip netns exec pod-a ip neigh show
# → 10.244.0.1  dev veth-a lladdr 02:42:0a:f4:00:01 REACHABLE
# → 10.244.0.11 dev veth-a lladdr aa:bb:cc:00:01:02 REACHABLE

# See packets crossing the bridge in real time
tcpdump -i br0 -n &
ip netns exec pod-a ping -c3 10.244.0.11
# → ARP request/reply, then ICMP echo/reply visible on br0

# Confirm routing table inside pod-a
ip netns exec pod-a ip route show
# → default via 10.244.0.1 dev veth-a
# → 10.244.0.0/24 dev veth-a proto kernel scope link src 10.244.0.10

# 5. Test pod-a → pod-b
ip netns exec pod-a ping -c3 10.244.0.11
# → PING 10.244.0.11: 3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Confirm environment is correct before testing
ip netns list        # → pod-a  pod-b
ip link show br0     # → br0: ... state UP
ip route show        # → 10.244.0.0/24 dev br0 proto kernel scope link src 10.244.0.1
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward  # → net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1

# 6. Cleanup
ip netns del pod-a
ip netns del pod-b
ip link del br0

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 persisted in /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes.conf and applied at boot via sysctl --system
  • net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 and br_netfilter module loaded before kubelet starts (verify with lsmod | grep br_netfilter)
  • nf_conntrack_max sized to at least 2 × max_pods_per_node × avg_connections_per_pod
  • rp_filter set to 0 or 2 on node interfaces used by CNI when asymmetric routing is in use (required for Calico)
  • ARP neighbor table limits (gc_thresh1, gc_thresh2, gc_thresh3) raised for nodes running 100+ pods
  • Veth pair naming convention verified with ip link show after every CNI upgrade to catch interface naming regressions
  • Kernel version ≥ 4.19 confirmed for stable veth/bridge behavior with eBPF-based CNIs

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Set ip_forward=1 at runtime only, skip persisting Reverts on reboot; cross-node pod routing fails silently after node restart Persist in /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes.conf; run sysctl --system after writing the file Assign the same /24 to both the pod namespace and the bridge's gateway address Overlapping subnet causes routing conflicts; ARP floods the bridge Assign a /32 host route for each pod IP on the bridge side, or use a /24 subnet for the bridge and /32 for pod IPs Leave veth host-side unattached to any bridge Pod is isolated; no traffic can leave the namespace Always run ip link set veth-X master br0 before bringing the interface up Forget ip link set lo up inside the namespace Loopback is DOWN; processes using localhost or 127.0.0.1 fail Include ip link set lo up in every namespace setup script Use identical bridge names across multiple nodes expecting them to sync Linux bridges are purely local; identical names have no network relationship Bridges are node-local; cross-node reachability requires routes or overlays (Lessons 02 and 05)

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] A veth pair is described as a "bidirectional virtual wire." What happens to a veth pair's peer interface when the namespace it lives in is deleted, and why does this matter for CNI cleanup?
Answer When a network namespace is deleted, all interfaces inside it are destroyed. Because a veth pair's two ends are linked, destroying the pod-side end (`eth0` inside the namespace) automatically removes the host-side end (e.g., `cali`) as well. This means CNI plugins do not need a separate step to delete the host-side veth — running `ip netns del ` or `ip link del ` cleans up both ends atomically.
  1. [Scenario question] You manually wire up a pod namespace with a veth pair and bridge, but pings from the pod to the bridge gateway IP (10.244.0.1) fail with 100% packet loss. The bridge is up, the veth pair is up, and the IP addresses are correct inside the namespace. What is the most likely remaining cause, and what command confirms it?
Answer The most likely cause is that IP forwarding is disabled on the host (`net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0`), so the kernel silently drops packets that need to be forwarded between the pod namespace and the rest of the network. Run `sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward` to confirm — if it returns `0`, enable it with `sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`. A secondary cause could be that `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=0` or the `br_netfilter` module is not loaded, preventing iptables FORWARD rules from seeing bridged traffic.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to verify that IP forwarding is currently enabled on a Kubernetes node?
Answer 
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
The output should show `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1`. A value of `0` means the node cannot forward packets between pod namespaces and external destinations, breaking cross-node pod communication.

docs.title: Lesson 02 — IP Routing and Forwarding in Linux
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Lesson 01 — Linux Networking Fundamentals · Time: ~2 hours

Goal: Trace a packet's exact path through the Linux routing subsystem and explain why CNI plugins choose between static routes, BGP, and VXLAN based on the underlying network topology.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Run all commands inside minikube
minikube ssh

# View live pod routes — these are real Calico-programmed routes
ip route show

docs.title: 1. How Linux Routes a Packet
docs.text:
When a process sends a packet, the kernel performs a longest-prefix match (LPM) lookup across policy rule tables:

flowchart TD
    A[Packet arrives at kernel] --> B{ip rule list\npriority 0: check local table}
    B -->|Match| C[Deliver locally\nINPUT hook]
    B -->|No match| D{priority 32766:\ncheck main table LPM}
    D -->|Match found| E[Resolve next-hop MAC\nvia ARP / neighbor table]
    D -->|No match| F{priority 32767:\ncheck default table}
    F -->|Default route 0.0.0.0/0| E
    F -->|No default| G[ICMP unreachable\npacket dropped]
    E --> H[Hand to outbound\ninterface driver]

    style A fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style G fill:#a53232,color:#fff
    style H fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
# Trace which route would be chosen for a destination
ip route get 10.244.1.5
# → 10.244.1.5 via 192.168.1.20 dev eth0 src 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Packet Routing Decision — Step by Step
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as Kernel
    participant RT as Routing Tables
    participant ARP as ARP/Neighbor
    participant NIC as Outbound NIC

    K->>RT: LPM lookup for dst=10.244.1.5
    RT-->>K: Next hop = 192.168.1.20 via eth0
    K->>ARP: Resolve MAC for 192.168.1.20
    ARP-->>K: MAC = aa:bb:cc:11:22:33
    K->>NIC: Transmit frame with outer MAC + IP packet
    Note over NIC: If ip_forward=0, transit packets<br/>are silently dropped here

docs.title: 2. Routing Tables and Rules
docs.text:
Linux supports multiple routing tables selected by policy rules evaluated in priority order.

# List policy rules (evaluated top-to-bottom)
ip rule list
# 0:      from all lookup local       ← loopback, broadcast
# 32766:  from all lookup main        ← normal routes
# 32767:  from all lookup default     ← fallback

# Show a specific table
ip route show table main
ip route show table local

# Add a rule: traffic from pod CIDR uses table 100
ip rule add from 10.244.0.0/16 lookup 100 priority 100
ip route add default via 192.168.1.1 table 100

Calico uses policy routing to steer pod traffic to the correct veth without IP masquerading.

See also: Lesson 03 — iptables and Netfilter for how conntrack interacts with routing decisions and why DNAT at PREROUTING must happen before the routing lookup.

docs.title: 3. Static Routes
docs.text:
# Host route — single destination IP (pod-specific routes in Calico/Cilium)
ip route add 10.244.1.5/32 via 192.168.1.20

# Network route — entire remote pod CIDR (Flannel host-gw mode)
ip route add 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.20 dev eth0

# ECMP — equal-cost multi-path (multiple next-hops for HA)
ip route add 10.244.1.0/24 nexthop via 192.168.1.20 nexthop via 192.168.1.21

# Delete a route
ip route del 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.20

# Blackhole route (drop traffic to unreachable pod CIDR)
ip route add blackhole 10.244.99.0/24

docs.title: 4. IP Forwarding
docs.text:
A Linux node acts as a router only when ip_forward is enabled.

# Check
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward

# Enable temporarily
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# Persist across reboots
echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1' > /etc/sysctl.d/99-ip-forward.conf
sysctl --system

Without this, pods on node A cannot reach pods on node B even if routes exist — the node will silently drop transit packets.

docs.title: Routing Kernel Parameter Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change net.ipv4.ip_forward 0 Enables IP packet forwarding between interfaces Must be 1 on every K8s node net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding 0 Same for IPv6 Required for IPv6 or dual-stack clusters net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy 0 (L3) ECMP hash uses L3 header only (src/dst IP) Set to 1 (L4) for per-flow load-balancing in K8s net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter 1 (strict) Drops packets with unexpected source interface Set to 2 (loose) or 0 for Calico/asymmetric routes net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects 1 Accepts ICMP redirects that could change routing Set to 0 on Kubernetes nodes to prevent redirect attacks net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range 32768 60999 Ephemeral source port range for outbound connections Widen to 1024 65535 on high-throughput nodes net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout 60 Time sockets linger in FIN_WAIT_2 state Reduce to 15 on nodes with many short-lived connections

docs.title: Flannel host-gw (pure L3, no overlay)
docs.text:
Node A (192.168.1.10) has pod CIDR 10.244.0.0/24
Node B (192.168.1.20) has pod CIDR 10.244.1.0/24

On Node A:
  ip route add 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.20   ← added by Flannel

On Node B:
  ip route add 10.244.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.10   ← added by Flannel
Requires all nodes to be on the same L2 segment (same VLAN/subnet). Fails across separate L3 networks.

docs.title: Calico with BGP
docs.text:
Calico runs bird (BGP daemon) on each node. Nodes peer with each other (or a Route Reflector) and exchange /32 host routes for each pod.

# View BGP peers
calicoctl node status

# View routes propagated by Calico
ip route show | grep bird

docs.title: Cilium native routing
docs.text:
Cilium programs the kernel routing table directly using BPF hooks. No separate routing daemon needed.

cilium status
cilium bpf tunnel list   # empty in native routing mode

See also: Lesson 05 — VXLAN and Overlay Networks for the alternative when nodes are not L2-adjacent and overlay encapsulation is used instead of static routes.

docs.title: 6. ECMP and Hashing
docs.text:
For high-availability setups, multiple paths to the same destination can be load-balanced.

# ECMP with weighted next-hops (Linux 3.6+)
ip route add 10.244.0.0/16 \
  nexthop via 192.168.1.10 weight 1 \
  nexthop via 192.168.1.11 weight 1

# Hash is per-flow by default (src IP, dst IP, protocol, ports)
# Check hash policy
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/fib_multipath_hash_policy
# 0 = L3 only (src/dst IP), 1 = L4 (recommended for Kubernetes)
sysctl -w net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy=1

docs.title: 7. Troubleshooting Routing
docs.text:
# Is ip_forward on?
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

# Which route will be used?
ip route get 10.244.3.7

# Is there a blackhole route blocking traffic?
ip route show | grep blackhole

# Watch routing table changes in real time
ip monitor route

# Is the packet leaving the right interface?
tcpdump -i eth0 -n 'host 10.244.3.7'
tcpdump -i cali1234abcd -n 'host 10.244.3.7'

# Check if kernel is dropping forwarded packets
watch -n1 'cat /proc/net/stat/rt_cache'
netstat -s | grep -i "forwarded\|route"

docs.title: AWS VPC
docs.text:
• Each EC2 instance has a VPC route table entry pointing to its ENI.
  • Pod routing options:
  • AWS VPC CNI: pods get real VPC IPs via secondary ENI IPs — no overlay needed, routes are in the VPC route table.
  • Overlay CNI (Flannel/Calico): pods use a secondary CIDR; traffic is encapsulated before leaving the node.
  • Requires disabling the Source/Destination Check on the EC2 instance when using non-VPC pod IPs.

docs.title: GCP VPC
docs.text:
• GCP uses a software-defined distributed router. Route tables are per-VPC and global.
  • Kubernetes on GKE injects per-node pod CIDR routes automatically.
  • Google's VPC supports custom-mode subnets with alias IP ranges for pods (similar to AWS VPC CNI).

docs.title: Azure VNet
docs.text:
• Azure CNI gives pods Azure VNet IPs from the subnet address space.
  • Kubenet (the basic option) uses a UDR (User Defined Route) for pod CIDRs — similar to Flannel host-gw.

docs.title: 9. Hands-On Lab: Cross-Namespace Routing
docs.text:
Simulate two nodes routing pods to each other (no overlay, pure L3).

# Two "nodes" = two namespaces with veth links to the host
ip netns add node1
ip netns add node2

# node1 veth
ip link add veth-n1 type veth peer name veth-n1-host
ip link set veth-n1 netns node1
ip link set veth-n1-host up
ip addr add 192.168.1.1/24 dev veth-n1-host
ip netns exec node1 ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev veth-n1
ip netns exec node1 ip link set veth-n1 up
ip netns exec node1 ip link set lo up
ip netns exec node1 ip route add default via 192.168.1.1

# node2 veth
ip link add veth-n2 type veth peer name veth-n2-host
ip link set veth-n2 netns node2
ip link set veth-n2-host up
ip addr add 192.168.1.2/24 dev veth-n2-host
ip netns exec node2 ip addr add 192.168.1.20/24 dev veth-n2
ip netns exec node2 ip link set veth-n2 up
ip netns exec node2 ip link set lo up
ip netns exec node2 ip route add default via 192.168.1.2

# "CNI" static routes — each node knows remote pod CIDR
ip netns exec node1 ip route add 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.20
ip netns exec node2 ip route add 10.244.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.10

# Enable forwarding on host
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

docs.title: Step-by-step Observation
docs.text:
# Verify routing tables in each "node"
ip netns exec node1 ip route show
# → default via 192.168.1.1 dev veth-n1
# → 192.168.1.0/24 dev veth-n1 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.10
# → 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.20 dev veth-n1       ← CNI-added route

ip netns exec node2 ip route show
# → 10.244.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.10 dev veth-n2       ← CNI-added route

# Test which route the kernel selects
ip netns exec node1 ip route get 10.244.1.1
# → 10.244.1.1 via 192.168.1.20 dev veth-n1 src 192.168.1.10

# Monitor routing decisions live while pinging
ip monitor route &
ip netns exec node1 ping -c3 -I 10.244.0.1 10.244.1.1

# Watch forwarding counters increment
watch -n1 "netstat -s | grep 'forwarded\|dropped'"
# → 3 outgoing packets forwarded

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Confirm routes are present and ip_forward is on
ip netns exec node1 ip route | grep 10.244.1
# → 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.20 dev veth-n1
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
# → net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1

# Clean up
ip netns del node1
ip netns del node2

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 persisted in sysctl.d and verified with sysctl -a | grep ip_forward after node boot
  • net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy=1 set when ECMP is used to ensure per-flow (not per-destination) load distribution
  • rp_filter set appropriately per interface when CNI uses asymmetric routing (Calico with BGP requires rp_filter=0 or 2)
  • No stale blackhole routes from failed CNI initialization — verify with ip route show | grep blackhole after cluster upgrades
  • Cloud provider-specific requirements met: AWS Source/Destination Check disabled; GCP alias IP ranges configured; Azure UDRs in place
  • ip monitor route output reviewed after each CNI update to confirm expected routes are added
  • ECMP next-hop weights balanced when nodes have differing pod densities

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Rely on default route for pod CIDR traffic Traffic exits via default gateway (internet); routers don't know pod IPs Add explicit host or network routes for each pod CIDR via the correct next-hop Use L3-only ECMP hash (policy=0) in Kubernetes All connections from one source IP always pick the same path; uneven load, broken failover Set fib_multipath_hash_policy=1 for L4 hashing so each flow is independently distributed Add pod routes with scope link without a reachable next-hop Packets go nowhere; kernel assumes direct delivery but no ARP succeeds Specify via <next-hop-ip> explicitly unless the pod is truly on the same L2 segment Forget to disable accept_redirects A rogue router can inject ICMP redirects and silently reroute pod traffic Set net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects=0 on all nodes Program pod routes inside pod namespace instead of host Only traffic from that pod benefits; other pods on the node remain unreachable to it Pod CIDR routes belong in the host network namespace, not inside the pod

docs.text: Use Case Command Show main routing table ip route show Show specific routing table ip route show table <N> Simulate routing decision for IP ip route get <dst-ip> Add static route ip route add <prefix> via <gw> dev <iface> Add host route (pod-specific) ip route add <pod-ip>/32 dev <veth> Add ECMP route ip route add <prefix> nexthop via <gw1> nexthop via <gw2> Delete route ip route del <prefix> via <gw> List policy routing rules ip rule list Add policy rule ip rule add from <src-cidr> lookup <table> Enable IP forwarding sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 Monitor routing table changes live ip monitor route Set L4 ECMP hash sysctl -w net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy=1

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is longest-prefix match (LPM) routing, and how does it determine which route is used when a packet could match both a /24 network route and a /32 host route in the routing table?
Answer Longest-prefix match means the kernel selects the route with the most specific (longest) prefix that covers the destination address. A `/32` host route is more specific than a `/24` network route, so if both are present, the `/32` wins regardless of which was added first. This is why Calico installs per-pod `/32` host routes — they always take precedence over broader subnet routes and ensure packets reach the exact pod without ambiguity.
  1. [Scenario question] Cross-node pod-to-pod traffic drops 100% even though ip route show on the sending node shows a route to the remote pod CIDR via the correct next-hop. No errors appear. What is the most likely cause, and what single command confirms it?
Answer The most likely cause is that `net.ipv4.ip_forward=0` on the node, so the kernel drops forwarded packets silently instead of routing them. Run `sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward` — if it returns `0`, the node is not acting as a router even though routes exist. A secondary cause is `rp_filter=1` (strict reverse path filtering) rejecting asymmetrically routed packets, confirmed with `sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter`.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to determine which route a Linux node would use to reach a pod at 10.244.3.7, including the outbound interface and next-hop IP?
Answer 
ip route get 10.244.3.7
The output shows the selected route, the next-hop IP (`via`), and the outbound interface (`dev`). If the route says `blackhole`, the CNI has installed a drop route for that CIDR because the node is unreachable.

docs.title: Lesson 03 — iptables and Netfilter Architecture
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Lesson 02 — IP Routing and Forwarding · Time: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Explain how kube-proxy translates a Kubernetes Service into iptables DNAT rules and trace a packet end-to-end from ClusterIP through conntrack to a backend pod.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Run all commands inside minikube
minikube ssh

# See kube-proxy iptables rules live
sudo iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n --line-numbers | head -20

docs.title: 1. Netfilter Hook Points
docs.text:
The Linux kernel's netfilter framework intercepts packets at five hook points in the network stack:

flowchart LR
    NIC_IN[NIC\nIngress] --> PRE[PREROUTING\nraw · mangle · nat]
    PRE --> RD{Routing\nDecision}
    RD -->|For local process| INP[INPUT\nmangle · filter · security]
    RD -->|Transit packet| FWD[FORWARD\nmangle · filter · security]
    INP --> LOC[Local\nProcess]
    LOC --> OUT[OUTPUT\nraw · mangle · nat · filter · security]
    FWD --> POST[POSTROUTING\nmangle · nat]
    OUT --> POST
    POST --> NIC_OUT[NIC\nEgress]

    style NIC_IN fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style NIC_OUT fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style PRE fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style RD fill:#6a4fa5,color:#fff
    style INP fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style FWD fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style OUT fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style POST fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff

docs.title: kube-proxy Packet Flow: ClusterIP → Pod
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Pod / Client
    participant PRE as PREROUTING (nat)
    participant FWD as FORWARD (filter)
    participant POST as POSTROUTING (nat)
    participant POD as Backend Pod

    P->>PRE: Packet dst=10.96.0.1:80 (ClusterIP)
    Note over PRE: KUBE-SERVICES chain<br/>→ KUBE-SVC-XXXX<br/>→ statistic 50% → KUBE-SEP-YYY<br/>→ DNAT to 10.244.0.5:8080
    PRE->>FWD: Packet dst=10.244.0.5:8080 (conntrack: NEW)
    Note over FWD: KUBE-FORWARD chain\nAccepts if src/dst in pod CIDR
    FWD->>POST: Forward to pod
    Note over POST: MASQUERADE if src is external
    POST->>POD: Packet delivered
    POD-->>P: Reply (conntrack: ESTABLISHED → auto reverse DNAT)

docs.title: 2. Tables and Chains
docs.text:
iptables organizes rules into tables (purpose) and chains (hook points).

Table Purpose Built-in Chains raw Skip conntrack; earliest hook PREROUTING, OUTPUT mangle Modify headers (TTL, TOS, marks) All 5 hooks nat SNAT / DNAT address translation PREROUTING, OUTPUT, POSTROUTING filter Allow / Drop / Reject INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT security SELinux MAC policy INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT

Processing order at PREROUTING: raw → mangle → nat → filter

docs.title: 3. kube-proxy iptables Rules
docs.text:
When you create a Service of type ClusterIP, kube-proxy writes rules like this:

ClusterIP: 10.96.0.1  Port: 80
Backend Pods: 10.244.0.5:8080, 10.244.1.3:8080

# Inspect kube-proxy chains
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n --line-numbers
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SVC-XXXX -n       # per-Service chain
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SEP-XXXX -n       # per-Endpoint chain

Packet flow for a ClusterIP request: 

Pod sends to 10.96.0.1:80
  → PREROUTING → nat/KUBE-SERVICES
    → matches KUBE-SVC-XXXX (the service chain)
      → statistic match (round-robin) → KUBE-SEP-YYY (endpoint 1)
        → DNAT to 10.244.0.5:8080
  → routing decision: forward to 10.244.0.5
  → POSTROUTING: MASQUERADE if leaving the node

docs.title: 4. Common iptables Commands
docs.text:
# List rules with line numbers and no DNS resolution
iptables -t nat -L -n --line-numbers -v

# Save and restore rules
iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4
iptables-restore < /etc/iptables/rules.v4

# Append a rule to FORWARD chain (allow pod traffic)
iptables -A FORWARD -s 10.244.0.0/16 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A FORWARD -d 10.244.0.0/16 -j ACCEPT

# Insert a logging rule at position 1 (before DROP)
iptables -I INPUT 1 -p tcp --dport 80 -j LOG --log-prefix "HTTP-IN: "

# Count packets matching a rule
iptables -t filter -L FORWARD -v -n

# Flush all rules (DANGEROUS — locks you out if no default ACCEPT)
# iptables -F

# Delete a specific chain
iptables -t nat -F KUBE-SVC-XXXX
iptables -t nat -X KUBE-SVC-XXXX

docs.title: iptables / Conntrack Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max 65536 Maximum tracked connections Raise to 524288+ for clusters with 100+ nodes net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_buckets 16384 Hash table size for conntrack Set to nf_conntrack_max / 4 net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established 432000 (5 days) TCP established session timeout Reduce to 86400 (1 day) for large busy clusters net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait 120 TIME_WAIT connection hold Reduce to 30 for high-connection-rate services net.ipv4.netfilter.ip_conntrack_tcp_timeout_close_wait 60 CLOSE_WAIT timeout Reduce if stale connections fill conntrack table net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables 0 Bridge traffic traverses iptables Must be 1 for kube-proxy to intercept pod traffic

docs.title: DNAT — ClusterIP to Pod IP
docs.text: Translates a virtual service IP to a real pod IP. Done in PREROUTING (for traffic arriving at the node) and OUTPUT (for traffic from local pods).

docs.title: SNAT / MASQUERADE — Pod to External
docs.text:
When a pod sends traffic to the internet, the pod IP must be replaced with the node's IP (since pod IPs are not routable externally).

# kube-proxy adds this for pod → external traffic
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.244.0.0/16 ! -d 10.244.0.0/16 -j MASQUERADE

# Check MASQUERADE rules
iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v | grep -i masq

docs.title: Hairpin NAT
docs.text: When a pod accesses its own service IP, the reply must loop back. kube-proxy handles this with MASQUERADE in POSTROUTING when src and dst are both pods.

docs.title: 6. Conntrack — Connection Tracking
docs.text:
Netfilter tracks connection state so reply packets can be automatically associated with their forward request.

# View conntrack table
conntrack -L
conntrack -L --proto tcp --state ESTABLISHED

# Monitor new connections
conntrack -E --event-mask NEW

# Table size (critical to tune for high-throughput clusters)
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=1000000

# Current usage
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count

# Bucket count (hash table size)
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_buckets

Conntrack exhaustion causes silent packet drops — one of the most common and hardest-to-diagnose issues in production Kubernetes clusters.

# Check for conntrack drops
dmesg | grep -i "nf_conntrack: table full"
cat /proc/net/stat/nf_conntrack | awk '{print $1, $2, $3}'

Conntrack state machine:

State Meaning Example NEW First packet of a new flow SYN packet ESTABLISHED Bidirectional traffic seen ACK after SYN-ACK RELATED Associated flow (FTP data, ICMP error) ICMP unreachable for TCP connection INVALID Does not match any known state Out-of-window RST UNTRACKED Marked with NOTRACK in raw table Intentionally bypassed traffic

docs.title: 7. ipset
docs.text:
kube-proxy uses ipset for efficient lookups when there are many endpoints. Instead of thousands of individual iptables rules, one rule matches against an ipset.

# List all ipsets
ipset list

# kube-proxy creates sets like KUBE-CLUSTER-IP, KUBE-NODE-PORT-TCP
ipset list KUBE-CLUSTER-IP

# Manual ipset
ipset create my-pods hash:ip
ipset add my-pods 10.244.0.5
ipset add my-pods 10.244.1.3

iptables -A INPUT -m set --match-set my-pods src -j ACCEPT

docs.title: 8. IPVS Mode (kube-proxy alternative)
docs.text:
IPVS (IP Virtual Server) is a kernel-level L4 load balancer — faster than iptables for large numbers of services.

# Check if kube-proxy is using IPVS
kubectl get cm -n kube-system kube-proxy -o yaml | grep mode
# mode: ipvs

# Inspect IPVS rules
ipvsadm -L -n
ipvsadm -L -n --stats

# Example output:
# TCP  10.96.0.1:80 rr
#   -> 10.244.0.5:8080           Masq    1      0          0
#   -> 10.244.1.3:8080           Masq    1      0          0

IPVS advantages over iptables: - O(1) lookup (hash table) vs O(n) iptables chain traversal - Native load-balancing algorithms: rr, lc, dh, sh, lblc, lblcr - Lower CPU for large clusters (1000+ services)

docs.title: 9. eBPF and the Post-iptables Era
docs.text:
Cilium replaces kube-proxy's iptables rules with eBPF programs attached directly to network interfaces:

# Check kube-proxy replacement mode in Cilium
cilium status | grep KubeProxy

# View eBPF-based service entries
cilium service list

# View NAT table in BPF
cilium bpf nat list

Benefits: no conntrack for pod-to-pod, no SNAT for intra-cluster traffic, lower latency.

See also: Lesson 04 — Network Namespaces Deep Dive for where iptables and eBPF programs get applied — they operate on the veth endpoints inside the pod namespace boundary.

docs.title: 10. Debugging Packet Flow
docs.text:
# Trace a packet through the netfilter hooks (requires kernel module)
modprobe nf_log_ipv4
iptables -t raw -A PREROUTING -s 10.244.0.5 -j TRACE
iptables -t raw -A OUTPUT -d 10.244.0.5 -j TRACE
# Then watch kernel logs
dmesg -wH | grep TRACE

# Count drops per chain
iptables -t filter -L FORWARD -v -n
# Pkts in and out columns show traffic; zero out means matching but passing

# Watch iptables rule hit counts live
watch -n1 'iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -v -n | head -30'

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Service ClusterIP unreachable from pods kube-proxy iptables rules missing or stale iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep <cluster-ip> Restart kube-proxy pod; check --iptables-sync-period Intermittent connection drops under load conntrack table exhaustion dmesg | grep "nf_conntrack: table full" Raise nf_conntrack_max; check nf_conntrack_count Pod can reach internet but external traffic can't reach pod MASQUERADE rule missing in POSTROUTING iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -v -n | grep MASQ Re-run kube-proxy or add MASQUERADE rule manually Pod-to-pod FORWARD drops Default FORWARD policy is DROP and no ACCEPT rule exists iptables -L FORWARD -v -n Add iptables -A FORWARD -s 10.244.0.0/16 -j ACCEPT iptables rules disappear after node reboot Rules not persisted ls /etc/iptables/ Use iptables-save / iptables-restore or switch to nftables with persistence kube-proxy IPVS mode — sessions not load balanced IPVS scheduler not set to rr or connection persistence active ipvsadm -L -n --stats Adjust scheduler in kube-proxy ConfigMap; check timeout with ipvsadm -L --timeout TRACE target shows packet entering PREROUTING but not exiting Packet dropped in nat or mangle rule before forwarding iptables -t nat -L PREROUTING -v -n Identify the rule with the highest packet count matching the src/dst

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• nf_conntrack_max sized to max_pods_per_node × max_services × connections_per_service; set nf_conntrack_buckets to max / 4
  • nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established reduced from default 5 days if the cluster handles high-churn short-lived connections
  • kube-proxy mode confirmed (iptables vs ipvs) and appropriate tuning applied — IPVS preferred for clusters with 500+ services
  • iptables-save output reviewed after every kube-proxy restart to confirm expected KUBE-SERVICES and KUBE-SEP rules are present
  • bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 and br_netfilter module loaded before kube-proxy starts
  • TRACE rules removed after debugging — they generate one kernel log line per packet and can flood the system log
  • iptables rules persisted via iptables-restore at boot if kube-proxy is not running as a DaemonSet

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Flush all iptables rules (iptables -F) on a live node Drops all KUBE-SERVICES and FORWARD rules; all service traffic fails instantly Never flush on a live node; use iptables-save to inspect and delete specific rules Leave default nf_conntrack_max=65536 on nodes with 200+ pods Conntrack exhaustion causes silent packet drops with no obvious error messages Size conntrack table at node provisioning time; alert on nf_conntrack_count / nf_conntrack_max > 80% Use iptables TRACE target in production One log line per packet per hook; can generate millions of kernel log entries per second Use TRACE only on development clusters; limit scope with specific src/dst filters Manually add kube-proxy iptables rules kube-proxy overwrites them on the next sync cycle (default 30s) Configure services via Kubernetes API; let kube-proxy manage rules Mix iptables and nftables rules on the same node Rule evaluation order is undefined; some packets bypass one or the other Choose one framework; migrating clusters use iptables-nft shim which routes iptables commands to nftables backend

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List nat table rules (no DNS lookup) iptables -t nat -L -n --line-numbers -v Inspect kube-proxy service chains iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n Watch rule hit counts live watch -n1 'iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -v -n' Save rules to file iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4 Restore rules from file iptables-restore < /etc/iptables/rules.v4 Check conntrack table usage cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count View conntrack entries for TCP conntrack -L --proto tcp Monitor new connections conntrack -E --event-mask NEW Check for conntrack table full dmesg \| grep nf_conntrack Trace packet through hooks iptables -t raw -A PREROUTING -s <ip> -j TRACE List IPVS rules ipvsadm -L -n Check kube-proxy mode kubectl get cm -n kube-system kube-proxy -o yaml \| grep mode

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Component Role in Kubernetes nat/PREROUTING DNAT service IP → pod IP nat/POSTROUTING SNAT pod IP → node IP (MASQUERADE) filter/FORWARD Allow/deny routed pod traffic conntrack Session state for NAT reverse translation ipset Efficient IP group matching for endpoints IPVS Fast kernel load balancing (kube-proxy IPVS mode) eBPF (Cilium) Bypass iptables entirely at the socket/TC layer

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] At which Netfilter hook does kube-proxy install its DNAT rules for ClusterIP services, and why must DNAT happen at that specific hook rather than at the FORWARD hook?
Answer kube-proxy installs DNAT rules in the `nat` table at both the `PREROUTING` hook (for traffic arriving from outside the node) and the `OUTPUT` hook (for traffic originating from local pods). DNAT must happen before the routing decision — if the kernel looked up a route for the original ClusterIP (e.g., `10.96.42.10`), it would find no route for a virtual IP. By rewriting the destination to a real pod IP at PREROUTING, the subsequent routing lookup correctly finds a path to `10.244.x.x`.
  1. [Scenario question] A pod can reach the internet but cannot communicate with a ClusterIP service at 10.96.42.10. The service has two healthy endpoints and kubectl get endpoints shows their IPs. iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES shows no entry for 10.96.42.10. What is the most likely cause?
Answer The kube-proxy rules are missing, most likely because kube-proxy is not running on that node or its iptables sync period has not fired since the service was created. Check `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy` to verify the pod is running. If kube-proxy is running but rules are absent, check for `bridge-nf-call-iptables=0` or the `br_netfilter` module not being loaded — without these, kube-proxy rules cannot intercept bridged pod traffic.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to inspect the per-service iptables load-balancing chain for a ClusterIP service and see the DNAT rules for each backend endpoint?
Answer 
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep 10.96.42.10
This shows the `KUBE-SVC-XXXX` chain name for the service. Then run `iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SVC-XXXX -n` to see the probabilistic load-balancing rules, and `iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SEP-YYYY -n` to see the DNAT rule for each individual endpoint.

Next: Lesson 04 — Network Namespaces Deep Dive

docs.title: Lesson 04 — Network Namespaces Deep Dive
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Lesson 01 — Linux Networking Fundamentals · Time: ~2 hours

Goal: Reproduce the complete pod network namespace lifecycle — from clone(CLONE_NEWNET) through CNI wiring — and debug a running pod's network state from the host using nsenter.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Run all commands inside minikube
minikube ssh

# See real pod namespaces
ip netns list

# Inspect a pod's namespace (find the pause PID first)
sudo crictl ps | head -5

docs.title: 1. What a Network Namespace Contains
docs.text:
A network namespace is a complete, isolated copy of the network stack:

Resource Isolated per namespace Network interfaces Yes (lo, eth0, etc.) IP addresses Yes Routing tables Yes iptables/nftables rules Yes Conntrack table Yes Sockets Yes (cannot be shared across namespaces) BPF programs attached to interfaces Yes

What is not isolated: the physical hardware, kernel sysctl net.* globals (partially), and network namespaces themselves (managed from the host).

docs.title: 2. Creating and Managing Network Namespaces
docs.text:
# Create a named namespace (creates /var/run/netns/<name>)
ip netns add red
ip netns add blue

# List all named namespaces
ip netns list
ip netns list -details     # show if namespace file is a bind mount

# Execute a command in a namespace
ip netns exec red ip link list
ip netns exec red bash     # interactive shell in the namespace

# Delete
ip netns del red

# Show which namespace a process is in
ls -la /proc/<pid>/ns/net

# List all namespaces known to the kernel
lsns -t net

docs.title: Architecture: Namespace / Pause / CNI Wiring
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph node [Host network namespace]
        K[kubelet]
        CRI[containerd / CRI-O]
        CNI[CNI plugin binary]
        HOST_VETH[veth-host-side\ne.g. cali1a2b3c]
        BRIDGE[bridge / VTEP\ne.g. cni0 or flannel.1]
        HOST_VETH --- BRIDGE
    end

    subgraph pod [Pod network namespace]
        PAUSE[pause container\nholds namespace open]
        APP[app container\nshares namespace]
        ETH0[eth0\n10.244.0.10/24]
        PAUSE --- ETH0
        APP --- ETH0
    end

    K -->|1. schedules pod| CRI
    CRI -->|2. creates namespace via clone CLONE_NEWNET| pod
    CRI -->|3. calls CNI ADD| CNI
    CNI -->|4. creates veth pair| HOST_VETH
    HOST_VETH <-->|veth pair| ETH0

    style node fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style pod fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff

docs.title: 3. How Kubernetes Uses Network Namespaces
docs.text:
The kubelet/container runtime creates a pod namespace using the pause container:

# Find the pause container for a pod
crictl ps | grep pause
# or:
docker ps | grep pause

# Get the pause container's PID
PAUSE_PID=$(crictl inspect <container-id> | jq '.info.pid')

# Access its network namespace
nsenter --target $PAUSE_PID --net -- ip addr
nsenter --target $PAUSE_PID --net -- ip route
nsenter --target $PAUSE_PID --net -- ss -tlnp

# Alternative: find the namespace path from the pod UID
ls /var/run/netns/   # on containerd-based nodes, the path may differ
# containerd: /proc/<pause_pid>/ns/net (accessed via nsenter or /proc)

All containers in the same pod share this namespace, which is why they can communicate via localhost and share port space.

docs.title: 4. Inspecting Pod Network Namespaces from the Host
docs.text:
# Method 1: nsenter (most reliable)
POD_NS=$(kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
PAUSE_PID=$(crictl inspect $(crictl ps | grep $POD_NS | head -1 | awk '{print $1}') | jq -r '.info.pid')

nsenter -t $PAUSE_PID -n ip addr
nsenter -t $PAUSE_PID -n ip route
nsenter -t $PAUSE_PID -n ss -s

# Method 2: netshoot (run a debug pod in the same namespace)
kubectl debug -it <pod-name> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container-name>

# Method 3: kubectl exec with network tools
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- sh
# Then: ip addr, ip route, ss, nslookup, curl

docs.title: Namespace / Runtime Configuration Reference
docs.text: Item Location / Command Notes Named namespace bind-mount /var/run/netns/<name> Created by ip netns add; CNI uses this path Pod namespace (containerd) /proc/<pause_pid>/ns/net Accessed via nsenter -t <pid> -n List namespaces (kernel) lsns -t net Shows PID, NSID, and process name Namespace inode ID stat /proc/<pid>/ns/net Same inode = same namespace Pause container image registry.k8s.io/pause:3.x Configured in kubelet --pod-infra-container-image CNI binary directory /opt/cni/bin/ CNI plugins must be executable here CNI config directory /etc/cni/net.d/ JSON config files; first sorted file is used

docs.title: Kernel Namespace Limit Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change user.max_net_namespaces unlimited (varies by distro) Maximum network namespaces the user namespace can create Set a cap on shared nodes to prevent namespace exhaustion attacks user.max_user_namespaces 7182 (distro-dependent) Caps nested user namespaces (affects rootless containers) Raise if rootless container runtimes are used (Podman, rootless containerd) net.core.default_qdisc pfifo_fast Default queueing discipline applied to new veth interfaces Set to fq_codel or noqueue on Kubernetes nodes for lower pod latency net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter 1 rp_filter value applied to newly created interfaces Set to 0 before CNI creates veths if CNI uses asymmetric routing net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding 0 IP forwarding default for new interfaces Set to 1 so veth pairs created by CNI forward without per-interface config

docs.title: 5. Network Namespace Lifecycle with CNI
docs.text:
When a pod is scheduled, this sequence occurs:

sequenceDiagram
    participant K as kubelet
    participant CRI as containerd / CRI-O
    participant CNI as CNI plugin
    participant NS as Pod namespace
    participant HOST as Host namespace

    K->>CRI: Create pod sandbox
    CRI->>NS: clone(CLONE_NEWNET) — new namespace
    CRI->>HOST: Bind-mount namespace at /var/run/netns/cni-UUID
    CRI->>CNI: Exec CNI binary with ADD + namespace path
    CNI->>HOST: ip link add eth0-host type veth peer name eth0
    CNI->>NS: ip link set eth0 netns <ns-path>
    CNI->>NS: ip addr add <pod-ip>/24 dev eth0
    CNI->>NS: ip route add default via <gateway>
    CNI->>HOST: ip link set eth0-host master cni0 (bridge)
    CNI-->>CRI: Return result JSON (pod IP, gateway)
    CRI->>NS: Start app containers sharing namespace
    Note over NS: Pod is Running
    K->>CRI: Delete pod
    CRI->>CNI: Exec CNI binary with DEL + namespace path
    CNI->>HOST: ip link del eth0-host (destroys veth pair)
    CRI->>HOST: Unlink /var/run/netns/cni-UUID
    Note over NS: Namespace freed by kernel

docs.title: hostNetwork pods
docs.text:
Some system pods (kube-proxy, CNI agents) run in the host network namespace:

spec:
  hostNetwork: true

# These pods appear in host routing/iptables
kubectl get pod -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E "kube-proxy|calico-node"
# Their IPs are node IPs, not pod CIDR IPs

Risks: a compromised hostNetwork pod can see and modify all host network state.

docs.title: Shared network between pods (non-standard)
docs.text:
Pods can share a namespace using shareProcessNamespace + init container tricks, but the standard model is one namespace per pod.

See also: Lesson 03 — iptables and Netfilter for how iptables rules are namespace-scoped — each pod namespace has its own iptables state independent of the host, though kube-proxy rules only exist in the host namespace.

docs.title: 7. Namespace File Descriptors and Pinning
docs.text:
A namespace exists as long as either: - A process is running inside it, or - A file descriptor referencing it is open (bind-mount counts)

# Bind-mount a namespace so it persists without a process
touch /tmp/netns-persist
mount --bind /proc/$$/ns/net /tmp/netns-persist

# Open a namespace from its bind-mount path
ip netns exec $(readlink /tmp/netns-persist) ip addr

# This is exactly how CNI keeps the pod namespace alive
# when the pause container hasn't started yet
ls -la /var/run/netns/

docs.title: 8. Debugging Namespace Leaks
docs.text:
After a node has been running a long time, stale namespace files can accumulate if cleanup fails.

# Count active namespaces
ls /var/run/netns/ | wc -l

# Check for orphaned namespaces (no pause container for them)
for ns in /var/run/netns/cni-*; do
  ns_id=$(basename $ns)
  pid=$(lsns -t net -o PID,NETNSID | grep $ns_id | awk '{print $1}')
  if [ -z "$pid" ]; then
    echo "ORPHAN: $ns"
  fi
done

# View all network namespaces the kernel knows about
lsns -t net

# Identify which pods use each namespace
crictl pods --no-trunc -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name + " " + .status.linux.namespaces[] | select(.type=="network") | .path'

docs.title: 9. Hands-On Lab: Full Pod Namespace Simulation
docs.text:
Reproduce the entire pod network namespace lifecycle manually.

# Step 1: Create the namespace (simulating CRI)
ip netns add cni-pod-sim

# Step 2: Create veth pair (simulating CNI ADD)
ip link add eth0-host type veth peer name eth0
ip link set eth0 netns cni-pod-sim

# Step 3: Set up bridge on host
ip link add cni0 type bridge
ip link set cni0 up
ip addr add 10.244.0.1/24 dev cni0
ip link set eth0-host master cni0
ip link set eth0-host up

# Step 4: Configure pod namespace
ip netns exec cni-pod-sim ip link set lo up
ip netns exec cni-pod-sim ip link set eth0 up
ip netns exec cni-pod-sim ip addr add 10.244.0.100/24 dev eth0
ip netns exec cni-pod-sim ip route add default via 10.244.0.1

docs.title: Step-by-step Observation
docs.text:
# Verify the namespace was created
ip netns list
# → cni-pod-sim (id: N)

# Confirm the veth pair spans both namespaces
ip link show eth0-host
# → eth0-host@if<N>: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> ...

ip netns exec cni-pod-sim ip link show eth0
# → eth0@if<M>: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> ...

# Step 5: Verify pod-side networking
ip netns exec cni-pod-sim ip addr
# → 2: eth0 ... inet 10.244.0.100/24 brd 10.244.0.255 scope global eth0

ip netns exec cni-pod-sim ip route
# → default via 10.244.0.1 dev eth0
# → 10.244.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.244.0.100

ip netns exec cni-pod-sim ping -c3 10.244.0.1
# → PING 10.244.0.1: 3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss

# Confirm namespace inode to verify isolation
readlink /proc/$$/ns/net
# → net:[<host-ns-inode>]
readlink /proc/$(ip netns exec cni-pod-sim sh -c 'echo $$')/ns/net
# → net:[<different-inode>]  ← proves separate namespace

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Confirm full setup
lsns -t net
# → host namespace + cni-pod-sim listed

# Step 6: Simulate CNI DEL (pod deletion)
ip link del eth0-host     # destroys veth pair; eth0 inside ns also gone
ip link del cni0
ip netns del cni-pod-sim

# Confirm cleanup
ip netns list   # → (empty or no cni-pod-sim)
lsns -t net     # → only host namespace remains

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Namespace count (ls /var/run/netns/ | wc -l) monitored and alerted when it diverges from running pod count by more than 10%
  • CNI plugin version pinned in node image; update tested in staging before rolling to production
  • hostNetwork: true restricted via PodSecurity admission or OPA/Gatekeeper policy — only approved system workloads allowed
  • Node-level debugging tooling (nsenter, crictl, lsns) pre-installed on all nodes; do not rely on cluster access alone for debugging
  • CNI binary directory /opt/cni/bin/ permissions verified (executable, owned by root) after every node image rebuild
  • Pause container image pinned to a specific digest in --pod-infra-container-image to prevent silent upgrades during node reboot
  • Namespace leak detection script run weekly; orphaned namespaces cleaned before they affect kernel namespace limit

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Run ip netns exec to debug pods directly On containerd nodes, pod namespaces are not registered in /var/run/netns/; command fails silently Use nsenter -t <pause_pid> -n <cmd> or kubectl debug with a netshoot sidecar Delete the pause container to "restart" networking Destroying the pause container destroys the namespace and all app container sockets; kubelet then terminates the entire pod Delete the pod via Kubernetes API and let the scheduler reschedule it Use hostNetwork: true for performance Bypasses all namespace isolation; a bug in the app can affect host routing/firewall state Use high-performance CNIs (Cilium with XDP, Multus + DPDK) that keep namespace isolation Assume CNI failure leaves no residue A partial CNI ADD can leave orphan veth interfaces and stale IPs in the IPAM store Always check CNI plugin exit codes in kubelet logs; implement CNI plugin liveness probes Hard-code pause container PID for scripting PID changes every time the pod is recreated; scripts break silently Use crictl inspect or /proc/<pid>/ns/net paths dynamically

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does the pause (infra) container serve as the holder of a pod's network namespace, rather than the first application container that starts?
Answer The pause container is started first and holds the network namespace open for the entire lifetime of the pod. If the application container held the namespace and then crashed and restarted, the namespace (along with its IP address, routes, and sockets) would be destroyed and recreated, breaking network state. The pause container does nothing except hold the namespace file descriptor open via a bind-mount at `/var/run/netns/cni-`, ensuring the namespace survives application container restarts.
  1. [Scenario question] You run ip netns list on a node running containerd and it shows no namespaces, but kubectl get pods shows many running pods. Where are the pod network namespaces, and how do you access one to inspect its routing table?
Answer On containerd-based nodes, pod namespaces are not registered in `/var/run/netns/` — they are referenced by the pause container's PID via `/proc//ns/net`. Find the pause container ID with `crictl ps | grep pause`, get its PID with `crictl inspect | jq '.info.pid'`, then run `nsenter -t -n ip route` to enter the namespace and inspect its routing table. The command `lsns -t net` lists all kernel-known network namespaces with their PIDs.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to inspect the IP addresses and routes of a running pod from the host node, given the pause container's PID?
Answer 
nsenter -t <pause_pid> -n ip addr
This enters the pod's network namespace and runs `ip addr` within it, showing the pod's `eth0` interface with its assigned IP. Follow with `nsenter -t -n ip route` to see the pod's routing table, which should show a default route via the bridge gateway (e.g., `10.244.0.1`).
