docs.title: Lesson 05 — VXLAN and Overlay Networks
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Lesson 02 — IP Routing and Forwarding · Time: ~2 hours

Goal: Build a working VXLAN tunnel between two Linux hosts, explain how the FDB maps pod MACs to VTEP IPs, and calculate the correct pod MTU to prevent silent fragmentation.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Two terminals:
# Terminal 1 — minikube Linux node
minikube ssh
ip link show | grep -E "vxlan|tunl|cali"

# Terminal 2 — Mac, kubectl
kubectl get pods -A -o wide   # see pod IPs and nodes

docs.title: 1. The Problem Overlay Networks Solve
docs.text:
Kubernetes assigns pods IPs from a private CIDR (e.g., 10.244.0.0/16). These IPs are not routable on the underlying physical network. Without overlays, cross-node pod traffic would need: - Routes programmed on every physical switch/router (BGP), or - VPC-level route tables updated for every node (cloud), or - An overlay that wraps pod-IP packets inside routable packets.

Overlay networks choose the third option: encapsulate first, route second.

See also: Lesson 02 — IP Routing and Forwarding for how CNI plugins using Flannel host-gw or Calico BGP avoid encapsulation entirely by programming the physical routing layer instead.

docs.title: 2. VXLAN Fundamentals
docs.text: VXLAN (Virtual eXtensible LAN) encapsulates L2 Ethernet frames inside UDP packets.

docs.title: Packet Structure
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph outer [Outer packet - routed on physical network]
        OE[Outer Ethernet Header\nnode MAC to next-hop MAC]
        OI[Outer IP Header\nsrc: node IP, dst: remote node IP]
        OU[Outer UDP Header\nsrc: ephemeral, dst: 4789]
        OV[VXLAN Header 8 bytes\nVNI 24-bit segment ID]
    end
    subgraph inner [Inner packet - original pod frame]
        IE[Inner Ethernet\npod src MAC to dst pod MAC]
        II[Inner IP Header\npod src IP to pod dst IP]
        IP2[Inner TCP/UDP\napplication payload]
    end
    outer --> inner

    style outer fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style inner fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff

Key facts: - VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier): 24-bit = up to 16 million segments (vs 4096 VLANs) - UDP destination port: 4789 (IANA standard); Flannel legacy uses 8472 - Each node runs a VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint) — a virtual NIC that handles encapsulation and decapsulation - Overhead: 50 bytes (outer Ethernet 14 + IP 20 + UDP 8 + VXLAN 8)

docs.title: Architecture: Two-Node VXLAN Overlay
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph nodeA [Node A — 192.168.1.10]
        PA[Pod A\n10.244.0.5]
        BRA[cni0\nbridge]
        VTEPA[flannel.1\nVTEP]
        PA --- BRA --- VTEPA
    end

    subgraph net [Physical Network]
        PHYS[UDP 4789\nencapsulated traffic]
    end

    subgraph nodeB [Node B — 192.168.1.20]
        VTEPB[flannel.1\nVTEP]
        BRB[cni0\nbridge]
        PB[Pod B\n10.244.1.7]
        VTEPB --- BRB --- PB
    end

    VTEPA <-->|outer src=192.168.1.10\nouter dst=192.168.1.20| PHYS
    PHYS <--> VTEPB

    style nodeA fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style nodeB fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style net fill:#4a4a4a,color:#fff

docs.title: 3. Creating a VXLAN Interface
docs.text:
# Create a VXLAN interface (VTEP)
ip link add vxlan0 type vxlan \
  id 100 \             # VNI
  dstport 4789 \       # UDP port
  local 192.168.1.10 \ # local node IP (tunnel source)
  dev eth0             # interface to use for outer IP

ip link set vxlan0 up
ip addr add 10.244.0.1/16 dev vxlan0

# Check interface details
ip -d link show vxlan0
# → vxlan id 100 local 192.168.1.10 dev eth0 srcport 0 0 dstport 4789

docs.title: 4. VXLAN FDB (Forwarding Database)
docs.text:
The VTEP needs to know which remote node has which pod MAC address.

# View the VXLAN FDB
bridge fdb show dev vxlan0

# Output example:
# 00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 192.168.1.20 self permanent  ← flood to this VTEP
# aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01 dst 192.168.1.20 self            ← specific pod MAC

# Add a unicast FDB entry (Flannel/Calico do this via their daemons)
bridge fdb add aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01 dev vxlan0 dst 192.168.1.20

# Add an anycast entry (flood unknown MACs to all VTEPs)
bridge fdb add 00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan0 dst 192.168.1.20
bridge fdb add 00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan0 dst 192.168.1.30

Flannel uses the Kubernetes API (node annotations) to watch node CIDRs and program FDB entries. When a new node joins, flanneld adds its VTEP MAC and node IP to the FDB of every other node.

docs.title: 5. Flannel VXLAN Mode — How It Works
Packet Journey: Pod A to Pod B
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PA as Pod A (10.244.0.5)
    participant BRA as cni0 bridge (Node A)
    participant VTEPA as flannel.1 VTEP (Node A)
    participant NET as Physical Network
    participant VTEPB as flannel.1 VTEP (Node B)
    participant BRB as cni0 bridge (Node B)
    participant PB as Pod B (10.244.1.7)

    PA->>BRA: Frame: src=10.244.0.5 dst=10.244.1.7
    BRA->>VTEPA: Routed to flannel.1 (ip route: 10.244.1.0/24 via flannel.1 onlink)
    Note over VTEPA: FDB lookup: dst MAC for 10.244.1.0 → Node B VTEP at 192.168.1.20
    VTEPA->>NET: UDP encap: outer 192.168.1.10→192.168.1.20 port 8472 VNI=1
    NET->>VTEPB: Physical delivery
    Note over VTEPB: Decap: strip outer headers, recover inner frame
    VTEPB->>BRB: Inner frame: 10.244.0.5→10.244.1.7
    BRB->>PB: Delivered via pod-side veth

docs.title: 6. MTU — The Most Common VXLAN Problem
docs.text:
VXLAN adds 50 bytes of overhead (outer Ethernet + IP + UDP + VXLAN header).

Physical NIC MTU: 1500 bytes
VXLAN overhead:    - 50 bytes
Pod/container MTU: 1450 bytes  ← must be configured explicitly

If pods use MTU 1500 (the default), large packets get fragmented or silently dropped (if the DF bit is set).

# Check MTU on VXLAN interface
ip link show flannel.1 | grep mtu

# Check pod-side MTU (inside pod namespace)
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- ip link show eth0 | grep mtu

# Test actual MTU with ping (don't fragment)
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- ping -M do -s 1422 <other-pod-ip>
# -M do = don't fragment, -s = payload size
# 1422 + 28 (ICMP+IP headers) = 1450 → succeeds
# 1423 + 28 = 1451 → fragmented or ICMP message too big received

# Fix: set CNI MTU in ConfigMap (Flannel example)
kubectl edit cm -n kube-system kube-flannel-cfg
# NET_CONF_JSON: "MTU": 1450

docs.title: MTU Reference by Environment
docs.text: Environment Physical MTU VXLAN Overhead Correct Pod MTU Standard Ethernet 1500 50 1450 AWS (most instances) 9001 (jumbo) 50 8951 GCP VPC 1460 50 1410 Azure VNet 1500 50 1450 On-prem jumbo frames 9000 50 8950 Geneve (instead of VXLAN) 1500 54 1446

docs.title: 7. Geneve — The Modern Alternative
docs.text:
Geneve (Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation) is similar to VXLAN but with extensible option headers. OVN, OpenShift, and Cilium support Geneve.

# Create a Geneve interface
ip link add geneve0 type geneve \
  id 100 \
  remote 192.168.1.20 \
  dstport 6081

ip link set geneve0 up

Cilium uses Geneve or VXLAN depending on configuration: 

cilium config view | grep tunnel
# tunnel-protocol: vxlan  (or geneve)

docs.title: VXLAN Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change VNI (id) — 24-bit segment identifier Use different VNIs to isolate tenant networks UDP port (dstport) 4789 (IANA) Destination UDP port for encapsulated traffic Use 4789 unless hardware offload requires 8472 (Flannel legacy) local IP — Source IP of outer UDP header Set to the node's primary IP; must be reachable from all other nodes MTU on vxlan device inherited Maximum frame size on the VTEP Set to physical_MTU - 50; CNI must propagate this to pods learning flag on VTEP learns remote MAC→VTEP mappings via flood-and-learn Disable (nolearning) when CNI uses explicit FDB population proxy flag off Respond to ARP on behalf of remote pods Enable (proxy) with l2miss/l3miss for ARP suppression UDP receive buffer system default Receive buffer for VTEP socket Increase net.core.rmem_max to 16777216 on high-throughput nodes

docs.title: 8. Bare Metal vs Cloud Overlay Considerations
Bare Metal
docs.text:
• Full control of MTU (configure jumbo frames end-to-end for best performance)
  • Overlay overhead matters more at 10/25/100 GbE
  • Consider native routing (BGP, host-gw) for performance-sensitive workloads
  • Ensure UDP 4789/8472 is allowed on host firewall rules
# Allow VXLAN on firewall (if using ufw/iptables)
ufw allow 4789/udp
# or:
iptables -I INPUT -p udp --dport 4789 -j ACCEPT

docs.title: Cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure)
docs.text:
• VPC Security Groups / Firewall Rules must allow UDP 4789 between nodes
  • NACLs (AWS) must allow it in both directions
  • Cloud load balancers don't forward raw UDP 4789 — VXLAN must be node-to-node
  • Some cloud providers offer native overlay bypass (AWS VPC CNI, GKE Dataplane v2)
# AWS: check Security Group allows VXLAN
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-xxxxx \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[0].IpPermissions[?FromPort==`4789`]'

docs.title: 9. Performance Tuning
docs.text:
# Enable hardware offload for VXLAN (if NIC supports it)
ethtool -k eth0 | grep tx-udp_tnl
# tx-udp_tnl-segmentation: on

# Enable checksum offload
ethtool -K eth0 tx-checksum-ip-generic on

# Increase UDP receive buffer for VTEP
sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=16777216
sysctl -w net.core.wmem_max=16777216

# Use RSS (Receive Side Scaling) so VXLAN decap is spread across CPUs
ethtool -l eth0
ethtool -L eth0 combined 8

docs.title: 10. Hands-On Lab: Manual VXLAN Tunnel
docs.text:
Build a VXLAN overlay between two Linux hosts (or VMs).

### On Host A (192.168.1.10)
ip link add vxlan10 type vxlan id 10 dstport 4789 \
  local 192.168.1.10 dev eth0
ip link set vxlan10 up
ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev vxlan10

bridge fdb add 00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan10 dst 192.168.1.20
ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 dev vxlan10

### On Host B (192.168.1.20)
ip link add vxlan10 type vxlan id 10 dstport 4789 \
  local 192.168.1.20 dev eth0
ip link set vxlan10 up
ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev vxlan10

bridge fdb add 00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan10 dst 192.168.1.10
ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 dev vxlan10

docs.title: Step-by-step Observation
docs.text:
### From Host A

# Verify VTEP interface details
ip -d link show vxlan10
# → vxlan id 10 local 192.168.1.10 dev eth0 srcport 0 0 dstport 4789 ...

# Confirm FDB flood entry
bridge fdb show dev vxlan10
# → 00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 192.168.1.20 self permanent

# Test overlay reachability
ping -c5 10.0.0.2
# → PING 10.0.0.2: 5 packets transmitted, 5 received, 0% packet loss

# Inspect encapsulated traffic on the physical interface
tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 -X
# → UDP packets visible; inner IP addresses 10.0.0.1→10.0.0.2 visible in hex

# Verify MTU: largest payload that passes without fragmentation
ping -M do -s 1422 10.0.0.2   # → succeeds (1422+28 = 1450 ≤ 1500-50)
ping -M do -s 1452 10.0.0.2   # → fails: "Frag needed" or message too big

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# After first ping, FDB should have learned remote MAC
bridge fdb show dev vxlan10
# → 00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 192.168.1.20 self permanent  (flood entry)
# → aa:bb:cc:11:22:33 dst 192.168.1.20 self            (learned entry for 10.0.0.2)

# Confirm no fragmentation occurs at correct MTU
ip -s link show vxlan10
# → RX: bytes/packets should match TX with 0 drops

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Cross-node pod traffic 100% loss UDP 4789 blocked by firewall/security group tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 on both nodes Open UDP 4789 in firewall; check AWS SG / Azure NSG Large requests fail, small ones work MTU mismatch — pod MTU not set to physical_MTU - 50 kubectl exec -- ping -M do -s 1422 <pod> Set CNI MTU in flannel/calico ConfigMap; restart CNI daemonset bridge fdb show shows no entries FDB not populated; flannel/calico daemon not running kubectl get pod -n kube-system | grep flannel Restart CNI daemon; check logs for API access errors VXLAN tunnel works but very high CPU Hardware offload disabled; all encap/decap in software ethtool -k eth0 | grep tx-udp_tnl Enable offload: ethtool -K eth0 tx-udp_tnl-segmentation on Intermittent drops under load UDP receive buffer overflow on VTEP netstat -su | grep errors Increase net.core.rmem_max and rmem_default ip -d link show vxlan0 shows wrong VNI Flannel used different VNI than expected ip -d link show flannel.1 Confirm VNI in flannel ConfigMap; recreate interface if mismatched ARP not resolving across VTEPs Flood-and-learn disabled but explicit FDB not populated bridge fdb show dev flannel.1 | wc -l vs node count Add zero-MAC flood entries or enable l2miss/l3miss with ARP proxy

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Pod MTU set to physical_MTU - 50 (VXLAN) or physical_MTU - 54 (Geneve) in CNI ConfigMap before cluster goes live
  • UDP 4789 (or 8472 for Flannel legacy) explicitly allowed between all nodes in firewall rules, security groups, and NACLs
  • Hardware VXLAN offload verified on the NIC model in use (ethtool -k eth0 | grep tx-udp_tnl) for performance-critical clusters
  • net.core.rmem_max and wmem_max raised to 16777216 on nodes expected to handle > 10 Gbps overlay throughput
  • FDB entry count monitored — unexpectedly low count means CNI daemon has lost sync with the cluster state
  • Jumbo frame configuration confirmed end-to-end (NIC → switch → NIC) before using MTU > 1500 to avoid hidden fragmentation
  • Cloud-specific MTU verified: GCP VPC uses 1460 baseline requiring pod MTU 1410, not 1450

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Leave pod MTU at default 1500 on a VXLAN overlay Large packets get fragmented or dropped; throughput collapses; hard to diagnose because small packets work fine Set CNI MTU to physical_MTU - 50 in the CNI ConfigMap; verify with ping -M do Use Flannel VXLAN on bare metal with jumbo frames but keep default CNI MTU Wastes jumbo frame benefit; pods limited to 1450 when they could use 8950 Set flannel.MTU: 8950 in kube-flannel-cfg when physical MTU is 9000 Allow only TCP in firewall rules between nodes VXLAN runs over UDP 4789; all overlay traffic is blocked Allow UDP 4789 (and 8472 for legacy) in both directions between node security groups Mix VNIs across clusters sharing the same physical network Different clusters use the same VNI; MAC/ARP entries bleed across cluster boundaries Assign a unique VNI range per cluster; use id parameter in VXLAN link creation Rely on flood-and-learn in large clusters Each unknown MAC causes a flood to all VTEPs; broadcast storm at scale Configure CNI daemon to use unicast FDB population (Flannel directRouting, Calico VXLAN with explicit FDB)

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command Create VXLAN VTEP interface ip link add vxlan0 type vxlan id <VNI> dstport 4789 local <node-ip> dev eth0 Show VTEP details ip -d link show vxlan0 View VXLAN FDB bridge fdb show dev vxlan0 Add unicast FDB entry bridge fdb add <mac> dev vxlan0 dst <remote-node-ip> Add flood FDB entry bridge fdb add 00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan0 dst <remote-node-ip> Test overlay reachability ping -c5 <overlay-ip> Test MTU (no fragment) ping -M do -s 1422 <dst-ip> Inspect encapsulated traffic tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 -X Check hardware VXLAN offload ethtool -k eth0 \| grep tx-udp_tnl Check MTU on flannel interface ip link show flannel.1 \| grep mtu Verify pod MTU kubectl exec <pod> -- ip link show eth0 Check CNI MTU config (Flannel) kubectl get cm -n kube-system kube-flannel-cfg -o yaml \| grep MTU

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail VXLAN overhead 50 bytes → subtract from physical MTU for pod MTU FDB Maps pod MAC → remote node VTEP IP VNI 24-bit segment ID; use unique values per cluster Flannel VXLAN Flood+learn or unicast FDB via Kubernetes API Geneve Extensible alternative (54 bytes overhead), used by OVN/Cilium MTU mismatch Most common VXLAN-related packet drop cause Cloud firewall Must allow UDP 4789 between all nodes Hardware offload tx-udp_tnl-segmentation reduces CPU for encap/decap

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] VXLAN adds 50 bytes of overhead per packet. Explain where those 50 bytes come from, and what pod MTU you must configure when the physical NIC MTU is 1500 bytes to prevent silent fragmentation.
Answer The 50-byte overhead breaks down as: outer Ethernet header (14 bytes) + outer IP header (20 bytes) + outer UDP header (8 bytes) + VXLAN header (8 bytes) = 50 bytes total. With a physical NIC MTU of 1500 bytes, the maximum pod payload is 1500 − 50 = **1450 bytes**. Pod interfaces must be configured with MTU 1450 — if left at the default 1500, any packet larger than 1450 bytes will either be fragmented (degrading performance) or silently dropped if the DF (Don't Fragment) bit is set.
  1. [Scenario question] Small HTTP requests between pods on different nodes succeed consistently, but large file transfers fail or hang partway through. VXLAN is in use with default configuration. No error messages appear in the application logs. What is the most likely cause, and how do you confirm it?
Answer The most likely cause is an MTU mismatch — pod interfaces are configured at MTU 1500 but should be 1450 for VXLAN. Small packets fit within the limit, but large packets exceed 1450 bytes, causing fragmentation or silent drops when the DF bit is set. Confirm with `kubectl exec -- ping -M do -s 1422 ` — a payload of 1422 bytes + 28 bytes (ICMP + IP headers) = 1450, which should succeed; `ping -M do -s 1452` should fail or return "Frag needed."
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to inspect the VXLAN FDB (Forwarding Database) on a Flannel node and verify that the remote VTEP for another node has been populated?
Answer 
bridge fdb show dev flannel.1
Look for entries mapping remote node VTEP MAC addresses to their node IPs (`dst` field). An entry like `00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 192.168.1.20 self permanent` is the flood entry for Node B. If the FDB is empty or missing entries for known nodes, the flanneld daemon is not syncing from the Kubernetes API.

Next: Lesson 06 — BGP Fundamentals for Kubernetes

docs.title: Lesson 06 — BGP Fundamentals for Kubernetes
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud Prereqs: Lesson 02 — IP Routing and Forwarding Time: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Configure Calico with BGP peering to a ToR switch so pod routes are reachable from physical network infrastructure without any overlay tunnel.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — kubectl (Mac)
kubectl get pods -n calico-system   # check Calico/BIRD is running

# Terminal 2 — minikube node (Linux)
minikube ssh
# Check if BIRD is running (Calico BGP agent)
sudo ps aux | grep bird
ip route show proto bird   # routes installed by BGP

See also: Lesson 07 — Bare Metal Network Infrastructure covers the ToR/spine-leaf physical layer that BGP peers with.

docs.title: 1. BGP Fundamentals
docs.text:
BGP is a path-vector protocol: routers advertise reachability to IP prefixes along with the path (list of AS numbers) used to reach them.

Term Definition AS (Autonomous System) A network under single administrative control ASN 16-bit (1–65535) or 32-bit identifier; 64512–65534 = private iBGP BGP between peers in the same AS eBGP BGP between peers in different ASes NLRI Network Layer Reachability Information — the prefix being advertised BGP Speaker Any router/daemon running the BGP protocol Hold Timer Max seconds between keepalives before session resets (default 90s)

docs.title: Architecture: Calico BGP on a Kubernetes Cluster
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph node_a["Node A (ASN 65001)"]
        PA[Pod 10.244.0.5/32]
        BIRD_A[BIRD daemon]
    end
    subgraph node_b["Node B (ASN 65002)"]
        PB[Pod 10.244.1.7/32]
        BIRD_B[BIRD daemon]
    end
    subgraph tor["ToR Switch (ASN 65000)"]
        TOR[BGP Router]
    end
    subgraph rr["Route Reflector (ASN 64512)"]
        RR[RR Node]
    end

    BIRD_A -- "eBGP advertise 10.244.0.0/24" --> TOR
    BIRD_B -- "eBGP advertise 10.244.1.0/24" --> TOR
    TOR -- "redistribute" --> BIRD_A
    TOR -- "redistribute" --> BIRD_B
    BIRD_A -- "iBGP (via RR)" --> RR
    BIRD_B -- "iBGP (via RR)" --> RR
    RR -- "reflect routes" --> BIRD_A
    RR -- "reflect routes" --> BIRD_B

docs.title: 2. BGP Session Establishment
docs.text: BGP uses TCP port 179. Peers must be manually configured — BGP does not auto-discover neighbors.

docs.title: Session State Machine
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Idle -->|"start"| Connect
    Connect -->|"TCP syn sent"| Active
    Active -->|"TCP established"| OpenSent
    OpenSent -->|"OPEN received"| OpenConfirm
    OpenConfirm -->|"KEEPALIVE received"| Established
    Active -->|"TCP reset"| Connect
    Established -->|"hold timer"| Idle
# Check BGP session states with BIRD (used by Calico)
birdc show protocols
# Name       Proto      Table      State  Since         Info
# Node_192_168_1_20  BGP  ---  up  2024-01-15  Established  # → healthy

# Check with FRRouting (used in some bare-metal setups)
vtysh -c "show bgp summary"

# Count established sessions
birdc show protocols | grep -c Established   # → number of peers up

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change holdTime 90s Seconds between keepalives before session resets Reduce to 9s for faster detection without BFD keepaliveTime 30s Interval for KEEPALIVE messages Usually 1/3 of holdTime connectRetryTime 120s Delay before retrying failed connections Reduce on stable links bfdEnabled false Enable BFD for sub-second failure detection Always true in production password (none) MD5 TCP session authentication Required in multi-tenant environments

docs.title: 3. How Calico Uses BGP
docs.text:
Calico runs a BGP agent (BIRD) on every node. Each node advertises the pod routes it owns.

Node A (ASN 64512) — podCIDR 10.244.0.0/24
Node B (ASN 64512) — podCIDR 10.244.1.0/24

Node A's BIRD advertises: 10.244.0.5/32 (each pod as a host route)
Node B receives this and installs: ip route add 10.244.0.5/32 via 192.168.1.10

No overlay needed — packets go directly at wire speed.

docs.title: Step-by-step: Pod Creation to Route Advertisement
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as kubelet
    participant CNI as Calico CNI
    participant BIRD as BIRD daemon
    participant Peer as BGP Peer (ToR)
    participant OS as Linux routing

    K->>CNI: CNI ADD (new pod)
    CNI->>OS: ip route add 10.244.0.5 dev cali1234 scope link
    CNI->>BIRD: notify via Felix / route update
    BIRD->>Peer: BGP UPDATE: advertise 10.244.0.5/32
    Peer->>BIRD: BGP UPDATE ACK
    Note over Peer: ToR installs route<br/>10.244.0.5 via node-IP
    BIRD->>OS: install received peer routes

docs.title: Full Mesh (default Calico, up to ~50 nodes)
docs.text:
Every node peers with every other node. Session count grows as n*(n-1)/2.

flowchart LR
    N1[Node 1] --- N2[Node 2]
    N1 --- N3[Node 3]
    N2 --- N3
    N1 --- N4[Node 4]
    N2 --- N4
    N3 --- N4

docs.title: Route Reflector (50+ nodes)
docs.text:
Dedicated RR nodes relay routes between peers. All nodes peer only with the RR(s).

# Calico: designate a node as a Route Reflector
kubectl annotate node rr-node projectcalico.org/RouteReflectorClusterID=244.0.0.1

# BGPPeer config: nodes peer with the RR only
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: BGPPeer
metadata:
  name: peer-with-rr
spec:
  peerIP: 192.168.1.100   # RR IP
  asNumber: 64512
EOF

docs.title: eBGP with ToR (Top-of-Rack) Switches — Most Scalable
docs.text:
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: BGPConfiguration
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  asNumber: 65001
  serviceLoadBalancerIPs:
    - cidr: 10.0.0.0/24   # advertise LB IPs to the ToR
Topology Max Nodes Sessions per Node Use When Full mesh ~50 n-1 Small clusters, simple setup Route Reflector ~1000 2–4 (to RRs) Medium clusters, same AS eBGP with ToR Unlimited 2 (to ToR pair) Production bare metal

docs.title: 5. BGP Path Attributes
docs.text:
Understanding these attributes is key for traffic engineering:

Attribute Type Use in Kubernetes AS_PATH Well-known mandatory Loop prevention; prefer shortest path LOCAL_PREF Well-known discretionary iBGP preference (higher = preferred); not sent in eBGP MED (MULTI_EXIT_DISC) Optional non-transitive Suggest preferred entry to external AS NEXT_HOP Well-known mandatory Next router to reach the prefix COMMUNITY Optional transitive Tag routes for policy (e.g., "no-export") WEIGHT Cisco-proprietary Local-only preference (highest wins) 
# View BGP routes with attributes in BIRD
birdc show route all
birdc show route for 10.244.0.5

# In FRRouting
vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 unicast 10.244.0.5"

docs.title: 6. BGP Communities for Kubernetes
docs.text:
BGP communities are 32-bit tags attached to routes. Calico and MetalLB use them for policy.

# MetalLB: advertise LoadBalancer IPs with a community tag
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BGPAdvertisement
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  communities:
    - my-community
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: Community
metadata:
  name: my-community
spec:
  communities:
    - name: web-tier
      value: "64512:100"

Upstream router policy on the ToR: 

If route has community 64512:100 → set LOCAL_PREF 200

docs.title: 7. BFD — Bidirectional Forwarding Detection
docs.text:
BFD provides subsecond failure detection for BGP sessions. Important for fast pod rerouting on bare metal.

# Calico BGP peer with BFD
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: BGPPeer
metadata:
  name: node-to-tor
spec:
  peerIP: 192.168.1.1
  asNumber: 65000
  bfdEnabled: true
Mechanism Detection Time CPU Cost Use When Hold timer (default 90s) 90 seconds Zero Never in production Tuned hold timer (9s) 9 seconds Minimal Acceptable if BFD unavailable BFD (300ms interval) ~1 second Low Always — production bare metal BFD (50ms interval) ~150ms Medium Critical latency-sensitive paths

docs.title: 8. Advertising Service IPs via BGP
docs.text:
One powerful pattern on bare metal: advertise Service LoadBalancer or ExternalIP ranges via BGP so they are reachable from the rest of the network.

Calico: 

apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: BGPConfiguration
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  serviceLoadBalancerIPs:
    - cidr: 10.100.0.0/24   # LB IP range
  serviceExternalIPs:
    - cidr: 10.200.0.0/24   # External IP range
  serviceClusterIPs:
    - cidr: 10.96.0.0/12    # cluster IP range (optional)

MetalLB (BGP mode): 

apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BGPPeer
metadata:
  name: tor-switch
spec:
  myASN: 64512
  peerASN: 65000
  peerAddress: 192.168.1.1

docs.title: 9. ECMP via BGP Multipath
docs.text:
ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) allows traffic to be distributed across multiple BGP paths, distributing pod traffic across all nodes advertising a service VIP.

# Enable ECMP in Calico BGP config
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: BGPConfiguration
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  asNumber: 64512
  listenPort: 179

# Verify ECMP routes on the ToR (FRRouting)
vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 unicast 10.100.0.100/32"
# Should show multiple NEXT_HOPs (one per node running the service)

# Check ECMP on Linux kernel
ip route show 10.100.0.100
# 10.100.0.100 proto bird
#   nexthop via 192.168.1.10 dev eth0 weight 1
#   nexthop via 192.168.1.11 dev eth0 weight 1

docs.title: 10. Cloud Provider BGP Considerations
docs.text:
BGP is typically not available in public cloud VPCs — cloud providers abstract away routing via their SDN. However:

  • AWS Direct Connect / Transit Gateway: BGP is used between on-prem and AWS. Kubernetes pod routes can be injected here via Calico or a transit VPC pattern.
  • GCP Cloud Router: supports BGP for Dedicated Interconnect and VPN — not for internal pod routing in GKE.
  • Azure ExpressRoute: BGP between on-prem and Azure. Azure CNI with BGP is possible in some hybrid scenarios.
  • Bare-metal in cloud (Equinix Metal, etc.): full BGP support — treat exactly like on-premises.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix BGP session stuck in Active TCP port 179 blocked telnet <peer-ip> 179 Open firewall rule for TCP/179 between peers Session flaps every 90 seconds Hold timer expiry, no BFD birdc show protocols all Tune hold timer or enable BFD Pod routes missing on peer node BIRD not advertising route birdc show route for <pod-ip> Check Felix is running; calicoctl node status BGP Established but no routes Route policy filtering birdc show route import <proto> Check import/export filters in BGP config BIRD: Unable to open configuration file Config syntax error birdc configure check Validate BIRD config syntax ToR not receiving service IPs serviceLoadBalancerIPs not set kubectl get bgpconfiguration default -o yaml Add CIDR to serviceLoadBalancerIPs Session connects then immediately drops ASN mismatch or OPEN message rejected tcpdump -i eth0 tcp port 179 -n Match asNumber in both peer configs

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• BGP hold timer reduced to ≤9s or BFD enabled on all BGP peers
  • Route Reflectors deployed (≥2 for HA) for clusters with more than 50 nodes
  • eBGP peering configured with ToR switches using per-node unique private ASNs (64512–65534)
  • serviceLoadBalancerIPs and serviceExternalIPs CIDRs published to ToR for external reachability
  • BGP MD5 authentication configured on all external-facing peers
  • ECMP multipath enabled on ToR switches for load distribution across nodes
  • Monitoring alert configured when any BGP session leaves Established state

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Leave default hold timer at 90s Pod rerouting takes 90+ seconds after node failure Enable BFD or set holdTime: 9 and keepaliveTime: 3 Use full mesh on 100+ node cluster n*(n-1)/2 = 4950 sessions; BIRD CPU spikes on route churn Deploy 2 Route Reflectors per failure domain Give all nodes the same ASN in eBGP with ToR ToR sees AS_PATH loop and rejects routes Assign each node a unique private ASN (Calico supports perNodeLabels for this) Advertise entire podCIDR block instead of host routes /16 advertisement hides individual pod failures Let Calico advertise per-pod /32 host routes (default behavior) Enable BGP without firewall rules Any host on the management network can peer Restrict TCP/179 to known peer IPs via iptables or switch ACL

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command Check all BGP session states birdc show protocols Show all BGP routes birdc show route Show route for specific pod IP birdc show route for 10.244.0.5 Show routes with full attributes birdc show route all Check Calico BGP status calicoctl node status Reload BIRD config birdc configure List IPAM blocks (Calico) calicoctl ipam show --show-blocks Test TCP/179 reachability telnet <peer-ip> 179 Capture BGP packets tcpdump -i eth0 tcp port 179 -n Show BGP summary (FRRouting) vtysh -c "show bgp summary" Show specific prefix (FRRouting) vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 unicast <prefix>" View kernel routes from BGP ip route show proto bird

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Kubernetes Application BGP speaker BIRD agent on each node (Calico) iBGP full mesh Default Calico (<50 nodes) Route Reflector Scalable Calico for 50+ nodes eBGP with ToR Enterprise bare-metal, wire-speed pod routing BGP community Traffic engineering, MetalLB policy BFD Fast failure detection (<1s) Service advertisement Make LB IPs routable from physical network ECMP multipath Distribute service traffic across multiple nodes

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is a BGP Route Reflector, and at what cluster size does Calico's documentation recommend switching from a full BGP mesh to a Route Reflector topology?
Answer In a full BGP mesh every node peers with every other node, resulting in n*(n-1)/2 sessions — 4,950 sessions in a 100-node cluster. A Route Reflector (RR) is a dedicated node that receives BGP routes from all peers and re-advertises (reflects) them back out to all other peers. This reduces each non-RR node to only 2–4 sessions (one per RR). Calico recommends switching to RR topology at approximately 50 nodes, where the mesh overhead begins causing BIRD CPU spikes on route churn.
  1. [Scenario question] A Calico node's BGP session is stuck in the Active state and never transitions to Established. The peer IP is reachable via ping. What is the most likely cause, and what command confirms it?
Answer The most likely cause is TCP port 179 being blocked by a firewall or security group between the nodes. BGP uses TCP port 179 for session establishment — ICMP (ping) may work while TCP 179 is blocked. Confirm with `telnet 179`; if it hangs or refuses, the port is blocked. A secondary cause is an ASN mismatch in the BGP peer configuration, which would cause the OPEN message to be rejected immediately after TCP connects.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run on a Calico node to verify that all BGP sessions are in the Established state?
Answer 
calicoctl node status
The output shows each BGP peer, their IP address, ASN, and session state. All peers should show `Established` in the `INFO` column. Any peer showing `Active`, `Connect`, or `Idle` indicates a problem. You can also run `kubectl exec -n calico-system calico-node-xxxxx -- birdcl show protocols` to see the raw BIRD BGP protocol states.

Next: Lesson 07 — Bare Metal Network Infrastructure for Kubernetes

docs.title: Lesson 07 — Bare Metal Network Infrastructure for Kubernetes
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal Prereqs: Lesson 05 — VXLAN, Lesson 06 — BGP Time: ~3 hours

Goal: Design and validate a spine-leaf Kubernetes cluster network with LACP bonding, VLAN segmentation, jumbo frames, and MetalLB load balancing so production bare-metal pods achieve wire-speed native routing.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — minikube Linux node
minikube ssh
ip link show bonding_masters 2>/dev/null || echo "No bonding on this node"
bridge vlan show 2>/dev/null
ip link show type vlan

# Terminal 2 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node minikube | grep -A5 "Addresses\|Capacity"

See also: Lesson 06 — BGP Fundamentals for configuring the BGP sessions between nodes and ToR switches in this topology.

docs.title: Single Rack (dev/small clusters, up to ~20 nodes)
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    INT[Internet / Uplink]
    CORE[Core Switch]
    TOR[ToR Switch<br/>10/25 GbE access ports]
    N1[Node 1]
    N2[Node 2]
    N3[Node 3]
    N4[Node 4]

    INT --> CORE --> TOR
    TOR --> N1
    TOR --> N2
    TOR --> N3
    TOR --> N4

docs.title: Spine-Leaf (production, 20–1000+ nodes)
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S1[Spine 1<br/>100 GbE uplinks]
    S2[Spine 2<br/>100 GbE uplinks]
    L1[Leaf 1<br/>25 GbE to nodes]
    L2[Leaf 2]
    L3[Leaf 3]
    L4[Leaf 4]
    NG1[Node Group 1]
    NG2[Node Group 2]
    NG3[Node Group 3]
    NG4[Node Group 4]

    S1 --- L1
    S1 --- L2
    S1 --- L3
    S1 --- L4
    S2 --- L1
    S2 --- L2
    S2 --- L3
    S2 --- L4
    L1 --> NG1
    L2 --> NG2
    L3 --> NG3
    L4 --> NG4

Each Leaf uplinks to every Spine (full mesh). Nodes connect only to their Leaf. Provides predictable latency and no STP convergence issues.

Topology Max Nodes Failure Domain Use When Single ToR ~20 Single switch Dev, edge, small clusters Dual ToR (MLAG) ~50 Switch pair Medium clusters, redundancy Spine-Leaf 1000+ Single leaf Production, any scale

Kubernetes recommendation: Spine-Leaf with ECMP — symmetric routing, no oversubscription bottleneck, no STP.

docs.title: Packet Flow: NIC to Pod
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Wire as Physical Wire
    participant NIC as NIC (eth0/eth1)
    participant Bond as bond0 (LACP)
    participant VLAN as eth0.20 (VLAN)
    participant Kernel as IP Stack
    participant Pod as Pod veth

    Wire->>NIC: Frame arrives
    NIC->>Bond: LACP selects active slave
    Bond->>VLAN: 802.1Q tag stripped
    VLAN->>Kernel: IP routing lookup
    Kernel->>Pod: forward via veth pair

docs.title: Single NIC (dev/small)
docs.text: Simple but no redundancy.

docs.title: LACP Bond (802.3ad) — Recommended for Production
docs.text:
# Check NIC speed and driver
ethtool eth0 | grep -E "Speed|Duplex|Link"
ethtool -i eth0 | grep driver

# Create a bond
ip link add bond0 type bond mode 802.3ad
ip link set eth0 master bond0
ip link set eth1 master bond0
ip link set bond0 up

# Verify bond status
cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0
# Active slaves, LACP state, link speeds   # → both slaves should be "up"

# Check LACP negotiation
cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0 | grep -E "802.3ad|LACP|Partner"

Switch side: configure the ports as a port-channel / LAG with LACP mode active.

docs.title: LACP Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Value Effect When to change mode 802.3ad Active LACP negotiation Use active-backup if switch does not support LACP lacp-rate fast 1s LACP PDUs (vs 30s slow) Always use fast for faster failover mii-monitor-interval 100 (ms) Link state polling interval 50ms for critical nodes xmit-hash-policy layer3+4 Hashing for load distribution layer3+4 for IP/port-based distribution min-links 1 Min active slaves before bond goes down Set to 2 for strict HA

docs.title: SR-IOV (High Performance)
docs.text:
SR-IOV partitions a physical NIC into Virtual Functions (VFs), each passed directly into a pod or VM.

# Check SR-IOV capability
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<pci-addr>/sriov_totalvfs

# Enable 8 VFs
echo 8 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<pci-addr>/sriov_numvfs

# VFs appear as additional PCI devices
lspci | grep -i ethernet                 # → VFs listed alongside PF

Kubernetes integration: use the SR-IOV Network Device Plugin + SR-IOV CNI for DPDK/low-latency workloads.

docs.title: 3. VLAN Design
docs.text:
VLANs segment traffic on the same physical switches. Common Kubernetes VLAN design:

VLAN Purpose MTU Notes 10 Management (SSH, iDRAC/iLO, BMC, IPMI) 1500 Out-of-band; restrict to ops team 20 Kubernetes node traffic (podCIDR routing, BGP) 9000 Main data plane 30 Storage (Ceph OSD, NFS, iSCSI) 9000 Jumbo frames required for RDMA 40 Tenant / application separation 9000 Optional; use NetworkPolicy otherwise 
# Configure VLAN on a node interface
ip link add link eth0 name eth0.20 type vlan id 20
ip link set eth0.20 up
ip addr add 192.168.20.10/24 dev eth0.20

# Or configure the switch to present VLAN 20 untagged to the port (access port)
# Node then uses eth0 directly

Switch config (Cisco NX-OS example): 

interface Ethernet1/1
  switchport mode access
  switchport access vlan 20
  spanning-tree port type edge
  no shutdown

docs.title: 4. MTU and Jumbo Frames
docs.text:
Production bare metal should use jumbo frames (MTU 9000) end-to-end.

# Set jumbo frames on NIC
ip link set eth0 mtu 9000

# Persist in network config (varies by distro)
# /etc/netplan/01-netcfg.yaml (Ubuntu)
network:
  ethernets:
    eth0:
      mtu: 9000

# Verify end-to-end (ping with DF bit)
ping -M do -s 8972 192.168.1.20
# 8972 + 28 = 9000 — if this works, jumbo frames are working end-to-end

# Verify from inside a pod
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- ping -M do -s 8972 <other-pod-ip>

# Set CNI MTU accordingly (subtract overlay overhead)
# VXLAN on 9000 MTU: 9000 - 50 = 8950
# Native routing on 9000 MTU: 9000 (no overhead)

Switch configuration: enable jumbo frames globally: 

# Cisco NX-OS
policy-map type network-qos jumbo
  class type network-qos class-default
    mtu 9216
system qos
  service-policy type network-qos jumbo

docs.title: MTU Reference Table
docs.text: Scenario NIC MTU CNI MTU Overhead Native routing (no overlay) 9000 9000 0 bytes VXLAN overlay 9000 8950 50 bytes IP-IP overlay 9000 8980 20 bytes WireGuard encryption 9000 8940 60 bytes Cloud (AWS default) 9001 8951 50 bytes VXLAN

docs.title: 5. Load Balancers on Bare Metal
docs.text: Cloud Kubernetes gets cloud-native LBs for free. Bare metal needs an alternative.

docs.title: MetalLB
docs.text:
MetalLB implements LoadBalancer service type for bare metal using BGP or L2 (ARP/NDP).

# MetalLB L2 mode (simple, no BGP required)
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: production
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 192.168.100.100-192.168.100.200
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: L2Advertisement
metadata:
  name: example
  namespace: metallb-system

# MetalLB BGP mode (recommended for production)
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta2
kind: BGPPeer
metadata:
  name: tor-switch
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  myASN: 64512
  peerASN: 65000
  peerAddress: 192.168.1.1
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BGPAdvertisement
metadata:
  name: example
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - production

docs.title: kube-vip
docs.text:
Alternative to MetalLB: uses VRRP/ARP for HA virtual IPs.

# kube-vip as a DaemonSet for LoadBalancer services
env:
  - name: vip_leasename
    value: plndr-svcs-lock
  - name: lb_enable
    value: "true"
  - name: lb_port
    value: "80"
Solution Mode ECMP HA Use When MetalLB L2 ARP/NDP No Single speaker Simple setups, no BGP on switches MetalLB BGP BGP Yes Via BGP multipath Production with BGP-capable ToR kube-vip VRRP No Active/standby Control plane VIP + services

docs.title: 6. External DNS and IP Planning
docs.text:
Plan your IP ranges before deploying:

Physical Network:    192.168.0.0/16
  Node management:   192.168.1.0/24   (node SSH, kubelet API)
  LoadBalancer VIPs: 192.168.100.0/24 (MetalLB pool)

Kubernetes Internal:
  Pod CIDR:          10.244.0.0/16    (never routable externally)
  Service CIDR:      10.96.0.0/12     (never routable externally)
  Node CIDR mask:    /24              (256 pods per node max)

# Calculate how many nodes fit in a pod CIDR
# podCIDR=10.244.0.0/16, nodeMask=/24
# 2^(24-16) = 256 nodes × 254 usable IPs/node
python3 -c "print(2**(24-16), 'nodes,', 2**8-2, 'IPs/node')"
# → 256 nodes, 254 IPs/node

docs.title: 7. Node Network Configuration at Scale
docs.text: For consistent bare-metal node networking, use automation:

docs.title: Netplan (Ubuntu)
docs.text:
# /etc/netplan/01-k8s-node.yaml
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    eth0:
      mtu: 9000
  bonds:
    bond0:
      interfaces: [eth0, eth1]
      mtu: 9000
      parameters:
        mode: 802.3ad
        lacp-rate: fast
        mii-monitor-interval: 100
        transmit-hash-policy: layer3+4
      addresses: [192.168.1.10/24]
      routes:
        - to: default
          via: 192.168.1.1
      nameservers:
        addresses: [8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4]

docs.title: NMState (Red Hat / OpenShift)
docs.text:
# NMState declarative network config
interfaces:
  - name: bond0
    type: bond
    state: up
    ipv4:
      address:
        - ip: 192.168.1.10
          prefix-length: 24
      enabled: true
    link-aggregation:
      mode: 802.3ad
      port:
        - eth0
        - eth1

docs.title: 8. RDMA and High-Performance Networking
docs.text:
For AI/ML workloads requiring InfiniBand or RoCE:

# Check RDMA devices
rdma dev
# Shows InfiniBand and RoCE devices with GIDs

# Install RDMA CNI plugin
# Use Multus + RDMA device plugin for secondary interfaces with RDMA
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep rdma

# Check RDMA queue pairs
rdma stat show

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Nodes can't reach each other VLAN mismatch between node and switch tcpdump -i eth0 -n vlan Verify switch port VLAN config matches node VLAN config Pod traffic drops silently MTU mismatch (black-hole routing) ping -M do -s 8972 <remote-ip> Set consistent MTU on all NIC, bond, VLAN, and CNI interfaces Bond shows only one active slave Switch not configured for LACP cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0 Configure switch port-channel with channel-group N mode active MetalLB service VIP unreachable BGP session not established kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l app=metallb Verify ASN and peer IPs in BGPPeer config iperf3 bandwidth low between nodes Only one LACP slave hashing to flow ethtool -S bond0 \| grep slave Tune xmit-hash-policy to layer3+4 on both bond and switch PXE boot fails at DHCP Management VLAN not assigned to port tcpdump -i eth0 port 67 or 68 Add VLAN 10 as native VLAN on switch port SR-IOV VF not visible in pod VF not created or device plugin not running echo 8 > .../sriov_numvfs then lspci Create VFs at node boot and ensure SR-IOV device plugin DaemonSet is running

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Spine-leaf topology deployed with no leaf-to-leaf direct links and full spine redundancy
  • LACP bonding (802.3ad) active on all nodes with lacp-rate fast and layer3+4 hashing
  • Jumbo frames (MTU 9000) set end-to-end: NIC, bond, switch ports, and CNI MTU adjusted accordingly
  • Separate VLANs for management, Kubernetes data, and storage traffic
  • MetalLB or kube-vip deployed with an IP pool plan that does not overlap pod/service CIDRs
  • Out-of-band management (IPMI/BMC) accessible on a dedicated VLAN with restricted firewall rules
  • Node network configuration managed by Netplan/NMState and version-controlled, not set manually

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Run all traffic on a single flat VLAN Storage floods degrade node communication; no blast radius isolation Separate VLANs 10/20/30 with ACLs between them Set MTU 1500 on storage NIC iSCSI/Ceph performance degrades 30–50% due to fragmentation Set MTU 9000 on storage VLAN end-to-end before deploying Ceph Use MetalLB L2 mode in production Single speaker is a bottleneck; no ECMP; ARP failover is slow (~10s) Use MetalLB BGP mode with ToR peering for ECMP and fast convergence Connect leaf switches to each other Creates STP loops and unpredictable latency; defeats spine-leaf design In spine-leaf, leaves ONLY connect to spines — never to each other Configure IP manually on each node Config drift leads to duplicate IPs and debugging nightmares Use Netplan/NMState templates applied by Ansible or cloud-init

docs.text: Component Bare Metal Decision Topology Spine-Leaf preferred for scale, ECMP routing NIC LACP bond (802.3ad) for redundancy; SR-IOV for DPDK/low-latency MTU Jumbo frames (9000) end-to-end; adjust CNI MTU per overlay VLANs Separate management (10), Kubernetes (20), storage (30) Load Balancer MetalLB BGP mode for ECMP; L2 for simple setups IP planning Separate physical, pod, service, and VIP ranges; plan before deploy Pod routing Native BGP preferred (no overhead); VXLAN for simpler setup

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is the purpose of LACP (802.3ad) bonding on a bare-metal Kubernetes node, and what does the xmit-hash-policy: layer3+4 setting control?
Answer LACP bonding aggregates two or more physical NICs into a single logical interface (`bond0`), providing both link redundancy (if one NIC or switch port fails, the bond continues on the remaining link) and increased bandwidth. The `xmit-hash-policy: layer3+4` setting determines how outbound packets are distributed across the active slave links — using a hash of source IP, destination IP, source port, and destination port. This ensures that multiple concurrent flows are spread across both links rather than all going to the same NIC, maximizing bandwidth utilization.
  1. [Scenario question] Two nodes in a spine-leaf cluster cannot reach each other. The bond interface on both nodes shows only one active slave instead of two. LACP is configured on the bond. What is the most likely cause, and what command on the node confirms it?
Answer The most likely cause is that the switch ports are not configured for LACP (port-channel with `channel-group N mode active`). When the switch does not send LACP PDUs, the bond falls back to only one active slave. Confirm on the node with `cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0` — look at the "MII Status" of each slave and the "Partner Key" field; if the Partner Key is `0`, the switch is not negotiating LACP. Run `tcpdump -i eth0 ether proto 0x8809` to verify LACP PDUs are (or are not) being exchanged.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to verify that jumbo frames (MTU 9000) are working end-to-end between two bare-metal Kubernetes nodes?
Answer 
ping -M do -s 8972 <remote-node-ip>
The `-M do` flag sets the Don't Fragment bit and `-s 8972` sends a payload of 8972 bytes. Adding the 28-byte ICMP and IP header overhead gives 9000 bytes total — the maximum for a jumbo frame MTU of 9000. A successful reply confirms end-to-end jumbo frame support. If you receive "Frag needed" or the ping times out, an intermediate interface (switch port, NIC, or bond) has not been configured for MTU 9000.

docs.title: Lesson 08 — Cloud Provider Networking Basics
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Cloud Provider Prereqs: Lesson 02 — IP Routing and Forwarding Time: ~3 hours

Goal: Explain how AWS VPC CNI, GKE Alias IPs, and Azure CNI assign pod IPs from cloud network resources, and configure security group and load balancer integrations for each provider.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — kubectl (Mac)
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | head -20

# Terminal 2 — cloud CLI (optional, Mac)
kubectl get cm -n kube-system amazon-vpc-cni -o yaml 2>/dev/null || echo "Not on AWS EKS"
kubectl get cm -n kube-system ip-masq-agent -o yaml 2>/dev/null || echo "Not on GKE"

See also: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification for how the cloud-specific CNI binaries plug into the kubelet ADD/DEL lifecycle.

docs.title: 1. The SDN Abstraction
docs.text:
Cloud VPCs implement routing in software, not on physical switches.

flowchart LR
    subgraph cloud["Cloud Provider SDN"]
        HV1[Hypervisor Node 1]
        HV2[Hypervisor Node 2]
        FABRIC[Virtual Network Fabric<br/>Software-defined routes]
    end
    subgraph k8s["Kubernetes Cluster"]
        N1[EKS/GKE/AKS Node]
        N2[EKS/GKE/AKS Node]
        P1[Pod 10.0.1.5]
        P2[Pod 10.0.2.7]
    end

    P1 --> N1 --> HV1 --> FABRIC
    FABRIC --> HV2 --> N2 --> P2

This means: - Routes are enforced by the hypervisor/network fabric — you do not configure ToR switches - IP-in-IP or VXLAN tunnels may already be used underneath (invisible to you) - Routing changes propagate in seconds (API calls), not minutes (BGP convergence) - Security is enforced at the VM NIC level (Security Groups, NACLs)

docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph vpc["VPC 10.0.0.0/16"]
        subgraph az1["us-east-1a"]
            SUB1[Subnet 10.0.1.0/24]
            N1[EC2 Node<br/>eth0=10.0.1.10<br/>Primary ENI]
            N1E2[eth1=10.0.1.20<br/>Secondary ENI]
            P1[Pod 10.0.1.21]
            P2[Pod 10.0.1.22]
        end
        subgraph az2["us-east-1b"]
            SUB2[Subnet 10.0.2.0/24]
            N2[EC2 Node<br/>eth0=10.0.2.10]

        NAT[NAT Gateway]

    N1E2 --> P2
    SUB1 --> NAT --> IGW

docs.title: AWS VPC CNI (amazon-vpc-cni-k8s)
docs.text:
Pods get real VPC IPs from secondary ENI private IPs.

Node (m5.xlarge): 2 ENIs × 15 IPs/ENI = 30 pod IPs max
                                         (limits vary by instance type)

# Check ENIs and secondary IPs on a node
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids <id> \
  --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].NetworkInterfaces'

# View pod IPs assigned via VPC CNI
kubectl get pods -o wide -A | head -20

# Check AWS VPC CNI version
kubectl get ds -n kube-system aws-node \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'

# VPC CNI configuration
kubectl get cm -n kube-system amazon-vpc-cni -o yaml

# Step-by-step: trace a pod IP back to its ENI
POD_IP=$(kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
echo "Pod IP: $POD_IP"                            # → 10.0.1.21
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=${POD_IP}" \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[0].{ENI:NetworkInterfaceId,Node:PrivateIpAddress}'
# → shows which ENI owns this pod IP

Source/Destination Check must be disabled (EKS does this automatically): 

aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute \
  --instance-id <id> \
  --no-source-dest-check

docs.title: ENI Limits per Instance Type
docs.text: Instance ENIs IPs/ENI Max Pods With Prefix Delegation t3.medium 3 6 15 54 m5.large 3 10 27 90 m5.xlarge 4 15 44 120 m5.4xlarge 8 30 232 480 c5.18xlarge 15 50 737 750

docs.title: AWS VPC CNI Configuration Reference
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect When to change WARM_IP_TARGET 1 IPs pre-warmed per node Increase for faster pod startup MINIMUM_IP_TARGET 0 Min IPs always allocated Set to expected pod count per node ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION false Allocate /28 blocks instead of single IPs Enable for high pod density nodes WARM_PREFIX_TARGET 1 /28 blocks pre-warmed Tune for burst workloads AWS_VPC_K8S_CNI_EXTERNALSNAT false Use VPC NAT for pod egress Set true when using NAT Gateway for pod egress 
# Enable prefix delegation for higher pod density
kubectl set env ds -n kube-system aws-node ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true
kubectl set env ds -n kube-system aws-node WARM_PREFIX_TARGET=1

docs.title: AWS Security Groups
docs.text:
Security Groups are stateful firewalls at the ENI level.

# Check which SGs are on a node
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids <id> \
  --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].SecurityGroups'

# EKS creates these SGs automatically:
# - Cluster SG (control plane ↔ nodes)
# - Node SG (node ↔ node, pod ↔ pod)

For pod-level security groups (Security Groups for Pods): 

# SecurityGroupPolicy CRD (requires VPC CNI trunk ENI mode)
apiVersion: vpcresources.k8s.aws/v1beta1
kind: SecurityGroupPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-sg-policy
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  securityGroups:
    groupIds:
      - sg-0123456789abcdef0

docs.title: GKE Networking
docs.text:
GKE uses Alias IP ranges — each node gets a /24 from the pod range, and pod IPs are real VPC addresses.

# View node pod CIDR allocations
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.podCIDR}{"\n"}{end}'
# → gke-node-1    10.100.0.0/24
# → gke-node-2    10.100.1.0/24

# GKE Dataplane v2 (uses Cilium eBPF under the hood)
kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml 2>/dev/null

# Check Dataplane version
gcloud container clusters describe <cluster> \
  --format='value(networkConfig.datapathProvider)'
# ADVANCED_DATAPATH = Dataplane v2 (eBPF/Cilium)
# LEGACY_DATAPATH = iptables kube-proxy

# Observe ip-masq-agent config
kubectl get configmap -n kube-system ip-masq-agent -o yaml

docs.title: GCP Firewall Rules
docs.text:
GCP firewall rules are global, applied at the VPC level, not per-instance.

# View firewall rules for the cluster
gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter="name~gke-"

# GKE auto-creates:
# gke-<cluster>-master      — kubelet API access from control plane
# gke-<cluster>-vms         — node ↔ node traffic
# gke-<cluster>-inkubelet   — control plane to nodes

docs.title: Azure CNI
docs.text:
Two modes:

Azure CNI (classic): Pods get IPs from the VNet subnet. 

# Each node pre-allocates pod IPs from the subnet
az aks show --resource-group rg --name aks \
  --query networkProfile.podCidr

Azure CNI Overlay: Pods get IPs from a separate overlay CIDR (less VNet IP exhaustion). 

az aks show --resource-group rg --name aks \
  --query networkProfile.networkMode
# overlay

# View node's pod CIDR in overlay mode
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.podCIDR}{"\n"}{end}'

docs.title: NSG (Network Security Group)
docs.text:
NSGs filter traffic at the subnet or NIC level.

# View NSG rules applied to AKS nodes
az network nsg rule list \
  --resource-group <node-resource-group> \
  --nsg-name <nsg-name>

# IMPORTANT: AKS manages these NSG rules — manual edits will be overwritten

docs.text:
# External LoadBalancer (Azure Standard LB)
service:
  type: LoadBalancer

# Internal
service:
  type: LoadBalancer
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-load-balancer-internal: "true"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-load-balancer-internal-subnet: "internal-subnet"

docs.title: AWS
docs.text:
# Gotcha 1: ENI limit → pod density limit
# m5.large: 3 ENIs × 10 IPs = 30 pods max (minus 1 per ENI for node)
# Check limits: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-eni.html

# Gotcha 2: Prefix delegation (increases pod density)
kubectl set env ds -n kube-system aws-node ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true

# Gotcha 3: externalTrafficPolicy=Local required for client IP preservation with NLB
kubectl patch svc <svc> -p '{"spec":{"externalTrafficPolicy":"Local"}}'

docs.title: GCP
docs.text:
# Gotcha 1: Default firewalls allow all internal traffic — add deny rules for segmentation
# Gotcha 2: Alias IP ranges must be sized before cluster creation (can't shrink)
# Gotcha 3: GKE uses MASQUERADE for pod egress by default
kubectl get configmap -n kube-system ip-masq-agent -o yaml

docs.title: Azure
docs.text:
# Gotcha 1: Azure CNI classic exhausts VNet IPs quickly
# 110 pods/node × 100 nodes = 11,000 IPs needed in subnet

# Gotcha 2: AKS requires pre-planned subnet for Azure CNI
# Use Overlay mode for large clusters
az aks create --network-plugin azure --network-plugin-mode overlay ...

# Gotcha 3: NSG rules are managed by AKS — manual edits get overwritten

docs.title: 7. Hands-On: Inspect Cloud Cluster Networking
docs.text:
# Any cloud cluster — trace a pod's IP back to the cloud resource

# Step 1: Get pod IP
POD_IP=$(kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
echo "Pod IP: $POD_IP"                                      # → 10.0.1.21

# Step 2: Find which node
NODE=$(kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}')
echo "Node: $NODE"                                          # → ip-10-0-1-10.ec2.internal

# Step 3: AWS — find the ENI that owns this secondary IP
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node $NODE \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=${POD_IP}" \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[0].{ENI:NetworkInterfaceId,Node:PrivateIpAddress}'
# → {"ENI": "eni-0abc123", "Node": "10.0.1.10"}

# Step 4: Verify security groups allow the traffic
aws ec2 describe-network-interface-attribute \
  --network-interface-id <eni-id> \
  --attribute groupSet

# GKE: verify alias IP assignment on the node
gcloud compute instances describe $NODE --format='value(networkInterfaces[0].aliasIpRanges)'
# → [{cidrRange: 10.100.1.0/24, subnetworkRangeName: pods}]

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Instance type selected with sufficient ENI/IP capacity for target pod density (AWS)
  • Prefix delegation enabled on EKS for clusters with >30 pods/node
  • Secondary IP range pre-sized for maximum cluster growth before cluster creation (GKE)
  • Azure CNI Overlay mode enabled for clusters with more than 50 nodes (AKS)
  • NetworkPolicy or Security Groups for Pods configured for pod-level isolation
  • Cloud NAT / NAT Gateway provisioned for private node subnets requiring egress
  • Load balancer health check ports opened in node security groups / firewall rules

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use default ENI limits on large EKS nodes Pod scheduling fails when ENI is full; no visible error until pods are stuck Plan instance type based on max pods needed; enable prefix delegation Size GKE secondary range too small at cluster creation Pod CIDR exhaustion as cluster grows; cannot resize Allocate a /14 secondary range (262k addresses) even for small clusters Edit NSG/firewall rules manually on AKS/GKE Cloud controller manager overwrites changes at next reconcile Use Kubernetes NetworkPolicy; only add non-managed rules outside the node resource group Use externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster with NLB on AWS Client source IP is masqueraded; hops add latency Use externalTrafficPolicy: Local with NLB and ip target type Rely on Security Groups alone for pod-to-pod isolation on EKS SGs apply at ENI (node) level, not pod level, without trunk ENI mode Enable Security Groups for Pods with trunk ENI mode, or use Calico NetworkPolicy

docs.text: Provider Key Concept AWS EKS VPC CNI gives pods real ENI IPs; ENI limit caps pod density per node GCP GKE Alias IP ranges; Dataplane v2 uses Cilium eBPF; secondary ranges pre-sized at creation Azure AKS Azure CNI Overlay recommended for large clusters; NSG at subnet managed by AKS All providers Cloud LBs integrate via CCM (Cloud Controller Manager) annotations on Service objects

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] How does the AWS VPC CNI plugin assign IP addresses to pods differently from an overlay-based CNI like Flannel, and what hardware resource on the EC2 instance limits the maximum number of pods per node?
Answer The AWS VPC CNI plugin assigns pods real VPC IP addresses by using secondary private IPs on Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) attached to the EC2 instance. Each secondary IP becomes a pod IP, and routes inside the VPC fabric deliver traffic directly — no VXLAN or overlay tunnel is needed. The limiting factor is the number of ENIs the instance type supports and the number of secondary IPs per ENI. For example, an `m5.xlarge` supports 4 ENIs × 15 IPs/ENI = 60 total IPs, minus 1 per ENI for the primary node IP = 44 maximum pod IPs.
  1. [Scenario question] Pods on an EKS node are stuck in ContainerCreating with no IP assigned. kubectl describe node shows the node is Ready. The VPC CNI DaemonSet pods are running. What is the most likely cause?
Answer The most likely cause is that the ENI warm IP pool is exhausted — the node has used all secondary IPs available on its attached ENIs and cannot allocate a new IP for the new pod. Check with `kubectl describe node | grep -i eni` or inspect the VPC CNI logs (`kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node`). The fix is either to scale to a larger instance type with more ENIs, or to enable prefix delegation (`ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true`) which allocates `/28` blocks of 16 IPs at a time instead of single IPs, increasing pod density.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to find which ENI on an EC2 instance owns a specific pod IP address (e.g., 10.0.1.21)?
Answer 
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=10.0.1.21" \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[0].{ENI:NetworkInterfaceId,Node:PrivateIpAddress}'
The output shows the ENI ID that holds this secondary IP. This is useful for correlating pod IPs to ENI security group rules when debugging connectivity issues at the VPC level.

docs.title: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification and Plugin Architecture
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud Prereqs: Lesson 04 — Network Namespaces Time: ~2 hours

Goal: Trace a Kubernetes pod creation through the full CNI ADD lifecycle — from kubelet invocation to IP assignment — and manually execute a CNI plugin to verify your understanding of the stdin/stdout JSON protocol.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — minikube node (inspect CNI config and binaries)
minikube ssh
ls /etc/cni/net.d/        # CNI config files (first alphabetically is used)
ls /opt/cni/bin/          # CNI plugin binaries

# Terminal 2 — kubectl (Mac)
kubectl get pods -A | grep calico   # the running CNI

See also: Lesson 10 — eBPF and XDP for how Cilium replaces iptables-based CNI plumbing with eBPF TC programs loaded during the ADD operation.

docs.title: 1. What CNI Is
docs.text:
CNI is a specification + set of libraries defining how container runtimes configure network interfaces for containers. It is intentionally minimal:

  • A CNI plugin is an executable (binary) placed in /opt/cni/bin/
  • It receives configuration via stdin (JSON)
  • It receives environment variables for context
  • It outputs results on stdout (JSON)
  • The runtime calls it on ADD (create pod), DEL (delete pod), and CHECK (verify) operations

docs.title: Architecture: CNI Plugin Ecosystem
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph node["Kubernetes Node"]
        KL[kubelet]
        subgraph cni_bin["/opt/cni/bin/"]
            CALICO[calico]
            BRIDGE[bridge]
            IPAM[host-local]
            BW[bandwidth]
            PM[portmap]
        end
        subgraph cni_conf["/etc/cni/net.d/"]
            CONF[10-calico.conflist]
        end
        subgraph netns["Network Namespaces"]
            NS1[/var/run/netns/cni-abc<br/>Pod eth0: 10.244.0.6]
        end
    end
    subgraph ipam_backends["IPAM Backends"]
        HL[host-local<br/>/var/lib/cni/networks/]
        CIPAM[calico-ipam<br/>Kubernetes CRDs]
        WA[whereabouts<br/>Cluster-wide]
        VPCNI[aws-vpc-cni<br/>EC2 ENI secondary IPs]
    end

    KL -- "reads first conf" --> CONF
    KL -- "exec with env vars" --> CALICO
    CALICO -- "calls IPAM" --> CIPAM
    CALICO -- "creates veth in" --> NS1
    CIPAM --> WA
    CALICO -.chain.-> BW
    CALICO -.chain.-> PM

docs.title: 2. CNI Environment Variables
docs.text:
CNI_COMMAND      ADD | DEL | CHECK | VERSION
CNI_CONTAINERID  Unique ID of the container (pod)
CNI_NETNS        Path to the network namespace: /var/run/netns/<id>
CNI_IFNAME       Interface name to create inside the container: eth0
CNI_ARGS         Extra K=V args (not widely used)
CNI_PATH         Colon-separated list of directories to search for CNI plugins
Variable Example Value Notes CNI_COMMAND ADD One of ADD / DEL / CHECK / VERSION CNI_CONTAINERID a1b2c3d4e5f6... Sandbox container ID from kubelet CNI_NETNS /var/run/netns/cni-abc123ef Pre-created by kubelet before CNI call CNI_IFNAME eth0 Always eth0 for primary pod interface CNI_PATH /opt/cni/bin Colon-separated; chained plugins also searched here

docs.title: 3. CNI Configuration File
docs.text:
Stored in /etc/cni/net.d/. The first file (alphabetically) is used.

{
  "cniVersion": "1.0.0",
  "name": "my-network",
  "type": "bridge",
  "bridge": "cni0",
  "isGateway": true,
  "ipMasq": true,
  "ipam": {
    "type": "host-local",
    "ranges": [
      [{"subnet": "10.244.0.0/24"}]
    ],
    "routes": [
      {"dst": "0.0.0.0/0"}
    ]
  }
}

For chained plugins (multiple plugins in sequence, .conflist format): 

{
  "cniVersion": "1.0.0",
  "name": "k8s-pod-network",
  "plugins": [
    {
      "type": "calico",
      "ipam": {"type": "calico-ipam"}
    },
    {
      "type": "bandwidth",
      "ingressRate": 10485760,
      "egressRate": 10485760
    },
    {
      "type": "portmap",
      "capabilities": {"portMappings": true}
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text: Field Required Default Effect cniVersion Yes — CNI spec version; must match plugin support name Yes — Network name; used as key for IPAM state type Yes — Binary filename in CNI_PATH to execute ipam.type Yes (usually) — IPAM plugin name; called by main plugin isGateway No false Assign gateway IP to bridge interface ipMasq No false Add iptables MASQUERADE for pod egress plugins Conflist only — Array of plugins to chain in sequence

docs.title: Step-by-step: kubelet to Running Pod Network
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant KB as kubelet
    participant FS as /etc/cni/net.d/
    participant BIN as /opt/cni/bin/calico
    participant IPAM as calico-ipam
    participant NS as Network Namespace
    participant OS as Linux kernel

    KB->>KB: Create pod sandbox (pause container)
    KB->>NS: ip netns add /var/run/netns/cni-abc123
    KB->>FS: Read first .conf/.conflist file
    KB->>KB: Set CNI_COMMAND=ADD, CNI_NETNS=..., CNI_IFNAME=eth0
    KB->>BIN: exec calico (config via stdin JSON)
    BIN->>IPAM: Call calico-ipam ADD
    IPAM-->>BIN: Return: ip=10.244.0.6/24, gw=10.244.0.1
    BIN->>OS: ip link add veth1234 type veth peer name eth0
    BIN->>NS: ip link set eth0 netns /var/run/netns/cni-abc123
    BIN->>NS: ip addr add 10.244.0.6/24 dev eth0 (inside ns)
    BIN->>OS: ip route add 10.244.0.6 dev veth1234 scope link
    BIN->>OS: Configure eBPF/iptables rules (Calico)
    BIN-->>KB: stdout: CNI result JSON
    KB->>KB: Store pod IP in pod.status.podIP

docs.text:
{
  "cniVersion": "1.0.0",
  "interfaces": [
    {
      "name": "eth0",
      "mac": "0a:58:0a:f4:00:06",
      "sandbox": "/var/run/netns/cni-abc123"
    }
  ],
  "ips": [
    {
      "interface": 0,
      "address": "10.244.0.6/24",
      "gateway": "10.244.0.1"
    }
  ],
  "routes": [
    {"dst": "0.0.0.0/0", "gw": "10.244.0.1"}
  ],
  "dns": {
    "nameservers": ["10.96.0.10"]
  }
}

docs.title: 6. IPAM Plugins
docs.text: IPAM (IP Address Management) plugins handle IP allocation, called by the main CNI plugin.

docs.title: host-local
docs.text:
Allocates IPs from a range, stored in flat files on each node. 

# IPAM state files
ls /var/lib/cni/networks/my-network/
# Files named after each allocated IP, containing container ID

# Check all allocated IPs
ls /var/lib/cni/networks/k8s-pod-network/
# → 10.244.0.2  10.244.0.3  10.244.0.6  last_reserved_ip.0

docs.title: calico-ipam
docs.text:
Uses Calico's IPAM blocks (by default /26 per node) with central coordination via Kubernetes CRDs. 

calicoctl ipam show --show-blocks
# → shows which /26 blocks are allocated to each node
calicoctl ipam show --ip 10.244.0.6
# → pod and node that owns this IP

docs.title: whereabouts
docs.text:
Cluster-wide IPAM with no per-node allocation boundaries (useful for Multus secondary networks). 

kubectl get ippools.whereabouts.cni.cncf.io
kubectl get overlappingrangeipreservations.whereabouts.cni.cncf.io

docs.title: AWS VPC CNI IPAM
docs.text:
Allocates IPs from EC2 secondary ENI IPs; keeps a warm pool pre-provisioned. 

kubectl get cm -n kube-system amazon-vpc-cni -o yaml | grep WARM_IP_TARGET
# Increasing WARM_IP_TARGET reduces pod startup time

IPAM Plugin Scope State Storage Use When host-local Per-node Node filesystem Simple setups, Flannel calico-ipam Cluster Kubernetes CRDs Calico CNI whereabouts Cluster etcd / Kubernetes Multus secondary interfaces aws-vpc-cni Per-node EC2 ENI API EKS only dhcp External DHCP server Bare metal with existing DHCP infra

docs.title: 7. Multus — Multiple CNI Plugins Per Pod
docs.text:
Multus is a meta-CNI that calls multiple CNI plugins for a single pod, giving it multiple network interfaces.

# Pod with extra SR-IOV NIC
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  annotations:
    k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: '[
      {
        "name": "sriov-net",
        "interface": "net1"
      }
    ]'
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: app:latest

# Check Multus installation
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep multus
ls /etc/cni/net.d/00-multus.conf    # Multus must be first alphabetically

# View network attachment definitions
kubectl get network-attachment-definitions -A

# Verify multi-NIC pod
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- ip addr
# → eth0: primary (from default CNI)
# → net1: secondary (from SR-IOV CNI)

docs.title: 8. Debugging CNI
docs.text:
# CNI logs (location varies by plugin)
journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i cni
cat /var/log/calico/cni/cni.log
cat /var/log/aws-routed-eni/ipamd.log

# Manually run a CNI plugin (simulate ADD operation)
export CNI_COMMAND=ADD
export CNI_CONTAINERID=test-container
export CNI_NETNS=/var/run/netns/test-ns
export CNI_IFNAME=eth0
export CNI_PATH=/opt/cni/bin

ip netns add test-ns                             # → create test namespace
echo '{"cniVersion":"1.0.0","name":"test","type":"bridge","bridge":"cni-test","ipam":{"type":"host-local","ranges":[[{"subnet":"10.99.0.0/24"}]]}}' \
  | /opt/cni/bin/bridge
# → stdout shows CNI result JSON with assigned IP   # → 10.99.0.2/24

# Verify the interface was created in the namespace
ip netns exec test-ns ip addr show eth0          # → 10.99.0.2/24

# Cleanup
ip netns del test-ns
# DEL the bridge
CNI_COMMAND=DEL CNI_CONTAINERID=test-container CNI_NETNS=/var/run/netns/test-ns \
  CNI_IFNAME=eth0 CNI_PATH=/opt/cni/bin \
  echo '{"cniVersion":"1.0.0","name":"test","type":"bridge","bridge":"cni-test","ipam":{"type":"host-local","ranges":[[{"subnet":"10.99.0.0/24"}]]}}' \
  | /opt/cni/bin/bridge

# Common CNI failure modes:
# 1. Binary not found in CNI_PATH
# 2. Network namespace not created yet
# 3. IPAM pool exhausted (host-local: check /var/lib/cni/networks/)
# 4. Interface name conflict (eth0 already exists in namespace)
# 5. Missing kernel modules (vxlan, bridge)

# Check if kernel modules are loaded
lsmod | grep -E "vxlan|bridge|8021q"
modprobe bridge vxlan

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Pod stuck in ContainerCreating CNI binary not found or exits non-zero journalctl -u kubelet --since "5m ago" \| grep cni Check binary exists in CNI_PATH and is executable failed to allocate for range 0 IPAM pool exhausted ls /var/lib/cni/networks/<name>/ Remove stale IPAM entries for deleted containers eth0 already exists in namespace Previous DEL failed; namespace reused ip netns exec <ns> ip link del eth0 Manually clean up stale namespace before retry Multus pod missing net1 interface NetworkAttachmentDefinition not found in pod namespace kubectl get net-attach-def -n <ns> Create NAD in same namespace as pod CNI version mismatch error Plugin supports older cniVersion CNI_COMMAND=VERSION /opt/cni/bin/<plugin> Upgrade CNI plugin binary to match conflist version Pod gets wrong IP subnet Wrong .conflist file being read (not alphabetically first) ls -1 /etc/cni/net.d/ Rename files so desired config sorts first alphabetically failed to dial Felix (Calico) Felix not running; IPAM depends on it kubectl get pods -n calico-system Restart Calico node DaemonSet; check Felix logs

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• CNI binaries version-pinned and distributed via DaemonSet init container (not host package)
  • IPAM pool sized for maximum expected pod count with 20% headroom
  • Stale IPAM entries cleaned up during node drain/delete via lifecycle hooks
  • cniVersion in conflist matches the installed binary's supported versions
  • Kernel modules (bridge, vxlan, ip_tables) confirmed loaded at node boot
  • CNI log rotation configured to prevent disk exhaustion on high-churn clusters
  • Multus NetworkAttachmentDefinition CRDs in the correct namespace for each workload

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Leave multiple .conf files in /etc/cni/net.d/ CNI uses only the first alphabetically; leftover files from old CNIs cause confusion Remove old CNI config files when switching CNI plugins Install CNI binaries via host package manager Binaries can be updated or removed by OS updates outside Kubernetes lifecycle Use an init DaemonSet to copy versioned CNI binaries to /opt/cni/bin/ Ignore IPAM exhaustion warnings Pod scheduling fails silently when pool is full Monitor IPAM utilization with calicoctl ipam show or alert on failed to allocate in CNI logs Use host-local IPAM on large multi-node clusters Per-node flat files have no cluster-wide leak detection Use calico-ipam or whereabouts for cluster-wide coordination and stale entry cleanup Forget to delete CNI state when removing nodes Stale IPs remain allocated; causes IP conflicts if address reused Run calicoctl ipam release or delete host-local state files during node decommission

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List CNI config files (sorted) ls -1 /etc/cni/net.d/ List CNI binaries ls /opt/cni/bin/ Check CNI logs (Calico) cat /var/log/calico/cni/cni.log Check CNI logs (kubelet) journalctl -u kubelet \| grep -i cni Show IPAM blocks (Calico) calicoctl ipam show --show-blocks Check specific IP ownership calicoctl ipam show --ip <ip> Check IPAM state files ls /var/lib/cni/networks/<name>/ List Multus NADs kubectl get network-attachment-definitions -A List whereabouts IP pools kubectl get ippools.whereabouts.cni.cncf.io Simulate CNI ADD manually CNI_COMMAND=ADD CNI_NETNS=... CNI_IFNAME=eth0 ... echo '{...}' \| /opt/cni/bin/<plugin> Check plugin supported versions CNI_COMMAND=VERSION /opt/cni/bin/<plugin> Check kernel modules for CNI lsmod \| grep -E "vxlan\|bridge\|8021q"

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail CNI binary location /opt/cni/bin/ CNI config location /etc/cni/net.d/ (first file alphabetically) Triggered by kubelet on pod ADD/DEL/CHECK Protocol Environment variables + stdin JSON config → stdout JSON result IPAM Subplugin handling IP allocation (host-local, calico-ipam, whereabouts, aws-vpc-cni) Chaining .conflist format runs plugins in sequence (main + bandwidth + portmap) Multus Meta-CNI for multiple interfaces per pod via NetworkAttachmentDefinition Debug CNI logs + manual binary execution with env vars

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What three environment variables does kubelet set when invoking a CNI plugin binary for the ADD operation, and what does each one convey to the plugin?
Answer The three most critical variables are: `CNI_COMMAND=ADD` (which operation to perform — ADD, DEL, or CHECK); `CNI_NETNS=/var/run/netns/cni-` (the path to the pre-created network namespace where the pod's interface should be configured); and `CNI_IFNAME=eth0` (the name to give the interface inside the namespace, always `eth0` for the primary pod interface). The plugin reads JSON configuration from stdin and writes the result JSON (including the assigned IP) to stdout.
  1. [Scenario question] A pod is stuck in ContainerCreating. The CNI plugin binary (/opt/cni/bin/calico) exists and is executable. journalctl -u kubelet shows a CNI error. What are the two most likely remaining causes, and how do you investigate each one?
Answer The two most likely causes are: (1) The IPAM pool is exhausted — no IP addresses remain to allocate. Check with `calicoctl ipam show --show-blocks` to see block utilization, or inspect `/var/lib/cni/networks//` for host-local IPAM. (2) There is a stale `eth0` interface already present in the target namespace from a failed previous attempt, causing the CNI to fail with "interface already exists." Inspect the namespace with `nsenter -t -n ip link` to see if `eth0` exists and manually delete it.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check which CNI configuration file will be used by kubelet on a Kubernetes node?
Answer 
ls -1 /etc/cni/net.d/
kubelet uses the first file alphabetically in `/etc/cni/net.d/`. The file with the lowest sort order (e.g., `10-calico.conflist`) wins. If multiple files exist from old CNI installations, the unexpected one may be active. Use `cat /etc/cni/net.d/` to confirm the plugin type and IPAM configuration.
