docs.title: Lesson 10 — eBPF and XDP in Kubernetes Networking
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud Prereqs: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification, Lesson 03 — iptables Time: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Attach an XDP program to drop traffic and inspect Cilium's TC eBPF programs with bpftool so you understand how eBPF replaces iptables for Kubernetes network policy and service load balancing.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — minikube node
minikube ssh
uname -r                          # kernel version (5.4+ needed, 5.10+ recommended)
bpftool version 2>/dev/null || echo "bpftool not installed"
mount | grep bpf                  # BPF filesystem must be mounted

# Terminal 2 — kubectl (Mac)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep cilium   # if using Cilium

See also: Lesson 03 — iptables for the legacy network stack that eBPF/Cilium replaces. Lesson 09 — CNI Specification for how the CNI ADD call loads eBPF programs onto new pod interfaces.

docs.title: 1. What eBPF Is
docs.text:
eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is a sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux kernel. You write programs in a restricted C-like language, compile them to eBPF bytecode, and attach them to kernel hook points. The kernel verifier checks programs for safety before loading.

flowchart LR
    subgraph userspace["User Space"]
        SRC[eBPF program<br/>C source]
        CLANG[clang -target bpf<br/>compile to bytecode]
        CTL[bpftool / libbpf<br/>load into kernel]
    end
    subgraph kernel["Kernel Space"]
        VER[Verifier<br/>safety checks]
        JIT[JIT compiler<br/>→ native machine code]
        subgraph hooks["Hook Points"]
            XDP[XDP<br/>NIC driver]
            TC[TC ingress/egress]
            SK[Socket layer]
            KP[kprobe / tracepoint]
            LSM[LSM hook]
        end
        MAPS[eBPF Maps<br/>kernel ↔ userspace<br/>shared state]
    end

    SRC --> CLANG --> CTL --> VER --> JIT --> hooks
    hooks <--> MAPS
    CTL <--> MAPS

docs.title: Hook Positions on the Linux Network Stack
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    APP[Application userspace<br/>write / read]
    SOCK[Socket layer<br/>BPF_PROG_TYPE_SK_SKB]
    PROTO[TCP / UDP / ICMP]
    ROUTE[IP routing]
    TC_IN[TC ingress<br/>BPF_PROG_TYPE_SCHED_CLS<br/>← Cilium policy / NAT]
    TC_EG[TC egress<br/>BPF_PROG_TYPE_SCHED_CLS<br/>← Cilium policy / NAT]
    XDP_H[XDP — eXpress Data Path<br/>BPF_PROG_TYPE_XDP<br/>← DDoS drop / L4 LB<br/>runs before sk_buff allocation]
    DRV[Network Driver / NIC]
    WIRE[Physical Wire]

    APP <--> SOCK <--> PROTO <--> ROUTE
    ROUTE --> TC_EG --> DRV
    DRV --> XDP_H --> TC_IN --> ROUTE
    DRV <--> WIRE
Hook Location Program Type Use in Kubernetes XDP NIC/driver receive path BPF_PROG_TYPE_XDP DDoS filter, L4 LB, fast packet drop TC ingress Before IP routing BPF_PROG_TYPE_SCHED_CLS Cilium network policy, service DNAT TC egress After IP routing BPF_PROG_TYPE_SCHED_CLS Cilium egress policy, source NAT Socket L4 socket layer BPF_PROG_TYPE_SK_SKB Cilium socket-level LB (bypass stack) kprobe/tracepoint Kernel function entry BPF_PROG_TYPE_KPROBE Tetragon security events, debugging LSM Linux Security Module BPF_PROG_TYPE_LSM Tetragon/Falco security enforcement

docs.title: 3. XDP — eXpress Data Path
docs.text:
XDP runs before the kernel allocates an sk_buff. Fastest possible hook.

// Simple XDP program: drop all ICMP
#include <linux/bpf.h>
#include <linux/if_ether.h>
#include <linux/ip.h>
#include <linux/icmp.h>
#include <bpf/bpf_helpers.h>

SEC("xdp")
int xdp_drop_icmp(struct xdp_md *ctx) {
    void *data = (void *)(long)ctx->data;
    void *data_end = (void *)(long)ctx->data_end;

    struct ethhdr *eth = data;
    if ((void *)(eth + 1) > data_end) return XDP_PASS;
    if (eth->h_proto != htons(ETH_P_IP)) return XDP_PASS;

    struct iphdr *ip = (void *)(eth + 1);
    if ((void *)(ip + 1) > data_end) return XDP_PASS;
    if (ip->protocol == IPPROTO_ICMP) return XDP_DROP;

    return XDP_PASS;
}

char LICENSE[] SEC("license") = "GPL";

# Compile with clang
clang -O2 -target bpf -c xdp_drop_icmp.c -o xdp_drop_icmp.o

# Attach to interface
ip link set dev eth0 xdp obj xdp_drop_icmp.o sec xdp

# Verify attachment
ip link show eth0 | grep xdp                     # → prog/xdp id <N> ...
bpftool net show dev eth0

# Test: ping from another node should now be dropped
ping -c3 <this-node-ip>                          # → 100% packet loss

# Detach
ip link set dev eth0 xdp off

docs.title: XDP Return Codes
docs.text: Return Code Numeric Action Performance XDP_DROP 1 Discard packet immediately Fastest — no sk_buff allocated XDP_PASS 2 Continue to normal network stack Normal path XDP_TX 3 Transmit packet back out same NIC Hardware loop XDP_REDIRECT 4 Redirect to another NIC or CPU Used for L4 LB XDP_ABORTED 0 Program error (like DROP + trace) Debugging only

docs.title: XDP Modes
docs.text: Mode Where it runs Requires Performance Native XDP NIC driver (before DMA) Driver support Highest (~25 Mpps) Generic XDP Software (after sk_buff alloc) Linux 4.12+ Lower; universal fallback Offloaded XDP SmartNIC hardware SmartNIC support Extreme (~100 Mpps)

docs.title: 4. TC Hook Programs
docs.text:
TC (Traffic Control) hooks run after sk_buff allocation, allowing full packet manipulation.

// TC egress: add a custom header
SEC("tc")
int tc_egress(struct __sk_buff *skb) {
    // Read packet data
    void *data = (void *)(long)skb->data;
    void *data_end = (void *)(long)skb->data_end;
    // ... packet manipulation
    return TC_ACT_OK;
}

# Attach TC eBPF program
tc qdisc add dev eth0 clsact
tc filter add dev eth0 egress bpf da obj tc_prog.o sec tc

# View TC filters
tc filter show dev eth0 egress
tc filter show dev eth0 ingress

# Cilium uses TC for all its per-pod programs
# View Cilium TC programs:
bpftool net show | grep cilium

# See programs on a specific pod interface
bpftool net show dev lxc1234abcd
TC Return Code Value Action TC_ACT_OK 0 Continue processing TC_ACT_SHOT 2 Drop packet TC_ACT_REDIRECT 7 Redirect to another interface TC_ACT_PIPE 3 Pass to next filter in chain

docs.title: 5. eBPF Maps
docs.text:
Maps are key-value stores shared between kernel eBPF programs and userspace.

// Define a map in eBPF program
struct {
    __uint(type, BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH);
    __uint(max_entries, 10000);
    __type(key, __u32);    // IP address
    __type(value, __u64);  // packet counter
} ip_counts SEC(".maps");

# List all eBPF maps
bpftool map list

# Inspect a map's contents
bpftool map dump id <map-id>

# Update a map entry
bpftool map update id <map-id> key hex 0a f4 00 06 value hex 00 01

# Cilium maps
cilium bpf map list
# Examples:
# cilium_lxc          — per-pod info (IP, MAC, endpoint ID)
# cilium_policy       — compiled policy rules
# cilium_lb4_services — service VIP → backend mapping
# cilium_ct_tcp4      — connection tracking
# cilium_nat          — NAT table

# View Cilium LB service map
cilium bpf lb list

docs.title: Common eBPF Map Types
docs.text: Map Type Lookup Use Case BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH O(1) hash IP/port lookup tables, conntrack BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY O(1) index Per-CPU stats, config flags BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH O(1) hash Conntrack with auto-eviction BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERF_EVENT_ARRAY n/a Stream events to userspace BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF n/a High-throughput event streaming BPF_MAP_TYPE_LPM_TRIE Longest prefix CIDR/routing lookups BPF_MAP_TYPE_PROG_ARRAY Index Tail calls (program chaining)

docs.title: 6. eBPF in Cilium — The Full Picture
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Wire as Physical Wire
    participant XDP as XDP hook
    participant TC_IN as TC ingress<br/>(cilium_netdev)
    participant RT as Kernel routing
    participant LXC_EG as TC egress<br/>(pod lxc interface)
    participant POD as Pod

    Wire->>XDP: Packet arrives on eth0
    XDP->>TC_IN: XDP_PASS (or drop DDoS)
    TC_IN->>TC_IN: Tail call: conntrack lookup
    TC_IN->>TC_IN: Tail call: service LB (DNAT VIP→pod)
    TC_IN->>TC_IN: Tail call: policy enforcement
    TC_IN->>RT: bpf_redirect / kernel route
    RT->>LXC_EG: forward to pod lxc interface
    LXC_EG->>LXC_EG: Egress policy check
    LXC_EG->>POD: deliver packet

    POD->>LXC_EG: Pod sends reply
    LXC_EG->>LXC_EG: Egress policy + SNAT
    LXC_EG->>RT: kernel route
    RT->>TC_IN: re-enter for encap/forward
    TC_IN->>Wire: out eth0
# View all Cilium eBPF programs loaded
bpftool prog list | grep -i cilium | wc -l
# Expect hundreds of programs on a node with many pods

# View program attached to a specific interface
bpftool net show dev lxc1234abcd

# Dump Cilium service table
cilium bpf lb list

# Dump conntrack table
cilium bpf ct list global

# View per-endpoint policy
cilium endpoint list
cilium endpoint get <id>

docs.title: 7. Tetragon — eBPF Security
docs.text:
Tetragon enforces security policies at the kernel level using LSM and kprobes.

# Install Tetragon
helm repo add cilium https://helm.cilium.io/
helm install tetragon cilium/tetragon \
  --namespace kube-system

# Watch all process executions
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact | grep exec

# Watch network connections
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact | grep connect

# TracingPolicy — alert on suspicious syscalls
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata:
  name: detect-exec
spec:
  kprobes:
    - call: "sys_execve"
      syscall: true
      args:
        - index: 0
          type: "string"
      selectors:
        - matchArgs:
            - index: 0
              operator: "Equal"
              values:
                - "/bin/bash"
                - "/bin/sh"
          matchActions:
            - action: Sigkill   # kill the process

# List all loaded programs

# Show program details (type, ID, name)
bpftool prog show id <id>

# Dump eBPF bytecode (before JIT)
bpftool prog dump xlated id <id>

# Dump JIT-compiled machine code

# Profile eBPF program performance

# View eBPF programs on network interfaces
bpftool net list

# Check all kernel BPF feature support

# Pin a program to BPF filesystem for persistence
bpftool prog pin id <id> /sys/fs/bpf/my_prog

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Kernel version 5.10 or higher on all nodes before deploying Cilium or XDP workloads
  • BPF filesystem mounted at /sys/fs/bpf and persisted across reboots (via /etc/fstab or systemd unit)
  • bpftool feature probe run on representative node to verify all required BPF map types are available
  • Cilium kube-proxy-replacement: strict enabled to fully disable kube-proxy iptables chains
  • eBPF map max_entries sized for peak concurrency (service count, connection count, pod count)
  • Tetragon TracingPolicies reviewed and tested in audit mode before enabling Sigkill actions
  • Node-level ulimit -l (locked memory) raised to accommodate all pinned eBPF maps

docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Run Cilium on kernel 4.x Missing LSM hooks, BTF, and map types; Cilium falls back to iptables silently Enforce minimum kernel 5.10 in node provisioning; check with uname -r Use XDP with virtual NICs (virtio, e1000) Generic XDP runs but software overhead negates performance benefit Use native XDP only on physical NICs with driver support; verify with bpftool net show Load eBPF programs without verifier bounds checks Kernel rejects program at load time with cryptic verifier error Always check data + sizeof(header) > data_end before dereferencing Mix Cilium and kube-proxy Duplicate NAT rules cause connection tracking conflicts Set --kube-proxy-replacement=strict and remove kube-proxy DaemonSet Ignore max_entries defaults Hash map silently drops entries when full (E2BIG returned to program) Instrument maps with perf counters; size to 2x peak concurrency

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is the difference between XDP and TC hook eBPF programs in terms of where they execute in the network stack, and why does Cilium use TC hooks rather than XDP for per-pod network policy enforcement?
Answer XDP runs at the NIC driver level before the kernel allocates an `sk_buff` structure — it is the earliest and fastest hook but only has access to raw packet bytes. TC (Traffic Control) hooks run after `sk_buff` allocation, giving full access to packet metadata, socket information, and the ability to redirect packets to other interfaces. Cilium uses TC hooks on each pod's `lxc` veth interface because policy enforcement requires matching packets by identity labels stored in BPF maps and redirecting accepted traffic — operations that need the richer context available at the TC layer. XDP is used by Cilium for DDoS mitigation and node-level L4 load balancing on the physical NIC.
  1. [Scenario question] After deploying Cilium with kubeProxyReplacement=strict, running cilium bpf lb list shows no service entries even though kubectl get svc shows many services. What is the most likely cause?
Answer The most likely cause is that the BPF filesystem is not mounted at `/sys/fs/bpf`. Cilium stores its BPF maps (including the service LB map `cilium_lb4_services`) on the BPF filesystem — if it is not mounted, maps cannot be pinned and service entries are lost. Verify with `mount | grep bpf`. A secondary cause is that kube-proxy is still running alongside Cilium, conflicting with the eBPF service maps. Check with `cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement` to confirm it shows `Strict`.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to list all eBPF programs currently loaded on a node and identify which ones belong to Cilium?
Answer 
bpftool prog list | grep cilium
Each entry shows the program ID, type (e.g., `sched_cls` for TC, `xdp`), and name. On a node with many pods, Cilium loads hundreds of programs — roughly two TC programs per pod interface (ingress and egress). You can also run `bpftool net list` to see programs attached to specific network interfaces.

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Control["Kubernetes Control Plane"]
        API[API Server]

    end

        KCC1[watches K8s objects\nupdates Calico CRDs]

docs.title: 2. Packet Flow: Pod-to-Pod Cross-Node
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PA as Pod A (node1\n10.244.0.5)
    participant VethA as cali<hash> veth\n(node1 host)
    participant Felix1 as Felix / iptables\n(node1)
    participant Net as Physical Network\n(BGP routes)
    participant Felix2 as Felix / iptables\n(node2)
    participant VethB as cali<hash> veth\n(node2 host)
    participant PB as Pod B (node2\n10.244.1.6)

    PA->>VethA: packet dst=10.244.1.6
    VethA->>Felix1: check cali-FORWARD policy
    Felix1->>Felix1: proxy_arp on veth → reply on behalf of gateway
    Felix1->>Net: route lookup → via node2 IP (BGP learned)
    Note over Net: IPIP/VXLAN encap if needed
    Net->>Felix2: decap + route to cali<hash>
    Felix2->>Felix2: check cali-FROM-ENDPOINT policy
    Felix2->>VethB: forward to pod veth
    VethB->>PB: packet delivered

docs.text:
Best performance. Requires L2 adjacency or BGP-capable switches.

docs.title: 4. Installation
docs.text:
# Install Calico via Tigera Operator (recommended)
kubectl create -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/tigera-operator.yaml

kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: operator.tigera.io/v1
kind: Installation
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  calicoNetwork:
    ipPools:
      - blockSize: 26
        cidr: 10.244.0.0/16
        encapsulation: VXLANCrossSubnet
        natOutgoing: Enabled
        nodeSelector: all()
EOF

# Verify operator is healthy
kubectl get tigerastatus

Felix is the per-node agent that programs the dataplane.

kubectl logs -n calico-system calico-node-xxxxx -c calico-node | grep felix

iptables -t nat -L cali-nat-outgoing -n -v      # masquerade rules

docs.text:
Calico divides each IPPool into /26 blocks (default) assigned per node.

# View IP pools
calicoctl get ippool -o wide
kubectl get ippool -o yaml

# View IPAM blocks (how the pool is divided per node)
calicoctl ipam show --show-blocks
# +----------+-------------------+----------+----------+

# +----------+-------------------+----------+----------+

# Which pod owns which IP?
calicoctl ipam show --ip 10.244.0.6

# Release a leaked IP (after pod deletion without cleanup)
calicoctl ipam release --ip=10.244.0.6

# View all allocations per node
calicoctl ipam show --show-borrowed

docs.text: Calico implements Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and also provides its own richer CRDs.

docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-allow-ingress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              role: frontend
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 80
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system

        - protocol: UDP

  name: default-deny-all

docs.text:
• Use Typha when cluster has 50+ nodes (spec.typhaDeployment.replicas >= 2)

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is Calico's default IPAM block size, and why does setting an overly large block size (e.g., /24) cause IP address starvation across a cluster with many small nodes?
Answer The default Calico IPAM block size is `/26`, which allocates 64 IP addresses per node. When a block is assigned to a node, all IPs in that block are reserved for that node — even if most are unused. With a `/24` block (256 IPs), a cluster where nodes run only 10–20 pods would waste 230+ IPs per node. A 100-node cluster with `/24` blocks needs a `/8` IP pool (16 million IPs) to avoid exhaustion. Using `/26` or `/27` blocks matched to the actual pods-per-node limit prevents IP starvation and allows more efficient pool utilization.
  1. [Scenario question] New pods cannot get IP addresses even though calicoctl ipam show --show-blocks shows blocks with available IPs. After investigation, you find that some IPs are allocated but have no corresponding running pods. How do you identify and release these leaked IPs?
Answer Run `calicoctl ipam show --ip ` for a suspected leaked IP — if it shows an allocation but the pod name no longer exists in Kubernetes, the IP has leaked. This happens when CNI DEL fails during pod deletion. Release the leaked IP with `calicoctl ipam release --ip=`. For bulk investigation, compare the allocated IPs in IPAM blocks against running pod IPs from `kubectl get pods -A -o wide`, or use `calicoctl ipam check` to automatically detect and optionally clean orphaned allocations.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check the IPAM block allocation across all nodes in a Calico cluster and see how many IPs are used versus free per block?
Answer 
calicoctl ipam show --show-blocks
The output table shows each CIDR block, which node it is assigned to, the number of IPs used, and the number free. A block showing `IPS USED: 64, IPS FREE: 0` on a node is fully exhausted — new pods on that node will fail to get an IP until a new block is allocated or existing IPs are released.

docs.title: Lesson 12 — Cilium CNI and eBPF Dataplane
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Lesson 10 — eBPF and XDP, Lesson 09 — CNI Specification · Time: ~3 hours

Goal: Deploy Cilium with kube-proxy replacement, write L7 CiliumNetworkPolicy, and use Hubble to observe and debug live traffic flows.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — minikube Linux node
minikube ssh
sudo bpftool prog list | grep -i cil | head -10
ip link show | grep -E "cilium|lxc"

# Terminal 2 — Mac (kubectl + cilium CLI)
cilium status 2>/dev/null || echo "cilium CLI not installed: brew install cilium-cli"
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "cilium|hubble"
hubble observe --last 10 2>/dev/null || echo "hubble not running"

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph CP["Kubernetes Control Plane"]
        API[API Server]
    end
    subgraph OP["cilium-operator\n1-2 replicas"]
        O1[IPAM\nCiliumNode mgmt\nCluster Mesh]
    end
    subgraph Agent["cilium-agent DaemonSet (every node)"]
        BPF[eBPF program loader]
        IDM[Identity management]
        IPAM[IPAM]
        KPR[kube-proxy replacement\neBPF service LB]
        HUB[Hubble server\nflow data export]
    end
    subgraph Envoy["Envoy (L7 policy)"]
        E1[HTTP / gRPC\npolicy enforcement]
    end
    API --> O1
    O1 --> BPF
    BPF --> eBPFmaps[(eBPF Maps\ncilium_lxc\ncilium_policy\ncilium_lb4_services)]
    Agent --> Envoy
    HUB --> HubbleRelay[Hubble Relay\nHubble UI]

See also: Lesson 10 — eBPF and XDP for eBPF program types and BPF map internals referenced throughout this lesson.

docs.title: 2. Identity-Based Policy (vs IP-based)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Traditional["Traditional: IP-based iptables"]
        PA1[Pod A\n10.0.0.5] -->|rule: allow 10.0.0.5/32| PB1[Pod B]
        note1["Problem: IP changes on reschedule"]
    end
    subgraph Cilium["Cilium: Identity-based eBPF"]
        PA2[Pod A\napp=frontend\nidentity: 1234] -->|TC egress stamps id=1234| TC1[TC egress\nBPF prog]
        TC1 -->|VXLAN/Geneve\nencap with identity| TC2[TC ingress\nBPF prog]
        TC2 -->|check id=1234 in policy map| PB2[Pod B\napp=backend]
    end

Cilium assigns a numeric identity to every pod based on its labels. Policy is enforced per identity, not per IP — policy survives pod restarts.

# View endpoint identities
cilium endpoint list
# ENDPOINT  POLICY (ingress)  POLICY (egress)  IDENTITY  LABELS
# 1234      Enabled           Enabled          12345     app=web,env=prod

# View all identities in the cluster
cilium identity list

# What is identity 12345?
cilium identity get 12345

docs.title: 3. eBPF Hook Points
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    NIC[NIC receive] -->|earliest hook| XDP[XDP\nDDoS / LB offload]
    XDP --> TCI[TC ingress\nbefore routing decision]
    TCI --> Route[Kernel routing]
    Route --> TCE[TC egress\nafter routing, before NIC transmit]
    TCE --> NIC2[NIC transmit]
    Route --> SOCK[Socket layer\nL4 bypass for local traffic]
# View eBPF programs loaded by Cilium
bpftool prog list | grep cilium
cilium bpf prog list

# View eBPF maps (key-value stores shared between kernel and userspace)
cilium bpf map list
# Examples:
#   cilium_lxc          — per-pod identity and endpoint info
#   cilium_policy       — compiled policy rules
#   cilium_ct_tcp4      — connection tracking table
#   cilium_lb4_services — service load balancing table
#   cilium_nat          — NAT table

# View service LB rules in eBPF (kube-proxy replacement)
cilium service list
cilium bpf lb list

docs.title: 4. Installation
docs.text:
# Install Cilium with Helm
helm repo add cilium https://helm.cilium.io/
helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=strict \
  --set k8sServiceHost=<API_SERVER_IP> \
  --set k8sServicePort=6443 \
  --set hubble.relay.enabled=true \
  --set hubble.ui.enabled=true

# Verify installation
cilium status --wait
cilium connectivity test   # end-to-end network tests (~5 min)

docs.title: Key Helm Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change kubeProxyReplacement disabled eBPF service LB mode Set strict to fully replace kube-proxy tunnel vxlan Overlay protocol Set disabled for native routing (needs BGP or same L2) autoDirectNodeRoutes false Auto-add routes for same-L2 nodes Enable with tunnel=disabled on bare metal hubble.relay.enabled false Cross-node flow aggregation Enable for multi-node Hubble visibility encryption.enabled false WireGuard node-to-node encryption Enable for untrusted networks loadBalancer.acceleration disabled XDP-level service LB Set native on supported NICs for best performance bpf.masquerade false eBPF-based masquerade (replaces iptables MASQ) Enable when kube-proxy is fully replaced

docs.title: Tunnel (default — works everywhere)
docs.text:
# VXLAN tunnel (default)
cilium config view | grep tunnel
# tunnel-protocol: vxlan

# Switch to Geneve
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --reuse-values \
  --set tunnel=geneve

docs.title: Native Routing (bare metal, cloud with routing support)
docs.text:
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --reuse-values \
  --set tunnel=disabled \
  --set autoDirectNodeRoutes=true \
  --set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.244.0.0/16

docs.title: WireGuard Transparent Encryption
docs.text:
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --reuse-values \
  --set encryption.enabled=true \
  --set encryption.type=wireguard

cilium encrypt status

docs.title: 6. CiliumNetworkPolicy (L3/L4/L7)
docs.text:
# More expressive than standard NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-policy
  namespace: default
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  ingress:
    - fromEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            app: frontend
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "80"
              protocol: TCP
          rules:
            http:
              - method: "GET"
                path: "/api/.*"    # L7 HTTP rule (Envoy enforces)
  egress:
    - toFQDNs:
        - matchName: "api.example.com"   # FQDN-based policy
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "443"
              protocol: TCP

# CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (global, all namespaces)
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}   # all pods
  ingress:
    - fromEntities:
        - cluster         # allow intra-cluster
  egress:
    - toEntities:
        - cluster
    - toFQDNs:
        - matchPattern: "*.amazonaws.com"

docs.title: 7. kube-proxy Replacement
docs.text:
Cilium implements Service load-balancing entirely in eBPF — no iptables, no kube-proxy process needed.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Pod / External client
    participant SK as Socket layer\n(BPF sock_ops)
    participant LB as cilium_lb4_services\neBPF map
    participant EP as Backend Pod

    P->>SK: connect to ClusterIP 10.96.0.10:80
    SK->>LB: lookup service → list of backends
    LB-->>SK: backend: 10.244.1.5:8080 (hash-selected)
    SK->>EP: direct socket to backend (no DNAT overhead)
    EP-->>P: response via conntrack
# Check if kube-proxy replacement is active
cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement
# KubeProxyReplacement: Strict

# View services handled by eBPF LB
cilium service list
# ID   Frontend               Service Type   Backend
# 1    10.96.0.1:443/TCP      ClusterIP      192.168.1.10:6443/TCP

# View backend set for a service
cilium bpf lb list | grep 10.96.0.1

# View NAT table (replaces conntrack for intra-cluster traffic)
cilium bpf nat list

docs.title: 8. Hubble — eBPF-Powered Observability
docs.text:
Hubble provides real-time flow visibility at the kernel level using eBPF ring buffers.

# Enable port-forward to Hubble relay
cilium hubble port-forward &

# Observe all flows in the cluster
hubble observe

# Filter by pod pair
hubble observe --from-pod default/frontend --to-pod default/backend

# Filter by policy verdict (dropped packets)
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED

# Filter by HTTP status
hubble observe --protocol http --http-status 500

# Output as JSON for processing
hubble observe -o json | jq '.flow | {src: .source.pod_name, dst: .destination.pod_name, verdict: .verdict}'

# Open Hubble UI
cilium hubble ui

docs.title: 9. Cluster Mesh
docs.text:
Connect multiple Kubernetes clusters so pods can communicate cross-cluster.

# Enable cluster mesh on cluster A
cilium clustermesh enable --service-type LoadBalancer
cilium clustermesh status

# Connect cluster A to cluster B
cilium clustermesh connect --context cluster-b

# Share a service across clusters
kubectl annotate svc my-service \
  service.cilium.io/global=true \
  service.cilium.io/shared=true

docs.title: 10. Cilium on Cloud Providers
docs.text:
# EKS — Cilium as CNI (replace aws-vpc-cni)
eksctl create cluster --config-file - <<EOF
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: cilium-cluster
  region: us-east-1
addons:
  - name: vpc-cni
    # don't install — Cilium replaces it
EOF

# GKE — Dataplane v2 uses Cilium automatically
gcloud container clusters create ... \
  --dataplane-v2

# AKS — Cilium option
az aks create \
  --network-plugin azure \
  --network-plugin-mode overlay \
  --network-dataplane cilium

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix cilium status shows agents not ready Kernel version <4.9 or missing BPF filesystem cilium version; uname -r Upgrade kernel to 5.4+; mount bpffs: mount bpffs /sys/fs/bpf -t bpf Policy not enforced — traffic passes that should be dropped Policy not compiled or identity mismatch cilium policy trace --src-pod ns/pod-a --dst-pod ns/pod-b --dport 80 Check endpoint selector label matches; re-apply policy Services not reachable after enabling kube-proxy replacement kube-proxy still running and conflicting cilium status \| grep KubeProxyReplacement Remove kube-proxy DaemonSet; ensure kubeProxyReplacement=strict hubble observe shows no flows Hubble relay not enabled cilium status \| grep Hubble Upgrade Cilium with hubble.relay.enabled=true Intermittent connection drops between pods conntrack table exhausted cilium metrics \| grep drop; cilium bpf ct list global \| wc -l Increase bpf-ct-global-tcp-max in Helm values L7 HTTP policy not blocking requests Envoy sidecar not injected kubectl logs cilium-pod -c cilium-envoy Check Envoy port 9090 is listening; verify CiliumNetworkPolicy has http rules XDP acceleration not working NIC driver not XDP-compatible cilium status \| grep XDP Use loadBalancer.acceleration=disabled or upgrade NIC drivers

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Run cilium connectivity test after every Cilium upgrade before returning to production
  • Set kubeProxyReplacement=strict and remove kube-proxy DaemonSet when enabling eBPF service LB
  • Enable Hubble relay (hubble.relay.enabled=true) so flows are visible across all nodes
  • Size the eBPF CT table for expected connection count (bpf-ct-global-tcp-max: default 512Ki)
  • Tune bpf.masquerade=true to move masquerade off iptables once kube-proxy is replaced
  • Deploy Tetragon alongside Cilium for runtime security audit of syscalls and file access
  • Use CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy default-deny with fromEntities: cluster before cluster goes to production

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Run kube-proxy alongside kubeProxyReplacement=strict Both programs service VIPs; iptables rules conflict with eBPF maps causing intermittent drops Remove kube-proxy DaemonSet completely when using strict replacement Write standard NetworkPolicy and CiliumNetworkPolicy for the same pods Both apply additively; unexpected intersections can over-restrict or leave gaps Migrate entirely to CiliumNetworkPolicy; use standard only when CNI portability is needed Use FQDN policy without DNS proxy enabled FQDN rules require Cilium's DNS proxy to intercept responses; without it rules never fire Ensure --enable-dns-proxy=true (default); verify with cilium config view \| grep dns-proxy Enable cluster mesh without unique cluster names/IDs Identity collisions across clusters cause policy bypasses Set unique cluster.name and cluster.id in Helm values before connecting clusters Leave hubble.retention at default on high-traffic cluster Hubble ring buffer fills; oldest flows are dropped before they can be inspected Tune hubble.eventBufferCapacity based on cluster throughput

docs.text: Use Case Command Overall Cilium health cilium status Run connectivity tests cilium connectivity test List pod endpoints with identities cilium endpoint list Trace policy between two pods cilium policy trace --src-pod ns/pod-a --dst-pod ns/pod-b --dport 80 Observe live flows hubble observe Observe dropped flows only hubble observe --verdict DROPPED List eBPF service LB rules cilium service list List eBPF backend map cilium bpf lb list List loaded eBPF programs bpftool prog list \| grep cilium Check WireGuard encryption status cilium encrypt status Get endpoint details cilium endpoint get <endpoint-id> View identity for a label set cilium identity list

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Feature Cilium Mechanism Pod networking eBPF programs at TC hook on each veth kube-proxy replacement eBPF service map + socket-level LB NetworkPolicy Identity-based eBPF programs (no IP dependency) L7 policy (HTTP/gRPC) Envoy sidecar managed by Cilium agent Observability Hubble (eBPF ring buffers → Hubble relay → UI) Encryption WireGuard or IPsec transparent node-to-node Multi-cluster Cilium Cluster Mesh (shared service discovery) Runtime security Tetragon (syscall-level eBPF audit)

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] How does Cilium's identity-based network policy differ from traditional IP-based iptables rules, and why does this make policy more resilient to pod restarts and rescheduling?
Answer Traditional IP-based iptables rules encode specific pod IP addresses — when a pod restarts or is rescheduled to a new node, it gets a new IP, and every rule referencing the old IP must be updated. Cilium assigns a numeric identity to each pod based on its Kubernetes labels (e.g., `app=frontend` → identity `1234`) and encodes that identity in the packet header during encapsulation. Policy enforcement compares identities, not IPs — so when a pod restarts with a new IP but the same labels, the same identity is assigned and all existing policies continue to apply without any rule updates.
  1. [Scenario question] You deploy a CiliumNetworkPolicy to block traffic from a pod labeled app=attacker to a pod labeled app=web, but traffic still flows through. cilium endpoint list shows both pods with correct labels. What is the first thing you should check?
Answer Run `cilium policy trace --src-pod /attacker --dst-pod /web --dport 80` to simulate the policy decision. This shows whether the policy is compiled, which identity labels are being matched, and what the final verdict is. If the trace shows `allow`, the policy selector may not be matching the endpoint labels (check for label key/value typos or namespace scope issues). If `cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement` shows kube-proxy is still active, conflicting iptables rules could be allowing traffic that Cilium's eBPF programs block.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to observe all dropped network flows in real time using Hubble?
Answer 
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED
Each line shows the source pod, destination pod, destination port, and the policy that caused the drop. This is the most efficient way to debug NetworkPolicy issues in Cilium — it pinpoints exactly which flows are being blocked and by which policy, without requiring packet captures or guesswork about selector matching.

docs.title: Lesson 13 — Kubernetes Services and kube-proxy
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Lesson 03 — iptables, Lesson 02 — IP Routing · Time: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Trace a ClusterIP packet through iptables DNAT chains, choose between iptables and IPVS modes, and diagnose service connectivity failures at the packet level.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — minikube Linux node
minikube ssh
sudo iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES | head -20
sudo iptables -t nat -L KUBE-NODEPORTS 2>/dev/null | head -10
ipvsadm -Ln 2>/dev/null | head -20  # if IPVS mode

# Terminal 2 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get svc -A
kubectl get endpointslices -A | head -10
kubectl get cm -n kube-system kube-proxy -o yaml | grep mode

docs.title: 1. The Service Problem
docs.text:
Pods have ephemeral IPs that change on restart. Services provide a stable virtual IP (VIP) that: - Never changes while the service exists - Automatically load-balances across healthy pod replicas - Is discoverable via DNS

flowchart LR
    subgraph Clients
        PA[Pod A\n10.244.1.5]
        EXT[External client]
    end
    subgraph SVC["Service (ClusterIP 10.96.42.10:80)"]
        KP[kube-proxy\nprograms iptables / IPVS]
    end
    subgraph Backends
        P1[Pod replica 1\n10.244.0.5:8080]
        P2[Pod replica 2\n10.244.1.3:8080]
        P3[Pod replica 3\n10.244.2.1:8080]
    end
    PA -->|dst: 10.96.42.10:80| KP
    KP -->|DNAT round-robin| P1
    KP --> P2
    KP --> P3
    EXT -->|NodePort :30080| KP

See also: Lesson 14 — CoreDNS for how the service name resolves to 10.96.42.10.

docs.title: ClusterIP (default)
docs.text:
Virtual IP reachable only from within the cluster. 

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

docs.title: NodePort
docs.text:
Exposes the service on a static port on every node's IP (range 30000–32767). 

spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
      nodePort: 30080

curl http://<any-node-ip>:30080

docs.title: LoadBalancer
docs.text:
Provisions an external load balancer (cloud LB or MetalLB on bare metal). 

spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

docs.title: ExternalName
docs.text:
DNS CNAME alias to an external hostname (no kube-proxy rules involved). 

spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: api.example.com

docs.title: Headless Service
docs.text:
No ClusterIP — DNS returns individual pod IPs directly. 

spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: db

# DNS returns all pod IPs directly (used by StatefulSets)
kubectl exec -it test -- nslookup db.default.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.244.0.5   ← pod IPs directly
# Address: 10.244.1.3

docs.title: Service Type Comparison
docs.text: Type Reachable From IP Assigned Use Case ClusterIP Inside cluster Service CIDR Internal microservice communication NodePort Outside (via node IP) Service CIDR + node port Dev/test, bare metal without LB LoadBalancer Outside (via LB IP) External IP from cloud/MetalLB Production external traffic ExternalName Inside cluster DNS CNAME (no IP) External service aliasing Headless Inside cluster (pod IPs) None StatefulSets, client-side LB

docs.title: 3. Endpoints and EndpointSlices
docs.text:
The Service controller watches pods matching the selector and creates EndpointSlices.

# View legacy Endpoints (still present)
kubectl get endpoints web
# NAME   ENDPOINTS                       AGE
# web    10.244.0.5:8080,10.244.1.3:8080  5m

# Modern: EndpointSlices (default since K8s 1.21, 100 endpoints/slice)
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
kubectl get endpointslice web-xxxxx -o yaml

# Check if endpoints are populated (empty = no matching pods)
kubectl describe endpoints web

EndpointSlices cap at 100 endpoints per slice. At scale this dramatically reduces the iptables/IPVS update payload compared to a single large Endpoints object.

docs.title: 4. kube-proxy: iptables Mode
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    PKT[Pod packet\ndst=10.96.42.10:80] --> PREROUTING[PREROUTING / OUTPUT\nnat table]
    PREROUTING --> KS[KUBE-SERVICES chain]
    KS -->|match 10.96.42.10:80| KSVC[KUBE-SVC-XXXXHASH\nload balance chain]
    KSVC -->|33% random| SEP1[KUBE-SEP-AAA\nDNAT → 10.244.0.5:8080]
    KSVC -->|33% random| SEP2[KUBE-SEP-BBB\nDNAT → 10.244.1.3:8080]
    KSVC -->|33% remaining| SEP3[KUBE-SEP-CCC\nDNAT → 10.244.2.1:8080]
    SEP1 --> ROUTE[Route to destination node]
    SEP2 --> ROUTE
    SEP3 --> ROUTE
    ROUTE --> POST[POSTROUTING MASQUERADE\nfor cross-node traffic]
# View kube-proxy mode
kubectl get cm -n kube-system kube-proxy -o yaml | grep mode

# Trace the iptables chain for a service (10.96.42.10:80)
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep 10.96.42.10
# KUBE-SVC-XXXX  tcp  10.96.42.10:80

# Service chain (round-robin via probabilistic match)
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SVC-XXXX -n
# KUBE-SEP-AAAA  all  --  statistic mode random probability 0.50000000000
# KUBE-SEP-BBBB  all  --  (second endpoint)

# Endpoint chain (DNAT)
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SEP-AAAA -n
# DNAT  tcp  --  to:10.244.0.5:8080

docs.title: 5. kube-proxy: IPVS Mode
docs.text:
IPVS is a kernel load balancer — O(1) hash lookup vs O(N) iptables rule scan.

# Enable IPVS mode
kubectl edit cm -n kube-system kube-proxy
# mode: "ipvs"
# ipvs:
#   scheduler: "rr"  # rr=round-robin, lc=least-conn, dh, sh, lblc

# View IPVS rules
ipvsadm -L -n
# TCP  10.96.42.10:80 rr
#   -> 10.244.0.5:8080           Masq    1      0          0
#   -> 10.244.1.3:8080           Masq    1      0          0

# IPVS uses a dummy interface (kube-ipvs0) to hold all ClusterIPs
ip addr show kube-ipvs0

docs.title: Mode Comparison
docs.text: Aspect iptables IPVS Lookup complexity O(N) — linear chain scan O(1) — kernel hash table Scheduling options Random, probabilistic rr, lc, dh, sh, lblc, lblcr Connection tracking Linux conntrack Linux conntrack Health checking None (relies on endpoints) None (relies on endpoints) Best for <1000 services >1000 services / high throughput

docs.title: 6. External Traffic Policy
docs.text:
Controls SNAT behavior and node-local routing for external (NodePort/LoadBalancer) traffic.

spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local    # or Cluster (default)

Cluster (default): - Traffic forwarded to pods on any node - Source IP replaced with node IP (SNAT) - Load balances evenly across all pods

Local: - Traffic only goes to pods on the node receiving the packet - Source IP is preserved (no SNAT) — critical for logging real client IPs - Load balancer must health-check each node; nodes without pods return unhealthy

# Check which nodes have local endpoints
kubectl get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web -o yaml | \
  grep -A5 "nodeName"

docs.title: 7. Service Topology and Traffic Distribution
docs.text:
# Prefer same-zone backends (K8s 1.27+)
spec:
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose

# Spread pods evenly across zones (reduce cross-zone traffic cost)
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: web

docs.title: 8. Session Affinity
docs.text:
Stick sessions to the same pod (useful for stateful apps).

spec:
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 3600

iptables implementation uses the --recent module to track source IPs and always DNAT to the same endpoint within the timeout window.

docs.title: 9. EndpointSlice Conditions and Graceful Drain
docs.text:
EndpointSlices carry per-endpoint health conditions that kube-proxy uses to handle pod termination gracefully.

# View EndpointSlice conditions
kubectl get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web -o yaml | \
  grep -A5 "conditions"
# conditions:
#   ready: true
#   serving: true
#   terminating: false

# A pod that is terminating has:
#   ready=false, serving=true, terminating=true
# kube-proxy keeps it in the LB table until ready=false AND serving=false
# This allows in-flight connections to drain before the pod is removed.
Condition ready serving terminating kube-proxy behavior Healthy pod true true false Included in load balancing Terminating pod false true true Kept for in-flight connections; excluded from new connections Failed pod false false false Removed from load balancing immediately

docs.title: 10. Services on Bare Metal vs Cloud
Bare Metal
docs.text:
• ClusterIP and NodePort work identically
  • LoadBalancer needs MetalLB or kube-vip
  • Use BGP mode MetalLB to advertise VIPs to upstream router

  networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal"

  service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-load-balancer-internal: "true"

docs.title: Troubleshooting

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Switch to IPVS mode for clusters with >1000 services or high churn
  • Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local on ingress-facing services to preserve client IPs for access logs
  • Use trafficDistribution: PreferClose to minimize cross-AZ bandwidth costs (K8s 1.27+)
  • Ensure NodePort range (30000-32767) is opened in node security groups / firewall rules
  • Monitor EndpointSlice count per service; alert if any service has 0 endpoints
  • Use headless services for StatefulSet pods so individual pod DNS names are resolvable
  • Annotate LoadBalancer services with cloud-specific annotations before deploying (NLB vs ALB, internal vs external)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Point Service selector at pods by name instead of labels Selectors only support label matching, not pod names Use consistent labels (app: web) on pods and match in Service selector Use NodePort in production without a frontend LB Direct NodePort exposure means client hits a specific node; if that node fails, client must try another IP Put a cloud LB or MetalLB in front of NodePorts; use LoadBalancer type instead Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local without health checks LB routes to all nodes equally; nodes with no pods silently drop packets Configure LB to use Kubernetes health check endpoint (kube-proxy health port 10256) clusterIP: None on a service that apps expect to get a stable IP Headless DNS returns pod IPs directly; each app connection may land on a different pod Only use headless for StatefulSets or client-side LB scenarios; use ClusterIP for normal services Ignore EndpointSlice max (100 endpoints/slice) in architecture Services with >100 pods silently cap if old Endpoints API is used Confirm EndpointSlice is used (kubectl get endpointslices); avoid code that reads only the Endpoints object

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] How does kube-proxy implement probabilistic load balancing across multiple endpoints for a ClusterIP service using iptables, and what chain structure does it use?
Answer kube-proxy creates a three-level chain structure: `KUBE-SERVICES` matches the destination ClusterIP and port, jumping to a per-service `KUBE-SVC-` chain. Inside that chain, each endpoint gets a `KUBE-SEP-` rule with a probabilistic `statistic mode random probability` match — the first endpoint gets `0.33`, the second gets `0.5` (of remaining), and the last gets `1.0` (all remaining traffic). Each `KUBE-SEP-` chain contains the actual `DNAT` rule rewriting the destination to the pod's IP and port (e.g., `DNAT tcp to 10.244.0.5:8080`).
  1. [Scenario question] A ClusterIP service with two healthy endpoints is unreachable from pods on one specific node, but works fine from pods on all other nodes. kubectl get endpoints shows both pod IPs. What is the first thing you should check on the failing node?
Answer Check whether the kube-proxy iptables rules exist on that specific node with `iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep `. If the KUBE-SERVICES chain is missing entries for the service, kube-proxy on that node may have failed to sync. Check `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy` for the node's kube-proxy pod status, and inspect its logs with `kubectl logs -n kube-system ` for sync errors. Also verify that `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1` is set on the failing node.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to find all iptables rules associated with a specific ClusterIP service (e.g., 10.96.42.10) and see the DNAT targets for its endpoints?
Answer 
iptables -t nat -S | grep 10.96.42.10
This shows the `KUBE-SVC-` chain name. Then run `iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SVC- -n` to see the per-endpoint probabilistic rules, and `iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SEP- -n` for each endpoint chain to confirm the DNAT target IP and port.

docs.title: Lesson 14 — CoreDNS and Service Discovery
docs.text:
Track: Kubernetes Networking · Prereqs: Lesson 13 — Services · Time: ~1h

Goal: Debug ndots:5 latency, tune CoreDNS for your cluster, and deploy NodeLocal DNSCache.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get cm -n kube-system coredns -o yaml
kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns

# Terminal 2 — debug pod
kubectl run dns-test --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it --restart=Never -- \
  sh -c "nslookup kubernetes && cat /etc/resolv.conf"

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
graph LR
    P[Pod
/etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.96.0.10] -->|UDP 53| NLD[NodeLocal DNSCache
169.254.20.10
per-node DaemonSet]
    NLD -->|cache miss| CD[CoreDNS

kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns   # CoreDNS pods
kubectl get svc  -n kube-system kube-dns               # ClusterIP 10.96.0.10

DNS name formats:

Type Format Example Service <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local web.default.svc.cluster.local StatefulSet pod <pod>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local db-0.db.default.svc.cluster.local Headless SVC Same — returns pod IP directly returns 10.244.1.5

docs.title: 2. The ndots:5 Latency Trap
docs.text:
Default /etc/resolv.conf in every pod: 

nameserver 10.96.0.10
search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5

Any hostname with fewer than 5 dots triggers search-domain expansion before the absolute lookup. External names waste 3 round trips (~90–300 ms):

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Pod
    participant C as CoreDNS
    Note over P,C: Internal — resolves on first try ✓
    P->>C: my-svc.default.svc.cluster.local?
    C-->>P: 10.96.0.42 ✓

    Note over P,C: External (api.example.com, 3 dots) — 4 queries!
    P->>C: api.example.com.default.svc.cluster.local?
    C-->>P: NXDOMAIN (+~30ms)
    P->>C: api.example.com.svc.cluster.local?
    C-->>P: NXDOMAIN (+~30ms)
    P->>C: api.example.com.cluster.local?
    C-->>P: NXDOMAIN (+~30ms)
    P->>C: api.example.com.?
    C-->>P: 203.0.113.1 ✓ (300ms wasted)

Fix: Lower ndots per pod or use FQDNs (trailing dot: api.example.com.).

# Per-pod dnsConfig
spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
      - name: ndots
        value: "1"

docs.title: 3. Corefile — Key Directives
docs.text:
kubectl get cm -n kube-system coredns -o yaml   # view current config
kubectl edit cm -n kube-system coredns           # edit (auto-reloads)
Directive What it does kubernetes cluster.local Answers *.cluster.local from K8s API forward . /etc/resolv.conf Sends external queries to node's upstream DNS cache 30 Caches positive responses for 30 s health / ready /health :8080 and /ready :8181 probes prometheus :9153 Metrics endpoint autopath @kubernetes Collapses search-list lookups into one query negative_ttl 5 Caches NXDOMAIN for 5 s (reduces repeat failures)

docs.title: Key Corefile Parameter Reference
4. NodeLocal DNSCache
docs.text:
Runs as a DaemonSet on 169.254.20.10 (link-local). Pods hit the local node cache instead of a ClusterIP — no conntrack overhead, ~10× lower p99 latency for cached queries.

# Deploy (official manifest)
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/master/cluster/addons/dns/nodelocaldns/nodelocaldns.yaml

# Verify — one pod per node
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=node-local-dns -o wide

# Confirm pod resolv.conf points to it
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 169.254.20.10

# Check NodeLocal DNSCache metrics
kubectl exec -n kube-system node-local-dns-xxxxx -- \
  curl -s http://169.254.20.10:9253/metrics | grep coredns_cache_hits_total

Cloud note: AWS EKS uses 169.254.20.10 with aws-k8s-cni automatically. GKE runs NodeLocal by default since 1.15. For bare metal, forward to your on-prem resolver: forward . <corp-dns-ip>.

docs.title: 5. Observing CoreDNS Live
docs.text:
# Enable query logging temporarily (adds "log" directive to Corefile)
kubectl edit cm -n kube-system coredns
# add "log" inside the .:53 block, then save

# Watch query logs in real time
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -f

# Count queries per second
kubectl exec -n kube-system coredns-xxxxx -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:9153/metrics | grep coredns_dns_requests_total

# Measure latency histogram
kubectl exec -n kube-system coredns-xxxxx -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:9153/metrics | grep coredns_dns_request_duration

# Verify autopath collapses search expansion
kubectl run -it --rm d --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  sh -c "time nslookup github.com"
# With ndots:5 — slow (~300ms)
# After ndots:1 — fast (<10ms)

docs.title: 6. Pod DNS Policy Options
docs.text:
The dnsPolicy field on a pod spec controls how /etc/resolv.conf is constructed.

dnsPolicy Behavior Use Case ClusterFirst (default) Cluster DNS first; unresolved queries forwarded upstream Standard — use for all workloads needing service discovery ClusterFirstWithHostNet Same as ClusterFirst, but for pods using hostNetwork: true Host-network pods that still need cluster DNS Default Inherits the node's /etc/resolv.conf directly Pods that must use the same DNS as the node None No DNS config at all; must supply dnsConfig manually Air-gapped, custom resolvers, or specific testing scenarios 
# Custom DNS config example (dnsPolicy: None)
spec:
  dnsPolicy: "None"
  dnsConfig:
    nameservers:
      - 10.100.0.53          # corporate DNS
    searches:
      - corp.internal
      - default.svc.cluster.local
      - svc.cluster.local
      - cluster.local
    options:
      - name: ndots
        value: "2"

docs.title: 7. Complete Production Corefile
docs.text:
.:53 {
    errors
    health {
       lameduck 5s
    }
    ready
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
       pods insecure
       fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
       ttl 30
    }
    prometheus :9153
    forward . /etc/resolv.conf {
       max_concurrent 1000
    }
    cache 300 {
       denial 30
    }
    loop
    reload
    loadbalance
}

# Stub zone for corporate domain
corp.internal:53 {
    errors
    cache 30
    forward . 10.100.0.53 10.100.0.54
}

Key additions over the default: - cache 300 — 300 s TTL for external names (reduces upstream load) - denial 30 — caches NXDOMAIN for 30 s (stops bad-hostname storms) - max_concurrent 1000 — caps upstream inflight queries; prevents amplification - loop — detects forwarding loops (always include) - loadbalance — randomizes A record order for simple client-side LB

docs.title: 8. CoreDNS Scaling and High Availability
docs.text:
CoreDNS is a Deployment, not a DaemonSet — it has a fixed replica count.

# Check current replica count
kubectl get deploy -n kube-system coredns
# NAME      READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
# coredns   2/2     2            2           30d

# Scale up for large clusters
kubectl scale deploy -n kube-system coredns --replicas=4

# Spread replicas across nodes (prevent both on same node)
kubectl patch deploy -n kube-system coredns --type=merge -p '{
  "spec": {
    "template": {
      "spec": {
        "affinity": {
          "podAntiAffinity": {
            "requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution": [{
              "labelSelector": {"matchLabels": {"k8s-app": "kube-dns"}},
              "topologyKey": "kubernetes.io/hostname"
            }]
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}'

docs.text: Cluster size Replicas Memory limit CPU request <100 nodes 2 170 MiB 100m 100–500 nodes 4 256 MiB 200m 500–1000 nodes 6 512 MiB 500m >1000 nodes NodeLocal DNSCache + 8+ replicas 512 MiB each 500m

docs.title: Key Metrics to Alert On
docs.text:
# Cache hit rate (target: >80%)
kubectl exec -n kube-system coredns-xxxxx -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:9153/metrics | \
  grep -E "coredns_cache_hits_total|coredns_cache_misses_total"

# Error rate (SERVFAIL responses — target: <0.1%)
kubectl exec -n kube-system coredns-xxxxx -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:9153/metrics | \
  grep coredns_dns_responses_total | grep SERVFAIL

# Request latency p99 (target: <10ms for cluster.local)
kubectl exec -n kube-system coredns-xxxxx -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:9153/metrics | \
  grep coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds_bucket

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix External names slow (~300 ms) ndots:5 search expansion kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf Set ndots:1 per pod or use FQDNs with trailing dot CoreDNS OOMKilled Traffic spike / cache overflow kubectl describe pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns Increase memory limits; add CoreDNS replicas i/o timeout for 10.96.0.10 kube-proxy DNAT rule for kube-dns missing iptables -t nat -S \| grep 10.96.0.10 Restart kube-proxy; verify DNS service has endpoints Intermittent NXDOMAIN for internal services UDP conntrack race condition kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache to bypass conntrack Corporate domain not resolving Missing stub zone in Corefile kubectl get cm -n kube-system coredns -o yaml Add stub zone block forwarding to corporate resolver SERVFAIL for external names Upstream DNS unreachable from nodes kubectl exec coredns-xxx -- dig @1.1.1.1 github.com Check node egress firewall; set working upstream in Corefile DNS works in some namespaces but not others Search domain missing or wrong in resolv.conf kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf Check dnsPolicy on pod spec; verify namespace is correct in search path

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache before production launch (eliminates conntrack UDP race)
  • Set ndots:1 via pod dnsConfig for pods making many external calls
  • Tune cache 300 for stable external hostnames; monitor cache hit rate in CoreDNS metrics
  • Add stub zones for all corporate/split-horizon domains before pods try to resolve them
  • Set CoreDNS memory limit to at least 170 MiB; alert on memory >80% — OOMKill drops all DNS
  • Run at least 2 CoreDNS replicas; use PodAntiAffinity to spread across nodes
  • Temporarily enable the log directive during incident investigation; disable after (high CPU cost)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Call external APIs with short names and ndots:5 3 extra NXDOMAIN queries per call add 90–300 ms of latency Use fully qualified names (api.example.com.) or set ndots:1 Set CoreDNS memory limit too low (e.g., 64 MiB) Cache fills up; OOMKill takes down all DNS, pods restart cluster-wide Start at 170 MiB; monitor and tune upward; alert at 80% usage Forward all queries including cluster.local to upstream Leaks internal service names to external DNS; also breaks resolution The kubernetes plugin must come before forward; use stub zones for corporate only Use dnsPolicy: None without setting nameserver Pod gets no DNS at all Only use dnsPolicy: None when providing a complete dnsConfig block Skip NodeLocal DNSCache and rely on ClusterIP DNS UDP to ClusterIP requires conntrack; under load, conntrack races cause SERVFAIL Always deploy NodeLocal DNSCache in production; it is a one-command install

docs.text: Use Case Command View current Corefile kubectl get cm -n kube-system coredns -o yaml Edit Corefile (hot-reload) kubectl edit cm -n kube-system coredns Test internal DNS kubectl run -it --rm d --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- nslookup kubernetes Test external DNS kubectl run -it --rm d --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- nslookup github.com Check resolv.conf in a pod kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf Verify NodeLocal DNSCache kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=node-local-dns -o wide Watch CoreDNS logs kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -f Check CoreDNS metrics kubectl exec coredns-xxx -- curl -s http://localhost:9153/metrics Test corporate stub zone kubectl run -it --rm d --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- nslookup svc.corp.internal Check DNS service endpoints kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system kube-dns Measure ndots latency kubectl run -it --rm d --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- sh -c "time nslookup api.example.com"

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail CoreDNS ClusterIP 10.96.0.10 (default) Search domains <ns>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local ndots:5 <5 dots → tries 3 search domains first (adds 90-300 ms for external names) Fix ndots dnsConfig.options ndots: "1" per pod, or use FQDNs with trailing dot NodeLocal DNSCache 169.254.20.10 per node — eliminates conntrack for DNS; ~10× lower p99 latency Stub zone corp.internal:53 { forward . <ip> } in Corefile Negative caching cache denial 30 caches NXDOMAIN to reduce repeat lookups autopath Collapses search-list expansion into a single query (Corefile plugin)

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does ndots:5 in a pod's /etc/resolv.conf cause up to 3 extra DNS queries for an external hostname like api.example.com, and what does each extra query attempt?
Answer `ndots:5` means any hostname with fewer than 5 dots is expanded against each search domain before the absolute lookup is tried. `api.example.com` has 2 dots (fewer than 5), so the resolver first tries `api.example.com.default.svc.cluster.local` (gets NXDOMAIN, ~30ms), then `api.example.com.svc.cluster.local` (NXDOMAIN, ~30ms), then `api.example.com.cluster.local` (NXDOMAIN, ~30ms), and finally `api.example.com.` (the absolute name, which succeeds). That is 3 wasted round trips adding 90–300ms of latency before the external name resolves.
  1. [Scenario question] An application pod is making external API calls and experiencing 200–300ms of extra latency on every new connection. No network errors appear. DNS queries eventually succeed. What is the most likely cause, and what is the simplest fix that does not require changing application code?
Answer The cause is `ndots:5` triggering search-domain expansion for external hostnames that have fewer than 5 dots. The simplest fix is to set `ndots:1` in the pod's `dnsConfig` — this means only hostnames with zero dots trigger search expansion, and `api.example.com` resolves directly on the first query. Add to the pod spec: `spec.dnsConfig.options: [{name: ndots, value: "1"}]`. Alternatively, use fully-qualified domain names with a trailing dot (`api.example.com.`) which bypass the ndots check entirely.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to verify that NodeLocal DNSCache is running on every node in the cluster?
Answer 
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=node-local-dns -o wide
There should be one pod per node, all in Running state. The `-o wide` flag shows which node each pod is on. Additionally, verify that pods on those nodes have `nameserver 169.254.20.10` in their `/etc/resolv.conf` by running `kubectl exec -- cat /etc/resolv.conf`.

docs.title: Lesson 15 — IPv6 and Dual-Stack Kubernetes
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Lesson 02 — IP Routing, Lesson 09 — CNI · Time: ~2 hours

Goal: Configure a dual-stack Kubernetes cluster, create dual-stack services with the correct ipFamilyPolicy, and diagnose IPv6 connectivity failures at the node and pod level.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.status.addresses[*].address}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | head -15

minikube ssh
ip -6 addr show

docs.title: 1. Dual-Stack vs IPv6-Only
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph SS["Single-Stack (IPv4 only)"]
        N1[Node\n192.168.1.10]
        P1[Pod\n10.244.1.5/24]
        S1[Service ClusterIP\n10.96.0.10/32]
    end
    subgraph DS["Dual-Stack (IPv4 + IPv6)"]
        N2[Node\n192.168.1.10\nfd00::10]
        P2[Pod\n10.244.1.5/24\nfd01::a:f405/96]
        S2[Service ClusterIPs\n10.96.0.10/32\nfd02::a/128]
    end

Dual-stack: Every pod and service has both an IPv4 and IPv6 address. Traffic uses IPv4 or IPv6 based on the caller's preference.

IPv6-only: No IPv4 at all. Less common, but increasingly required by some cloud regions, carriers, and mobile networks.

NDP replaces ARP in IPv6: - IPv4: ARP broadcast — "who has 10.244.1.1?" - IPv6: ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation — "who has fd01::1?" (multicast, not broadcast)

docs.title: 2. IPv6 Address Types
docs.text: Type Prefix Scope Use in Kubernetes Link-local fe80::/10 Same link only NDP, router discovery; not routable ULA (Unique Local) fc00::/7 Private network Pod CIDRs, service CIDRs in private clusters Global unicast 2000::/3 Internet-routable Public-facing node addresses, cloud-assigned Loopback ::1/128 Host only Localhost equivalent Multicast ff00::/8 Group NDP neighbor solicitation uses ff02::1:ff.../104

docs.title: 3. Enabling Dual-Stack at the Cluster Level
docs.text:
# kubeadm: enable dual-stack at init
cat <<EOF > kubeadm-config.yaml
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta3
kind: ClusterConfiguration
networking:
  podSubnet: "10.244.0.0/16,fd00:10:244::/56"      # IPv4 + IPv6 pod CIDR
  serviceSubnet: "10.96.0.0/12,fd00:10:96::/108"    # IPv4 + IPv6 service CIDR
EOF

kubeadm init --config kubeadm-config.yaml

Kubelet flags required (one IPv4, one IPv6 node address): 

--node-ip=192.168.1.10,fd00::1


# Verify node has both pod CIDRs
kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDRs}'
# ["10.244.0.0/24","fd00:10:244::/96"]

docs.title: 5. Dual-Stack Services
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    POD[Pod] -->|IPv4 dst 10.96.42.10:80| SVC4[Service ClusterIP\n10.96.42.10]
    POD -->|IPv6 dst fd00:10:96::1:80| SVC6[Service ClusterIP\nfd00:10:96::1]

# Prefer IPv6, fall back to IPv4
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack   # SingleStack | PreferDualStack | RequireDualStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv6
    - IPv4
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80

kubectl get svc web
# NAME   TYPE        CLUSTER-IP           CLUSTER-IPS                              PORT(S)
# web    ClusterIP   10.96.42.10          10.96.42.10,fd00:10:96::1               80/TCP

docs.title: ipFamilyPolicy Reference
docs.text: Policy Behavior Use Case SingleStack One IP family (default) Existing services; no migration needed PreferDualStack Dual-stack if cluster supports it; falls back to single Gradual migration to dual-stack RequireDualStack Fails if cluster doesn't support dual-stack Enforce dual-stack requirement in manifests

docs.text:
# Check pod has both addresses
kubectl get pod web-pod -o jsonpath='{.status.podIPs}'
# [{"ip":"10.244.0.6"},{"ip":"fd00:10:244::6"}]

# Inside the pod — verify both addresses visible
kubectl exec -it web-pod -- ip addr
# inet  10.244.0.6/24  brd 10.244.0.255 scope global eth0
# inet6 fd00:10:244::6/64 scope global dynamic

# Check IPv6 routing table inside pod
kubectl exec -it web-pod -- ip -6 route
# fd00:10:244::/64 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src fd00:10:244::6
# default via fd00:10:244::1 dev eth0

# Ping a peer pod over IPv6
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping6 fd00:10:244::7

  name: web-policy-v6
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web

docs.title: 8. Bare Metal IPv6 Considerations
docs.text:
# Enable IPv6 forwarding on nodes (required)
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.eth0.forwarding=1

# Allow iptables to see bridged IPv6 traffic
sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables=1

# Check IPv6 routes
ip -6 route show

# Check NDP neighbor table (IPv6 ARP equivalent)
ip -6 neigh show

# NDP proxy (if needed for routing without BGP)
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.eth0.proxy_ndp=1

metadata:
  name: v6-peer
spec:

  asNumber: 65000
  sourceAddress: "fd00::10"

docs.title: 10. SLAAC vs DHCPv6
docs.text:
IPv6 nodes and pods can receive addresses through two mechanisms:

Mechanism How it works Kubernetes usage SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) Node derives address from router advertisement prefix + EUI-64 or random suffix Node link-local and global addresses on bare metal DHCPv6 Stateful DHCP server assigns specific address + options Enterprise environments requiring tracked address assignments DHCPv6 Stateless Router provides prefix; DHCP provides options only (NTP, DNS) Hybrid — SLAAC for addresses, DHCP for config Static Manually configured via kubelet --node-ip Recommended for Kubernetes nodes to ensure stable node IPs

For Kubernetes pods, the CNI plugin handles IPv6 address assignment from the configured pod CIDR — SLAAC and DHCPv6 are not used for pod addresses.

# Check which address assignment method a node interface uses
ip -6 addr show eth0
# inet6 fd00::10/64 scope global dynamic   ← SLAAC/DHCPv6
# inet6 fd00::10/64 scope global           ← static (no "dynamic")

# Check router advertisements being received
rdisc6 eth0    # or: ip -6 route show | grep ra

docs.title: 11. Verification Steps
docs.text:
After configuring dual-stack, run these checks in order:

# Step 1: Verify nodes have both address families
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=\
"NAME:.metadata.name,ADDRESSES:.status.addresses[*].address"

# Step 2: Verify pods have dual IPs
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns=\
"NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,IPs:.status.podIPs[*].ip" | head -20

# Step 3: Verify services have dual ClusterIPs
kubectl get svc -A -o custom-columns=\
"NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,CLUSTER-IPS:.spec.clusterIPs"

# Step 4: Test pod-to-pod IPv6 connectivity
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping6 -c3 <pod-b-ipv6-addr>
# Expected: 3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss

# Step 5: Test service resolution over IPv6
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup -type=AAAA web.default.svc.cluster.local
# Expected: an fd00:... address in the Answer section

# Step 6: Verify ip6tables service rules exist
# (run on the node via minikube ssh or kubectl debug)
ip6tables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | head -10
# Expected: KUBE-SVC-* entries for IPv6 ClusterIPs

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Pod missing IPv6 address CNI doesn't have IPv6 pool configured kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIPs}' Add IPv6 pool to CNI config (Calico/Cilium/Flannel) IPv6 ping between pods fails IPv6 forwarding disabled on node sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding Set net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1; persist in /etc/sysctl.d/ Service has only one ClusterIP ipFamilyPolicy is SingleStack kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml \| grep ipFamily Update service to ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack ip6tables rules missing for service kube-proxy not generating IPv6 rules ip6tables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n Verify --cluster-cidr includes IPv6 CIDR; restart kube-proxy NDP resolution fails (neighbor unreachable) IPv6 proxy NDP not configured ip -6 neigh show and look for FAILED entries Enable proxy_ndp on the interface or configure upstream router DNS AAAA query returns nothing CoreDNS doesn't have IPv6 ClusterIP kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIPs}' Re-install with dual-stack service CIDRs configured Cloud VPC rejects IPv6 traffic VPC doesn't have IPv6 CIDR block assigned Cloud console: check VPC IPv6 CIDR block Assign IPv6 CIDR to VPC and subnets in cloud console

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Enable IPv6 forwarding persistently on all nodes (/etc/sysctl.d/99-k8s-ipv6.conf)
  • Assign IPv6 CIDR blocks to cloud VPC and subnets before creating the cluster
  • Configure CNI with both IPv4 and IPv6 pools before the first pod starts
  • Set ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack on new services as the migration baseline
  • Verify ip6tables KUBE-SERVICES rules exist alongside iptables rules after kube-proxy starts
  • Test AAAA DNS resolution from pods: nslookup -type=AAAA web.default.svc.cluster.local
  • Confirm MTU is consistent across IPv4 and IPv6 paths — IPv6 may require a different MTU (NDP Path MTU Discovery)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Enable dual-stack at cluster init but leave CNI with only IPv4 pool Pods get IPv4 addresses only; IPv6 ClusterIPs are unreachable Configure CNI IPv6 pool before the first pod starts Use link-local (fe80::/10) addresses for pod CIDRs Link-local addresses are not routable beyond the local link; cross-node traffic fails Use ULA (fc00::/7) or globally routable (2000::/3) prefixes for pod and service CIDRs Hardcode IPv4 service IPs in application configs App breaks when migrated to dual-stack or IPv6-only cluster Use DNS service names (svc.ns.svc.cluster.local) — never hardcode IPs Set RequireDualStack on all services immediately Services fail to create on single-stack clusters or during partial migration Use PreferDualStack for gradual rollout; switch to RequireDualStack only after full cluster dual-stack is verified Ignore ip6tables when debugging service connectivity IPv6 service path uses ip6tables; iptables commands show nothing for IPv6 traffic Always check both iptables and ip6tables when debugging dual-stack service issues

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command Check node has both address families kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses}' Check pod dual-stack IPs kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIPs}' Ping over IPv6 between pods kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping6 <ipv6-addr> DNS AAAA lookup kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup -type=AAAA web.default.svc.cluster.local View IPv6 routes on node ip -6 route show View NDP neighbor table ip -6 neigh show Check ip6tables service rules ip6tables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n Verify service has dual ClusterIPs kubectl get svc <svc> -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIPs}' Check IPv6 forwarding enabled sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding List pod CIDRs on a node kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDRs}' Enable dual-stack in Cilium helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --set ipv4.enabled=true --set ipv6.enabled=true

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail Dual-stack cluster Requires --pod-cidr and --service-cidr with both families at init ipFamilyPolicy PreferDualStack for gradual migration; RequireDualStack to enforce NDP IPv6 equivalent of ARP — ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation (multicast, not broadcast) IPv6 forwarding net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 required on every node Address types Link-local fe80::/10 (non-routable), ULA fc00::/7 (private), Global 2000::/3 Cloud support EKS (IPv6-only 1.21+), GKE dual-stack (1.21+), AKS dual-stack (1.21+) ip6tables kube-proxy writes parallel KUBE-SERVICES chains in ip6tables for IPv6 service VIPs

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] How does IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) differ from IPv4 ARP in its communication model, and why does Kubernetes require net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 on every node in a dual-stack cluster?
Answer ARP uses Layer 2 broadcast to ask "who has IP X?" — every device on the segment must process the broadcast. NDP uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation messages sent to a solicited-node multicast address derived from the target IP, so only the target host (and devices explicitly subscribed to that multicast group) process the message. This is more efficient and scales better. The `net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1` sysctl is required because, without it, the node's kernel drops IPv6 packets that need to be forwarded between pod namespaces and the external network — the same requirement as `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` for IPv4.
  1. [Scenario question] A dual-stack cluster has pods with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses assigned. IPv4 pings between pods on different nodes work correctly, but ping6 between pods on different nodes fails with 100% packet loss. What sysctl parameter should you check on the nodes first?
Answer Check `sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding` on the nodes — if it returns `0`, the kernel is not forwarding IPv6 packets between interfaces, causing all cross-node IPv6 traffic to be silently dropped. Set it with `sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1` and persist in `/etc/sysctl.d/99-k8s-ipv6.conf`. Also check `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables=1` and that `ip6tables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n` shows rules for IPv6 service ClusterIPs.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to verify that a service has been assigned both an IPv4 and an IPv6 ClusterIP in a dual-stack cluster?
Answer 
kubectl get svc <service-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIPs}'
The output should show two IPs — one IPv4 (e.g., `10.96.42.10`) and one IPv6 (e.g., `fd00:10:96::1`). If only one IP appears, check the service's `ipFamilyPolicy` with `kubectl get svc -o yaml | grep -A3 ipFamily` — it may be set to `SingleStack` instead of `PreferDualStack` or `RequireDualStack`.
