docs.title: Lesson 16 — Network Policies: Microsegmentation
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud Prerequisites: Lesson 13 — Kubernetes Services Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Configure NetworkPolicy resources to implement microsegmentation, enforce default-deny namespaces, test connectivity enforcement with Cilium and Calico tooling, and avoid common selector and DNS egress pitfalls.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get netpol -A
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | head -15

# Terminal 2 — minikube Linux node
minikube ssh
# Inspect CNI-enforced iptables rules (Calico)
sudo iptables -L | grep -i cali | head -20
# Or for Cilium: sudo bpftool map dump name cilium_policy 2>/dev/null | head -20

Observation commands — run after deploying test pods to see enforcement live:

# Deploy test pods with labels
kubectl run web --image=nginx --labels="app=web" --expose --port=80
kubectl run frontend --image=nicolaka/netshoot --labels="app=frontend" -- sleep 3600
kubectl run attacker --image=nicolaka/netshoot --labels="app=other" -- sleep 3600

# Confirm connectivity BEFORE any policy (all pods reachable — flat network)
kubectl exec frontend -- curl -s --max-time 2 http://web   # expect: nginx HTML
kubectl exec attacker -- curl -s --max-time 2 http://web   # expect: nginx HTML

# Apply default-deny + selective allow (Section 4), then verify isolation
kubectl exec frontend -- curl -s --max-time 2 http://web   # expect: nginx HTML (allowed)
kubectl exec attacker -- curl -s --max-time 2 http://web   # expect: silence / timeout (blocked)
echo "Enforcement confirmed if attacker timed out"

# Watch live events as policies are applied
kubectl get events --watch --field-selector reason=NetworkPolicyUpdated 2>/dev/null &

See also: Lesson 03 — iptables and Netfilter for CNI enforcement mechanics.

docs.title: 1. The Default Model
docs.text:
Without any NetworkPolicy, all ingress and all egress between pods is allowed (flat network model). Applying a NetworkPolicy to a pod's selector activates enforcement and denies all traffic not explicitly permitted.

No policy applied → pod is non-isolated → all traffic allowed
Policy applied    → pod is isolated → only specified traffic allowed

The CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, etc.) — not the Kubernetes API server — performs the actual enforcement. The API server stores and validates policy objects; the CNI agent on each node translates them into iptables rules or eBPF programs.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ns["Namespace: default"]
        FE["frontend\napp=frontend"]
        ATK["attacker\napp=other"]
        WEB["web pod\napp=web\n[isolated by policy]"]
        DB["db pod\napp=db\n[isolated by policy]"]
    end
    DNS["kube-dns\nkube-system"]

    FE -->|"TCP 80 ✓ allowed"| WEB
    ATK -->|"TCP 80 ✗ dropped"| WEB
    WEB -->|"TCP 5432 ✓ allowed"| DB
    ATK -->|"TCP 5432 ✗ dropped"| DB
    WEB -->|"UDP 53 ✓ DNS exception"| DNS

    style ATK fill:#fcc,stroke:#c00
    style WEB fill:#cfc,stroke:#090
    style DB fill:#cfc,stroke:#090

docs.title: 2. NetworkPolicy Anatomy
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-policy
  namespace: default         # policies are namespace-scoped
spec:
  podSelector:               # pods this policy applies TO
    matchLabels:
      app: web

  policyTypes:               # which directions this policy governs
    - Ingress
    - Egress

  ingress:                   # whitelist of allowed inbound connections
    - from:
        - podSelector:       # from pods with these labels (same namespace)
            matchLabels:
              app: frontend
        - namespaceSelector: # from pods in namespaces with this label
            matchLabels:
              env: production
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 80

  egress:                    # whitelist of allowed outbound connections
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: db
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 5432
    - to: []                 # DNS egress (required or DNS breaks)
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53

docs.title: Key Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect When to change podSelector: {} (none) Selects ALL pods in namespace Use for namespace-wide default-deny baseline policyTypes: [Ingress] Ingress-only Egress remains open Add Egress whenever restricting outbound traffic policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] — Both directions enforced Full microsegmentation from: [] / to: [] empty list — Denies ALL traffic in that direction Default-deny pattern alongside podSelector: {} namespaceSelector alone — Allows all pods from matching namespaces Cross-namespace access; pair with podSelector for AND logic ipBlock: cidr — Allows/blocks CIDR ranges External traffic, on-prem resources, monitoring agents ipBlock: except — Excludes sub-ranges from the CIDR block Carve out sensitive sub-networks within an allowed CIDR port: 53 protocol: UDP/TCP — DNS exception Required whenever an egress policy is applied

The packet journey through CNI enforcement:

sequenceDiagram
    participant SP as Source Pod
    participant K as Kernel (iptables / eBPF)
    participant CNI as CNI Agent\n(Calico Felix / Cilium Agent)
    participant TP as Target Pod

    SP->>K: send TCP SYN packet
    K->>CNI: policy table lookup (src/dst labels + port)
    CNI-->>K: allow / deny decision
    alt Allowed by NetworkPolicy
        K->>TP: deliver packet
        TP-->>SP: TCP SYN-ACK — connection established
    else Denied (drop — default)
        Note over K,SP: Packet silently dropped — sender sees timeout
    else Denied (reject — Calico action: Reject)
        K-->>SP: TCP RST or ICMP unreachable
    end

docs.title: 3. Selector Combinations
docs.text:
# AND condition: pod must have BOTH labels
from:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: frontend
        env: production

# OR condition: separate from entries
from:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: frontend
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: api

# AND between podSelector AND namespaceSelector
# (pod must match AND be in a matching namespace)
from:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        role: db-client
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        project: billing

# Note: if podSelector and namespaceSelector are SEPARATE from entries,
# they are ORed. If they are in the SAME from entry, they are ANDed.

docs.title: Default Deny All (namespace baseline)
docs.text:
# Apply first — sets default deny for the namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}      # matches all pods
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress

docs.title: Allow DNS (almost always needed with egress policies)
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - port: 53
          protocol: UDP
        - port: 53
          protocol: TCP

egress:
  - to:
      - ipBlock:
          cidr: 10.100.0.0/16    # corporate internal
          except:
            - 10.100.1.0/24      # exclude sensitive subnet

docs.title: 5. CNI Plugin Support
docs.text:
NetworkPolicy enforcement is the CNI plugin's responsibility — the Kubernetes API accepts any policy, but only plugins that implement it will enforce it.

CNI Plugin NetworkPolicy Support Calico Full (Kubernetes + its own CRDs) Cilium Full (Kubernetes + its own CRDs + L7) Weave Net Full Flannel None (use with Calico or Calico policy-only mode) AWS VPC CNI Partial (use Calico or Cilium on top) GKE Dataplane v2 Full (Cilium under the hood)

docs.title: 6. Testing Network Policies
docs.text:
# Method 1: netcat connectivity test from inside a pod
kubectl run -it --rm tester --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  nc -vz web.default.svc.cluster.local 80

# Method 2: Policy trace with Calico
calicoctl policy trace \
  --src-pod default/frontend \
  --dst-pod default/backend \
  --dst-port 8080

# Method 3: Cilium policy trace
cilium policy trace \
  --src-identity <id> \
  --dst-identity <id> \
  --dport 80

# Method 4: Use network-policy-api conformance tests
# https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/network-policy-api

docs.title: 7. Calico NetworkPolicy Extras
docs.text:
# Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy — cluster-wide, pre-namespace policies
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: GlobalNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-node-ports
spec:
  selector: all()
  ingress:
    - action: Allow
      protocol: TCP
      destination:
        ports: [30000-32767]   # NodePort range
  order: 100   # lower = higher priority

# Calico HostEndpoint — apply policy to node interfaces
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: HostEndpoint
metadata:
  name: node1-eth0
spec:
  interfaceName: eth0
  node: node1
  profiles:
    - node-profile

docs.title: 8. Cilium L7 Network Policy
docs.text:
Cilium can enforce policy at Layer 7 (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka).

apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: http-policy
  namespace: default
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  ingress:
    - fromEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            app: frontend
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "8080"
              protocol: TCP
          rules:
            http:
              - method: "GET"
                path: "/api/v1/.*"
              - method: "POST"
                path: "/api/v1/data"
                headers:
                  - "X-API-Key: .*"

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix DNS lookups fail after adding egress policy Missing DNS egress exception kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup kubernetes Add allow-dns NetworkPolicy to allow port 53 to kube-system/kube-dns Traffic blocked even though policy looks correct CNI plugin does not enforce NetworkPolicy (e.g., Flannel) kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico\|cilium\|weave' Switch to or layer Calico/Cilium on top of Flannel Policy applies to unintended pods Broad podSelector: {} catches all pods kubectl describe netpol <name> and check Affecting Pods Narrow podSelector with specific matchLabels Traffic still blocked after deleting the policy A second policy also selects the pod kubectl get netpol -n default -o yaml | grep -A5 podSelector Delete all policies selecting that pod or add an explicit allow rule AND logic not working (namespaceSelector + podSelector) Both selectors placed as separate from entries (OR logic) kubectl get netpol -o yaml and inspect from list structure Nest both selectors in the same from list item for AND behavior Cloud LB health checks fail after egress restriction Health probe IPs blocked by egress policy kubectl describe svc <lb-svc> → check health probe CIDR Add egress allow for cloud health check IP ranges Calico shows deny but no Kubernetes NetworkPolicy present Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy (cluster-scoped) is blocking calicoctl get globalnetworkpolicy Review GNP order and action; adjust or add an explicit Allow with lower order number

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Default-deny-all policy applied to every application namespace before any workloads are deployed
  • Explicit allow-dns NetworkPolicy deployed alongside every egress restriction
  • CNI plugin verified as NetworkPolicy-capable (kubectl describe pod -n kube-system <cni-pod>) before relying on enforcement
  • Every policy tested with both allowed and blocked traffic paths before promoting to production
  • Cloud LB health check IP ranges added to egress allowlist when using externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  • Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy or Cilium ClusterwideNetworkPolicy audited for cluster-wide rules that could silently override namespace policies
  • NetworkPolicy YAML reviewed with editor.networkpolicy.io or validated via kubectl apply --dry-run=server before applying in production

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Apply egress policy without a DNS exception All DNS lookups time out; every service call that uses a hostname fails with "name not resolved" Always deploy allow-dns as a companion policy whenever you restrict egress Place podSelector and namespaceSelector as separate from entries expecting AND logic Separate entries create OR conditions — either selector alone is sufficient to allow access, defeating the intent Nest both selectors inside the same from list item to enforce AND (pod must match AND be in the matching namespace) Use Flannel without an overlay policy engine and expect NetworkPolicy to work Flannel has no policy enforcement engine; the API accepts the resource silently but nothing is blocked Install Calico in policy-only mode on top of Flannel, or switch to Cilium or Weave Omit the policyTypes field Kubernetes infers policyTypes from the presence of ingress/egress rules, but explicit declaration prevents subtle bugs when rules are empty Always declare both Ingress and Egress in policyTypes when you intend to restrict both directions Write a temporary "allow-all" to unblock an incident and forget to remove it Leaves a permanent open hole; the next policy added assumes the allow-all is gone but it is still there, silently granting access Use labels + GitOps tracking to give every temporary policy an expiry annotation; automate cleanup

docs.text: Use Case Command List all NetworkPolicies in a namespace kubectl get netpol -n <ns> Describe a policy (selector, rules, affected pods) kubectl describe netpol <name> -n <ns> Test TCP connectivity from a pod kubectl exec <pod> -- nc -vz <host> <port> Launch netshoot debug pod kubectl run -it --rm tester --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash Watch Cilium dropped flows hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --namespace default Trace a Calico policy decision calicoctl policy trace --src-pod ns/pod --dst-pod ns/pod --dst-port 80 Get Cilium endpoint identity for a pod cilium endpoint list | grep <pod-name> Watch deny events in Calico Felix kubectl logs -n calico-system -l app=calico-node -c calico-node | grep Deny Check workload endpoint policies (Calico) calicoctl get workloadendpoint -n default <pod> -o yaml Check if a pod is isolated by any policy kubectl get netpol -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -B2 -A5 podSelector Validate NetworkPolicy YAML without applying kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f policy.yaml List all pods selected by a policy kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l <selector-from-policy>

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail Default behavior All pod-to-pod traffic allowed (no policies present) Policy activation ANY policy selecting a pod isolates it in that direction Selector logic Same from entry = AND; separate from entries = OR DNS egress Must be explicitly allowed when any egress policy is applied L7 policy Cilium only via CiliumNetworkPolicy (Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is L4 only) Testing nc, Cilium Hubble observe, Calico calicoctl policy trace Cloud providers AWS: Calico on VPC CNI; GKE: enable at cluster level; AKS: Calico or Azure NPM

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] By default, what is the network policy behavior for a pod that has no NetworkPolicy selecting it, and what changes the moment the first NetworkPolicy is applied to that pod?
Answer By default, all pod-to-pod traffic is allowed — the network is "flat" with no restrictions. This is the non-isolated state. The moment any NetworkPolicy with a `podSelector` matching that pod is applied, the pod becomes **isolated** in the direction(s) specified by `policyTypes`. From that point, only traffic explicitly whitelisted by the policy's `ingress` or `egress` rules is permitted; all other traffic in that direction is silently dropped. A second (or third) NetworkPolicy selecting the same pod is unioned additively — traffic is allowed if any matching policy permits it.
  1. [Scenario question] After applying a default-deny-all egress NetworkPolicy to a namespace, all application pods immediately lose the ability to resolve service names via DNS. No other egress policy exists. What rule is missing, and what is the most specific way to add it?
Answer The missing rule is an egress exception for DNS. When an egress policy is applied, all outbound traffic — including DNS queries to CoreDNS — is blocked unless explicitly allowed. The most specific fix is a companion NetworkPolicy that allows egress to `kube-system` namespace pods with label `k8s-app=kube-dns` on UDP and TCP port 53. Using both UDP and TCP port 53 is important because large DNS responses can fall back to TCP. Without this exception, every application call that uses a hostname fails with "name not resolved" rather than a connection error.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to test whether a pod named frontend in the default namespace can establish a TCP connection to web-service on port 80?
Answer 
kubectl exec frontend -- nc -vz web-service 80
A successful connection prints `Connection to web-service 80 port [tcp/http] succeeded!`. A timeout (hanging with no output) indicates a NetworkPolicy is silently dropping the traffic. A `Connection refused` means the pod is reachable but nothing is listening on port 80 — a service or pod configuration issue, not a network policy issue.

Next: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers and L7 Load Balancing

docs.title: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers and L7 Load Balancing
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud Prerequisites: Lesson 13 — Kubernetes Services Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Deploy an NGINX or Traefik ingress controller, configure host-based and path-based routing with TLS termination via cert-manager, and diagnose 502/503/504 errors in the routing chain.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl + minikube tunnel)
kubectl get ingress -A
kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx 2>/dev/null || kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep ingress

# To expose an Ingress locally (bare metal simulation):
minikube tunnel   # run in a dedicated terminal, requires sudo

# Terminal 2 — Mac
kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx -o wide 2>/dev/null
curl -H "Host: myapp.local" http://$(minikube ip)/

Observation commands — run after deploying NGINX Ingress to see routing live:

# Watch the NGINX controller pod as Ingress objects are applied
kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -f &

# Deploy sample backends
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --port=80
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80
kubectl create deployment api --image=hashicorp/http-echo --port=5678 \
  -- /http-echo -text="api response"
kubectl expose deployment api --port=5678

# Apply and inspect routing
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: demo
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: demo.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api
            port:
              number: 5678
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

kubectl describe ingress demo                       # check rules and backend status
kubectl get endpoints web api                       # confirm pods are ready
curl -H "Host: demo.local" http://$(minikube ip)/  # expect: nginx HTML
curl -H "Host: demo.local" http://$(minikube ip)/api  # expect: "api response"

See also: Lesson 19 — MetalLB and kube-vip for assigning the Ingress controller a real EXTERNAL-IP on bare metal.

docs.title: 1. The Ingress Architecture
docs.text:
NodePort and LoadBalancer services give you L4 load balancing — they know TCP/UDP but nothing about HTTP. An Ingress controller adds L7 awareness: routing by hostname, URL path, TLS termination, authentication, rate limiting, and more.

flowchart LR
    Client["External Client"]
    LB["Cloud LB or MetalLB VIP\n(Service: LoadBalancer / NodePort)"]
    IC["Ingress Controller Pod\nNGINX / Traefik / Envoy / HAProxy"]
    API["Kubernetes API\n(watches Ingress objects)"]
    SVC1["api-service :8080"]
    SVC2["frontend-service :80"]
    P1["api pods"]
    P2["frontend pods"]

    Client --> LB
    LB --> IC
    IC -->|"Host: web.example.com\npath: /api"| SVC1
    IC -->|"Host: web.example.com\npath: /"| SVC2
    SVC1 --> P1
    SVC2 --> P2
    API -.->|"watch + sync config"| IC

The Ingress controller is itself a Kubernetes application (Deployment + Service). It watches Ingress resources and programs its proxy configuration dynamically.

docs.title: 2. Ingress Resource
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx        # which controller handles this
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - web.example.com
      secretName: web-tls-cert   # TLS certificate
  rules:
    - host: web.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 8080
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: frontend-service
                port:
                  number: 80
    - host: admin.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: admin-service
                port:
                  number: 80

docs.title: Key Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect When to change ingressClassName (cluster default IngressClass) Selects which controller processes this Ingress Multiple controllers installed; set explicitly to avoid ambiguity pathType: Prefix — Matches path and all sub-paths Use Exact for precise path matching with no sub-path bleed pathType: Exact — Matches only the exact path string Strict API endpoints where sub-paths should 404 tls.secretName — Secret containing tls.crt and tls.key Required for HTTPS; pair with cert-manager for auto-renewal nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target (no rewrite) Rewrites URL before forwarding to backend Strip path prefix before sending to backend service nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect "true" Redirects HTTP to HTTPS Set to "false" for plain HTTP environments nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size "1m" Maximum request body size Increase for file uploads ("100m") nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity (none) Enables sticky sessions via cookie Use when backend has session state

The request flow through the Ingress controller:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant LB as Cloud LB / MetalLB
    participant IC as Ingress Controller
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API
    participant SVC as Backend Service

    K8s-->>IC: watch Ingress objects (continuous)
    IC-->>IC: regenerate nginx.conf from Ingress rules

    C->>LB: HTTP GET /api (Host: web.example.com)
    LB->>IC: forward to controller pod (port 80/443)
    IC->>IC: match rule: host=web.example.com, path prefix /api
    IC->>SVC: proxy_pass to api-service:8080
    SVC-->>IC: 200 OK + response body
    IC-->>C: 200 OK (adds X-Request-ID, removes internal headers)

docs.title: 3. NGINX Ingress Controller
docs.text:
The most widely used. Can run on bare metal or cloud.

# Install via Helm
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx \
  --create-namespace \
  --set controller.service.type=LoadBalancer

# Verify
kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx
kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx ingress-nginx-controller
# Check EXTERNAL-IP — this is the IP your DNS should point to

# IngressClass resource
kubectl get ingressclass

# Bare metal: use NodePort or HostPort
helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --set controller.service.type=NodePort \
  --set controller.hostPort.enabled=true  # bind port 80/443 on each node

docs.title: NGINX Annotations
docs.text:
annotations:
  # Rate limiting
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "10"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "5"

  # Timeouts
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-connect-timeout: "30"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "60"

  # Auth
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-type: basic
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-secret: basic-auth-secret

  # Redirect HTTP to HTTPS
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"

  # Backend protocol
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS"   # for HTTPS backends
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "GRPC"    # for gRPC backends

  # Upload size
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "100m"

  # Sticky sessions
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity: "cookie"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/session-cookie-name: "INGRESSCOOKIE"

docs.title: 4. Traefik Ingress Controller
docs.text:
Popular in bare-metal and edge environments. Supports both Ingress and its own IngressRoute CRD.

# Install via Helm
helm repo add traefik https://helm.traefik.io/traefik
helm install traefik traefik/traefik \
  --namespace traefik \
  --create-namespace

# Traefik IngressRoute (more expressive than standard Ingress)
apiVersion: traefik.io/v1alpha1
kind: IngressRoute
metadata:
  name: web-route
spec:
  entryPoints:
    - web
    - websecure
  routes:
    - match: "Host(`web.example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/api`)"
      kind: Rule
      services:
        - name: api-service
          port: 8080
      middlewares:
        - name: rate-limit
  tls:
    certResolver: letsencrypt

docs.title: 5. TLS Termination and cert-manager
docs.text:
# Install cert-manager
helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io
helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager \
  --namespace cert-manager \
  --create-namespace \
  --set installCRDs=true

# ClusterIssuer for Let's Encrypt
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: admin@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            class: nginx
---
# Ingress with automatic TLS certificate
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - web.example.com
      secretName: web-tls    # cert-manager will create this Secret

# Check certificate status
kubectl get certificate
kubectl describe certificate web-tls
kubectl get certificaterequest

docs.title: 6. Ingress on Bare Metal
docs.text: The main challenge: no cloud LB to assign an EXTERNAL-IP.

docs.title: Option A: NodePort + DNS round-robin
docs.text:
# Service type NodePort — expose on every node
helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --set controller.service.type=NodePort \
  --set controller.service.nodePorts.http=30080 \
  --set controller.service.nodePorts.https=30443

# DNS round-robin to all node IPs
# web.example.com → 192.168.1.10, 192.168.1.11, 192.168.1.12

docs.title: Option B: MetalLB + LoadBalancer
docs.text:
# Install MetalLB (see Lesson 19)
# Then service type=LoadBalancer works

helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --set controller.service.type=LoadBalancer
# MetalLB assigns EXTERNAL-IP from pool

docs.title: Option C: HostPort (DaemonSet mode)
docs.text:
# Runs NGINX on every node, bound to ports 80/443
controller:
  kind: DaemonSet
  hostPort:
    enabled: true
  service:
    type: ClusterIP   # no LB needed — traffic goes direct to node

docs.title: AWS — AWS Load Balancer Controller (ALB)
docs.text:
# ALB Ingress (creates an Application Load Balancer)
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:...
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP":80},{"HTTPS":443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"

docs.title: GKE — GCE Ingress Controller
docs.text:
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "gce"
    kubernetes.io/ingress.global-static-ip-name: "my-static-ip"

docs.title: AKS — Application Gateway Ingress Controller (AGIC)
docs.text:
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: azure/application-gateway
    appgw.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> on NGINX service No cloud LB or MetalLB configured kubectl describe svc -n ingress-nginx ingress-nginx-controller On bare metal: install MetalLB (L19) or switch to NodePort 502 Bad Gateway from NGINX Backend pod not ready or port mismatch kubectl get endpoints <service> and kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx <controller> Check pod readiness, correct targetPort in Service spec 503 Service Unavailable No healthy backend endpoints kubectl get endpoints <service> — look for empty <none> Fix pod labels to match Service selector; check readinessProbe 504 Gateway Timeout Backend too slow or proxy-read-timeout too short kubectl exec -n ingress-nginx <pod> -- curl -v <backend>:port Increase proxy-read-timeout annotation; tune app performance TLS certificate shows "Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate" cert-manager not running or ClusterIssuer not ready kubectl get clusterissuer; kubectl describe certificate <name> Fix ClusterIssuer ACME credentials; check cert-manager pod logs 404 Not Found from NGINX Path or host does not match any Ingress rule kubectl describe ingress <name> and check Rules section Add correct host/path rule; verify ingressClassName Admission webhook error on kubectl apply NGINX admission webhook pod not ready kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx and check webhook pod status Delete and recreate the ValidatingWebhookConfiguration if pod is healthy

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• ingressClassName explicitly set on every Ingress resource (do not rely on cluster default in multi-controller clusters)
  • TLS configured for all public-facing Ingress resources; HTTP redirected to HTTPS via ssl-redirect: "true"
  • cert-manager ClusterIssuer tested with a staging Let's Encrypt endpoint before switching to production
  • Readiness probes on all backend pods so NGINX removes unhealthy endpoints automatically
  • Rate limiting annotations (limit-rps, limit-connections) applied to public endpoints
  • NGINX ConfigMap tuned for worker-processes, keep-alive, and upstream-keepalive-connections based on expected traffic
  • Ingress controller Deployment or DaemonSet tested for rolling updates without dropping connections (minReadySeconds, PodDisruptionBudget)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use ingressClassName: nginx without verifying which IngressClass is installed Multiple controllers (nginx + traefik) may both pick up or both ignore the resource depending on installed classes Run kubectl get ingressclass to confirm the class name and controller before deploying Ingress objects Skip TLS and rely on HTTP in production Traffic between client and cluster is unencrypted; modern browsers block mixed content Always terminate TLS at the ingress controller; use cert-manager for automatic certificate lifecycle Reuse a single Ingress resource across many teams by adding annotation overrides Annotations apply to the whole Ingress object; one team's rate-limit annotation affects all hosts in that object Give each team or service its own Ingress resource; use ingressClassName to share one controller Set proxy-body-size: "0" (unlimited) globally in the ConfigMap Exposes the cluster to memory exhaustion from large request bodies Set a reasonable default globally; override per-Ingress only for specific upload endpoints Deploy NGINX in Deployment mode (not DaemonSet) on bare metal with HostPort Only the nodes running NGINX pods receive traffic; other nodes are dead ends Use DaemonSet + HostPort on bare metal so every node can accept traffic, or use MetalLB to route to only ready nodes

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List all Ingress objects cluster-wide kubectl get ingress -A Describe an Ingress (rules, backends, TLS) kubectl describe ingress <name> -n <ns> Check NGINX controller external IP kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx ingress-nginx-controller View generated nginx.conf kubectl exec -n ingress-nginx <pod> -- nginx -T Tail NGINX access and error logs kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx <pod> --tail=100 -f Test routing with a Host header curl -H "Host: web.example.com" http://<controller-ip> Check certificate status kubectl get certificate -A Describe a cert-manager Certificate kubectl describe certificate <name> Verify TLS certificate from CLI openssl s_client -connect web.example.com:443 -servername web.example.com < /dev/null Check backend endpoints kubectl get endpoints <service-name> Reload NGINX manually (graceful) kubectl exec -n ingress-nginx <pod> -- nginx -s reload List IngressClass resources kubectl get ingressclass

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Feature Bare Metal Cloud External IP MetalLB or NodePort Cloud LB (auto) TLS cert-manager (LE or internal CA) ACM/Cloud certificates L7 LB NGINX/Traefik/Envoy ALB (AWS), GCE LB, App Gateway Ingress class Configure manually Provided by cloud controller Path routing Standard across all Standard across all

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is an IngressClass resource, and why must ingressClassName be explicitly specified on each Ingress object when multiple Ingress controllers are deployed in the same cluster?
Answer An `IngressClass` is a cluster-scoped resource that maps a class name (e.g., `nginx`, `traefik`) to a specific Ingress controller. Each Ingress controller watches only for Ingress objects that reference its IngressClass. Without explicit `ingressClassName`, both controllers may try to process the same Ingress object — or neither will, if neither is configured as the default. Run `kubectl get ingressclass` to see installed classes and check the `ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"` annotation to identify the cluster default.
  1. [Scenario question] The NGINX Ingress controller returns a 502 Bad Gateway error for a specific host/path rule. The Ingress object exists, the backend Service exists, and kubectl get svc shows the correct port. What is the most likely cause, and how do you confirm it?
Answer A 502 means the NGINX controller reached the backend Service but got an error from the backend pod — most likely the pod is not ready, is crashing, or the Service's `targetPort` does not match the port the pod is actually listening on. Check `kubectl get endpoints ` to confirm pods are listed and their ports are correct. If endpoints show ``, the pod selector in the Service does not match any pods. Check pod readiness with `kubectl get pods -l -o wide` and look at the READY column.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to view the full NGINX configuration that the ingress controller has generated from all deployed Ingress resources?
Answer 
kubectl exec -n ingress-nginx <controller-pod> -- nginx -T
This dumps the complete `nginx.conf` including all `server` blocks, `location` blocks, and upstream definitions generated from Ingress resources. It is the definitive way to verify that path rewrites, SSL settings, timeout annotations, and backend proxy targets are configured as expected.

Next: Lesson 18 — Gateway API: Next-Generation Ingress

docs.title: Lesson 18 — Gateway API: Next-Generation Ingress
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud Prerequisites: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers Duration: ~2 hours

Goal: Build a multi-role traffic management system using GatewayClass, Gateway, and HTTPRoute resources, implement canary deployments with weighted traffic splitting, and migrate workloads from Ingress to Gateway API.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl)
# Check if Gateway API CRDs are installed
kubectl api-resources | grep -E "gateway|httproute|grpcroute|tcproute"
kubectl get gatewayclass 2>/dev/null || echo "Gateway API not installed — run: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.1.0/standard-install.yaml"

# Terminal 2 — Mac
kubectl get gateway,httproute -A 2>/dev/null

Observation commands — run after creating a Gateway and HTTPRoute:

# Install Gateway API CRDs if not present
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.0/standard-install.yaml

# Watch Gateway and HTTPRoute status conditions as they are applied
kubectl get gateway -A -w &
kubectl get httproute -A -w &

# After creating resources (Sections 3-5), check status:
kubectl describe gateway prod-gateway -n infra
# Look for: "Programmed: True" and "ResolvedRefs: True" conditions

kubectl describe httproute web-route -n default
# Look for: "Accepted: True" and "ResolvedRefs: True" conditions

# Test weighted traffic split (Section 5)
for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -H "Host: web.example.com" http://<gateway-ip>/ | grep -o 'v[12]'; done
# Expect roughly 18 × v1 and 2 × v2 (90/10 split)

See also: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers for the Ingress API that Gateway API supersedes.

docs.title: 1. Why Gateway API Replaces Ingress
docs.text: Limitation Ingress API Gateway API Roles No separation of concerns Infrastructure, cluster, app teams separated Cross-namespace routing Not supported Supported via ReferenceGrant TCP/UDP routing Not supported TCPRoute, UDPRoute gRPC routing Not supported GRPCRoute Traffic splitting Annotation hacks Weight-based, natively in spec Header modification Annotation hacks RequestHeaderModifier filter Extensibility Annotations (string blobs) Extension points + custom filters

docs.title: 2. Resource Hierarchy
docs.text:
The Gateway API uses a three-layer role model — infrastructure teams own the top, application teams own the bottom:

flowchart TD
    GC["GatewayClass (cluster-scoped)\nowned by: controller (NGINX, Istio, Envoy)\ndefines: which implementation handles Gateways"]
    GW["Gateway (namespace-scoped)\nowned by: infrastructure team\ndefines: listeners, ports, protocols, TLS, allowed routes"]
    HR["HTTPRoute / TCPRoute / GRPCRoute (namespace-scoped)\nowned by: application team\ndefines: routing rules → backend Services"]
    SVC["Service → Pods"]

    GC --> GW
    GW --> HR
    HR --> SVC

The request path at runtime:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant GW as Gateway (listener :443)
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API
    participant HR as HTTPRoute rules
    participant SVC as Backend Service

    K8s-->>GW: watch GatewayClass + Gateway + HTTPRoute (continuous)
    GW-->>GW: program data-plane (Envoy / NGINX)

    C->>GW: HTTPS GET /api (Host: web.example.com)
    GW->>HR: evaluate route rules (host + path + headers)
    HR-->>GW: matched rule → backendRef: api-service:8080 weight:100
    GW->>SVC: forward request
    SVC-->>C: 200 OK

docs.title: 3. GatewayClass
docs.text:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  controllerName: k8s.io/ingress-nginx   # controller that manages this class

# Install NGINX Gateway Fabric (Gateway API implementation)
helm install nginx-gateway oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-gateway-fabric \
  --namespace nginx-gateway \
  --create-namespace

kubectl get gatewayclass
# NAME    CONTROLLER                    ACCEPTED
# nginx   k8s.io/ingress-nginx          True

docs.title: GatewayClass Parameters
docs.text: Field Default Effect When to change controllerName — Binds this class to a running controller Match exactly the controller's advertised name (see controller docs) spec.parametersRef (none) Points to a controller-specific config CRD Use for controller-specific defaults (timeouts, logging) .status.conditions[Accepted] — Controller acknowledged the class If False, check controller logs for name mismatch

docs.title: 4. Gateway
docs.text:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: prod-gateway
  namespace: infra
spec:
  gatewayClassName: nginx
  listeners:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      protocol: HTTP
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: All      # or: Same | Selector
    - name: https
      port: 443
      protocol: HTTPS
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: web-tls-cert
            namespace: infra
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Selector
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              gateway-access: allowed

docs.title: Gateway Listener Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change allowedRoutes.namespaces.from: All — Any namespace can attach HTTPRoutes Development clusters; restrict to Selector in production allowedRoutes.namespaces.from: Same — Only routes in the Gateway's namespace attach Single-team gateways allowedRoutes.namespaces.from: Selector — Only namespaces with matching labels attach Multi-tenant: label namespaces with gateway-access: allowed tls.mode: Terminate — TLS terminated at the gateway; plain HTTP forwarded to backends Standard web apps tls.mode: Passthrough — TLS forwarded unchanged to backend (requires TLSRoute) mTLS all the way to pods; backend owns the certificate

docs.title: 5. HTTPRoute
docs.text:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: web-route
  namespace: default
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: prod-gateway
      namespace: infra
      sectionName: https     # bind to the https listener
  hostnames:
    - "web.example.com"
  rules:
    # Path-based routing
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /api
      backendRefs:
        - name: api-service
          port: 8080
          weight: 100

    # Header-based routing (canary)
    - matches:
        - headers:
            - name: X-Canary
              value: "true"
      backendRefs:
        - name: api-service-canary
          port: 8080

    # Traffic splitting (weighted)
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /
      backendRefs:
        - name: frontend-v1
          port: 80
          weight: 90
        - name: frontend-v2
          port: 80
          weight: 10    # 10% canary traffic

docs.title: 6. HTTPRoute Filters
docs.text:
rules:
  - filters:
      # Add/remove request headers
      - type: RequestHeaderModifier
        requestHeaderModifier:
          add:
            - name: X-Gateway-Version
              value: "v2"
          remove:
            - X-Internal-Token

      # Redirect HTTP to HTTPS
      - type: RequestRedirect
        requestRedirect:
          scheme: https
          statusCode: 301

      # URL rewrite
      - type: URLRewrite
        urlRewrite:
          path:
            type: ReplacePrefixMatch
            replacePrefixMatch: /v2

      # Mirror traffic to another service (for testing)
      - type: RequestMirror
        requestMirror:
          backendRef:
            name: shadow-service
            port: 8080

docs.title: 7. TCPRoute and GRPCRoute
docs.text:
# TCPRoute — route raw TCP (databases, message queues)
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: TCPRoute
metadata:
  name: postgres-route
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: prod-gateway
      sectionName: postgres   # listener on port 5432
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: postgres-service
          port: 5432
---
# GRPCRoute — route gRPC by service and method
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GRPCRoute
metadata:
  name: grpc-route
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: prod-gateway
      sectionName: grpc
  rules:
    - matches:
        - method:
            service: "myapp.UserService"
            method: "GetUser"
      backendRefs:
        - name: user-service
          port: 50051

docs.title: 8. Cross-Namespace Routing with ReferenceGrant
docs.text:
# HTTPRoute in namespace "app" references Service in namespace "shared"
# → requires ReferenceGrant in "shared" namespace

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ReferenceGrant
metadata:
  name: allow-from-app
  namespace: shared          # in the target namespace
spec:
  from:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: HTTPRoute
      namespace: app         # the source namespace
  to:
    - group: ""
      kind: Service

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Gateway stuck with Programmed: False GatewayClass controller not running or name mismatch kubectl describe gatewayclass <name> → check Accepted condition Verify controller pod is running and controllerName matches exactly HTTPRoute Accepted: False parentRefs namespace/name wrong, or listener allowedRoutes does not permit this namespace kubectl describe httproute <name> → check status conditions Fix parentRefs.namespace, or add namespace label for Selector-mode allowedRoutes Cross-namespace backend ResolvedRefs: False Missing ReferenceGrant in the target Service's namespace kubectl get referencegrant -n <target-ns> Create ReferenceGrant granting access from route's namespace to target Service Traffic not splitting at expected weights Old connections stick to one backend (keep-alive) Use short-lived connections: curl --no-keepalive Test with fresh connections; configure session affinity intentionally if needed TLS: certificate not served (fake cert) Gateway TLS certificateRefs Secret does not exist or is in wrong namespace kubectl get secret <name> -n infra Create or copy the TLS Secret into the Gateway's namespace; use cert-manager BackendTLSPolicy 404 on valid route HTTPRoute hostnames does not match request Host header exactly curl -v -H "Host: web.example.com" http://<gw-ip>/ Ensure hostnames in HTTPRoute matches the Host header sent by client GRPCRoute not accepted Using standard CRDs — GRPCRoute requires experimental channel kubectl api-resources | grep grpcroute Apply experimental CRDs: experimental-install.yaml from the Gateway API release

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• GatewayClass Accepted status confirmed before creating Gateway resources that reference it
  • Gateway listener allowedRoutes set to Selector in production (not All) to prevent unauthorized namespace attachment
  • ReferenceGrant created in every target namespace before cross-namespace routes are deployed
  • HTTPRoute and Gateway status conditions checked (Accepted, Programmed, ResolvedRefs) after each change
  • Canary traffic splits validated with real request sampling before increasing canary weight
  • TLS certificates managed via cert-manager BackendTLSPolicy or external secret sync; not manually created
  • Ingress and HTTPRoute objects not duplicated for the same hostname during migration (can cause split-brain routing)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Give app teams permission to create Gateway objects App teams can open arbitrary ports and protocols on the shared infrastructure; this defeats role separation Only the infrastructure team creates Gateway objects; app teams create HTTPRoutes that attach to pre-approved Gateways Reference a Service in another namespace without a ReferenceGrant The route silently fails with ResolvedRefs: False; traffic does not flow but no error is surfaced to the caller Always create ReferenceGrant in the target namespace before deploying a cross-namespace backendRef Use Ingress annotation workarounds on HTTPRoute objects HTTPRoute does not support annotations for behavior tuning; they are ignored silently Use HTTPRoute filters (RequestHeaderModifier, URLRewrite, RequestMirror) for all routing behavior Set allowedRoutes.from: All on the production Gateway Any namespace in the cluster (including compromised ones) can attach routes and receive production traffic Label trusted namespaces and use from: Selector with explicit label matching Skip checking status conditions after applying resources Resources may appear created but be non-functional if the controller rejects them Always run kubectl describe gateway/httproute and verify Accepted: True and Programmed: True before testing

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List all GatewayClasses kubectl get gatewayclass List all Gateways cluster-wide kubectl get gateway -A List all HTTPRoutes cluster-wide kubectl get httproute -A Describe Gateway (check status conditions) kubectl describe gateway <name> -n <ns> Describe HTTPRoute (check Accepted/ResolvedRefs) kubectl describe httproute <name> -n <ns> List ReferenceGrants kubectl get referencegrant -A Install standard Gateway API CRDs kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.0/standard-install.yaml Install experimental CRDs (TCPRoute, UDPRoute, GRPCRoute) kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.0/experimental-install.yaml Test weighted traffic split (20 requests) for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -H "Host: web.example.com" http://<gw-ip>/; done Test header-based canary routing curl -H "X-Canary: true" -H "Host: web.example.com" http://<gw-ip>/ Get Gateway API conformance test results kubectl get gatewayclass <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Resource Scope Purpose GatewayClass Cluster Defines the controller implementation Gateway Namespace Defines listeners (ports, protocols, TLS) HTTPRoute Namespace HTTP/S routing rules → backends TCPRoute Namespace TCP routing rules GRPCRoute Namespace gRPC routing rules ReferenceGrant Namespace Grants cross-namespace routing permission

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does the Gateway API use three separate resource types (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute) instead of a single Ingress-like object?
Answer The three-layer hierarchy maps to real organizational boundaries: infrastructure teams own GatewayClass (which controller handles traffic) and Gateway (listener ports, TLS, allowed namespaces), while application teams own HTTPRoute (routing rules to their backends). This separation means an app team cannot change TLS settings or open new ports on shared infrastructure. The old Ingress API collapsed all roles into one object, forcing teams to use annotation hacks for features like traffic splitting.
  1. [Scenario question] An HTTPRoute you just applied shows ResolvedRefs: False in its status conditions and traffic is not flowing. What is the most likely cause, and how do you fix it?
Answer The most common cause is a missing ReferenceGrant when the HTTPRoute references a backend Service in a different namespace. Without a ReferenceGrant in the target namespace explicitly allowing the route's namespace to reference its Services, the controller rejects the cross-namespace backendRef. Create a `ReferenceGrant` in the Service's namespace with `from.namespace` set to the HTTPRoute's namespace. Verify with `kubectl get referencegrant -n ` and re-check `kubectl describe httproute `.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to verify that a weighted 90/10 traffic split between frontend-v1 and frontend-v2 is actually working as configured?
Answer 
for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -H "Host: web.example.com" http://<gateway-ip>/ | grep -o 'v[12]'; done | sort | uniq -c
Look for approximately 18 responses tagged `v1` and 2 responses tagged `v2`; if all 20 return `v1`, the HTTPRoute weights are not being applied by the controller (check `kubectl describe httproute` for status conditions).

Next: Lesson 19 — Load Balancing on Bare Metal: MetalLB and kube-vip

docs.title: Lesson 19 — Load Balancing on Bare Metal: MetalLB and kube-vip
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal Prerequisites: Lesson 06 — BGP Fundamentals, Lesson 13 — Kubernetes Services Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Configure MetalLB in L2 and BGP modes to provide LoadBalancer services on bare-metal clusters, compare with kube-vip for control-plane HA, and diagnose ARP and BGP announcement failures.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get pods -n metallb-system 2>/dev/null || echo "MetalLB not installed"
kubectl get ipaddresspools,l2advertisements -n metallb-system 2>/dev/null
kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=LoadBalancer

# Terminal 2 — minikube Linux node (inspect ARP for L2 mode)
minikube ssh
arp -n | head -20
ip neigh show

Observation commands — run after installing MetalLB and creating a LoadBalancer service:

# Watch MetalLB speaker announcements in real time
kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=speaker -f &

# Create a test LoadBalancer service
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment web --type=LoadBalancer --port=80

# Watch the service get an EXTERNAL-IP assigned from the pool
kubectl get svc web -w
# Expect: EXTERNAL-IP changes from <pending> to 192.168.100.xxx

# From outside the cluster, verify ARP resolution (L2 mode)
# arping -I eth0 192.168.100.100   # should respond from the elected speaker node

# Check which node is currently serving the VIP
kubectl get events -n metallb-system | grep -i announcing

See also: Lesson 06 — BGP Fundamentals for BGP session setup and ECMP concepts used by MetalLB BGP mode.

docs.title: 1. The Bare Metal LB Problem
docs.text:
# Without a LB controller, LoadBalancer services hang:
kubectl get svc web
# NAME   TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)        AGE
# web    LoadBalancer   10.96.42.10   <pending>     80:30080/TCP   10m

The Cloud Controller Manager (CCM) provisions cloud LBs. On bare metal, you need to run your own LB controller.

flowchart LR
    subgraph cloud["Cloud Cluster"]
        SVC1["Service\ntype: LoadBalancer"]
        CCM["Cloud Controller Manager"]
        CLB["Cloud LB\n(AWS NLB / GCP / Azure)"]
    end
    subgraph bare["Bare Metal Cluster"]
        SVC2["Service\ntype: LoadBalancer"]
        MLB["MetalLB / kube-vip"]
        VIP["VIP (ARP/BGP)\n192.168.100.100"]
    end

    SVC1 -->|"triggers provisioning"| CCM --> CLB
    SVC2 -->|"triggers provisioning"| MLB --> VIP

    style CLB fill:#cce,stroke:#66c
    style VIP fill:#cec,stroke:#6c6

docs.title: 2. MetalLB Overview
docs.text:
MetalLB implements LoadBalancer by either: - L2 mode: answers ARP/NDP for the VIP on the local subnet - BGP mode: advertises VIP routes to upstream routers

# Install MetalLB
helm repo add metallb https://metallb.github.io/metallb
helm install metallb metallb/metallb \
  --namespace metallb-system \
  --create-namespace

kubectl get pods -n metallb-system
# metallb-controller-xxx  (allocates IPs)
# metallb-speaker-xxx     (announces IPs — DaemonSet)

docs.title: 3. MetalLB L2 Mode
docs.text:
The speaker pod on the node holding the VIP responds to ARP requests for that IP.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Router as Upstream Router
    participant Node1 as Node 1 (elected speaker)
    participant Node2 as Node 2
    participant Spk as MetalLB Speaker (Node 1)
    participant Pod as Backend Pod

    Note over Spk: Leader election: Node 1 wins for 192.168.100.100

    Router->>Node1: ARP request: who has 192.168.100.100?
    Spk-->>Router: ARP reply: 192.168.100.100 is at <node1-MAC>
    Router->>Node1: TCP packet to 192.168.100.100:80
    Node1->>Pod: forward via kube-proxy (may DNAT to Node 2 pod)

    Note over Node1,Node2: On node failure:
    Spk-->>Router: gratuitous ARP from Node 2 (new leader)
    Note over Router: Router updates ARP cache (~10 s)
# Configure an IP address pool
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: production-pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 192.168.100.100-192.168.100.200
    - 192.168.200.0/24
---
# Enable L2 advertisement
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: L2Advertisement
metadata:
  name: l2-advert
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - production-pool
  nodeSelectors:               # optional: which nodes can announce
    - matchLabels:
        node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: ""

L2 mode limitations: - Single node holds the VIP at a time (failover on node failure, ~10s) - All traffic enters through one node (no true load balancing at the LB layer) - Works only within the same L2 broadcast domain

docs.title: 4. MetalLB BGP Mode
docs.text:
Announces VIPs via BGP to upstream routers. Multiple nodes can announce the same VIP via ECMP.

# BGP Peer (ToR switch)
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta2
kind: BGPPeer
metadata:
  name: tor-switch
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  myASN: 64512
  peerASN: 65000
  peerAddress: 192.168.1.1
  holdTime: 30s
  keepaliveTime: 10s
---
# Advertise pool via BGP
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BGPAdvertisement
metadata:
  name: bgp-advert
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - production-pool
  communities:
    - 64512:100       # tag with community for upstream policy
  aggregationLength: 32   # advertise host routes (/32)

BGP mode advantages: - ECMP: multiple nodes announce same VIP → load balancing at router level - Fast failover (BFD sub-second) - Works across L3 boundaries (across routers, not just L2)

docs.title: Key BGP/Pool Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change myASN — Local AS number for the BGP session Use private ASN (64512-65535); must match router config peerASN — Upstream router's AS number Match the ToR switch configuration holdTime 90s BGP session dead timer Reduce to 30s for faster failover detection aggregationLength 32 (IPv4) Prefix length for advertised routes Use 32 for per-VIP /32 host routes; aggregate with /24 to reduce BGP table size communities (none) BGP community strings appended to routes Signal upstream policy (e.g., no-export, local-pref) bfdProfile (none) Enables BFD for sub-second failure detection Production BGP — combine with fast BFD for <1s failover IPAddressPool.addresses — CIDR or range of allocatable IPs Must not overlap with node or pod subnets

docs.title: 5. Using the LoadBalancer Service
docs.text:
# Assign from a specific pool
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    metallb.io/address-pool: production-pool
    metallb.io/loadBalancerIPs: 192.168.100.105  # request specific IP
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

kubectl get svc web
# NAME   TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP       PORT(S)   AGE
# web    LoadBalancer   10.96.42.10   192.168.100.105   80/TCP    30s

docs.title: 6. kube-vip
docs.text:
kube-vip provides VIP management using VRRP (ARP-based HA) or BGP. Also handles HA for the Kubernetes control plane API server.

# Install kube-vip as a DaemonSet for LoadBalancer services
kubectl apply -f https://kube-vip.io/manifests/rbac.yaml

# Generate kube-vip DaemonSet manifest
docker run --network host --rm \
  ghcr.io/kube-vip/kube-vip:latest \
  manifest daemonset \
  --services \
  --arp \
  --leaderElection \
  | kubectl apply -f -

# kube-vip ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: kube-vip
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  range-global: "192.168.100.100-192.168.100.200"

kube-vip vs MetalLB:

Feature kube-vip MetalLB Control-plane VIP (HA API server) Yes No L2 / ARP mode Yes (VRRP) Yes BGP mode Yes Yes (more mature) IP pool management CRDs Basic (ConfigMap range) Full (IPAddressPool, L2Advertisement, BGPAdvertisement) Recommended for Control-plane HA + simple LB Production LoadBalancer services

docs.title: 7. Shared IPs Across Services
docs.text:
Both tools support multiple services sharing one IP (different ports).

# MetalLB shared IP
metadata:
  annotations:
    metallb.io/allow-shared-ip: "web-group"   # same key = shared IP
---
# Service 1: port 80
# Service 2: port 443
# Both get the same EXTERNAL-IP

docs.title: 8. Production Considerations
docs.text:
# Separate the LB VIP range from node IPs to avoid conflicts
# Node subnet:  192.168.1.0/24
# VIP pool:     192.168.100.0/24  (different subnet, routed via ToR)

# Use BGP mode for production — no single point of failure
# Use L2 mode for dev/lab — simpler, no BGP required

# MetalLB BGP with BFD for fast failover
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta2
kind: BGPPeer
spec:
  bfdProfile: fast-bfd
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BFDProfile
metadata:
  name: fast-bfd
spec:
  receiveInterval: 300    # 300ms
  transmitInterval: 300
  detectMultiplier: 3     # 3 × 300ms = 900ms failure detection

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> after MetalLB install No IPAddressPool or L2Advertisement/BGPAdvertisement created kubectl get ipaddresspools,l2advertisements -n metallb-system Create IPAddressPool and the appropriate Advertisement CRD VIP assigned but unreachable from outside cluster VIP is in a different subnet than clients (L2 mode) or BGP session is not established arping -I eth0 <VIP> from outside; kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l component=speaker | grep bgp For L2: ensure VIP is in same broadcast domain; for BGP: check session with router ARP not responding for VIP Speaker not elected or port security on switch blocking gratuitous ARP kubectl get events -n metallb-system | grep announcing Check speaker pod logs; disable port-security / ARP inspection on the connected switch port BGP session not established Firewall blocking TCP 179 between node and router telnet <router-ip> 179 from node Open TCP 179 on host firewall and network ACLs IP pool exhausted — service stays pending All IPs in pool are allocated kubectl describe ipaddresspool production-pool -n metallb-system Expand pool address range or add a second IPAddressPool Traffic only reaches one pod (L2 mode) L2 mode is single-node ingress; kube-proxy distributes after the node kubectl get pods -o wide -l app=web — all traffic enters one node Accept this limitation for L2; switch to BGP mode with ECMP for true per-node distribution kube-vip leader not switching after node failure Leader lease stuck or ARP cache not refreshed on upstream router kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=kube-vip | grep -E 'leader|VIP' Increase ARP probe frequency in kube-vip config; check upstream router ARP cache timeout

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• VIP address pool configured in a separate subnet from node and pod CIDRs to prevent IP conflicts
  • BGP mode used for production workloads (L2 mode is for dev/lab only — single ingress node is a bottleneck)
  • BGP peer holdTime and keepaliveTime tuned; BFDProfile configured for sub-second failover
  • Switch port security and gratuitous ARP inspection disabled (or explicitly permitted) for nodes running MetalLB speakers
  • IP address pool size planned with headroom — allocating 100% causes new services to stay pending
  • kube-vip deployed for control-plane HA if running a multi-master bare-metal cluster
  • MetalLB speaker resource limits set (DaemonSet pods run on every node — size accordingly)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use L2 mode in production expecting high availability L2 mode is single-node: only one node holds the VIP at a time; failover takes ~10 s and traffic is not distributed across nodes Use BGP mode with ECMP in production for true multi-node load distribution and sub-second failover with BFD Put VIP pool in the same /24 as the node IPs The LB may assign an IP already used by a node or another static device on the subnet Always allocate the VIP pool from a dedicated subnet or range that is not shared with node addresses Forget to open TCP 179 (BGP) on node firewalls BGP sessions never establish; MetalLB speaker logs show repeated connection refused; VIPs stay unannounced Pre-open TCP 179 between all nodes and each BGP peer (ToR switch) in the host firewall before installing MetalLB Use MetalLB and kube-vip for LoadBalancer services simultaneously Both tools race to handle the same Service resources; one or both fail to announce correctly Pick one tool per cluster for LoadBalancer services; kube-vip for control-plane HA can coexist if LoadBalancer mode is disabled in one of them Request a specific IP with metallb.io/loadBalancerIPs without first checking pool availability Service stays pending with an event saying the requested IP is not in any pool Verify the IP is within a configured IPAddressPool range before annotating the Service

docs.title: Quick Reference

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Tool Mode Failover Load Distribution MetalLB L2 ARP/NDP ~10s (leader election) Single node (ingress point) MetalLB BGP BGP routes <1s (with BFD) ECMP across nodes kube-vip ARP/BGP VRRP ~1s Single or ECMP

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does MetalLB L2 mode result in a single ingress node rather than true load balancing, and how does BGP mode solve this?
Answer In L2 mode, MetalLB uses leader election so that exactly one node's speaker answers ARP requests for the VIP. All external traffic therefore enters through that one node, which then uses kube-proxy to forward to pods — the LB layer itself is a single point of ingress. BGP mode solves this by having each speaker on multiple nodes advertise the same /32 host route via BGP; the upstream router installs ECMP routes for the VIP and distributes flows across all announcing nodes, giving true per-node load balancing.
  1. [Scenario question] A LoadBalancer service stays in EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> even after MetalLB pods are running. What two CRDs should you check first?
Answer Check that an `IPAddressPool` exists with a valid address range and that an `L2Advertisement` (or `BGPAdvertisement` for BGP mode) references that pool. Without both CRDs, MetalLB's controller will not allocate an IP or advertise it. Run `kubectl get ipaddresspools,l2advertisements -n metallb-system` to confirm both are present. A missing advertisement CRD is the most common oversight after install.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to find which node is currently announcing a specific VIP in L2 mode?
Answer 
kubectl get events -n metallb-system | grep announcing
Look for event messages of the form `announcing from node worker-X` — the node named in that event is the current elected speaker for the VIP. You can also watch speaker logs with `kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=speaker -f` for real-time announcement events.

docs.title: Practice Setup

# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=LoadBalancer
kubectl describe svc <your-lb-svc> | grep -E "LoadBalancer|Ingress|Annotations"

# Terminal 2 — cloud CLI (optional)
aws elb describe-load-balancers 2>/dev/null | jq '.LoadBalancerDescriptions[].LoadBalancerName' || \
  echo "Configure AWS CLI or use GCP/Azure equivalent"

Observation commands — run after creating a LoadBalancer service to watch the provisioning lifecycle:

# Watch service until EXTERNAL-IP is assigned
kubectl get svc web -w
# Expect: EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> → 203.0.113.100 (takes 30-120 seconds)

# Watch CCM events on the Service object
kubectl describe svc web
# Look for Events:
#   Normal  EnsuredLoadBalancer  Successfully ensured load balancer
#   Warning FailedToEnsure       ...  ← examine this on failure

# Stream CCM logs (shows cloud API calls)
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cloud-controller-manager -f

# AWS: watch NLB target group registration in real time
aws elbv2 describe-target-health \
  --target-group-arn $(aws elbv2 describe-target-groups \
    --query 'TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn' --output text) \
  --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[*].{Target:Target.Id,Health:TargetHealth.State}'

docs.title: Classic Load Balancer (CLB) — legacy
docs.text: Created by default before the AWS Load Balancer Controller.

docs.title: Network Load Balancer (NLB) — L4
docs.text:
Recommended for TCP/UDP. Very high throughput, static IPs.

service:
  type: LoadBalancer
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "external"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip"   # pod IP targets
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internet-facing"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-protocol: "TCP"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-port: "traffic-port"
    # Cross-zone load balancing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"
    # Preserve client IP
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-target-group-attributes: "preserve_client_ip.enabled=true"

docs.title: Application Load Balancer (ALB) — L7
docs.text:
Created via the AWS Load Balancer Controller (Ingress resource).

# Install AWS LBC
helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts
helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set clusterName=my-cluster \
  --set serviceAccount.create=true \
  --set serviceAccount.annotations."eks\.amazonaws\.com/role-arn"=arn:aws:iam::123:role/alb-role

# ALB Ingress
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip      # pod-level targets
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123:certificate/xxx
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP": 80}, {"HTTPS": 443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /healthz
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: "shared-alb"  # share one ALB across Ingresses

docs.text: Target Type Traffic Path Use Case instance LB → NodePort → pod Default; simpler, no VPC CNI requirement ip LB → pod IP directly Lower latency; requires AWS VPC CNI; preserves client IP natively

docs.title: Key AWS Annotations
docs.text: Annotation Default Effect When to change aws-load-balancer-type: "external" "" (CLB) Creates an NLB via AWS LBC Use for all new NLB deployments aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip" "instance" Routes directly to pod IPs Preferred for latency-sensitive workloads with VPC CNI aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internet-facing" "internal" Creates internet-accessible LB Public-facing services aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true" "false" Distributes traffic across all AZs Multi-AZ clusters with uneven pod distribution aws-load-balancer-target-group-attributes: "preserve_client_ip.enabled=true" disabled Preserves real client IP in target group Needed for ip target type to pass client IP to pods

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> indefinitely CCM cannot call cloud API (IAM/RBAC permission missing) kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cloud-controller-manager | grep -i error Attach the required IAM role/policy to the node instance profile or workload identity LB provisioned but traffic does not reach pods Security Group / Firewall rule not allowing health check probe IPs kubectl describe svc <name> → check Events for health check failures Add ingress rule for cloud health check IPs (AWS: 100.64.0.0/10; GCP: 35.191.0.0/16 + 130.211.0.0/22) ExternalTrafficPolicy: Local — some nodes receive no traffic Cloud LB correctly removes nodes where no ready pods exist; uneven pod distribution kubectl get pods -o wide -l <selector> Distribute pods across all nodes (remove nodeSelector/affinity constraints) or switch to Cluster policy AWS NLB: client IP is the node IP, not the real client target-type: instance mode SNATs traffic at the node Check annotation aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type Switch to ip target type; ensure pods have VPC-routable IPs (AWS VPC CNI) AKS internal LB stuck pending Missing subnet annotation for internal LB kubectl describe svc <name> → look for subnet error Add azure-load-balancer-internal-subnet annotation with correct subnet name GKE: LB health checks fail Backend pod readiness probe path differs from health check path kubectl describe backendconfig <name> Add BackendConfig with correct healthCheck.requestPath matching pod readiness probe Cloud LB account limit reached Cloud provider quota on number of LBs (e.g., AWS default 20 CLBs per region) AWS: aws service-quotas list-service-quotas --service-code elasticloadbalancing Request quota increase or consolidate services behind a single Ingress/ALB using group.name

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• NLB target type set to ip for VPC CNI clusters to avoid double-hop through NodePort
  • externalTrafficPolicy: Local used only when client IP preservation is required AND pods are evenly distributed across nodes
  • Cross-zone load balancing enabled for multi-AZ clusters to prevent traffic imbalance during pod scheduling
  • Cloud LB health check path and port configured to match pod readiness probes (use BackendConfig on GKE)
  • Security Groups / Firewall rules explicitly allow cloud health check probe IP ranges to reach all node ports
  • Internal LB used for services that do not need internet exposure (avoid default internet-facing scheme)
  • IAM permissions for the CCM or AWS LBC service account tested in a staging environment before production deployment

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Create a separate LoadBalancer Service for every microservice Each service creates a new cloud LB — costs multiply quickly; AWS default NLB quota is 50/region Expose multiple services through a single Ingress (ALB/NGINX) using path or host routing; use group.name on AWS ALB Use externalTrafficPolicy: Local without ensuring pods on every node Nodes without pods fail LB health checks and receive zero traffic; app appears down on those nodes Only use Local when pods are deployed as DaemonSets or when node pinning is intentional; otherwise use Cluster Leave the default CLB on AWS EKS (no annotations) CLBs are legacy, more expensive, have no cross-zone load balancing by default, and do not support modern target types Always annotate with aws-load-balancer-type: external to get NLB, and specify nlb-target-type: ip Use instance target type on NLB with many pods per node Traffic is DNAT'd to NodePort then kube-proxy picks a random pod — extra hop, SNAT loses client IP, uneven distribution Use ip target type to route directly to pod IPs and preserve client IP Skip the AKS SKU selection (use Basic LB) Azure Basic LB does not support multiple availability zones or outbound rules for large clusters Always create AKS clusters with --load-balancer-sku standard; Basic LB is deprecated

docs.text: Use Case Command List all LoadBalancer services kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=LoadBalancer Watch LB provisioning kubectl get svc <name> -w Check CCM events on a service kubectl describe svc <name> Stream CCM logs kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cloud-controller-manager -f AWS: list all NLBs aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --query 'LoadBalancers[*].{Name:LoadBalancerName,DNS:DNSName}' AWS: check NLB target health aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn> GCP: list forwarding rules gcloud compute forwarding-rules list GKE: check NEG status kubectl describe svc <name> | grep neg Azure: list load balancers az network lb list --resource-group <node-rg> -o table Check externalTrafficPolicy kubectl get svc <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalTrafficPolicy}' Get LB ingress IP/hostname kubectl get svc <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0]}' Patch externalTrafficPolicy kubectl patch svc <name> -p '{"spec":{"externalTrafficPolicy":"Local"}}'

docs.text: Provider L4 LB L7 LB Internal AWS EKS NLB ALB (LBC controller) NLB internal GCP GKE Passthrough NLB Cloud LB (GCE Ingress) ILB Azure AKS Standard LB App Gateway / AGIC Internal SLB Bare metal MetalLB / kube-vip NGINX/Traefik Same (private pool)

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserve the real client IP while externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster does not?
Answer With `Cluster` policy, any node can receive the traffic and kube-proxy SNATs the source IP to the node's own IP before forwarding to a pod on a different node — the original client IP is lost at that SNAT step. With `Local` policy, the cloud LB's health check only marks nodes with ready pods as healthy, so traffic is only sent to nodes that already have a pod; kube-proxy does not SNAT because no cross-node hop is needed. The trade-off is that `Local` can cause uneven distribution if pods are not spread across all nodes.
  1. [Scenario question] An AWS NLB is working but pod logs show the source IP as the EC2 node IP, not the original client IP. Which annotation is most likely misconfigured?
Answer The NLB is using `target-type: instance` mode, which routes through NodePort and kube-proxy, causing SNAT. Switch to `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip"` so the NLB routes directly to pod IPs (bypassing NodePort). You may also need `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-target-group-attributes: "preserve_client_ip.enabled=true"` to ensure the NLB passes the client IP through to the pod.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to watch the progression of an EXTERNAL-IP being assigned to a LoadBalancer service?
Answer 
kubectl get svc web -w
Watch for the `EXTERNAL-IP` column to change from `` to an actual IP or DNS hostname; this transition typically takes 30–120 seconds and is driven by the Cloud Controller Manager calling the cloud provider API to provision the load balancer.
