docs.title: Sidecar Injection + mTLS Handshake Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as kubectl apply
    participant API as API Server
    participant MWC as MutatingWebhook (istiod)
    participant POD as Pod (running)
    participant ISTIOD as istiod CA
    participant ENVOY_A as Envoy A (sidecar)
    participant ENVOY_B as Envoy B (sidecar)

    K->>API: Create pod spec
    API->>MWC: Admission webhook call
    MWC-->>API: Mutated spec + istio-proxy container + init container
    API->>POD: Schedule pod
    POD->>ISTIOD: CSR for SPIFFE cert (spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/frontend)
    ISTIOD-->>POD: X.509 SVID cert issued
    ENVOY_A->>ENVOY_B: TLS ClientHello + SPIFFE cert
    ENVOY_B->>ISTIOD: Verify cert against CA bundle
    ISTIOD-->>ENVOY_B: Valid
    ENVOY_B-->>ENVOY_A: TLS ServerHello + own SPIFFE cert
    ENVOY_A->>ISTIOD: Verify cert against CA bundle
    ISTIOD-->>ENVOY_A: Valid
    ENVOY_A-->>ENVOY_B: mTLS session established — data flows

docs.title: 2. Installation
docs.text:
# Install Istio using istioctl
curl -L https://istio.io/downloadIstio | sh -
export PATH=$PWD/istio-*/bin:$PATH

# Install with default profile
istioctl install --set profile=default -y

# Verify
istioctl verify-install
kubectl get pods -n istio-system
# expect: istiod Running, istio-ingressgateway Running

# Enable sidecar injection for a namespace
kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled

# Check injection is working
kubectl get namespace default --show-labels
# expect: istio-injection=enabled

# Ambient mode installation
istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y
# No sidecar injection needed — ztunnel handles it per-node
kubectl label namespace default istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient

docs.title: 3. mTLS with PeerAuthentication
docs.text:
# Require mTLS for all services in a namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: default
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT     # PERMISSIVE allows plain text too (migration period)

# Verify mTLS is active
istioctl authn tls-check <pod-name>.default
# HOST:PORT                                     STATUS     SERVER     CLIENT
# web.default.svc.cluster.local:80             OK         STRICT     STRICT

# Check certificate used
istioctl proxy-config secret <pod-name>.default
# expect: cert validity, SPIFFE URI in SAN

# See all mTLS CONFLICT states cluster-wide
istioctl authn tls-check --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null | grep CONFLICT
# empty = no conflicts

docs.title: PeerAuthentication Mode Reference
docs.text: Mode Behavior When to use STRICT mTLS only; plain text rejected Full mesh — all sidecars injected PERMISSIVE Accept both mTLS and plain text Migration: external clients still plain DISABLE Plain text only Debug only — never in production

docs.title: 4. AuthorizationPolicy
docs.text:
# Allow only specific services to call the web service
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-allow
  namespace: default
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals:               # service account identity
              - "cluster.local/ns/default/sa/frontend"
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: ["GET", "POST"]
            paths: ["/api/*"]
---
# Default deny everything not explicitly allowed
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: default
spec:
  {}  # empty = deny all

docs.title: VirtualService
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  hosts:
    - web
  http:
    # Canary: route 10% to v2
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: web
            subset: v1
          weight: 90
        - destination:
            host: web
            subset: v2
          weight: 10

    # Fault injection (testing resilience)
    - fault:
        delay:
          percentage:
            value: 10.0
          fixedDelay: 5s
        abort:
          percentage:
            value: 5.0
          httpStatus: 503
      route:
        - destination:
            host: web

    # Retry policy
    - retries:
        attempts: 3
        perTryTimeout: 2s
        retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure
      timeout: 10s
      route:
        - destination:
            host: web

docs.title: DestinationRule
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  host: web
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        h2UpgradePolicy: UPGRADE
        http2MaxRequests: 1000
    outlierDetection:        # circuit breaker
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
  subsets:
    - name: v1
      labels:
        version: v1
    - name: v2
      labels:
        version: v2

docs.title: VirtualService / DestinationRule Key Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change retries.attempts 2 Max retry count Increase for idempotent reads retries.perTryTimeout 25s Timeout per attempt Match upstream SLA outlierDetection.consecutiveGatewayErrors 5 Errors before ejection Lower for fast failover outlierDetection.baseEjectionTime 30s How long host stays ejected Increase for slow recovery connectionPool.tcp.maxConnections 2^32-1 Max TCP connections Set for connection limiting connectionPool.http.http1MaxPendingRequests 2^32-1 Max queued HTTP/1 requests Tune to prevent queue buildup

docs.title: 6. Ingress with Istio Gateway
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: web-gateway
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
    - port:
        number: 443
        name: https
        protocol: HTTPS
      tls:
        mode: SIMPLE
        credentialName: web-tls-cert
      hosts:
        - web.example.com
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: web-vs
spec:
  hosts:
    - web.example.com
  gateways:
    - web-gateway
  http:
    - match:
        - uri:
            prefix: /
      route:
        - destination:
            host: web
            port:
              number: 80

docs.title: 7. Observability
docs.text:
# Install Kiali (topology dashboard), Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/prometheus.yaml
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/grafana.yaml
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/jaeger.yaml
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/kiali.yaml

# Access Kiali (service mesh topology)
istioctl dashboard kiali
# expect: topology graph with traffic flows and mTLS lock icons

# Access Jaeger (distributed tracing)
istioctl dashboard jaeger

# Access Grafana (metrics)
istioctl dashboard grafana

# CLI observability
# Envoy access logs (per sidecar)
kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy | head -20
# expect: JSON log lines with method, path, response_code, upstream_cluster

# Proxy config dump
istioctl proxy-config cluster <pod>.default
# expect: table with FQDN, PORT, SUBSET, DIRECTION, TYPE

istioctl proxy-config listener <pod>.default
# expect: virtual listeners 0.0.0.0:15001 (outbound) and per-port entries

istioctl proxy-config route <pod>.default
# expect: virtual host routing rules

# Check for traffic issues
istioctl analyze   # validates Istio config — reports errors and warnings
# expect: "No validation issues found" or list of issues

kubectl patch svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system \
  --type='json' \

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Sidecar not injected Namespace missing label kubectl get ns <ns> --show-labels kubectl label ns <ns> istio-injection=enabled 503 Service Unavailable mTLS conflict (one side STRICT, other plain) istioctl authn tls-check <pod>.default Add PeerAuthentication PERMISSIVE or inject sidecar in caller upstream connect error DestinationRule subset has no matching pods istioctl proxy-config cluster <pod>.default \| grep <service> Verify label selector in subset matches pod labels Envoy not synced to istiod istiod unavailable or network partition istioctl proxy-status — look for NOT SENT Check kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod AuthorizationPolicy blocking DENY rule or missing ALLOW rule kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy \| grep RBAC Add explicit ALLOW or check principal format High latency after mesh enable Envoy sidecar CPU/memory starved kubectl top pod <pod> --containers Increase values.global.proxy.resources limits Certificate expired SVID cert not rotated istioctl proxy-config secret <pod>.default Restart istiod to force rotation 
# 1. Is sidecar injected?
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep istio-proxy

# 2. Is Istiod healthy?
kubectl get pods -n istio-system
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod | grep -E "WARN|ERROR"

# 3. Is mTLS the problem?
# Temporarily set PERMISSIVE mode
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: default
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: PERMISSIVE
EOF
# If traffic flows now → certificate or policy issue

# 4. Check Envoy configuration
istioctl proxy-config cluster <pod>.default | grep <service-name>

# 5. Enable Envoy access logging
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: access-logging
spec:
  accessLogging:
    - providers:
        - name: envoy
EOF

# 6. Run connectivity test
istioctl experimental envoy-stats <pod>

See also: Lesson 16 — Network Policies for base NetworkPolicy before layering Istio AuthorizationPolicy.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• PeerAuthentication set to STRICT in all application namespaces (not PERMISSIVE)
  • AuthorizationPolicy default-deny applied per namespace before deploying workloads
  • istioctl analyze runs clean in CI — zero errors or warnings
  • Envoy sidecar CPU/memory requests and limits set to prevent noisy-neighbor starvation
  • Distributed tracing (Jaeger/Zipkin) sampling rate tuned — not 100% in high-RPS production
  • Istio ingress gateway has a PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 1
  • Certificate rotation tested — SVID expiry handled without service interruption

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Apply PeerAuthentication STRICT before all pods have sidecars Non-injected pods cannot complete mTLS handshake — 503 errors Enable PERMISSIVE first, verify all pods have sidecar, then switch to STRICT Use namespace-wide deny-all AuthorizationPolicy without allow rules Blocks health checks and monitoring, causing cascading failures Add explicit ALLOW for health check paths and monitoring principals first Deploy VirtualService subsets before DestinationRule is applied Envoy has no subset configuration — 503 on subset routing Apply DestinationRule before or simultaneously with VirtualService Run Istio control plane (istiod) with a single replica istiod failure causes cert rotation and config push to stop Set replicaCount: 2 or more and add PodAntiAffinity Forget to annotate sidecar resource limits Envoy sidecar consumes unbounded CPU — evicts application containers Always set sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPU and proxyCPULimit annotations

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command Check sidecar injection status for all pods istioctl proxy-status Inspect Envoy cluster config for a pod istioctl proxy-config cluster <pod>.default Check mTLS status for a service istioctl authn tls-check <pod>.default Validate all Istio configs istioctl analyze View Envoy access logs kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy Open Kiali topology dashboard istioctl dashboard kiali Check secret/cert for a sidecar istioctl proxy-config secret <pod>.default Enable sidecar injection on namespace kubectl label ns <ns> istio-injection=enabled Temporarily disable mTLS for debugging Apply PeerAuthentication mode: PERMISSIVE Force Envoy config re-push from istiod kubectl rollout restart deployment -n istio-system istiod Get Envoy listener table istioctl proxy-config listener <pod>.default Install observability stack kubectl apply -f samples/addons/

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Feature Istio Mechanism mTLS Envoy sidecar intercepts all traffic, presents SPIFFE cert AuthorizationPolicy Envoy enforces at request time per-service Traffic splitting VirtualService weights Circuit breaker DestinationRule outlierDetection Tracing Envoy propagates B3/W3C trace headers Ambient mode ztunnel (L4) + waypoint (L7), no sidecar

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is the difference between PeerAuthentication modes PERMISSIVE and STRICT, and when should each be used?
Answer `PERMISSIVE` mode accepts both mTLS-encrypted connections and plain-text connections, which allows non-injected clients (such as external services or pods without sidecars) to still communicate during a migration. `STRICT` mode rejects all plain-text — only connections with valid SPIFFE X.509 certificates are accepted. Use `PERMISSIVE` during the rollout period while injecting sidecars into all workloads, then switch to `STRICT` once every pod in the namespace has an injected Envoy sidecar to guarantee end-to-end mTLS.
  1. [Scenario question] After applying PeerAuthentication with mode: STRICT to a namespace, several services start returning 503 errors. What is the most likely cause?
Answer Some caller pods are missing the Istio sidecar — either their namespace does not have the `istio-injection=enabled` label or they were created before the label was applied. Without a sidecar, those pods send plain-text requests that STRICT mode rejects. Run `istioctl authn tls-check .default` to identify CONFLICT rows and `kubectl describe pod | grep istio-proxy` to confirm whether the sidecar was injected. The fix is to label the namespace and restart affected pods to trigger injection.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to verify that mTLS is active and in STRICT mode between a specific pod and the web service?
Answer 
istioctl authn tls-check <pod-name>.default
Look for the row `web.default.svc.cluster.local:80` and confirm the `STATUS` column shows `OK` with both `SERVER` and `CLIENT` columns showing `STRICT`; a `CONFLICT` status means one side is not enforcing mTLS.

docs.title: Lesson 22 — Multi-Cluster Networking
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud | Prerequisites: Lesson 12 — Cilium, Lesson 06 — BGP | Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Connect two Kubernetes clusters with Cilium Cluster Mesh or Submariner and reach services across cluster boundaries using the MCS API.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl with multiple contexts)
kubectl config get-contexts
# expect: list with cluster-1 and cluster-2 entries

kubectl config use-context <cluster-1>
kubectl get pods -A | head -10

# Terminal 2 — Mac (second cluster context)
kubectl config use-context <cluster-2>
cilium clustermesh status 2>/dev/null || echo "Cluster Mesh not enabled on this cluster"
kubectl get serviceimports -A 2>/dev/null || echo "MCS API not installed"

# Verify cross-cluster DNS (MCS)
kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup web.default.svc.clusterset.local 2>/dev/null || echo "MCS DNS not configured"

docs.title: 1. Multi-Cluster Patterns
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Flat["Flat Network"]
        c1a["Cluster A\nPods routable"]
        c1b["Cluster B\nPods routable"]
        c1a <-- "direct pod IP" --> c1b
    end

    subgraph GW["Gateway-Based"]
        c2a["Cluster A"] --> gwa["Egress\nGateway"]
        gwa -- "encrypted tunnel" --> gwb["Ingress\nGateway"]
        gwb --> c2b["Cluster B"]
    end

    subgraph Mesh["Cluster Mesh (Cilium)"]
        c3a["Cluster A\neBPF + etcd"]
        c3b["Cluster B\neBPF + etcd"]
        c3a <-- "shared identity\nglobal service" --> c3b
    end

    style Flat fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
    style GW fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
    style Mesh fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
Pattern Description Use Case Flat network Pod IPs routable across clusters Same VPC, low latency Gateway-based Traffic goes through ingress/egress gateways Different VPCs, encrypted Service mirroring Service objects mirrored across clusters East-west service discovery Cluster Mesh Full interconnect with shared identity Cilium native DNS-based federation DNS routes to nearest healthy cluster Geo-distributed apps

docs.title: 2. Multi-Cluster Services API (MCS)
docs.text:
The Kubernetes Multi-Cluster Services API (SIG-Multicluster KEP-1645) provides a standard for cross-cluster service export/import.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CA as Cluster A
    participant Ctrl as MCS Controller
    participant CB as Cluster B
    participant DNS as DNS (clusterset.local)

    CA->>CA: Create ServiceExport "web"
    CA->>Ctrl: Notify: web is exported
    Ctrl->>CB: Create ServiceImport "web"
    CB->>DNS: Register web.default.svc.clusterset.local
    CB->>CA: DNS query for web.default.svc.clusterset.local
    CA-->>CB: Returns ClusterSetIP
    CB->>CA: Traffic via ClusterSetIP
# In cluster A — export a service
apiVersion: multicluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ServiceExport
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
---
# In cluster B — import it
apiVersion: multicluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ServiceImport
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
spec:
  type: ClusterSetIP
  ports:
    - port: 80
      protocol: TCP

# DNS name for imported service:
# web.default.svc.clusterset.local
kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup web.default.svc.clusterset.local
# expect: returns a ClusterSetIP address (virtual IP)

docs.title: MCS API Parameter Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change ServiceImport.spec.type ClusterSetIP Virtual IP for cross-cluster LB Use Headless for direct pod routing ServiceExport annotation multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service auto Maps to derived ClusterIP service Do not modify manually DNS domain clusterset.local Search domain for cross-cluster names Configured in DNS operator

docs.title: 3. Cilium Cluster Mesh
docs.text:
Cilium's Cluster Mesh connects clusters so pods can communicate using their cluster-internal pod IPs and DNS names.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ClusterA["Cluster A"]
        cilA["Cilium Agent"]
        etcdA["etcd / KVStore"]
        cilA --> etcdA
    end
    subgraph ClusterB["Cluster B"]
        cilB["Cilium Agent"]
        etcdB["etcd / KVStore"]
        cilB --> etcdB
    end
    etcdA <-- "clustermesh-apiserver\nTLS mutual auth" --> etcdB
    cilA -- "eBPF policy + routing" --> cilB

    style ClusterA fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style ClusterB fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
# Enable Cluster Mesh on cluster A
cilium clustermesh enable \
  --service-type LoadBalancer
cilium clustermesh status --wait
# expect: "Cluster Mesh: OK"

# Connect cluster B to cluster A
# (run with context pointing to cluster A)
cilium clustermesh connect \
  --destination-context cluster-b \
  --source-context cluster-a

# Verify mesh is connected
cilium clustermesh status
# Cluster A ←→ Cluster B  CONNECTED
# expect: "Global services: N" showing shared services count

# Share a service globally (available in all mesh clusters)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    service.cilium.io/global: "true"
    service.cilium.io/shared: "true"   # include this cluster's endpoints
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80

# Global service load balances across all clusters
# Affinity to local cluster:
annotations:
  service.cilium.io/global: "true"
  service.cilium.io/affinity: "local"   # prefer local cluster, fall back cross-cluster

docs.title: Cilium Cluster Mesh Parameter Reference
docs.text: Annotation / Parameter Default Effect When to change service.cilium.io/global "false" Make service visible across all mesh clusters Set "true" for HA global services service.cilium.io/shared "false" Include this cluster's endpoints in global LB Set "true" to contribute backends service.cilium.io/affinity "none" Prefer local ("local") or remote ("remote") endpoints Use "local" to reduce cross-region latency clustermesh.cilium.io/global-service — Alternative annotation form Same as service.cilium.io/global

docs.title: Primary-Remote Model
docs.text:
One cluster has the control plane; remote clusters use it.

# Install Istio on primary cluster
istioctl install --set profile=default \
  --set values.pilot.env.EXTERNAL_ISTIOD=true

# Install remote cluster config
istioctl install --set profile=remote \
  --set values.global.remotePilotAddress=<primary-pilot-ip>

docs.title: Multi-Primary (Recommended for HA)
docs.text:
Each cluster runs its own Istiod.

# Step 1: Create a shared root CA
# (both clusters must trust the same root)

# Step 2: Install Istio on cluster 1
istioctl install -f cluster1.yaml

# Step 3: Install Istio on cluster 2
istioctl install -f cluster2.yaml

# Step 4: Cross-cluster east-west gateway
kubectl apply -n istio-system -f eastwest-gateway.yaml

# Step 5: Expose services for cross-cluster discovery
istioctl x create-remote-secret \
  --context=cluster1 \
  --name=cluster1 | kubectl apply --context=cluster2 -f -

# Services become reachable via their FQDN across clusters
# Verify remote clusters registered:
istioctl remote-clusters
# expect: cluster1 and cluster2 listed as CONNECTED

docs.title: 5. Submariner
docs.text:
Submariner provides direct pod-to-pod connectivity between clusters using encrypted tunnels.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ClusterA["Cluster A"]
        podA["Pod A\n10.244.1.5"]
        gwA["Gateway Node\n(subctl)"]
        podA --> gwA
    end
    subgraph Broker["Broker Cluster"]
        broker["Broker CRD\n(discovery)"]
    end
    subgraph ClusterB["Cluster B"]
        gwB["Gateway Node\n(subctl)"]
        podB["Pod B\n10.244.2.7"]
        gwB --> podB
    end

    gwA -- "IPsec/WireGuard\nencrypted tunnel" --> gwB
    gwA <-- "register endpoints" --> broker
    gwB <-- "register endpoints" --> broker

    style ClusterA fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
    style ClusterB fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
    style Broker fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
# Install subctl CLI
curl -Ls https://get.submariner.io | bash

# Deploy broker (coordinates cluster registration)
subctl deploy-broker --kubeconfig broker-cluster.kubeconfig

# Join cluster A
subctl join broker-info.subm --kubeconfig cluster-a.kubeconfig \
  --clusterid cluster-a \
  --natt-discovery-port 4900 \
  --globalnet   # if pod CIDRs overlap

# Join cluster B
subctl join broker-info.subm --kubeconfig cluster-b.kubeconfig \
  --clusterid cluster-b \
  --globalnet

# Verify connectivity
subctl verify --kubeconfig cluster-a.kubeconfig --toconfig cluster-b.kubeconfig
# expect: all connectivity checks PASS

# Export service for cross-cluster access
subctl export service --namespace default web
# Creates ServiceExport → Lighthouse DNS resolves across clusters
# DNS: web.default.svc.clusterset.local

docs.title: 6. AWS Multi-Cluster (EKS)
docs.text:
# Option 1: VPC Peering — flat network, pod IPs routable
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection \
  --vpc-id vpc-cluster-a \
  --peer-vpc-id vpc-cluster-b

# Update route tables in both VPCs
aws ec2 create-route \
  --route-table-id rtb-xxxxxx \
  --destination-cidr-block 10.1.0.0/16 \
  --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-xxxxxx

# Option 2: AWS Transit Gateway — hub-and-spoke for many VPCs
aws ec2 attach-vpc-to-transit-gateway \
  --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxxxx \
  --vpc-id vpc-cluster-a

# Option 3: AWS VPC Lattice (new, service-level)
# Service-to-service connectivity without VPC peering

docs.title: 7. GCP Multi-Cluster (GKE)
docs.text:
# GKE Hub — register clusters to a fleet
gcloud container hub memberships register cluster-a \
  --gke-cluster us-central1/cluster-a

gcloud container hub memberships register cluster-b \
  --gke-cluster us-east1/cluster-b

# Enable Multi-Cluster Services
gcloud container hub multi-cluster-services enable

# Enable Multi-Cluster Ingress
gcloud container hub ingress enable \
  --config-membership=cluster-a

# MultiClusterIngress resource (deployed to config cluster)
apiVersion: networking.gke.io/v1
kind: MultiClusterIngress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      backend:
        serviceName: web
        servicePort: 80

docs.title: 8. Overlapping Pod CIDRs Problem
docs.text:
When clusters have overlapping pod CIDRs (common in independent deployments), you need NAT or Globalnet.

Cluster A: pods 10.244.0.0/16
Cluster B: pods 10.244.0.0/16  ← SAME CIDR

Solution 1: Globalnet (Submariner)
  — Each cluster gets a unique global CIDR
  — Pods are SNATed to the global CIDR for cross-cluster traffic

Solution 2: Service-based communication only
  — Expose services, not pods — services have cluster-unique IPs

Solution 3: Re-IP pods (if possible)
  — Reinitialize clusters with non-overlapping CIDRs

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix cilium clustermesh status shows DISCONNECTED TLS cert mismatch or network block on port 2379 cilium clustermesh status --wait; kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/clustermesh-apiserver Regenerate clustermesh secrets: cilium clustermesh enable --service-type LoadBalancer Cross-cluster pod unreachable but service works Pod CIDR overlaps, Globalnet needed subctl diagnose all Re-join with --globalnet flag Hubble shows no cross-cluster flows Hubble relay not reaching remote cluster hubble observe --from-cluster cluster-b Verify clustermesh status and Hubble relay ports Istio remote cluster shows ERROR Shared root CA mismatch or remote secret expired istioctl remote-clusters Rotate remote secret: istioctl x create-remote-secret MCS DNS (clusterset.local) not resolving MCS controller not installed or ServiceExport missing kubectl get serviceexport -A; kubectl get serviceimport -A Install MCS controller, verify ServiceExport exists in source cluster Submariner tunnel flapping UDP 4500/4490 (IPsec) blocked between gateway nodes subctl show connections; subctl diagnose firewall inter-cluster Open UDP 4490, 4500, 4800 between gateway node IPs 
# Cilium Cluster Mesh
cilium clustermesh status
# Check "Clusters" section for CONNECTED status

hubble observe --from-cluster cluster-b   # cross-cluster flows

# Istio
istioctl remote-clusters   # check registered remote clusters
istioctl proxy-config cluster <pod> | grep cluster-b

# Submariner
subctl show connections
subctl show endpoints
subctl diagnose all   # comprehensive health check

# DNS cross-cluster
# MCS: nslookup web.default.svc.clusterset.local
# Cilium: nslookup web.default.svc.cluster.local (global service)
# Submarine: nslookup web.default.svc.clusterset.local (Lighthouse)

See also: Lesson 21 — Istio for Istio multi-cluster east-west gateway configuration. Lesson 23 — Network Security Hardening for encrypting cross-cluster tunnels.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Pod CIDRs are non-overlapping across all clusters — or Globalnet is enabled
  • Cross-cluster traffic is encrypted (WireGuard in Cilium, IPsec in Submariner, mTLS in Istio)
  • Cluster identity verification in place — certificates from shared CA or per-cluster identity
  • Global services have service.cilium.io/affinity: local to avoid unnecessary cross-region traffic
  • MCS ServiceExport resources are version-controlled and reviewed before deployment
  • Failover behavior tested: shut down one cluster's endpoints and verify traffic shifts
  • Cross-cluster DNS TTL is low enough for fast failover (≤30s)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Expose all services as global without affinity Every request potentially crosses regions — high latency and cost Only export services that genuinely need cross-cluster HA; set affinity: local Use overlapping pod CIDRs without Globalnet Pod IP collisions make routing ambiguous — traffic goes to wrong cluster Plan non-overlapping CIDRs at day zero or enable Globalnet in Submariner Share a single root CA between clusters without rotation plan Compromised CA affects all clusters simultaneously Use intermediate CAs per cluster, rotate quarterly Deploy MCS controller without RBAC review ServiceExport allows any namespace to expose services to other clusters Restrict ServiceExport creation to cluster-admins or dedicated operators Rely only on DNS for cross-cluster health detection Stale DNS cache serves dead endpoints during outage Combine DNS failover with health-check-based endpoint removal

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What DNS suffix does the Multi-Cluster Services (MCS) API use for cross-cluster service discovery, and what two objects must exist before the DNS name resolves?
Answer Cross-cluster services resolve under the `clusterset.local` domain — for example, `web.default.svc.clusterset.local`. Two objects must exist: a `ServiceExport` in the source cluster (which signals that the service should be shared) and a corresponding `ServiceImport` in the destination cluster (which the MCS controller creates automatically). Without the ServiceExport in the originating cluster, the MCS controller never notifies other clusters, so the ServiceImport and DNS record are never created.
  1. [Scenario question] A Cilium Cluster Mesh shows DISCONNECTED between cluster-a and cluster-b even though both clusters are running. What port and protocol should you verify is open between nodes?
Answer The Cluster Mesh API server uses TCP port 2379 (etcd) for the clustermesh-apiserver mutual TLS connection between clusters. If a firewall or security group blocks TCP 2379 between the node IPs of the two clusters, the mesh will show DISCONNECTED. Run `kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/clustermesh-apiserver` to see TLS or connection refused errors, and open TCP 2379 bidirectionally between the clusters' node CIDR ranges.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check whether two Cilium Cluster Mesh-connected clusters are CONNECTED and how many global services are shared?
Answer 
cilium clustermesh status
Look for lines showing each connected cluster with status `CONNECTED` and a count of `Global services: N`; a `DISCONNECTED` or `PENDING` state indicates an API server reachability or certificate issue that needs further investigation.

docs.title: Lesson 23 — Network Security Hardening
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud | Prerequisites: Lesson 16 — Network Policies, Lesson 21 — Istio | Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Apply layered network security controls — default-deny policies, metadata API blocks, encrypted transit, and runtime enforcement — that satisfy PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark requirements.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl — audit current posture)
kubectl get netpol -A

kubectl get peerauthentication -A 2>/dev/null || echo "Istio not installed"

docs.title: 2. Default Deny Network Policies
docs.text:
Start with deny-all and explicitly allow required traffic.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant NS as Namespace (production)
    participant NP as NetworkPolicy engine
    participant Pod as Pod

    Dev->>NS: Apply default-deny-all policy
    NS->>NP: Ingress DENY all, Egress DENY all
    Dev->>NS: Apply allow-dns-egress policy
    NP->>Pod: DNS port 53 egress ALLOWED
    Dev->>NS: Apply allow-healthchecks policy
    NP->>Pod: Ingress from kube-system ALLOWED
    Dev->>NS: Apply app-specific allow rules
    NP->>Pod: Specific ingress/egress ALLOWED
    Note over NP,Pod: Default position: DENY unless explicitly ALLOWED
# Namespace-level default deny
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
---
# Allow only DNS egress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - ports:
        - port: 53
          protocol: UDP
        - port: 53
          protocol: TCP
---
# Allow health check probes from kube-system
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-healthchecks
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system

docs.title: NetworkPolicy Parameter Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change podSelector: {} Selects ALL pods Policy applies namespace-wide Use label selector for per-app granularity policyTypes: [Ingress] Only ingress controlled Egress remains open Always add Egress to policyTypes for full control namespaceSelector Not set (any namespace) Restricts by namespace labels Required for cross-namespace allow rules ipBlock.except Not set Allow all IPs in CIDR Use to carve out cloud metadata API port: 53, protocol: UDP UDP DNS Allow DNS resolution Add TCP 53 for large DNS responses

docs.title: 3. Block Cloud Metadata API
docs.text:
The cloud metadata API (169.254.169.254) exposes credentials and configuration. Block it from pods.

# Block access to cloud metadata service
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-metadata-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except:
              - 169.254.169.254/32   # AWS/GCP/Azure metadata
              - 169.254.170.2/32     # AWS ECS metadata

# Verify block works
kubectl run -it --rm test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
# expect: connection timed out (or refused) — NOT a valid metadata response

# Verify DNS still works after block
kubectl run -it --rm dns-test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
# expect: resolves successfully (DNS egress port 53 is still open)

docs.title: Cilium WireGuard
docs.text:
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --reuse-values \
  --set encryption.enabled=true \
  --set encryption.type=wireguard \
  --set encryption.nodeEncryption=true   # encrypt node-to-node too

# Verify encryption
cilium encrypt status
# Encryption: Wireguard
# Keys in use: 1
# expect: all nodes show WireGuard active

docs.title: Calico WireGuard
docs.text:
kubectl patch felixconfiguration default \
  --type='merge' \
  -p '{"spec":{"wireguardEnabled":true}}'

# Verify
kubectl get node <node> -o yaml | grep wireguard
calicoctl node status | grep WireGuard
# expect: "WireGuard: Active" per node

docs.title: Istio mTLS
docs.text:
# Enforce strict mTLS cluster-wide
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: istio-system   # applies to all namespaces
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

docs.title: Encryption Method Comparison
docs.text: Method Layer Scope Key Management Performance Cost WireGuard (Cilium/Calico) L3 Node-to-node Automatic per-node keys ~3-5% CPU overhead IPsec (Cilium/Submariner) L3 Node-to-node Manual or operator-managed ~5-8% CPU overhead Istio mTLS L7 Pod-to-pod istiod CA (SPIFFE) Envoy sidecar overhead TLS (application) L7 Service-to-service App-managed certs Minimal if hardware offloaded

docs.title: 5. Egress Control with FQDN Policies
docs.text:
Cilium allows restricting outbound traffic to specific domain names.

apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-external-apis
  namespace: production
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: worker
  egress:
    - toFQDNs:
        - matchName: "api.github.com"
        - matchPattern: "*.amazonaws.com"
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "443"
              protocol: TCP

# Verify FQDN policy is active
kubectl exec -it -n production worker-pod -- curl -v https://api.github.com
# expect: HTTP 200 — allowed by FQDN policy

kubectl exec -it -n production worker-pod -- curl -v https://evil.example.com
# expect: connection refused or timeout — not in FQDN allowlist

Calico also supports DNS-based policy in Enterprise edition.

docs.title: 6. Pod Security and Network Interaction
docs.text:
Kubernetes PodSecurity Admission enforces security at the pod level, which complements network controls.

# Apply baseline security to a namespace
kubectl label namespace production \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

# Restricted: prevents hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged
kubectl label namespace production \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

Network-relevant pod spec hardening: 

spec:
  hostNetwork: false       # don't share host network namespace
  hostPID: false           # don't share host PID namespace
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
  containers:
    - name: app
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
          add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]  # only if binding ports < 1024

docs.title: PodSecurity Level vs Network Risk
docs.text: Level hostNetwork hostPID Privileged Net Risk privileged Allowed Allowed Allowed Critical — bypasses all pod-level controls baseline Blocked Blocked Blocked Moderate — container escape still possible restricted Blocked Blocked Blocked Low — combined with NetworkPolicy = strong

docs.title: 7. Audit Logging for Network Events
docs.text:
# Cilium flow audit (all denied flows)
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces -o json | \
  jq '{src: .flow.source.pod_name, dst: .flow.destination.pod_name,
       dport: .flow.l4.TCP.destination_port, verdict: .flow.verdict}'
# expect: JSON lines showing blocked flows — use to build allow rules

# Tetragon network audit
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents --event-types PROCESS_ACCEPT,PROCESS_CONNECT -o json
# expect: process-level network events including binary path and args

# kube-apiserver audit log — network policy changes
kubectl get events --all-namespaces | grep NetworkPolicy

docs.title: 8. Network Security Checklist Automation
docs.text:
# 1. Default deny policies in all namespaces
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
  count=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -n $ns 2>/dev/null | grep deny | wc -l)
  echo "$ns: $count deny policies"
done
# expect: each namespace shows ≥1 deny policy

# 2. Pod → metadata API is blocked
kubectl run -it --rm meta-test --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/
# expect: timeout

# 3. Encryption is active
cilium encrypt status   # for Cilium/WireGuard
# expect: "Encryption: Wireguard" and "Keys in use: 1"

# 4. mTLS is enforced (Istio)
istioctl authn tls-check --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null | grep CONFLICT
# expect: empty — no CONFLICT rows

# 5. No hostNetwork pods (except system components)
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces \
  -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostNetwork == true) |
    .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name'
# expect: only kube-system / openshift-* components

# 6. No pods with excessive capabilities
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces \
  -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities.add // empty'
# expect: empty or only NET_BIND_SERVICE

# 7. Egress to internet is controlled
kubectl run -it --rm egress-test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -m 5 https://ifconfig.me
# expect: timeout (if egress blocked) or only expected exit IPs

docs.text:
Requirement Kubernetes Control PCI-DSS 1.2 NetworkPolicy: segment cardholder data environment PCI-DSS 4.1 Istio/Calico mTLS: encrypt cardholder data in transit HIPAA NetworkPolicy + mTLS: isolate PHI workloads SOC 2 Audit logs: Hubble + Tetragon for network events CIS Benchmark Default deny policies, no hostNetwork for user pods

# 5.3.2 Ensure all namespaces have network policies

# Automated scan with kube-bench
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/main/job.yaml
kubectl logs -f job.kube-bench | grep -A3 "5.3"
# expect: PASS for 5.3.1 and 5.3.2

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Pods can't do DNS after default-deny Missing allow-dns-egress NetworkPolicy kubectl exec pod -- nslookup kubernetes Apply allow-dns-egress policy (port 53 UDP+TCP) Health checks failing after deny-all Kubelet probe traffic blocked from kube-system kubectl describe pod <pod> \| grep Events Add ingress from namespaceSelector: kube-system WireGuard not encrypting between nodes Kernel < 5.6 (no built-in WireGuard) or module missing cilium encrypt status Upgrade kernel or use IPsec fallback Tetragon not capturing events eBPF program not loaded or kernel too old kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/tetragon Check kernel version ≥ 4.19 for eBPF support FQDN egress policy allows wrong IPs DNS cache poisoning or stale entry kubectl exec pod -- nslookup api.github.com and compare to Cilium's cached IPs Add fromEndpoints restriction and flush Cilium DNS cache PodSecurity restricted blocks all pods Pods not compliant (privileged, hostNetwork, etc.) kubectl describe pod <pod> \| grep "violates PodSecurity" Add runAsNonRoot, drop ALL capabilities, remove hostNetwork Hubble shows flows but no drop verdicts PeerAuthentication in PERMISSIVE — policy not enforced kubectl get peerauthentication -A Switch to STRICT after confirming all sidecars injected

See also: Lesson 16 — Network Policies for base NetworkPolicy syntax. Lesson 21 — Istio for mTLS STRICT enforcement.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Default-deny NetworkPolicy applied in every application namespace before workloads deploy
  • Metadata API (169.254.169.254) blocked via ipBlock.except in egress policy
  • Node-to-node encryption enabled (WireGuard in Cilium/Calico or IPsec in Submariner)
  • Istio PeerAuthentication set to STRICT cluster-wide (not per-namespace permissive)
  • pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted on all application namespaces
  • Hubble or Tetragon audit log exported to SIEM for network event retention
  • kube-bench run on all nodes — CIS checks 5.3.1 and 5.3.2 pass

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Apply default-deny without testing first Breaks DNS, monitoring, and health checks immediately Use hubble observe --verdict DROPPED to discover required flows before enforcing Encrypt only pod-to-pod traffic, not node-to-node Host-level processes (kubelet, CNI) still send plain traffic on the wire Enable nodeEncryption: true in Cilium WireGuard config Use PERMISSIVE mTLS permanently No actual encryption guarantee — legacy clients silently bypass mTLS Set a migration deadline; switch to STRICT within sprint Block metadata API only in default namespace Pods in other namespaces still reach metadata API Apply deny-metadata-api NetworkPolicy in every namespace or use Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy Run Tetragon/Hubble but never export to SIEM Audit data only lives in ephemeral pod logs — lost on restart Configure Hubble to export to Kafka/Elasticsearch; Tetragon to Falco/Splunk

docs.text: Control Tool What It Prevents Default deny NetworkPolicy Lateral movement Metadata block NetworkPolicy (ipBlock except) Credential theft FQDN egress Cilium CiliumNetworkPolicy Exfiltration Encryption WireGuard / mTLS Eavesdropping Pod security PodSecurity Admission hostNetwork bypass Audit Hubble / Tetragon Detecting incidents

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why must you explicitly add a DNS egress policy (allowing port 53 UDP and TCP) when deploying a default-deny NetworkPolicy, and what breaks if you omit it?
Answer A default-deny policy with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` and an empty `podSelector: {}` blocks all outbound traffic including DNS queries to CoreDNS. Without an explicit allow for UDP port 53 (and TCP port 53 for large responses), pods cannot resolve any service names — `nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local` will hang or return SERVFAIL. The allow-dns-egress policy must target `0.0.0.0/0` (or specifically the CoreDNS ClusterIP) on ports 53 UDP and TCP, and must be applied in the same namespace simultaneously with or before the deny-all policy.
  1. [Scenario question] A penetration tester demonstrates that a pod in the production namespace can query the cloud metadata API at 169.254.169.254 and retrieve an IAM role credential. What NetworkPolicy construct blocks this while still allowing all other internet egress?
Answer Use an `ipBlock` with an `except` clause in an egress NetworkPolicy: allow `cidr: 0.0.0.0/0` with `except: [169.254.169.254/32]` (and also `169.254.170.2/32` for AWS ECS metadata). This allows egress to all destinations except the metadata API addresses. Apply this policy with `podSelector: {}` to cover all pods in the namespace, and include it in every application namespace — not just the default namespace.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to see all currently dropped network flows across all namespaces in real time?
Answer 
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces
Each output line shows the source pod, destination pod, destination port, and the drop reason (such as `POLICY_DENIED`); use this to identify which flows are being blocked so you can build the precise allow rules needed before enforcing a default-deny posture.

docs.title: Lesson 24 — Network Observability and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud | Prerequisites: All previous lessons — this is the capstone | Duration: ~3 hours

Goal: Diagnose any Kubernetes network failure — from pod unreachability to DNS timeouts — using a structured L1-to-L7 methodology and tools including Hubble, netshoot, tcpdump, and Prometheus metrics.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — minikube Linux node
minikube ssh
ss -s           # socket summary — total established/closed counts
ss -tlnp        # listening TCP sockets with process names
conntrack -L 2>/dev/null | head -10  # conntrack table — expect: NAT entries

# Terminal 2 — Mac (kubectl + hubble)
hubble observe --last 20 2>/dev/null || echo "hubble not running — try: cilium hubble enable"
kubectl run netshoot --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it --restart=Never -- bash
# expect: bash prompt inside netshoot — all network debug tools available

docs.title: 1. Systematic Troubleshooting Methodology
docs.text:
Work from the bottom of the stack up:

flowchart TD
    L1["L1/L2: Physical / Link\nNIC up? Interface up? veth wired?"]
    L3["L3: IP\nRoute correct? ip_forward on? MTU ok?"]
    L4["L4: TCP/UDP\nconntrack full? iptables blocking?"]
    L7["L7: Application\nDNS resolving? TLS cert valid? HTTP 200?"]
    K8S["Kubernetes\nService exists? Endpoint healthy? NetworkPolicy denying?"]
    CNI["CNI\nPod IP assigned? veth wired? IPAM exhausted?"]

    L1 --> L3 --> L4 --> L7 --> K8S --> CNI

    style L1 fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
    style L3 fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style L4 fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
    style L7 fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
    style K8S fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#E91E63
    style CNI fill:#e0f2f1,stroke:#009688

The golden rule: confirm each layer before moving up. Don't start at Kubernetes if you haven't confirmed the node NIC is up.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Eng as Engineer
    participant Node as Node
    participant CNI as CNI (Cilium/Calico)
    participant K8S as Kubernetes API
    participant App as Application

    Eng->>Node: ip link / ss / ping gateway
    Node-->>Eng: L2/L3 OK or FAIL
    Eng->>CNI: cilium status / calicoctl node status
    CNI-->>Eng: CNI OK or FAIL
    Eng->>K8S: kubectl get ep / netpol / svc
    K8S-->>Eng: Service+Endpoint present or missing
    Eng->>App: nslookup / curl -v
    App-->>Eng: DNS resolved / HTTP status
    Note over Eng,App: Stop at first layer that fails — fix before proceeding up

docs.title: 2. The Diagnostic Pod
docs.text:
Keep a debug pod manifest ready:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: netshoot
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
    - name: netshoot
      image: nicolaka/netshoot
      command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: "node-to-debug"  # pin to specific node

# Or one-liner:
kubectl run -it --rm netshoot --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
# expect: bash prompt with curl, nslookup, tcpdump, ss, traceroute, iperf3

# In the same network namespace as a running pod:
kubectl debug -it <pod-name> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container-name>
# expect: shares network namespace of target — same IP, same routes

# nsenter trick (from node — sees pod network namespace):
NODE_PID=$(kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
# SSH to node, find PID:
crictl inspect $(crictl ps | grep <pod-name> | awk '{print $1}') | jq '.info.pid'
nsenter -n -t <PID> -- ss -tlnp
# expect: socket table from inside the pod

docs.title: 3. Pod Connectivity Checklist
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: Pod A cannot reach Pod B

# Step 1: Can Pod A reach its own gateway?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -c3 $(ip route | grep default | awk '{print $3}')
# expect: 0% packet loss

# Step 2: Can Pod A reach Pod B's IP directly?
POD_B_IP=$(kubectl get pod pod-b -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -c3 $POD_B_IP
# If fail → routing or NetworkPolicy issue

# Step 3: Is there a NetworkPolicy blocking traffic?
# Check policies selecting pod-a (egress) and pod-b (ingress)
kubectl get networkpolicy -n default -o yaml | grep -A10 "podSelector"
# Use Cilium policy trace:
cilium policy trace --src-pod default/pod-a --dst-pod default/pod-b --dport 80
# expect: "Final verdict: allowed" or "Final verdict: denied — reason: ..."

# Step 4: Is the route present?
NODE=$(kubectl get pod pod-b -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}')
# SSH to node
ssh $NODE
ip route get $POD_B_IP
# expect: a valid route showing the veth or tunnel interface

# Step 5: Cross-node — is VXLAN/BGP working?
# Check CNI status
calicoctl node status   # or: cilium status
# expect: BGP peer state Established, VXLAN/WireGuard active

# Step 6: Packet capture
# On pod-b's node:
tcpdump -i any -n host $POD_B_IP
# expect: ICMP packets arriving from Pod A's IP

docs.title: 4. Service Connectivity Checklist
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: Pod cannot reach Service

# Step 1: Does the service exist?
kubectl get svc web -n default
# expect: ClusterIP shows an IP address (not <none>)

# Step 2: Does it have endpoints?
kubectl get endpoints web -n default
# expect: IP:port entries — if empty: selector doesn't match pods or pods not Ready
kubectl describe endpoints web -n default
# shows notReadyAddresses if pods are failing health checks

# Step 3: Is the DNS name resolving?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup web.default.svc.cluster.local
# expect: returns ClusterIP address
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup web   # short name
# expect: same result via search domain

# Step 4: Is the ClusterIP reachable?
CLUSTER_IP=$(kubectl get svc web -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- curl -v http://$CLUSTER_IP:80
# expect: HTTP response — if fails: iptables DNAT rule missing

# Step 5: Are iptables DNAT rules present?
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep $CLUSTER_IP
# expect: rule with "/* web/default:http cluster IP */"

# Step 6: Is kube-proxy running and healthy?
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy | tail -20
# expect: "Syncing iptables rules" messages without ERROR

docs.title: 5. DNS Troubleshooting
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: DNS lookups failing or slow

# Step 1: Can pod reach CoreDNS?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nc -vzu 10.96.0.10 53
# expect: "open" (UDP) — if fails: NetworkPolicy blocking CoreDNS

# Step 2: Does a simple lookup work?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
# expect: returns 10.96.0.1 (or configured API server ClusterIP)

# Step 3: Enable CoreDNS query logging
kubectl edit cm -n kube-system coredns
# Add: log  (inside the .:53 { block)
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n kube-system coredns

# Watch queries
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -f | grep -v "NOERROR"
# expect: each query logged — look for NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL

# Step 4: Check ndots behavior
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# expect: "ndots:5" — means short names trigger 5 search domain tries before bare lookup
# high ndots:5 → many fallback queries for external names

# Step 5: Check CoreDNS metrics
kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/kube-dns 9153:9153 &
curl -s http://localhost:9153/metrics | grep coredns_dns_request_duration
# expect: histogram buckets with 95th percentile < 5ms for healthy DNS

# Step 6: Check for conntrack UDP race condition
# (symptom: 5-second DNS timeouts)
dmesg | grep "nf_conntrack: table full"
# if present: conntrack exhaustion is causing DNS drops
sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count
sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
# expect: count < 80% of max

docs.title: 6. Latency Investigation
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: High latency between pods

# Step 1: Baseline measurement
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- \
  for i in $(seq 10); do curl -w "%{time_total}\n" -o /dev/null -s http://web; done
# expect: p99 < 5ms for in-cluster pod-to-pod on modern hardware

# Step 2: Check for packet loss
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -c100 -f $POD_B_IP
# "%" column shows packet loss
# expect: 0% loss for healthy cluster

# Step 3: MTU mismatch (causes fragmentation → latency)
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -M do -s 1422 $POD_B_IP  # VXLAN
# If "Message too long" → MTU mismatch
# Check effective MTU
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
# expect: 1450 (VXLAN) or 1360 (WireGuard over VXLAN) or 1500 (native)

# Step 4: CPU throttling on pods (affects packet processing)
kubectl top pod pod-a
kubectl describe pod pod-a | grep -A5 "Limits\|Requests"
# expect: CPU usage well below limits — high throttling causes tail latency

# Step 5: conntrack contention
# High conntrack lookup latency on busy nodes:
cat /proc/net/stat/nf_conntrack
# expect: low "searched" vs "found" ratio

# Step 6: Node CPU for network interrupts
# On node:
watch -n1 'cat /proc/interrupts | grep -E "eth0|mlx5"'
# expect: interrupts spread evenly across CPUs (RSS/multi-queue working)

docs.title: 7. Packet Capture Techniques
docs.text:
# Capture on a specific pod's veth (from the host)
# First, find the veth
POD_ID=$(kubectl get pod pod-a -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
# Find matching veth on node:
ip link show | grep -i cali
# Then capture:
tcpdump -i cali1234abcd -n -w /tmp/pod-a.pcap
# expect: raw packets — open in Wireshark to decode

# Capture inside pod
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- tcpdump -i eth0 -n -w /tmp/capture.pcap
# Copy out:
kubectl cp pod-a:/tmp/capture.pcap ./pod-a.pcap
# expect: pcap file on local disk

# ksniff — kubectl plugin for pod packet capture
kubectl sniff pod-a -n default -o ./pod-a.pcap
# expect: live capture piped to Wireshark (requires krew install sniff)

# Capture VXLAN encapsulated traffic (between nodes)
tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 -w /tmp/vxlan.pcap
# expect: UDP frames with inner IP headers visible in Wireshark

# View in Wireshark
# wireshark ./pod-a.pcap
# or analyze with tshark:
tshark -r pod-a.pcap -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e tcp.dstport
# expect: columns showing inner IP flow src/dst/port

docs.title: 8. Hubble — Flow-Level Observability
docs.text:
# Install Hubble CLI
curl -L --fail --remote-name-all \
  https://github.com/cilium/hubble/releases/download/v0.13.0/hubble-linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar xzvf hubble-linux-amd64.tar.gz
mv hubble /usr/local/bin/

# Forward Hubble relay
cilium hubble port-forward &

# Watch all flows
hubble observe
# expect: stream of src → dst flows with verdict (FORWARDED/DROPPED)

# Watch denied flows (policy violations)
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces
# expect: flows that NetworkPolicy or Istio AuthorizationPolicy blocked

# Flow for specific pod
hubble observe --from-pod default/frontend --to-pod default/backend
# expect: flows between those two pods with HTTP method and status

# Count flows per destination
hubble observe --all-namespaces -o json | \
  jq -r '.flow | .destination.namespace + "/" + .destination.pod_name' | \
  sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
# expect: top-N pods by received flow count

# HTTP flows
hubble observe --protocol http --all-namespaces | head -20
# expect: HTTP method, path, response code for each flow

# Service connectivity map (Hubble UI)
cilium hubble ui
# expect: browser opens at localhost:12000 with service topology graph

docs.title: Hubble Key Metrics
docs.text: Metric PromQL What it shows Total drop rate rate(cilium_drop_count_total[5m]) Policy drops per second Drop by reason sum by (reason) (rate(cilium_drop_count_total[5m])) Why traffic is dropped iptables rule count felix_iptables_rules_total Calico iptables rule count conntrack entries node_nf_conntrack_entries Current conntrack table usage DNS error rate rate(coredns_dns_responses_total{rcode!="NOERROR"}[5m]) CoreDNS failures

docs.title: 9. Key Metrics to Monitor
docs.text:
# Kubernetes network metrics (from kube-state-metrics + node-exporter)
# In Prometheus/Grafana:

# Node network throughput
rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total{device="eth0"}[5m])
rate(node_network_transmit_bytes_total{device="eth0"}[5m])
# expect: matches expected app traffic patterns

# Network errors
rate(node_network_receive_errs_total[5m])
rate(node_network_transmit_errs_total[5m])
# expect: near-zero; spikes indicate hardware/driver issues

# conntrack usage
node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit
# expect: < 0.8 (80%) — above this DNS and new connections start dropping

# DNS query rate
rate(coredns_dns_requests_total[5m])
# baseline this per-pod for capacity planning

# DNS error rate
rate(coredns_dns_responses_total{rcode!="NOERROR"}[5m])
# expect: near-zero; NXDOMAIN spike = broken service names

# kube-proxy sync latency
rate(kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])
# expect: < 100ms p99; spikes correlate with iptables rule churn

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Pod can't ping pod NetworkPolicy block or missing route cilium policy trace --src-pod ns/a --dst-pod ns/b --dport 80 Add NetworkPolicy allow rule or fix CNI route Pod can't reach service No endpoints or kube-proxy not synced kubectl get endpoints <svc>; iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n \| grep <clusterIP> Fix pod readiness probe or restart kube-proxy DNS timeout (5s) conntrack UDP race or CoreDNS crash dmesg \| grep conntrack; kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns Increase conntrack table size or scale CoreDNS replicas Intermittent connections conntrack table exhausted cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count vs max sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=524288 High latency MTU fragmentation (VXLAN overhead ignored) ping -M do -s 1422 <pod-ip> Lower pod MTU to 1450 for VXLAN or 1360 for WireGuard LoadBalancer pending CCM not installed or cloud IAM insufficient kubectl describe svc <svc> \| grep Events Install cloud CCM or grant IAM role for LB provisioning BGP not established TCP/179 blocked or ASN mismatch calicoctl node status \| grep BGP; telnet <peer> 179 Open TCP 179 and verify peer ASN config VXLAN drops UDP/4789 blocked on firewall or MTU exceeded tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 Open UDP 4789 and set CNI MTU to 1450

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Hubble or equivalent flow exporter deployed and exporting to centralized log store
  • Prometheus alerts configured for cilium_drop_count_total and node_nf_conntrack_entries
  • netshoot (or equivalent debug image) added to cluster image pull policy allowlist
  • ss -tlnp and conntrack -L available on nodes — conntrack-tools package installed
  • MTU set correctly for CNI overlay (1450 VXLAN, 1360 WireGuard+VXLAN) — not default 1500
  • CoreDNS scaled to minimum 2 replicas with PodAntiAffinity across nodes
  • Network troubleshooting runbook stored in team wiki with this lesson's methodology

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Start troubleshooting at Kubernetes layer (services, policies) Lower layers (MTU, routing, CNI) may be broken — Kubernetes can't fix a missing route Always start at L1/L2 and work up: NIC → route → conntrack → K8s Use kubectl exec curl as the only test Passes through kube-proxy DNAT — hides raw routing issues Also test pod-IP directly and use tcpdump on the node Run tcpdump without specifying interface Captures loopback and all interfaces — overwhelming noise Always specify -i cali1234 (veth) or -i eth0 udp port 4789 Ignore MTU for overlay networks 1500-byte packets are fragmented in VXLAN tunnels — silent performance loss Calculate: physical MTU (1500) − VXLAN header (50) = 1450 max pod MTU Assume DNS failure = CoreDNS issue conntrack table exhaustion or NetworkPolicy blocking DNS are more common Check dmesg \| grep conntrack and netpol before touching CoreDNS config

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command Watch denied flows real-time hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces Trace Cilium policy decision cilium policy trace --src-pod ns/pod-a --dst-pod ns/pod-b --dport 80 Check service endpoints kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns> Verify ClusterIP DNAT rule iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n \| grep <clusterIP> Capture pod traffic from node tcpdump -i cali<veth> -n -w /tmp/out.pcap Check conntrack table usage cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count Test DNS resolution from pod kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup <svc>.default.svc.cluster.local Inspect socket table inside pod kubectl exec -it pod -- ss -tlnp Run netshoot debug pod kubectl run -it --rm netshoot --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash Debug in target pod network ns kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container> Check MTU fragmentation kubectl exec -it pod -- ping -M do -s 1422 <dest-ip> View Hubble service topology cilium hubble ui

docs.title: Summary and Graduation
docs.text:
You have covered the full Kubernetes networking stack:

Lessons 01-04: Linux primitives — namespaces, veth, routing, iptables
Lessons 05-06: Overlay networks and BGP
Lessons 07-08: Bare metal infrastructure and cloud provider networking
Lesson  09:    CNI specification
Lessons 10-11: Calico and Cilium — the two dominant CNIs
Lessons 12-13: Services and DNS — the discovery layer
Lesson  14:    Network Policies — microsegmentation
Lessons 15-16: Ingress and Gateway API — L7 traffic
Lessons 17-18: Load balancers — bare metal and cloud
Lesson  19:    Istio service mesh
Lesson  20:    eBPF/XDP — the kernel layer
Lesson  21:    IPv6 and dual-stack
Lesson  22:    Multi-cluster networking
Lesson  23:    Security hardening
Lesson  24:    Observability and troubleshooting ← you are here

You can now trace a packet from a pod's application socket all the way to its destination across any infrastructure — and diagnose where it breaks.

See also: Lesson 23 — Network Security Hardening for Hubble verdict filtering to build security policies. Lesson 21 — Istio for istioctl proxy-config and Envoy access log troubleshooting.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does the L1-to-L7 troubleshooting methodology require confirming each layer before moving up, rather than starting at the Kubernetes service layer where the symptom is visible?
Answer Higher-layer Kubernetes components (Services, NetworkPolicies, kube-proxy) depend on lower-layer correctness — if a route is missing or a veth pair is not wired to the OVS bridge, no amount of Kubernetes-level fixes will restore connectivity. Starting at L1/L2 (interface up, veth connected) and L3 (route present, ip_forward enabled) rules out the most fundamental issues before you spend time debugging iptables rules or Kubernetes endpoints that are actually fine. The golden rule is: confirm each layer is working before moving up, so you stop at the first layer that fails.
  1. [Scenario question] DNS lookups from a pod occasionally time out with exactly a 5-second delay. CoreDNS pods are running and healthy. What two root causes should you check first?
Answer The two most common causes of 5-second DNS timeouts in Kubernetes are: (1) conntrack table exhaustion — when the nf_conntrack table is full, new UDP connections (including DNS queries) are dropped silently and the client waits for the timeout; check with `dmesg | grep "nf_conntrack: table full"` and compare `nf_conntrack_count` to `nf_conntrack_max`. (2) The conntrack UDP race condition with parallel DNS queries on the same socket — the kernel can SNAT both A and AAAA queries to the same 5-tuple and drop one; check CoreDNS logs for `NXDOMAIN` or timeout patterns, and consider setting `ndots:3` or enabling NodeLocal DNSCache.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to watch all denied network flows across the entire cluster in real time?
Answer 
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces
Each line shows the source and destination pod names, namespace, destination port, and drop reason (such as `POLICY_DENIED` or `UNSUPPORTED_L3_PROTOCOL`); use this output to identify which flows are being blocked and by what policy, then work down the stack with `cilium policy trace` or `tcpdump` if the reason is not a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: Lesson 25 — OpenShift Networking Overview
docs.text:
Track: OpenShift Networking | Prerequisites: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification, Lesson 12 — Services | Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Understand how OpenShift's Cluster Network Operator manages OVN-Kubernetes, explain how OpenShift namespace isolation differs from vanilla Kubernetes, and use oc commands to inspect and troubleshoot network configuration.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — OpenShift CLI (oc)
oc get network.operator cluster -o yaml | grep -A10 defaultNetwork
# expect: type: OVNKubernetes, clusterNetwork, serviceNetwork fields

oc get pods -n openshift-network-operator
# expect: network-operator pod Running

oc get clusternetwork 2>/dev/null
# only present in legacy OpenShiftSDN clusters

# Terminal 2 — oc
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes | head -10
# expect: ovnkube-node DaemonSet pods per node, ovnkube-master pods

oc get hostsubnet 2>/dev/null || echo "OVN-Kubernetes mode (no hostsubnet)"
# hostsubnet only exists in OpenShiftSDN legacy mode

docs.title: 1. OpenShift vs Vanilla Kubernetes Networking
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Vanilla["Vanilla Kubernetes"]
        v_cni["CNI: User Choice\n(Calico/Cilium/Flannel)"]
        v_ing["Ingress: Ingress API\n(nginx/traefik/etc)"]
        v_np["NetworkPolicy: Optional\n(no default isolation)"]
        v_eg["Egress: via CNI\n(no built-in EgressIP)"]
    end

    subgraph OCP["OpenShift"]
        o_cni["CNI: OVN-Kubernetes\n(default, managed by CNO)"]
        o_ing["Ingress: Route CRD\n+ HAProxy Router"]
        o_np["NetworkPolicy: Enforced\n(namespace isolation default)"]
        o_eg["Egress: EgressIP + EgressFirewall\n(CRDs)"]
    end

    style Vanilla fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
    style OCP fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#E91E63
Feature Vanilla Kubernetes OpenShift Default CNI None (you choose) OVN-Kubernetes Ingress Ingress API Route CRD + HAProxy Router NetworkPolicy Optional Enforced by default (namespace isolation) Egress control Via CNI EgressIP, EgressFirewall CRDs DNS CoreDNS CoreDNS (same) Load Balancer Cloud CCM / MetalLB Same + MetalLB on bare metal Security PodSecurity Admission Security Context Constraints (SCCs) SDN history N/A OpenShift SDN (deprecated) → OVN-Kubernetes Network config entry point Edit CNI configs directly Edit network.operator.openshift.io CR only Pod CIDR default 10.244.0.0/16 (kubeadm) 10.128.0.0/14 Service CIDR default 10.96.0.0/12 (kubeadm) 172.30.0.0/16

docs.title: 2. OpenShift Network Operator (CNO)
docs.text:
OpenShift manages its network configuration through the Cluster Network Operator (CNO). You never edit CNI configs directly — you edit the Network.operator.openshift.io custom resource.

flowchart TD
    Admin["oc edit network.operator.openshift.io/cluster"]
    CNO["Cluster Network Operator\n(openshift-network-operator)"]
    OVN_DS["ovnkube-node DaemonSet\n(openshift-ovn-kubernetes)"]
    OVN_Master["ovnkube-master Deployment\n(NB DB + SB DB + ovn-northd)"]
    OVS["OVS (ovs-vswitchd)\nbr-int bridge per node"]
    OVN_CTRL["ovn-controller\n(translates logical → physical flows)"]

    Admin --> CNO
    CNO -- "manages" --> OVN_DS
    CNO -- "manages" --> OVN_Master
    OVN_DS --> OVS
    OVN_DS --> OVN_CTRL
    OVN_Master -- "NB→SB sync" --> OVN_CTRL

    style Admin fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
    style CNO fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
    style OVN_DS fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style OVN_Master fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
sequenceDiagram
    participant Admin as Cluster Admin
    participant CNO as Cluster Network Operator
    participant OVN_N as ovn-northd (control plane)
    participant OVN_C as ovn-controller (node)
    participant OVS as OVS br-int (node)

    Admin->>CNO: Edit network.operator CR (e.g. change MTU)
    CNO->>OVN_N: Update NorthBound DB logical topology
    OVN_N->>OVN_C: Compile logical flows → SouthBound DB
    OVN_C->>OVS: Program OpenFlow rules on br-int
    OVS-->>Admin: New MTU active on all nodes
    Note over CNO,OVS: Never edit OVS or OVN directly — CNO will overwrite
# View current network configuration
oc get network.operator.openshift.io cluster -o yaml
# Key fields:
# spec.defaultNetwork.type: OVNKubernetes
# spec.clusterNetwork: pod CIDR
# spec.serviceNetwork: service CIDR
# spec.networkType: OVNKubernetes

# View the cluster-level network config (read-only summary)
oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster -o yaml
# status.clusterNetwork:
#   - cidr: 10.128.0.0/14
#     hostPrefix: 23          ← /23 per node = 512 pods max per node
# status.serviceNetwork:
#   - 172.30.0.0/16
# status.networkType: OVNKubernetes
# expect: matches install-config.yaml values set at cluster creation

docs.title: CNO / OVN-Kubernetes Key Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change spec.defaultNetwork.type OVNKubernetes Active CNI plugin Set at install time only — migration requires maintenance window spec.clusterNetwork[].cidr 10.128.0.0/14 Pod IP CIDR Set at install time — cannot change post-install spec.clusterNetwork[].hostPrefix 23 Subnet size per node Smaller = more nodes; larger = more pods per node spec.serviceNetwork 172.30.0.0/16 ClusterIP range Set at install time only spec.defaultNetwork.ovnKubernetesConfig.mtu 1400 (Geneve) Pod network MTU Lower if physical MTU < 1450 (e.g. VPN overhead) spec.defaultNetwork.ovnKubernetesConfig.genevePort 6081 UDP tunnel port Change if 6081 is blocked

docs.title: 3. Default Pod and Service CIDRs
docs.text:
OpenShift uses different default CIDRs from vanilla Kubernetes:

Pod CIDR:      10.128.0.0/14   (4 × /16 blocks)
Service CIDR:  172.30.0.0/16
Node prefix:   /23             (512 IPs per node)

Each node gets a /23 from the pod CIDR: 

Node 1: 10.128.0.0/23   (pods 10.128.0.1 – 10.128.1.254)
Node 2: 10.128.2.0/23
Node 3: 10.128.4.0/23
...


# See per-node pod CIDR allocations
oc get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.podCIDRs}{"\n"}{end}'
# expect: each node shows its /23 subnet

# Verify service CIDR
oc get svc kubernetes -n default -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'
# expect: 172.30.0.1 (or first IP in service CIDR)

docs.title: 4. Namespace Network Isolation
docs.text:
OpenShift enforces namespace isolation by default using NetworkPolicy. When you create a namespace, OpenShift automatically creates policies that: - Allow traffic within the same namespace - Deny traffic from other namespaces - Allow ingress from the router namespace - Allow ingress from the monitoring namespace

# View auto-created NetworkPolicies
oc get networkpolicy -n my-namespace
# NAME                                    POD-SELECTOR   AGE
# allow-from-openshift-ingress            <none>         5m
# allow-from-openshift-monitoring         <none>         5m
# allow-same-namespace                    <none>         5m
# expect: these three policies in every new namespace

# Verify traffic between namespaces is blocked by default
# (without an explicit allow policy)
oc exec -it -n namespace-a pod-a -- curl -m5 http://<pod-b-ip>
# expect: timeout (blocked by auto-created isolation policy)

To allow traffic between namespaces: 

# Allow namespace B to receive from namespace A
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-namespace-a
  namespace: namespace-b
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: namespace-a

docs.title: 5. OpenShift DNS
docs.text:
CoreDNS is used but configured via the DNS operator:

# View DNS operator config
oc get dns.operator.openshift.io default -o yaml
# expect: spec.servers empty (no custom upstream) by default

# Custom upstream DNS servers
oc edit dns.operator.openshift.io default
# spec:
#   servers:
#     - name: corporate-dns
#       zones:
#         - corp.example.com
#       forwardPlugin:
#         upstreams:
#           - 10.100.0.53
# expect: CoreDNS CoreFile updated automatically by DNS operator

# DNS service (runs on each node via NodeLocal DNSCache)
oc get svc -n openshift-dns
# dns-default   ClusterIP   172.30.0.10   53/UDP,53/TCP

# NodeLocal cache address: 10.0.0.10 (or the node's local DNS cache)
# Verify pods use the local cache:
oc exec -it pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# expect: nameserver 172.30.0.10 (or NodeLocal DNSCache IP)

docs.title: 6. OpenShift Monitoring Network
docs.text:
OpenShift's built-in monitoring stack (Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana) lives in openshift-monitoring and needs network access to scrape all pods.

# Check monitoring pods
oc get pods -n openshift-monitoring
# expect: prometheus-k8s, alertmanager-main, grafana pods Running

# NetworkPolicy allows monitoring ingress automatically
oc get networkpolicy -A | grep monitoring
# expect: "allow-from-openshift-monitoring" in every namespace

# Check monitoring scrape targets
oc port-forward -n openshift-monitoring svc/prometheus-k8s 9090
# Browse to localhost:9090 → Status → Targets
# expect: all namespace/pod targets UP

docs.title: 7. OpenShift SDN (Legacy — Deprecated)
docs.text:
Before OVN-Kubernetes, OpenShift used its own SDN plugin with three modes:

Mode Description subnet Flat network, no isolation between namespaces multitenant Per-namespace VXLAN VNI — full isolation networkpolicy NetworkPolicy API — selective isolation 
# Check if a cluster still uses OpenShift SDN (older clusters)
oc get network.operator.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.defaultNetwork.type}'
# OpenShiftSDN  ← legacy
# OVNKubernetes ← current

# expect: OVNKubernetes on any cluster >= 4.12

Migration from OpenShift SDN to OVN-Kubernetes is supported but requires a maintenance window.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does OpenShift manage OVN-Kubernetes through the Cluster Network Operator (CNO) rather than allowing administrators to edit CNI configuration files directly on nodes?
Answer The CNO acts as the single source of truth for network configuration: it continuously reconciles the `network.operator.openshift.io/cluster` custom resource against the actual state of OVN pods, ConfigMaps, and node settings. If you edit OVS or OVN files directly on a node, the CNO's next reconciliation loop will overwrite your changes. This design ensures consistency across all nodes, makes upgrades safe (the CNO knows how to roll out new OVN versions), and prevents configuration drift that would be impossible to audit through GitOps.
  1. [Scenario question] A pod in namespace-a cannot reach a pod in namespace-b even though both pods are running. No custom NetworkPolicies have been created. What three auto-created NetworkPolicies does OpenShift place in every new namespace, and which one is preventing this traffic?
Answer OpenShift automatically creates `allow-same-namespace` (allows traffic within the same namespace), `allow-from-openshift-ingress` (allows the HAProxy router to reach pods), and `allow-from-openshift-monitoring` (allows Prometheus scraping). The policy preventing cross-namespace traffic is the absence of any explicit allow between namespaces — `allow-same-namespace` only permits intra-namespace traffic, and there is no auto-created policy that allows arbitrary cross-namespace traffic. Add a NetworkPolicy in `namespace-b` with a `namespaceSelector` allowing ingress from `namespace-a`.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check the current CNI type, pod CIDR, and service CIDR of an OpenShift cluster?
Answer 
oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster -o yaml
Look for `status.networkType` (should be `OVNKubernetes`), `status.clusterNetwork[].cidr` (default `10.128.0.0/14` with `/23` host prefix), and `status.serviceNetwork` (default `172.30.0.0/16`); these values are set at install time and cannot be changed post-install.
