docs.title: Lesson 26 — OVN-Kubernetes: OpenShift's Default CNI
docs.text:
Track: OpenShift Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 25 — OpenShift Networking Overview, Lesson 03 — iptables Duration: ~3 hours

Goal: Inspect the OVN/OVS control and data planes on a live OpenShift cluster, trace a packet from source pod to destination pod, and explain how NetworkPolicy is enforced without iptables.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — verify OVN-Kubernetes is running
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -o wide
# Expect: ovnkube-node on every node, ovnkube-master on control-plane nodes

# Terminal 2 — open a node debug shell (keep open throughout)
oc debug node/<worker-node-name>
# Inside: chroot /host

# Terminal 3 — exec into ovnkube-master for northbound commands
MASTER=$(oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -l app=ovnkube-master \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
echo "Master pod: $MASTER"

See also: Lesson 03 — iptables and Netfilter for why OVN replaces iptables entirely.

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Control["Control Plane (master nodes)"]
        NB["OVN Northbound DB\nLogical switches, routers, ACLs, LBs"]
        NORTHD["ovn-northd\n(translates logical → physical)"]
        SB["OVN Southbound DB\nChassis bindings, flows, BFD"]
    end
    subgraph Node1["Worker Node 1"]
        OC1["ovn-controller\n(reads SB, programs OVS)"]
        OVS1["OVS br-int\n(kernel flow tables)"]
        POD1["Pod A\nveth → OVS port"]
    end
    subgraph Node2["Worker Node 2"]
        OC2["ovn-controller"]
        OVS2["OVS br-int"]
        POD2["Pod B\nveth → OVS port"]
    end
    NB --> NORTHD --> SB
    SB --> OC1 --> OVS1 --- POD1
    SB --> OC2 --> OVS2 --- POD2
    OVS1 -- "Geneve tunnel\nport 6081" --> OVS2

Components per worker node: - ovn-controller — reads Southbound DB, programs OVS flows - ovs-vswitchd — OVS daemon implementing the dataplane - ovsdb-server — OVS local database

Components on control-plane nodes only: - ovn-northd — translates logical network to physical bindings - nbdb — OVN Northbound database (logical topology) - sbdb — OVN Southbound database (physical topology)

docs.title: 2. OVN-Kubernetes Pods in OpenShift
docs.text:
# View OVN-Kubernetes pods — confirm all Running
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -o wide
# NAME                          NODE           STATUS
# ovnkube-node-aaaaa            worker-1       Running   <- per worker node
# ovnkube-node-bbbbb            worker-2       Running
# ovnkube-master-ccccc          master-1       Running   <- control-plane only

# Check health (any non-Running pods are a problem)
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes | grep -v Running

# Inspect individual containers in ovnkube-node
oc get pod -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $OVNNODE \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'
# ovn-controller ovs-vswitchd ovsdb-server ovnkube-node

docs.title: 3. The OVS Bridge (br-int)
docs.text:
Each node has an OVS integration bridge (br-int) that connects all pods and handles all forwarding:

# From the node debug shell (chroot /host):
ovs-vsctl show
# Bridge "br-int"
#   Port eeb73ac0d1e3789      <- pod veth port (hex = iface ID)
#       Interface eeb73ac0d1e3789
#   Port k8s-worker-1
#       Interface k8s-worker-1  <- node's own port
#   Port patch-br-int-to-breth0_worker-1
#       Interface patch-br-int-to-breth0_worker-1
#           type: patch          <- connects to external bridge

# List ports with their OF port numbers
ovs-vsctl list-ports br-int

# Show OpenFlow tables (actual forwarding rules — 1000s of entries)
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | wc -l       # count
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | head -30    # first few rules

# Show all OVS interfaces with metadata
ovs-vsctl list Interface | grep -E "^name|external_ids|ofport" | head -40

docs.title: 4. Logical Network Topology
docs.text:
OVN creates a virtual topology mirroring Kubernetes objects — changes to pods/services trigger updates here:

# View entire logical network (run against master pod)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl show | head -60
# switch <uuid> (egressip-no-reroute-node-subnets)
# switch <uuid> (node-local-switch)
#     port node-local-switch-to-join ...
# router <uuid> (ovn_cluster_router)
#     port rtoj-ovn_cluster_router ...

# List logical switches (one per node + cluster-wide switches)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl ls-list

# List logical routers
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl lr-list
# <uuid> (ovn_cluster_router)   <- routes between all nodes/pods
# <uuid> (GR_worker-1)          <- gateway router per node

# List load balancers (each Service = one LB entry)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl lb-list | head -20
# <uuid>  None   tcp    10.96.0.1:443 = 192.168.0.5:6443,...

# View Southbound DB — physical chassis bindings
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-sbctl show | head -40

docs.title: 5. Pod Traffic Flow — Same Node
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PA as Pod A<br/>10.128.0.5
    participant OVS as OVS br-int<br/>(flow tables)
    participant PB as Pod B<br/>10.128.0.6

    PA->>OVS: Ethernet frame via veth
    Note over OVS: Table 0: in_port match<br/>Table 8: IP destination<br/>Action: direct output
    OVS->>PB: Frame via pod-b veth
    Note over PA,PB: No tunnel, no routing —<br/>same OVS bridge

docs.title: 6. Pod Traffic Flow — Cross-Node (Geneve Tunnel)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PA as Pod A<br/>10.128.0.5 (Node1)
    participant OVS1 as OVS Node1<br/>br-int
    participant TUN as Geneve Tunnel<br/>UDP port 6081
    participant OVS2 as OVS Node2<br/>br-int
    participant PB as Pod B<br/>10.128.2.5 (Node2)

    PA->>OVS1: veth frame
    Note over OVS1: Flow: route via ovn_cluster_router<br/>Encapsulate with Geneve header<br/>Outer src: Node1 IP, dst: Node2 IP<br/>Tunnel key (VNI) encodes metadata
    OVS1->>TUN: UDP/Geneve encapsulated
    TUN->>OVS2: Delivered to Node2
    Note over OVS2: Decapsulate<br/>Match inner dst IP<br/>Output to pod-b port
    OVS2->>PB: Frame via veth
# Verify Geneve tunnels exist on a node
ip link show type geneve     # Geneve tunnel interfaces
ovs-vsctl list-ports br-int | grep -i tun

# Confirm Geneve port (6081) is open between nodes
ss -ulnp | grep 6081

# View tunnel endpoints in OVN Southbound DB
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-sbctl list Encap | grep -E "ip|type"

docs.title: 7. NetworkPolicy Implementation — OVN ACLs
docs.text:
OVN implements NetworkPolicy using ACLs in the Northbound DB — not iptables. ovn-northd compiles ACLs → Southbound logical flows → ovn-controller programs OVS.

# Find the logical switch for a namespace
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl ls-list | grep production

# View ACLs on that switch (derived from NetworkPolicy objects)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl acl-list <ls-name> | head -20
# to-lport  1000 (ip4 && ip4.dst == 10.128.1.5 && tcp.dst == 80) allow-related
# to-lport  0    (ip4 && ip4.dst == {10.128.1.5}) drop   <- default deny

# Count total ACLs in the cluster
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl find ACL | grep -c "^_uuid"

# Trace what happens to a specific packet (ovn-trace — no actual traffic)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-trace <ls-name> \
  'inport == "pod-a-port"; ip4; ip4.src=10.128.0.5; ip4.dst=10.128.1.5; tcp; tcp.dst=80'
# output: "Policy drop" or "output to pod-b-port"

ACL to NetworkPolicy mapping: | NetworkPolicy field | OVN ACL field | |---------------------|--------------| | podSelector | ip4.src / ip4.dst match on port | | namespaceSelector | address set for namespace pod IPs | | ports | tcp.dst == X or udp.dst == X | | policyType: Ingress | to-lport direction | | policyType: Egress | from-lport direction |

docs.title: Local Gateway Mode (default OpenShift 4.10+)
docs.text: Egress traffic leaves via each node's own interface. Preserves pod source IPs for external traffic. Recommended.

docs.title: Shared Gateway Mode (legacy)
docs.text:
All external traffic routes through master nodes. Single bottleneck. Not recommended for production.

# Check current gateway mode
oc get network.operator.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.defaultNetwork.ovnKubernetesConfig.gatewayConfig}'
# {"routingViaHost": true}   <- local gateway (recommended)
# {"routingViaHost": false}  <- shared gateway (legacy)

# Change to local gateway (rolling restart of ovnkube-node pods)
oc patch network.operator.openshift.io cluster \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"defaultNetwork":{"ovnKubernetesConfig":{"gatewayConfig":{"routingViaHost":true}}}}}'

docs.title: 9. IPsec Encryption
docs.text:
OVN-Kubernetes supports transparent IPsec encryption for all Geneve tunnel traffic between nodes. No application changes required.

# Enable IPsec (takes 10-15 min — rolls out per node)
oc patch network.operator.openshift.io cluster \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"defaultNetwork":{"ovnKubernetesConfig":{"ipsecConfig":{"mode":"Full"}}}}}'

# Check IPsec pod status
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes | grep ipsec

# Verify IPsec is active on a node
oc debug node/<node> -- chroot /host \
  ip xfrm state | head -20
# src 192.168.0.1 dst 192.168.0.2
#     proto esp ... <- IPsec ESP state

# Check OVS certificate used for IPsec
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes ovnkube-node-xxxxx -- \
  ovs-vsctl get Open_vSwitch . other_config:certificate

docs.title: 10. Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change gatewayConfig.routingViaHost false (shared) Routes egress via node NIC vs master Set true for local gateway in production ipsecConfig.mode Disabled Encrypts Geneve tunnels with IPsec ESP Enable for compliance (PCI, HIPAA) mtu auto-detected Overlay MTU (subtract Geneve overhead ~50B) Lower if jumbo frames unavailable hybridOverlayConfig.enabled false Allows Windows nodes using VXLAN hybrid Enable for mixed Linux/Windows clusters v4InternalSubnet 100.64.0.0/16 Transit subnet for OVN join switch Change only if 100.64.x conflicts egressIPConfig.reachabilityTotalTimeoutSeconds 1 Time to detect EgressIP node failure Lower for faster HA failover

docs.title: 11. OVN-Kubernetes vs Other CNIs
docs.text: Feature OVN-Kubernetes Calico Cilium Dataplane OVS flow tables iptables / eBPF eBPF Policy engine OVN ACLs Felix (iptables/eBPF) eBPF Encapsulation Geneve (port 6081) VXLAN / IPIP / None VXLAN / Geneve / None Load balancing OVN logical LB kube-proxy / eBPF eBPF Observability ovn-trace, OVS flows Calico flow logs Hubble OpenShift default Yes Optional Optional Kernel dependency OVS module iptables / kmod eBPF verifier

  ovn-appctl -t ovn-controller connection-status

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• All ovnkube-node pods Running on every worker node — zero CrashLoopBackOff
  • All ovnkube-master pods Running on control-plane nodes with no restarts in 24 h
  • Geneve UDP port 6081 allowed between all node security groups / firewall rules
  • Gateway mode set to routingViaHost: true (local gateway) for production traffic
  • IPsec enabled if workloads are subject to data-in-transit compliance requirements

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Edit OVS flows directly with ovs-ofctl mod-flows ovn-controller overwrites manual flows on next reconcile All changes go through OVN NB via operator (network.operator.openshift.io) Delete OVN pods to "restart networking" NBDB or SBDB pod restart triggers full re-sync — brief outage on all nodes Restart only the specific container (ovn-controller) when needed Mix shared and local gateway mode expectations Shared gateway NATs egress through masters; local gateway does not — source IPs differ Pick one mode at cluster install time; migration requires rolling restart Allow only TCP 6081 for Geneve Geneve uses UDP — TCP 6081 does nothing Allow UDP 6081 between all node IPs Expect iptables -L to show NetworkPolicy rules OVN uses ACLs + OVS flows, not iptables — iptables is empty Use ovn-nbctl acl-list and ovs-ofctl dump-flows

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail Data plane Open vSwitch (OVS) flow tables — kernel module Control plane OVN: Northbound DB → ovn-northd → Southbound DB → ovn-controller Encapsulation Geneve tunnels between nodes (UDP port 6081) NetworkPolicy Compiled to OVN ACLs — no iptables involved Services OVN Logical Load Balancers (DNAT in flow tables) Encryption IPsec transparent mode over Geneve tunnels Configuration Via Cluster Network Operator — never edit OVS/OVN directly Packet tracing ovn-trace for logical simulation; ovs-appctl ofproto/trace for dataplane

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] How does OVN-Kubernetes enforce NetworkPolicy without using iptables, and what is the control-plane path from a NetworkPolicy object to an enforced flow rule?
Answer OVN-Kubernetes compiles NetworkPolicy objects into OVN ACLs stored in the Northbound database. `ovn-northd` reads those ACLs and translates them into logical flows in the Southbound database. Each node's `ovn-controller` reads the Southbound DB and programs OpenFlow rules into the OVS `br-int` bridge. The result is that packet filtering happens in the OVS kernel dataplane flow tables — `iptables -L` shows no NetworkPolicy rules because they are enforced entirely within OVS, not netfilter.
  1. [Scenario question] Cross-node pod-to-pod traffic fails but pods on the same node can communicate. What port and protocol must be open between all nodes, and how would you verify it is the issue?
Answer OVN-Kubernetes uses Geneve tunnels on **UDP port 6081** for cross-node encapsulation. If a firewall or security group blocks UDP 6081 between nodes, intra-node traffic (which stays on the OVS bridge without tunneling) works fine while cross-node traffic silently drops. Verify by running `ss -ulnp | grep 6081` on a node to confirm the port is listening, and use `tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 6081` on both nodes to check whether tunnel packets are arriving. The fix is to open UDP 6081 bidirectionally between all node IPs.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to simulate a packet from pod-a to pod-b on port 8080 without sending real traffic, to see whether OVN ACLs would allow or drop it?
Answer 
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-trace <ls-name> \
  'inport=="pod-a-port"; ip4; ip4.src=10.128.0.5; ip4.dst=10.128.1.5; tcp; tcp.dst=8080'
The output shows each logical flow table that the simulated packet passes through; look for `output to pod-b-port` for an allow result or `Policy drop` / `drop` for a deny result, which tells you which ACL matched.

docs.title: Lesson 27 — OpenShift Routes and HAProxy Router
docs.text:
Track: OpenShift Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers, Lesson 25 — OpenShift Overview Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Create edge, passthrough, and reencrypt Routes on OpenShift, configure a custom IngressController for router sharding, and read HAProxy backend stats to diagnose a 503 error.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — verify router is running and has an external IP
oc get pods -n openshift-ingress
oc get svc -n openshift-ingress router-default
# EXTERNAL-IP should be populated (NLB address or IP)

# Terminal 2 — inspect IngressController
oc get ingresscontroller default -n openshift-ingress-operator -o yaml \
  | grep -E "domain|replicas|endpointPublishing|conditions" | head -20

# Terminal 3 — peek at live HAProxy config inside the router
ROUTER=$(oc get pods -n openshift-ingress -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
echo "Router pod: $ROUTER"
oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- \
  cat /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config | head -60

See also: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers for Kubernetes Ingress API comparison. See also: Lesson 28 — OpenShift Egress for controlling outbound traffic from the same namespace.

docs.title: 1. Route vs Kubernetes Ingress
docs.text: Feature OpenShift Route Kubernetes Ingress API group route.openshift.io/v1 networking.k8s.io/v1 Controller HAProxy Router Any Ingress Controller TLS passthrough Native Requires SNI-based annotation TLS reencrypt Native Not standard A/B weight splitting Native (alternateBackends) Controller-specific annotation Wildcard host Native Via annotation Admission status Per-route .status.ingress LB IP in .status.loadBalancer Path-based routing Yes Yes

docs.title: 2. Route Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Client
        BR["Browser / Client"]
    end
    subgraph DNS
        WDNS["*.apps.cluster.example.com\n→ router EXTERNAL-IP"]
    end
    subgraph OpenShift
        SVC_LB["LoadBalancer Service\nrouter-default\n(NLB / MetalLB)"]
        subgraph IC["openshift-ingress namespace"]
            RP1["router-default-pod-1\nHAProxy"]
            RP2["router-default-pod-2\nHAProxy"]
        end
        subgraph App["application namespace"]
            SVC["Service\n(ClusterIP)"]
            POD1["Pod"]
            POD2["Pod"]
        end
        ROUTE["Route CR\nhost, TLS mode, weight"]
    end

    BR -- "HTTPS web.apps..." --> DNS
    DNS --> SVC_LB --> RP1
    SVC_LB --> RP2
    RP1 -- "watches / reconciles" --> ROUTE
    RP2 -- "watches / reconciles" --> ROUTE
    RP1 --> SVC --> POD1
    RP1 --> SVC --> POD2

docs.title: 3. The IngressController Operator
docs.text:
OpenShift manages routers via the IngressController CRD — never edit router pods directly.

# View the default IngressController
oc get ingresscontroller default -n openshift-ingress-operator -o yaml
# spec.domain: apps.cluster.example.com   <- wildcard DNS base
# spec.replicas: 2
# spec.endpointPublishingStrategy.type: LoadBalancerService
# status.conditions: Available True

# View router pods created by the operator
oc get pods -n openshift-ingress -o wide
# router-default-xxxxx-yyyyy   (one per replica, spread across infra nodes)

# View the LoadBalancer service (holds EXTERNAL-IP)
oc get svc -n openshift-ingress router-default

# Create a custom IngressController for internal traffic
oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: operator.openshift.io/v1
kind: IngressController
metadata:
  name: internal
  namespace: openshift-ingress-operator
spec:
  domain: internal.cluster.example.com
  replicas: 2
  endpointPublishingStrategy:
    type: LoadBalancerService
    loadBalancer:
      scope: Internal     # Internal LB (AWS: internal NLB)
  nodePlacement:
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        node-role.kubernetes.io/infra: ""
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      router: internal    # only routes in namespaces with this label
EOF

docs.title: 4. IngressController Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change spec.replicas 2 Number of HAProxy router pods Increase for high throughput spec.domain cluster install value Wildcard DNS base for auto-generated hostnames Set at install; changing disrupts all routes endpointPublishingStrategy.type LoadBalancerService How the router is exposed (LB, NodePort, HostNetwork) Use HostNetwork on bare metal tuningOptions.maxConnections 50000 HAProxy global maxconn Increase for high-connection workloads tuningOptions.threadCount auto HAProxy worker threads Set to vCPU count of infra nodes httpHeaders.forwardedHeaderPolicy Append Handling of X-Forwarded-For Set Replace if upstream proxy already sets it logging.access.destination.type Container Access log destination Use Syslog for centralized logging routeAdmission.wildcardPolicy WildcardsDisallowed Whether *.example.com routes are accepted Set WildcardsAllowed for multi-tenant platforms routeAdmission.namespaceOwnership InterNamespaceAllowed Whether routes can claim hostnames across namespaces Set Strict for tenant isolation

docs.title: Edge — TLS terminates at the router
docs.text:
apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: web-edge
  namespace: default
spec:
  host: web.apps.cluster.example.com
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: web
    weight: 100
  port:
    targetPort: 8080
  tls:
    termination: edge
    insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy: Redirect   # HTTP → HTTPS 301
    # Optional: provide custom certificate
    # certificate: |-
    #   -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
    # key: |-
    #   -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
    # caCertificate: |-   (chain if needed)

docs.title: Passthrough — TLS goes all the way to the pod
docs.text:
spec:
  tls:
    termination: passthrough
  # Router does NOT decrypt — routes by SNI hostname only
  # Cannot use path-based routing in passthrough mode
  # Pod must present a valid certificate

docs.title: Reencrypt — terminate at router, then re-establish TLS to pod
docs.text:
spec:
  tls:
    termination: reencrypt
    destinationCACertificate: |-   # CA cert to verify the pod's server cert
      -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
      ...
    # Optional: custom cert for the client-facing side

docs.title: 6. Route Lifecycle — Admission Sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User / CI
    participant API as API Server
    participant RO as Route Operator
    participant RP as Router Pod (HAProxy)

    U->>API: oc apply -f route.yaml
    API->>RO: Route created event
    RO->>RO: Validate hostname ownership<br/>Check routeAdmission policy
    RO->>API: Update route.status.ingress<br/>Admitted: True / False
    RP->>API: Watch Route objects (every 10s)
    RP->>RP: Regenerate haproxy.config<br/>Reload HAProxy (soft reload)
    Note over RP: HAProxy reload is zero-downtime:<br/>old process drains, new one takes over
# Check if a route was admitted
oc describe route web-edge | grep -A 15 "Status:"
# Ingress:
#   Host:  web.apps.cluster.example.com
#   Conditions:
#     Type: Admitted  Status: True
#     RouterName: default

# Check route admission across all routes
oc get routes -A -o custom-columns=\
'NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,HOST:.spec.host,ADMITTED:.status.ingress[0].conditions[0].status'

docs.title: 7. Route Management Commands
docs.text:
# Expose a service as a route (auto-generates hostname from service name + domain)
oc expose svc web
# → web.apps.cluster.example.com

# Expose with explicit hostname
oc expose svc web --hostname=web.apps.cluster.example.com

# Create a TLS edge route with custom certificates
oc create route edge web-tls \
  --service=web \
  --hostname=web.apps.cluster.example.com \
  --cert=tls.crt \
  --key=tls.key

# View all routes across all namespaces
oc get routes -A

# Delete
oc delete route web-edge -n default

docs.title: 8. Weighted Routes — A/B Traffic Splitting
docs.text:
OpenShift Routes support native A/B splits — no service mesh required.

apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: web-ab
spec:
  host: web.apps.cluster.example.com
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: web-v1
    weight: 80          # 80% to v1
  alternateBackends:
    - kind: Service
      name: web-v2
      weight: 20        # 20% to v2
  port:
    targetPort: 8080
  tls:
    termination: edge

# Verify weights are reflected in HAProxy
oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- \
  grep -A5 "web.apps.cluster.example.com" /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config \
  | grep "weight"
# server pod-v1-xxx 10.128.0.5:8080 weight 256  <- 80% → 256
# server pod-v2-xxx 10.128.0.6:8080 weight 64   <- 20% → 64

docs.title: 9. HAProxy Annotations
docs.text:
metadata:
  annotations:
    # Connection timeouts
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/timeout: 60s
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/connect-timeout: 5s

    # Load balancing algorithm
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/balance: "leastconn"   # roundrobin, source, leastconn

    # Sticky sessions (source IP based)
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/balance: "source"

    # Rate limiting
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/rate-limit-connections: "true"
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/rate-limit-connections.rate-http: "100"

    # IP allowlist (space-separated CIDRs)
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/ip_whitelist: "192.168.1.0/24 10.0.0.1"

    # HTTP Strict Transport Security
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/hsts_header: "max-age=31536000;includeSubDomains;preload"

    # CORS
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/cors-allow-origin: "https://example.com"

    # Rewrite incoming request path
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/rewrite-target: /

docs.title: 10. IngressController Tuning
docs.text:
apiVersion: operator.openshift.io/v1
kind: IngressController
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: openshift-ingress-operator
spec:
  replicas: 3
  tuningOptions:
    headerBufferBytes: 32768
    headerBufferMaxRewriteBytes: 8192
    maxConnections: 50000
    threadCount: 4
  logging:
    access:
      destination:
        type: Container    # stdout — scrape with Fluentd/Vector
      httpLogFormat: >-
        %ci:%cp [%t] %ft %b/%s %B %tsc %ac/%fc/%bc/%sc/%rc %{+Q}r
  httpHeaders:
    forwardedHeaderPolicy: Append

docs.title: 11. Router Sharding
docs.text:
Deploy multiple IngressControllers on different node groups, each serving different namespaces:

# Label namespace so the internal IngressController picks it up
oc label namespace my-app router=internal

# Confirm the internal router has admitted the route
oc describe route my-route -n my-app | grep RouterName
# RouterName: internal

docs.title: 12. Wildcard Routes
docs.text:
# Allow wildcard routes on the IngressController
oc patch ingresscontroller default \
  -n openshift-ingress-operator \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"routeAdmission":{"wildcardPolicy":"WildcardsAllowed"}}}'

# Create a wildcard route
oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: wildcard-route
spec:
  host: "*.apps.cluster.example.com"
  wildcardPolicy: Subdomain
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: web
  tls:
    termination: edge
EOF

docs.title: 13. Standard Kubernetes Ingress on OpenShift
docs.text:
OpenShift accepts standard Ingress resources — the router automatically converts them to Routes:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
  annotations:
    route.openshift.io/termination: edge   # OpenShift TLS annotation
spec:
  ingressClassName: openshift-default
  rules:
    - host: web.apps.cluster.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Route not admitted Hostname claimed by another route / admission policy oc describe route <name> \| grep Conditions Check routeAdmission.namespaceOwnership; delete conflicting route 503 Service Unavailable No healthy pod endpoints behind service echo "show stat" \| socat - /var/lib/haproxy/run/haproxy.sock \| cut -d, -f1,2,18 Check pod readiness probes; check service selector Certificate error (browser) Custom cert doesn't match hostname oc get route <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls.certificate}' \| openssl x509 -noout -subject Re-create route with correct cert No EXTERNAL-IP on router service Cloud LB not provisioned / MetalLB missing oc get svc -n openshift-ingress router-default Check IngressController endpointPublishingStrategy; install MetalLB on bare metal Route admitted but traffic returns 404 Wrong targetPort or missing path in backend oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- curl -s http://<svc-ip>:<port>/path Verify service port and pod HTTP server path HAProxy 502 Bad Gateway Pod starts but not yet ready oc get endpoints <service> — check address count Add/tune readiness probe; check haproxy.router.openshift.io/connect-timeout 
# Check HAProxy backend health via UNIX socket
oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- \
  bash -c 'echo "show stat" | socat - /var/lib/haproxy/run/haproxy.sock | \
  cut -d, -f1,2,18,19 | grep -v "^#"'
# be_<namespace>_<service>_<port>,pod-name,UP,0  <- UP = healthy
# be_<namespace>_<service>_<port>,pod-name,DOWN,-- <- DOWN = no connection

# Check router log for 5xx errors
oc logs -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER | grep " 5[0-9][0-9] " | tail -20

# Test route from inside cluster (bypass DNS)
oc run -it --rm test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -Hv "Host: web.apps.cluster.example.com" \
  http://router-default.openshift-ingress.svc

# Check all route status at once
oc get routes -A -o json \
  | jq '.items[] | select(.status.ingress[0].conditions[0].status != "True") | .metadata.name'

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• At least 2 router replicas spread across infra nodes (spec.replicas >= 2)
  • maxConnections tuned to expected peak concurrent connections per router pod
  • All production routes use TLS (edge minimum; passthrough/reencrypt for mTLS)
  • Custom certificates loaded for non-wildcard hostnames; wildcard cert for *.apps.*
  • routeAdmission.namespaceOwnership: Strict for multi-tenant environments
  • HAProxy access logs enabled and forwarded to centralized log aggregation
  • IngressController podDisruptionBudget reviewed — router upgrades must not cause full outage

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use passthrough TLS for a path-based route HAProxy cannot inspect SNI beyond hostname — no path routing Use reencrypt if path routing + TLS to pod is needed Set insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy: Allow on public routes Allows plain HTTP to production services — credentials in transit Use Redirect or None on all production routes Create routes directly instead of via IngressController Router sharding and admission policies are bypassed Always use oc expose or YAML; let the operator manage routing Expect X-Forwarded-For to show real client IP without cloud LB proxy protocol Cloud NLB replaces source IP unless proxy protocol or PROXY header is configured Enable PROXY protocol on the NLB and set httpHeaders.forwardedHeaderPolicy: Replace Ignore the Admitted condition A route can exist but be silently unserved if the router rejects it Monitor oc get routes -A and alert on Admitted != True

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List all routes oc get routes -A Expose service as route oc expose svc <name> --hostname=<host> Check route admitted oc describe route <name> \| grep Admitted Create TLS edge route oc create route edge <name> --service=<svc> --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key View IngressController oc get ingresscontroller -n openshift-ingress-operator -o yaml HAProxy backend stats echo "show stat" \| socat - /var/lib/haproxy/run/haproxy.sock View HAProxy config oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- cat /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config Router logs (5xx only) oc logs -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER \| grep ' 5[0-9][0-9] ' Enable wildcard routes oc patch ingresscontroller default -n openshift-ingress-operator --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"routeAdmission":{"wildcardPolicy":"WildcardsAllowed"}}}' Test route internally oc run --rm -it test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- curl -H "Host: <host>" http://router-default.openshift-ingress.svc Scale router replicas oc patch ingresscontroller default -n openshift-ingress-operator --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"replicas":3}}'

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail Route CRD route.openshift.io/v1 — OpenShift's first-class Ingress equivalent TLS modes edge (terminate at router), passthrough (pod handles TLS), reencrypt (router re-encrypts to pod) A/B routing Native weight-based splitting via alternateBackends IngressController Operator-managed HAProxy deployment — openshift-ingress-operator Wildcard DNS *.apps.cluster.example.com — base domain set in IngressController spec.domain Router sharding Multiple IngressControllers with namespaceSelector / routeSelector for multi-tenant isolation Standard Ingress Also supported — auto-converted to Routes by the router

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What are the three TLS termination modes for OpenShift Routes, and in which mode is path-based routing impossible?
Answer The three modes are: **edge** (TLS terminates at the HAProxy router; plain HTTP is forwarded to the backend pod), **reencrypt** (TLS terminates at the router, and HAProxy opens a new TLS connection to the pod using a destination CA certificate), and **passthrough** (the encrypted stream is forwarded unchanged to the pod based solely on SNI hostname). Path-based routing is impossible in **passthrough** mode because HAProxy never decrypts the connection and therefore cannot inspect the HTTP path — it can only route by the hostname in the TLS SNI field.
  1. [Scenario question] A Route shows Admitted: True but users receive 503 Service Unavailable. How would you check whether the backend pods are healthy from the HAProxy router's perspective?
Answer Connect to the HAProxy stats socket inside the router pod using `echo "show stat" | socat - /var/lib/haproxy/run/haproxy.sock | cut -d, -f1,2,18,19` — the output shows each backend server entry with `UP` or `DOWN` status. A `DOWN` entry means HAProxy cannot reach the pod (readiness probe failing, wrong targetPort, or pod not yet ready). Also check `oc get endpoints ` to verify that at least one pod IP is in the `Addresses` list rather than `NotReadyAddresses`.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check whether a specific Route was admitted by the HAProxy router?
Answer 
oc describe route web-edge | grep -A 15 "Status:"
Look for the `Admitted: True` condition under the `Ingress` section and confirm the `RouterName` field shows which IngressController accepted it; `Admitted: False` means the router rejected the route due to a hostname conflict or admission policy violation, and the `Message` field will explain why.

docs.title: Lesson 28 — OpenShift EgressIP and EgressFirewall
docs.text:
Track: OpenShift Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 16 — Network Policies, Lesson 25 — OpenShift Overview Duration: ~2 hours

Goal: Assign a stable egress IP to a namespace so external firewall rules remain valid across pod rescheduling, and restrict outbound destinations per namespace using EgressFirewall with CIDR and DNS-based rules.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — check existing egress resources
oc get egressip -o wide 2>/dev/null
oc get egressfirewall -A 2>/dev/null

# Terminal 2 — check which nodes are egress-assignable
oc get nodes -o custom-columns=\
'NAME:.metadata.name,EGRESS:.metadata.labels.k8s\.ovn\.org/egress-assignable'
# NAME        EGRESS
# worker-1    <present>   <- assignable
# worker-2    <none>      <- not assignable yet

# Terminal 3 — confirm OVN-Kubernetes is the network type
oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.networkType}'
# OVNKubernetes

See also: Lesson 26 — OVN-Kubernetes for how OVN ACLs underpin both EgressIP and EgressFirewall. See also: Lesson 16 — Network Policies for controlling ingress traffic.

docs.title: 1. The Egress Problem
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Without["Without EgressIP"]
        P1A["billing-pod
(on worker-1)
src: 192.168.1.10"]
        P1B["billing-pod
(on worker-2)
src: 192.168.1.11"]
        FW["External DB
Firewall
whitelist: ???"]
    end
    P1A -- "SNAT to node IP
192.168.1.10" --> FW
    P1B -- "SNAT to node IP
192.168.1.11" --> FW
    note1["Pod reschedules
→ source IP changes
→ firewall rules break"]
flowchart LR
    subgraph With["With EgressIP"]
        P2A["billing-pod
(on any node)"]
        EIP["EgressIP: 192.168.1.100
assigned to worker-1
(moves on node failure)"]
        FW2["External DB
Firewall
whitelist: 192.168.1.100 ✓"]
    end
    P2A -- "SNAT to EgressIP
192.168.1.100 always" --> EIP --> FW2

Core principle: EgressIP decouples outbound source IP from the node the pod runs on. The IP floats between eligible nodes using OVN SNAT rules.

docs.title: 2. EgressIP Configuration
docs.text:
# Step 1 — mark worker nodes as EgressIP candidates
oc label node worker-1 k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable=""
oc label node worker-2 k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable=""

# Step 2 — verify nodes appear as assignable
oc get nodes -l k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable

# Step 3 — create the EgressIP resource
apiVersion: k8s.ovn.org/v1
kind: EgressIP
metadata:
  name: billing-egress
spec:
  egressIPs:
    - 192.168.1.100     # must be in the same subnet as the egress node
    - 192.168.1.101     # second IP → HA: each IP lands on a different node
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      egress: billing   # namespaces with this label use these IPs
  podSelector:          # optional: restrict to specific pods within the namespace
    matchLabels:
      app: billing-processor

# Step 4 — label the target namespace
oc label namespace billing egress=billing

# Step 5 — apply and verify
oc apply -f egress-ip.yaml
oc get egressip billing-egress -o yaml
# status:
#   items:
#     - egressIP: 192.168.1.100
#       node: worker-1          <- which node holds this IP now
#     - egressIP: 192.168.1.101
#       node: worker-2          <- second IP on a different node

# Step 6 — confirm source IP from inside the pod
oc exec -n billing billing-pod -- curl -s ifconfig.me
# 192.168.1.100   <- EgressIP, not the node IP

docs.title: 3. EgressIP Assignment Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API
    participant OVN as OVN-Kubernetes Controller
    participant NB as OVN Northbound DB
    participant Node as Worker Node\n(ovn-controller)

    K8s->>OVN: EgressIP created event
    OVN->>OVN: Select eligible nodes\n(egress-assignable label)
    OVN->>Node: Add secondary IP to node NIC\n(e.g. 192.168.1.100 on eth0)
    OVN->>NB: Add SNAT rule:\npods in namespace → 192.168.1.100
    NB->>Node: ovn-controller programs OVS SNAT flow
    Note over Node: All egress from billing namespace\nnow SNATs to 192.168.1.100

docs.title: 4. EgressIP High Availability
docs.text:
EgressIP is automatically HA when multiple nodes are assignable and multiple IPs are configured. Failover uses BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) for sub-second node failure detection.

# View current IP-to-node assignment
oc get egressip -o wide
# NAME             EGRESSIPS                     ASSIGNED NODE    ASSIGNED EGRESSIPS
# billing-egress   192.168.1.100,192.168.1.101   worker-1         192.168.1.100
#                                                worker-2         192.168.1.101

# Simulate node failure — cordon worker-1 to trigger reassignment
oc adm cordon worker-1
# OVN detects node failure via BFD (~1 second)
# 192.168.1.100 moves to another egress-assignable node

# Confirm reassignment
oc get egressip billing-egress -o jsonpath='{.status.items}' | jq .

# Verify continuous egress (from a pod, while cordon is active)
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  oc exec -n billing billing-pod -- curl -s --connect-timeout 2 ifconfig.me
  sleep 0.5
done
# Should return 192.168.1.100 on all requests (brief gap < 2s during failover)

# Restore
oc adm uncordon worker-1

docs.title: 5. EgressFirewall
docs.text:
EgressFirewall restricts which external destinations a namespace's pods can reach. It is enforced via OVN ACLs — no iptables involved.

apiVersion: k8s.ovn.org/v1
kind: EgressFirewall
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: production
spec:
  egress:
    # Rule order matters — first match wins
    - type: Allow
      to:
        cidrSelector: 10.100.0.0/16    # corporate internal network

    - type: Allow
      to:
        dnsName: api.example.com       # DNS-based rule (wildcard supported)
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443

    # Always allow DNS resolution — without this, DNS lookups fail
    - type: Allow
      to:
        cidrSelector: 0.0.0.0/0
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53

    # Implicit deny-all for everything else
    - type: Deny
      to:
        cidrSelector: 0.0.0.0/0

# Apply and verify
oc apply -f egress-firewall.yaml
oc get egressfirewall -n production
# NAME      EGRESSFIREWALL STATUS
# default   EgressFirewall Rules applied

# Test: allowed traffic
oc exec -n production app-pod -- curl -m5 https://api.example.com    # allowed
oc exec -n production app-pod -- curl -m5 https://10.100.0.5         # allowed

# Test: blocked traffic (times out — Deny rule drops silently)
oc exec -n production app-pod -- curl -m5 https://google.com
# curl: (28) Connection timed out after 5001 milliseconds

# View OVN ACLs generated from EgressFirewall
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl find ACL external_ids:egressFirewall=production | head -30

docs.title: 6. EgressFirewall Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Values Effect When to change spec.egress[].type Allow / Deny Permit or block matching traffic First match wins — order rules carefully spec.egress[].to.cidrSelector CIDR string Match by destination IP range Use for RFC1918 or known IP blocks spec.egress[].to.dnsName FQDN or *.example.com Match by DNS name (OVN resolves it) Use for SaaS APIs with dynamic IPs spec.egress[].ports[].protocol TCP / UDP / SCTP Protocol filter per rule Omit to match all protocols spec.egress[].ports[].port 1–65535 Port filter per rule Combine with CIDR for precise control

docs.title: 7. DNS-Based EgressFirewall Rules
docs.text:
DNS-based rules are resolved by the OVN-Kubernetes DNS interceptor — it polls DNS and updates ACLs when IPs change:

egress:
  - type: Allow
    to:
      dnsName: "*.amazonaws.com"   # wildcard DNS names supported
    ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 443

# Check how OVN resolves DNS names for the firewall
oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -c northd | grep -i dns | tail -20

# Check DNS cache TTL used by OVN
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl find DNS | grep -E "records|external_ids"

# Important: DNS rules are eventually consistent (up to TTL seconds)
# For highly dynamic IPs, use CIDR rules instead

docs.title: 8. EgressFirewall on Legacy OpenShift SDN
docs.text:
On older clusters using OpenShift SDN, EgressFirewall is a different resource:

# Check which network type you have
oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.networkType}'
# OVNKubernetes → use EgressFirewall (k8s.ovn.org/v1)
# OpenShiftSDN  → use EgressNetworkPolicy (network.openshift.io/v1)

# Legacy — OpenShift SDN only
apiVersion: network.openshift.io/v1
kind: EgressNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: production
spec:
  egress:
    - type: Allow
      to:
        cidrSelector: 10.100.0.0/16
    - type: Deny
      to:
        cidrSelector: 0.0.0.0/0

docs.title: 9. EgressRouter (Legacy — Redirect Mode)
docs.text:
EgressRouter is an older mechanism that deploys a dedicated pod acting as a fixed-destination traffic redirector. Largely superseded by EgressIP + EgressFirewall.

# Check if any EgressRouter resources exist
oc get egressrouter -A 2>/dev/null

# EgressRouter use case: redirect all traffic from a namespace to a fixed IP
# Rarely needed in OVN-Kubernetes deployments
# Prefer EgressIP for stable source IP + EgressFirewall for destination control

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix EgressIP not assigned to any node No nodes labeled k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable oc get nodes -l k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable Label at least 2 worker nodes with the egress-assignable label EgressIP assigned but pod still uses node IP Namespace not labeled / label mismatch oc get ns <ns> --show-labels Match namespace label to egressIPs.spec.namespaceSelector.matchLabels EgressIP not in node subnet IP not routable on node's NIC — OVN can't add it oc get egressip <name> -o yaml \| grep conditions Use an IP from the same subnet as the egress node EgressFirewall blocking DNS Missing UDP/TCP port 53 Allow rule at top oc exec -n <ns> pod -- nslookup google.com — SERVFAIL Add explicit Allow rule for 0.0.0.0/0 port 53 before the Deny-all DNS-based rule not matching dynamic IP OVN DNS cache hasn't refreshed yet oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -c northd \| grep dns Wait for TTL expiry; for critical rules use CIDR instead of DNS name EgressFirewall not found Running OpenShift SDN not OVN-Kubernetes oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster -o jsonpath='{.status.networkType}' Use EgressNetworkPolicy for OpenShift SDN EgressIP failover not working Only one egress-assignable node configured oc get egressip -o wide — only one node listed Label a second node; configure a second EgressIP address 
# Full egress diagnostic sequence

# 1. Verify EgressIP assignment
oc get egressip -o wide

# 2. Verify namespace selector matches
oc get ns -l egress=billing

# 3. Test actual source IP from pod
oc exec -n billing billing-pod -- curl -s ifconfig.me

# 4. Check OVN SNAT rules
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl find NAT external_ip=192.168.1.100 | head -20

# 5. Test EgressFirewall allow/deny
oc exec -n production app-pod -- curl -m5 https://allowed-host.com
oc exec -n production app-pod -- curl -m5 https://blocked-host.com

# 6. View EgressFirewall OVN ACLs
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl find ACL "external_ids:egressFirewall=production" | grep -E "action|match"

# 7. Check OVN logs for ACL activity
oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes ovnkube-node-xxxxx -c ovn-controller \
  | grep -i "acl\|drop\|reject" | tail -30

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• At least 2 nodes labeled k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable for EgressIP HA
  • EgressIPs are within the subnet CIDR of their assigned nodes and not used by other hosts
  • Each critical namespace has an EgressFirewall with explicit Deny-all as the final rule
  • All EgressFirewall rules include an explicit Allow for DNS (UDP/TCP port 53) before the Deny-all
  • EgressIP failover tested by cordoning the primary egress node and verifying the IP moves
  • DNS-based EgressFirewall rules reviewed — high-TTL domains only; use CIDR for dynamic IPs
  • oc get egressip and oc get egressfirewall -A included in cluster health monitoring

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use a single egress-assignable node No HA — node failure removes the EgressIP entirely Label at least 2 nodes; configure 2 EgressIPs (one per node) Put EgressIP in a different subnet than the node OVN cannot attach the IP as a secondary NIC address Coordinate with network team — EgressIP must be from the node's subnet Write DNS-based EgressFirewall rules for fast-TTL hostnames ACL misses traffic until OVN's DNS cache refreshes Use CIDR-based rules for rapidly changing IP sets; DNS rules for stable SaaS endpoints Forget the DNS Allow rule before the Deny-all All DNS lookups fail — application breaks on first name resolution Always put UDP/TCP port 53 Allow to 0.0.0.0/0 before any broad Deny Use EgressRouter for new deployments EgressRouter is a legacy single-pod redirect — no HA, no policy Use EgressIP (stable source) + EgressFirewall (destination policy) together

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List EgressIP resources oc get egressip -o wide List EgressFirewall resources oc get egressfirewall -A Label node as egress-assignable oc label node <name> k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable="" Label namespace for EgressIP oc label namespace <ns> <key>=<value> Check which node holds an EgressIP oc get egressip <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.items}' Test pod source IP oc exec -n <ns> <pod> -- curl -s ifconfig.me Test EgressFirewall allow/deny oc exec -n <ns> <pod> -- curl -m5 https://<host> View OVN ACLs for a namespace firewall oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl find ACL "external_ids:egressFirewall=<ns>" Check OVN SNAT rules for EgressIP oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl find NAT external_ip=<ip> Determine CNI type oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster -o jsonpath='{.status.networkType}' View EgressIP failover conditions oc get egressip <name> -o yaml \| grep -A5 conditions

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Resource Purpose Scope HA model EgressIP Stable outbound source IP — survives pod rescheduling Namespace or pod selector Multiple IPs spread across egress-assignable nodes EgressFirewall Restrict external destinations by CIDR or DNS name Per namespace (one per namespace) N/A — OVN ACLs are replicated EgressNetworkPolicy Legacy EgressFirewall for OpenShift SDN Per namespace N/A EgressRouter Fixed-destination traffic redirect (legacy) Per namespace None — single-pod

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why must the EgressIP address be from the same subnet as the egress-assignable node, and what happens if you configure an IP from a different subnet?
Answer OVN-Kubernetes implements EgressIP by adding the EgressIP as a secondary address to the node's physical NIC (via `ip addr add`). For this to be reachable by the upstream router, the IP must be within the subnet already associated with that NIC — otherwise the router has no route to deliver return traffic back to the EgressIP address, and the SNAT flows will never complete. If you configure an EgressIP from a foreign subnet, the OVN controller will fail to assign it and the EgressIP resource will show an error in its `status.conditions` field.
  1. [Scenario question] An EgressFirewall is applied to the production namespace with an Allow rule for a specific CIDR and a final Deny-all rule. After deployment, all pods fail DNS resolution. What rule is missing?
Answer The EgressFirewall is missing an explicit Allow rule for DNS traffic before the Deny-all. Because EgressFirewall rules are evaluated in order and the first match wins, the Deny-all blocks UDP/TCP port 53 egress to `0.0.0.0/0` before the pods can reach CoreDNS. Add an `Allow` rule targeting `cidrSelector: 0.0.0.0/0` with `ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]` placed before the Deny-all rule. This is a mandatory addition to every EgressFirewall that uses a final deny.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check which node is currently holding a specific EgressIP and whether both EgressIPs in an HA pair are assigned to different nodes?
Answer 
oc get egressip billing-egress -o wide
The output shows the `ASSIGNED NODE` column for each EgressIP address; for HA you should see two rows with different node names. If both IPs are assigned to the same node or one shows no assignment, check whether at least two nodes are labeled `k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable` with `oc get nodes -l k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable`.

Next: Lesson 29 — AWS EKS Networking Deep Dive

docs.title: Lesson 29 — AWS EKS Networking Deep Dive
docs.text:
Track: AWS Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 08 — Cloud Provider Networking, Lesson 09 — CNI Duration: ~3 hours

Goal: Explain how the AWS VPC CNI assigns real VPC IPs to pods via ENI secondary IPs, calculate the pod density limit for a given instance type, enable prefix delegation to increase that limit, and assign per-pod Security Groups using SecurityGroupPolicy.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — verify aws-node DaemonSet is running
kubectl get ds -n kube-system aws-node -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node -o wide
# One pod per node — all should be Running

# Terminal 2 — check cluster identity
aws sts get-caller-identity
kubectl config current-context

# Terminal 3 — view ENIs attached to a node
NODE=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
INSTANCE_TYPE=$(kubectl get node $NODE \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.node\.kubernetes\.io/instance-type}')
echo "Node: $NODE  Instance type: $INSTANCE_TYPE"

aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters "Name=description,Values=aws-K8s-*" \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[*].[NetworkInterfaceId,PrivateIpAddresses[*].PrivateIpAddress]' \
  --output table 2>/dev/null || echo "Configure AWS CLI with EKS cluster credentials first"

See also: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification for how CNI plugins attach to the kubelet. See also: Lesson 30 — AWS VPC Design for subnet sizing and secondary CIDR configuration.

docs.title: 1. EKS Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph AWS_Account["AWS Account"]
        subgraph VPC["VPC 10.0.0.0/16"]
            subgraph Pub["Public Subnets"]
                NAT["NAT Gateway"]
                NLB["NLB / ALB"]
            end
            subgraph Priv["Private Subnets (nodes + pods)"]
                subgraph Node1["EC2 Worker Node"]
                    ETH0["Primary ENI eth0\n10.0.10.5 (node IP)\n10.0.10.11 (pod IP)\n10.0.10.12 (pod IP)"]
                    ETH1["Secondary ENI eth1\n10.0.10.50 (primary)\n10.0.10.51 (pod IP)\n10.0.10.52 (pod IP)"]
                    AWSNODE["aws-node\n(IPAMD)"]
                end
            end
            subgraph CP_NET["AWS-managed VPC (EKS Control Plane)"]
                CP["EKS Control Plane\n(API server, etcd)"]
                CPENI["Cross-account ENI\n→ customer VPC"]
            end
        end
    end
    CP -- "cross-account ENI" --> CPENI --> Node1
    AWSNODE -- "EC2 API:\nAttach ENI,\nAssign secondary IPs" --> ETH1

Control Plane: Managed by AWS — lives in an AWS-owned VPC, connected to your VPC via a cross-account ENI per subnet. You do not manage control plane nodes.

docs.title: 2. AWS VPC CNI — How Pod IPs Are Assigned
docs.text:
Pods receive real VPC IP addresses from EC2 ENI secondary IPs. No overlay network, no NAT for pod-to-pod traffic within the VPC.

sequenceDiagram
    participant K as kubelet
    participant CNI as VPC CNI Plugin
    participant IPAMD as IPAMD (aws-node)
    participant EC2 as EC2 API

    Note over IPAMD,EC2: Node startup — warm pool pre-fill
    IPAMD->>EC2: AttachNetworkInterface (secondary ENIs)
    EC2->>IPAMD: ENI attached (e.g. eth1)
    IPAMD->>EC2: AssignPrivateIpAddresses (secondary IPs)
    EC2->>IPAMD: IPs assigned (warm pool ready)

    Note over K,IPAMD: Pod scheduled
    K->>CNI: ADD (pod name, namespace, netns)
    CNI->>IPAMD: Request IP from warm pool
    IPAMD->>CNI: 10.0.10.11 (from warm pool)
    CNI->>CNI: Create veth pair\nMove one end to pod netns\nAssign 10.0.10.11\nAdd /32 host route on node
    CNI->>K: Result: IP=10.0.10.11
# Check IPAMD logs (IP assignment events)
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node -c aws-node | \
  grep -E "AssignPrivateIp|warm|allocated" | tail -20

# View current warm pool status
kubectl exec -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node -c aws-node -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:61678/v1/nodeIPStats 2>/dev/null | jq .
# totalIPAddresses: N
# assignedIPAddresses: M
# coolDownIPs: 0

docs.title: 3. ENI Secondary IP — Node Layout
docs.text:
EC2 Node (m5.large: max 3 ENIs × 10 IPs per ENI)

Primary ENI (eth0)          Secondary ENI (eth1)
┌─────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐
│ 10.0.10.5 (node)│         │ 10.0.10.50       │
│ 10.0.10.11 → Pod│         │ 10.0.10.51 → Pod│
│ 10.0.10.12 → Pod│         │ 10.0.10.52 → Pod│
│ ...             │         │ ...             │
└─────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘
  -1 IP per ENI for node's own use

Max pods = (ENIs × IPs_per_ENI) − ENIs
m5.large = (3 × 10) − 3 = 27 pods

# Check this node's pod capacity
kubectl describe node $NODE | grep -E "pods:" | head -3
# pods: 29   (aws-node uses formula + 2 for host-network pods)

# Check actual formula values for this instance type
kubectl get node $NODE -o json | \
  jq '.metadata.annotations["vpc.amazonaws.com/eniIPv4Limit"]'

docs.title: 4. Pod Density Limits by Instance Type
docs.text:
Instance ENIs IPs/ENI Standard Max Pods With Prefix Delegation t3.small 3 4 11 48 t3.medium 3 6 15 48 m5.large 3 10 27 48 m5.xlarge 4 15 58 64 m5.4xlarge 8 30 234 234+ c5.2xlarge 4 15 58 64 r5.2xlarge 4 15 58 64

Formula (standard): (ENIs × IPs_per_ENI) − ENIs

Formula (prefix delegation): (ENIs × prefixes_per_ENI × 16) − ENIs

docs.title: 5. VPC CNI Environment Variables
docs.text: Variable Default Effect When to change WARM_IP_TARGET 1 Min unused IPs to keep in warm pool Increase (e.g. 5) for bursty workloads to reduce IP attach latency MINIMUM_IP_TARGET 0 Absolute minimum IPs to maintain Set to expected pod count for stable baseline WARM_ENI_TARGET 1 Min unused ENIs to keep attached Set to 0 on small instances to avoid wasting IPs WARM_PREFIX_TARGET 1 Min unused /28 prefixes (prefix delegation only) Set to 2 for burst tolerance ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION false Assign /28 CIDR blocks instead of individual IPs Set true for large clusters — 16x more IPs per ENI slot ENABLE_POD_ENI false Enable trunk ENI for Security Groups for Pods Set true to use SecurityGroupPolicy CRD AWS_VPC_K8S_CNI_CUSTOM_NETWORK_CFG false Use ENIConfig CRD for pod subnet selection Set true for custom networking / secondary CIDR ENI_CONFIG_LABEL_DEF k8s.amazonaws.com/eniConfig Node label to match ENIConfig Set to topology.kubernetes.io/zone for per-AZ config ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY_CONTROLLER false Enable eBPF-based network policy enforcement Set true to replace kube-proxy NetworkPolicy (v1.14+)

docs.title: 6. Prefix Delegation
docs.text:
Assign /28 CIDR blocks (16 IPs) per ENI slot instead of individual secondary IPs. Dramatically increases pod density.

# Enable prefix delegation
kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system \
  ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true \
  WARM_PREFIX_TARGET=1

# After enabling, check node capacity change
kubectl describe node $NODE | grep "pods:"
# Before: pods: 27  (m5.large standard)
# After:  pods: 48  (m5.large with prefix delegation)

# View /28 prefixes attached to ENIs on the node
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node $NODE -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=$NODE_IP" \
  --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].NetworkInterfaces[*].Ipv4Prefixes'

# IPAMD logs showing prefix assignment
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node -c aws-node | \
  grep -i prefix | tail -20

docs.title: 7. Security Groups for Pods
docs.text:
By default all pods on a node share the node's Security Group. With Security Groups for Pods, individual pods get their own SG via ENI trunking.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Standard["Standard (node SG shared)"]
        N1["Node SG\nsg-node-xxx"]
        P1["Pod A"]
        P2["Pod B"]
        P3["Pod C"]
        N1 --- P1
        N1 --- P2
        N1 --- P3
    end
    subgraph SGPods["Security Groups for Pods"]
        TRUNK["Trunk ENI\n(one per node)"]
        BRANCH1["Branch ENI\n+ sg-db-xxx\n→ Pod A (DB client)"]
        BRANCH2["Branch ENI\n+ sg-web-xxx\n→ Pod B (web)"]
        TRUNK --- BRANCH1
        TRUNK --- BRANCH2
    end
# Step 1 — enable trunk ENI mode
kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_POD_ENI=true
# Restart node group to activate trunk ENI (rolling replacement)

# Step 2 — SecurityGroupPolicy: assign SG to specific pods
apiVersion: vpcresources.k8s.aws/v1beta1
kind: SecurityGroupPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-sg-policy
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: database-client
  securityGroups:
    groupIds:
      - sg-0123456789abcdef0   # SG with RDS port 5432 ingress rule

# Step 3 — verify pod has the right SG
POD_IP=$(kubectl get pod <pod> -n production -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=$POD_IP" \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[0].Groups'
# [{"GroupId": "sg-0123456789abcdef0", "GroupName": "db-access"}]

docs.title: 8. EKS Node Networking
docs.text:
# View all ENIs attached to a node
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node $NODE -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=$NODE_IP" \
  --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].NetworkInterfaces[*].{ENI:NetworkInterfaceId,IPs:PrivateIpAddresses[*].PrivateIpAddress}'

# View routes on the node — /32 host routes per pod IP
# (SSH to node via SSM or bastion)
aws ssm start-session --target <instance-id>
ip route show | grep -v docker | grep scope
# 10.0.10.11 dev eth0 scope link  <- pod IP host route
# 10.0.10.51 dev eth1 scope link
# 10.0.10.52 dev eth1 scope link

# Source/destination check must be DISABLED on EKS nodes
aws ec2 describe-instance-attribute \
  --instance-id <instance-id> \
  --attribute sourceDestCheck
# "Value": false   <- correct; true breaks pod routing

docs.title: 9. VPC CNI Network Policies (eBPF)
docs.text:
Since VPC CNI v1.14, AWS includes a built-in eBPF network policy controller:

# Enable network policy controller
kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system \
  ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY_CONTROLLER=true

# Standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources are enforced
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-only
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: database
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: api
      ports:
        - port: 5432
EOF

# Verify eBPF programs are loaded
kubectl exec -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node -- \
  bpftool prog list | grep aws 2>/dev/null | head -10

docs.title: 10. IRSA — IAM Roles for Service Accounts
docs.text:
Pods need AWS API access without storing static credentials. IRSA uses OIDC federation to map Kubernetes service accounts to IAM roles.

# Associate OIDC provider with cluster
eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider \
  --cluster my-cluster --approve

# Create IAM role for a service account
eksctl create iamserviceaccount \
  --name s3-reader \
  --namespace production \
  --cluster my-cluster \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess \
  --approve

# Verify the annotation on the service account
kubectl get sa s3-reader -n production -o yaml | grep eks.amazonaws.com
# eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/my-cluster-s3-reader

# Pod uses the service account — AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE is auto-injected
kubectl run test-irsa --rm -it --image=amazon/aws-cli \
  --serviceaccount=s3-reader -n production \
  -- s3 ls

docs.title: 11. EKS with Alternative CNI Plugins
docs.text:
# Option 1: Keep VPC CNI for pod IPs; add Calico for NetworkPolicy only
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/amazon-vpc-cni-k8s/master/config/master/calico-operator.yaml

# Option 2: Cilium replacing VPC CNI entirely (overlay mode)
kubectl -n kube-system delete daemonset aws-node
helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set eni.enabled=true \
  --set ipam.mode=eni \
  --set egressMasqueradeInterfaces=eth0 \
  --set tunnel=disabled

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Pods stuck Pending — "0/N nodes are available: N Too many pods" Node at ENI/IP capacity kubectl describe node $NODE \| grep "pods:" and compare to running count Use larger instance type or enable prefix delegation Pod gets no IP — CNI timeout in kubelet IPAMD warm pool empty / EC2 API throttling kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node -c aws-node \| grep ERROR Increase MINIMUM_IP_TARGET; check EC2 API rate limits Pod IP unreachable from another pod Source/destination check enabled on node aws ec2 describe-instance-attribute --instance-id <id> --attribute sourceDestCheck Disable source/destination check on all node ENIs Security Groups for Pods not working Trunk ENI not provisioned kubectl get node $NODE -o yaml \| grep vpc.amazonaws.com/trunk Restart node (rolling) after setting ENABLE_POD_ENI=true Pods can't reach ECR on private cluster Missing VPC endpoint for ECR aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints \| grep ecr Create interface endpoints for ecr.api, ecr.dkr, and S3 gateway Node shows Ready but pod IPs exhaust quickly WARM_ENI_TARGET too high — IPs reserved but unused curl localhost:61678/v1/nodeIPStats on node Lower WARM_ENI_TARGET to 0; tune WARM_IP_TARGET NetworkPolicy not enforced Network policy controller not enabled kubectl get ds aws-node -n kube-system -o yaml \| grep ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY Set ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY_CONTROLLER=true and restart aws-node 
# Full VPC CNI diagnostic sequence

# 1. Check IPAMD health
kubectl exec -n kube-system $(kubectl get pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -c aws-node -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:61678/v1/nodeIPStats | jq .

# 2. Check for IPAMD errors
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node -c aws-node | \
  grep -E "ERROR|WARN" | tail -30

# 3. Check ENI attachment status
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters "Name=description,Values=aws-K8s-*" \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[*].{ID:NetworkInterfaceId,Status:Status,Description:Description}' \
  --output table

# 4. Check pod IP assignment from VPC side
POD_IP=$(kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=$POD_IP" \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[0].{ID:NetworkInterfaceId,Node:Attachment.InstanceId}'

# 5. Connectivity test
kubectl run -it --rm debug --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -v http://<service-clusterip>:<port>

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Instance types sized for expected pod density — verify max pods with prefix delegation enabled
  • MINIMUM_IP_TARGET set to expected average pod count per node to reduce cold-start IP attach latency
  • Prefix delegation enabled (ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true) for clusters with >30 pods/node
  • Source/destination check disabled on all node ENIs (managed automatically by EKS Managed Node Groups)
  • IRSA configured for all pods accessing AWS APIs — no static credentials in environment variables or Secrets
  • VPC endpoints created for ECR (api + dkr), S3 (gateway), STS, and EC2 to avoid NAT Gateway costs
  • Network policy controller enabled and baseline NetworkPolicies applied to all production namespaces

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use t3.small for production nodes Only 11 max pods standard, 48 with prefix delegation — quickly exhausts for real workloads Use m5.large or larger; always enable prefix delegation Leave WARM_IP_TARGET=1 on bursty workloads Pod scheduling stalls waiting for IPAMD to attach IPs (5-10s delay) Set WARM_IP_TARGET=5 and MINIMUM_IP_TARGET to expected average Share one SG for all pods on a node Cannot scope DB access to specific pods — entire node has DB access Use SecurityGroupPolicy with ENABLE_POD_ENI=true for sensitive workloads Store AWS credentials in K8s Secrets Credentials rotate; Secrets can be read by other pods Use IRSA — service account token exchanged for temporary IAM credentials Run all pods in public subnets Pods have public IPs — dramatically increases attack surface Nodes and pods in private subnets; only NLBs/ALBs in public subnets

docs.text: Use Case Command Check aws-node DaemonSet kubectl get ds -n kube-system aws-node View IPAMD warm pool stats kubectl exec -n kube-system <aws-node-pod> -c aws-node -- curl -s localhost:61678/v1/nodeIPStats Enable prefix delegation kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true Enable SGs for Pods kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_POD_ENI=true Check pod SG assignment aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=<pod-ip>" --query 'NetworkInterfaces[0].Groups' View ENIs on a node aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=private-ip-address,Values=<node-ip>" --query '...NetworkInterfaces' Enable eBPF network policy kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY_CONTROLLER=true Create IRSA service account eksctl create iamserviceaccount --name <sa> --namespace <ns> --cluster <cluster> --attach-policy-arn <arn> --approve Check IPAMD errors kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node -c aws-node \| grep ERROR Node max pods kubectl describe node <name> \| grep pods: VPC CNI version kubectl get ds -n kube-system aws-node -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail Pod IP model Real VPC IPs from ENI secondary IPs — no overlay, no NAT for pod-to-pod IP assignment IPAMD (aws-node) maintains a warm pool; CNI plugin draws from it on pod create Pod density Limited by instance ENI/IP limits — use prefix delegation (16x IPs per ENI slot) Security Groups for Pods SecurityGroupPolicy CRD + trunk ENI — per-pod SG without overlay Network Policy VPC CNI eBPF controller (v1.14+) or Calico overlay IAM IRSA: service account → IAM role (OIDC — no stored credentials) Encryption In transit via TLS; pod-to-pod: add Calico/Cilium WireGuard

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does the AWS VPC CNI assign real VPC IP addresses to pods instead of using an overlay network, and what is the main pod density constraint this introduces?
Answer Real VPC IPs eliminate NAT and tunneling overhead: pod-to-pod traffic stays native L3 routing within the VPC, reducing latency and simplifying security group rules (SGs apply directly to pod IPs). The main constraint is that each IP must come from an ENI secondary IP slot, and each EC2 instance type has hard limits on the number of ENIs and IPs per ENI. For example, an `m5.large` supports 3 ENIs × 10 IPs − 3 (one per ENI for the node) = 27 pods maximum, far less than the default Kubernetes limit of 110. Prefix delegation (`ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true`) assigns /28 blocks instead of individual IPs, raising the `m5.large` limit to 48.
  1. [Scenario question] Pods are stuck in Pending with the reason "0/3 nodes are available: 3 Too many pods." The cluster uses m5.large nodes without prefix delegation. What is the current maximum pod count per node, and what is the simplest way to raise it?
Answer An `m5.large` supports 3 ENIs × 10 secondary IPs per ENI, minus 3 (one primary IP per ENI reserved for the node) = 27 pods. Enable prefix delegation by setting `ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true` and `WARM_PREFIX_TARGET=1` on the `aws-node` DaemonSet with `kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true`; this assigns /28 CIDR blocks (16 IPs each) per ENI slot, raising the `m5.large` limit to 48 pods without changing instance type.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check the current IP warm pool status — how many IPs are assigned versus available — on a specific node?
Answer 
kubectl exec -n kube-system $(kubectl get pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -c aws-node -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:61678/v1/nodeIPStats | jq .
Look for `totalIPAddresses`, `assignedIPAddresses`, and `coolDownIPs` fields; if `totalIPAddresses` minus `assignedIPAddresses` is at or near zero, the warm pool is exhausted and new pods will stall while IPAMD attaches more IPs from the EC2 API.
