docs.title: Lesson 30 — AWS VPC Design for Kubernetes
docs.text:
Track: AWS Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 29 — EKS Networking Deep Dive Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Design a production VPC for EKS — size subnets correctly for pod density, apply the required EKS subnet tags, attach a secondary CIDR to avoid RFC1918 exhaustion, and configure VPC endpoints so pods never traverse a NAT Gateway to reach ECR or S3.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — verify AWS CLI and EKS access
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws ec2 describe-vpcs \
  --query 'Vpcs[*].{ID:VpcId,CIDR:CidrBlock,Secondary:CidrBlockAssociationSet[*].CidrBlock}' \
  --output table

# Terminal 2 — check EKS-tagged subnets
aws ec2 describe-subnets \
  --query 'Subnets[?Tags[?Key==`kubernetes.io/role/elb`]].[SubnetId,CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone]' \
  --output table 2>/dev/null || echo "Configure AWS CLI first"

# Terminal 3 — check VPC endpoints
aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints \
  --query 'VpcEndpoints[*].{Type:VpcEndpointType,Service:ServiceName,State:State}' \
  --output table 2>/dev/null

See also: Lesson 29 — AWS EKS Networking for ENI/IP limits that drive subnet sizing.

docs.title: 1. Why VPC Design Matters for EKS
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Problem["Common mistakes"]
        S1["/24 subnet per AZ\n(254 IPs)"]
        S2["No subnet tags\n(LBs fail to provision)"]
        S3["Single VPC CIDR\n(exhausted by pods)"]
        S4["No VPC endpoints\n(NAT costs $0.045/GB)"]
    end
    subgraph Solution["Correct design"]
        T1["/22 or larger\n(1022+ IPs per AZ)"]
        T2["kubernetes.io/role/* tags\non all subnets"]
        T3["Secondary CIDR 100.64.0.0/16\nfor pod IPs"]
        T4["Interface endpoints\nfor ECR, STS, EC2"]
    end
    S1 --> T1
    S2 --> T2
    S3 --> T3
    S4 --> T4

Root cause of most EKS network failures: subnets exhausted, missing tags, or missing VPC endpoints.

docs.title: 2. IP Planning Formula
docs.text:
Required IPs per subnet =
  (nodes_per_AZ × 1)              <- node primary IPs
  + (pods_per_node × nodes_per_AZ)  <- pod secondary IPs (VPC CNI)
  + (LBs × 1)                     <- one IP per NLB/ALB per AZ
  + 20% buffer

Example: 20 nodes/AZ, 29 pods/node (m5.large), 5 LBs
  = 20 + (29 × 20) + 5 + 20% buffer
  = 20 + 580 + 5 = 605 × 1.2 = ~726 IPs
  → need /22 (1022 IPs) minimum per AZ

# Calculate IPs available in a subnet
python3 -c "
import ipaddress
n = ipaddress.IPv4Network('10.0.10.0/22')
print(f'Network: {n}')
print(f'Usable hosts: {n.num_addresses - 2}')
# AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet (first 4 + last 1)
print(f'AWS usable: {n.num_addresses - 5}')
"

docs.title: 3. Recommended VPC Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph VPC["VPC 10.0.0.0/16 + 100.64.0.0/16 (secondary)"]
        subgraph AZ_A["us-east-1a"]
            PUB_A["Public Subnet\n10.0.0.0/24 (254 IPs)\nNAT GW, ALB nodes"]
            PRIV_A["Private Subnet — Nodes\n10.0.10.0/22 (1022 IPs)\nWorker nodes + pod IPs"]
            POD_A["Pod Subnet (optional)\n100.64.0.0/18\nPod IPs from secondary CIDR"]
        end
        subgraph AZ_B["us-east-1b"]
            PUB_B["Public Subnet\n10.0.1.0/24"]
            PRIV_B["Private Subnet\n10.0.14.0/22"]
            POD_B["Pod Subnet\n100.64.64.0/18"]
        end
        subgraph AZ_C["us-east-1c"]
            PUB_C["Public Subnet\n10.0.2.0/24"]
            PRIV_C["Private Subnet\n10.0.18.0/22"]
            POD_C["Pod Subnet\n100.64.128.0/18"]
        end
        IGW["Internet Gateway"]
        NATGW["NAT Gateway\n(one per AZ)"]
        EP["VPC Endpoints\nECR, S3, STS, EC2"]
    end
    IGW --> PUB_A
    PUB_A --> NATGW --> PRIV_A
    EP -.-> PRIV_A
    EP -.-> PRIV_B
    EP -.-> PRIV_C

docs.title: 4. Subnet Tagging — Required for EKS
docs.text:
Missing tags are the #1 reason LoadBalancer services fail to provision.

# Tag private subnets — internal NLBs and ALBs (EKS-managed LBs)
aws ec2 create-tags \
  --resources subnet-private-1a subnet-private-1b subnet-private-1c \
  --tags \
    Key=kubernetes.io/cluster/my-cluster,Value=shared \
    Key=kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb,Value=1

# Tag public subnets — internet-facing NLBs and ALBs
aws ec2 create-tags \
  --resources subnet-public-1a subnet-public-1b subnet-public-1c \
  --tags \
    Key=kubernetes.io/cluster/my-cluster,Value=shared \
    Key=kubernetes.io/role/elb,Value=1

# Verify tags
aws ec2 describe-subnets \
  --filters "Name=tag:kubernetes.io/cluster/my-cluster,Values=shared" \
  --query 'Subnets[*].{ID:SubnetId,CIDR:CidrBlock,Tags:Tags[?Key==`kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb`||Key==`kubernetes.io/role/elb`]}' \
  --output table
Tag Value Required for kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name> shared or owned EKS to discover subnets kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb 1 Internal NLBs and ALBs kubernetes.io/role/elb 1 Internet-facing NLBs and ALBs

shared vs owned: Use shared when multiple EKS clusters share the same subnets. Use owned when only one cluster uses the subnet (allows the cluster to delete it on cluster deletion).

docs.title: 5. Secondary CIDR — Avoiding RFC1918 Exhaustion
docs.text:
Large clusters consume VPC IPs at scale (1 IP per pod). A secondary CIDR from RFC 6598 (100.64.0.0/10 — "shared address space") adds non-RFC1918 IPs that don't conflict with on-premises ranges.

# Attach secondary CIDR to VPC
aws ec2 associate-vpc-cidr-block \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxxxx \
  --cidr-block 100.64.0.0/16

# Verify
aws ec2 describe-vpcs --vpc-ids vpc-xxxxx \
  --query 'Vpcs[0].CidrBlockAssociationSet'
# [{"CidrBlock": "10.0.0.0/16", ...}, {"CidrBlock": "100.64.0.0/16", ...}]

# Create pod subnets in the secondary CIDR (one per AZ)
aws ec2 create-subnet \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxxxx \
  --cidr-block 100.64.0.0/18 \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a

# Configure VPC CNI to use secondary CIDR for pod IPs
kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system \
  AWS_VPC_K8S_CNI_CUSTOM_NETWORK_CFG=true \
  ENI_CONFIG_LABEL_DEF=topology.kubernetes.io/zone

docs.title: 6. ENIConfig — Custom Networking per AZ
docs.text:
When pods must use a different subnet than nodes (secondary CIDR scenario or separated pod/node subnets):

# One ENIConfig per AZ — name must match the AZ name exactly
apiVersion: crd.k8s.amazonaws.com/v1alpha1
kind: ENIConfig
metadata:
  name: us-east-1a       # must match topology.kubernetes.io/zone label
spec:
  subnet: subnet-pod-1a   # subnet for pod ENIs in this AZ (100.64.0.0/18)
  securityGroups:
    - sg-pod-xxxxx         # SG to attach to pod ENIs
---
apiVersion: crd.k8s.amazonaws.com/v1alpha1
kind: ENIConfig
metadata:
  name: us-east-1b
spec:
  subnet: subnet-pod-1b
  securityGroups:
    - sg-pod-xxxxx
---
apiVersion: crd.k8s.amazonaws.com/v1alpha1
kind: ENIConfig
metadata:
  name: us-east-1c
spec:
  subnet: subnet-pod-1c
  securityGroups:
    - sg-pod-xxxxx

# Apply ENIConfigs
kubectl apply -f eniconfig-us-east-1a.yaml
kubectl apply -f eniconfig-us-east-1b.yaml
kubectl apply -f eniconfig-us-east-1c.yaml

# Verify ENIConfigs exist
kubectl get eniconfig

# Nodes automatically pick the right ENIConfig based on their AZ label
kubectl get node $NODE -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.topology\.kubernetes\.io/zone}'
# us-east-1a  <- matches ENIConfig name "us-east-1a"

docs.title: 7. Security Groups for EKS
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph SGs["Security Group Layers"]
        CLUSTERSG["Cluster SG\n(control-plane ↔ nodes)\nAuto-created by EKS"]
        NODESG["Node SG\n(node ↔ node traffic)\nAuto-created by EKS"]
        PODSG["Pod SG\n(SecurityGroupPolicy)\nYou create this"]
        LBSG["LB SG\n(ALB/NLB → nodes)\nCreated by LB Controller"]
    end
    CLUSTERSG --> NODESG
    NODESG --> PODSG
    LBSG --> NODESG
# List EKS-managed security groups
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --filters "Name=tag:kubernetes.io/cluster/my-cluster,Values=owned,shared" \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[*].{Name:GroupName,ID:GroupId,Tags:Tags[?Key==`Name`].Value|[0]}'

# Allow DB access from node SG (for pods without per-pod SG)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-db-xxxxx \
  --protocol tcp \
  --port 5432 \
  --source-group sg-node-xxxxx  # node SG ID

# If using CNI overlay plugins (Cilium/Calico VXLAN)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-node-xxxxx \
  --protocol udp --port 4789 \
  --source-group sg-node-xxxxx

# Allow NodePort range from load balancers
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-node-xxxxx \
  --protocol tcp --port 30000-32767 \
  --cidr 10.0.0.0/8

docs.title: 8. VPC Endpoints — Keep Traffic Off the NAT Gateway
docs.text:
Pods accessing AWS services go via NAT Gateway by default ($0.045/GB + NAT GW hourly cost). VPC Endpoints keep traffic private and free (gateway) or low-cost (interface).

# Create S3 Gateway endpoint (free — route-table based)
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxxxx \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-private-1a rtb-private-1b rtb-private-1c

# Create ECR API interface endpoint (required for image pulls on private clusters)
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxxxx \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ecr.api \
  --subnet-ids subnet-private-1a subnet-private-1b subnet-private-1c \
  --security-group-ids sg-endpoint-xxxxx \
  --private-dns-enabled

# Create ECR DKR interface endpoint (actual image layer pulls)
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxxxx \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ecr.dkr \
  --subnet-ids subnet-private-1a subnet-private-1b subnet-private-1c \
  --security-group-ids sg-endpoint-xxxxx \
  --private-dns-enabled

# Verify endpoints are available
aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints \
  --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-xxxxx" \
  --query 'VpcEndpoints[*].{Type:VpcEndpointType,Service:ServiceName,State:State}' \
  --output table

Required endpoints for a fully private EKS cluster:

Endpoint Type Why needed com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.api Interface Authenticate ECR image pulls com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.dkr Interface Pull image layers from ECR com.amazonaws.<region>.s3 Gateway (free) Pull image layers (ECR uses S3 backend) com.amazonaws.<region>.sts Interface IRSA token exchange com.amazonaws.<region>.ec2 Interface VPC CNI calls EC2 API com.amazonaws.<region>.elasticloadbalancing Interface AWS Load Balancer Controller

docs.title: 9. EKS Fully Private Cluster
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant DEV as Developer
    participant VPN as VPN / Direct Connect
    participant PRIV as Private Subnet
    participant EKS as EKS API Server\n(private endpoint)
    participant EC2 as EC2 Worker Nodes

    DEV->>VPN: Connect to corporate VPN
    VPN->>PRIV: Route to VPC CIDR
    PRIV->>EKS: kubectl commands via private endpoint
    EKS->>EC2: Schedule workloads via cross-account ENI
    Note over EC2: Nodes pull images via ECR endpoint<br/>No internet access required
# Create a cluster with only private API endpoint
aws eks create-cluster \
  --name private-cluster \
  --resources-vpc-config \
    "subnetIds=subnet-private-1a,subnet-private-1b,\
     securityGroupIds=sg-cluster-xxxxx,\
     endpointPrivateAccess=true,\
     endpointPublicAccess=false"

# Access requires VPN, Direct Connect, or bastion
# Use SSM Session Manager for node access (no SSH required)
aws ssm start-session --target i-xxxxx

docs.title: 10. Network ACLs vs Security Groups
docs.text:
Security Groups Network ACLs Scope ENI level (per interface) Subnet level (all traffic) Stateful Yes — return traffic auto-allowed No — must allow both directions Default behavior Deny all inbound, allow all outbound Allow all (default NACL) Rules Allow only Allow + Deny EKS use Primary access control Secondary; rarely needed Order All rules evaluated Rule number order (lowest wins) 
# NACLs break EKS when stateless return traffic is blocked
# Allow ephemeral ports (1024-65535) for return traffic on outbound-restricted NACLs
aws ec2 authorize-network-acl-entry \
  --network-acl-id acl-xxxxx \
  --rule-number 900 \
  --protocol tcp \
  --port-range From=1024,To=65535 \
  --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --egress \
  --rule-action allow

# Same for inbound return traffic
aws ec2 authorize-network-acl-entry \
  --network-acl-id acl-xxxxx \
  --rule-number 900 \
  --protocol tcp \
  --port-range From=1024,To=65535 \
  --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --ingress \
  --rule-action allow

docs.title: 11. VPC Flow Logs for Kubernetes Debugging
docs.text:
# Enable VPC flow logs to CloudWatch
aws ec2 create-flow-logs \
  --resource-type VPC \
  --resource-ids vpc-xxxxx \
  --traffic-type ALL \
  --log-destination-type cloud-watch-logs \
  --log-group-name /aws/vpc/flowlogs/my-cluster

# Query: find REJECT traffic from a specific pod IP
aws logs filter-log-events \
  --log-group-name /aws/vpc/flowlogs/my-cluster \
  --filter-pattern "[version, account_id, interface_id, srcaddr=\"10.0.10.25\", ...]" | \
  jq '.events[].message' | grep REJECT

# CloudWatch Insights query for pod connectivity debugging:
# fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action
# | filter action = "REJECT"
# | filter srcAddr like "10.0.10."
# | sort @timestamp desc
# | limit 50

docs.title: 12. Subnet Sizing Reference
docs.text:
Cluster Size Nodes per AZ Pods per Node Recommended Subnet IPs Available Small (dev) 3 29 (m5.large) /24 251 Medium 10 29 /23 507 Large 25 29 /22 1019 XL 50 58 (m5.xlarge) /21 2043 Cluster with prefix delegation 50 110+ /20 4091

Rule of thumb: At least /22 per AZ for any production EKS cluster. Add secondary CIDR if you anticipate > 500 pods per AZ.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix LoadBalancer service stuck Pending Missing subnet tags aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids <id> --query 'Subnets[0].Tags' Add kubernetes.io/role/elb or internal-elb tag Node group fails to launch Subnet exhausted aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids <id> --query 'Subnets[0].AvailableIpAddressCount' Expand subnet or add new subnet Image pull fails on private cluster Missing ECR VPC endpoint aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters "Name=service-name,Values=*ecr*" Create interface endpoints for ecr.api and ecr.dkr Cross-AZ pod latency high Pods and nodes in different AZs due to bad ENIConfig kubectl get pods -o wide and compare AZ of pod IP vs node Verify ENIConfig names match AZ labels exactly IRSA token exchange fails on private cluster Missing STS VPC endpoint kubectl logs <pod> | grep sts Create interface endpoint for sts NLB health checks fail NACL blocking return traffic aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filter "Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc>" Allow ephemeral ports 1024-65535 inbound and outbound in NACL Pod IP from wrong AZ subnet ENIConfig name mismatch kubectl get node <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.topology\.kubernetes\.io/zone}' Rename ENIConfig to match exact AZ string 
# Full VPC diagnostic sequence

# 1. Check subnet capacity
aws ec2 describe-subnets \
  --filters "Name=tag:kubernetes.io/cluster/my-cluster,Values=shared" \
  --query 'Subnets[*].{ID:SubnetId,AZ:AvailabilityZone,Free:AvailableIpAddressCount,CIDR:CidrBlock}' \
  --output table

# 2. Verify all required subnet tags
aws ec2 describe-subnets \
  --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc-id>" \
  --query 'Subnets[*].{ID:SubnetId,Tags:Tags}' \
  --output json | jq '.[] | select(.Tags | map(.Key) | contains(["kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb"]) | not) | .ID'

# 3. Check VPC endpoints
aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints \
  --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc-id>" \
  --query 'VpcEndpoints[*].{Service:ServiceName,State:State}' \
  --output table

# 4. Check flow logs for REJECT on pod IPs
aws logs filter-log-events \
  --log-group-name /aws/vpc/flowlogs/my-cluster \
  --filter-pattern "REJECT" \
  --start-time $(($(date +%s) - 300))000 | jq '.events[].message' | head -20

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Private subnets sized at /22 or larger per AZ — AvailableIpAddressCount > 20% of capacity at all times
  • All private subnets tagged kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1 and kubernetes.io/cluster/<name>=shared
  • All public subnets tagged kubernetes.io/role/elb=1 and kubernetes.io/cluster/<name>=shared
  • Secondary CIDR (100.64.0.0/16) attached if primary CIDR is /16 and cluster has >500 pods
  • VPC endpoints created for ECR (api + dkr), S3 (gateway), STS, EC2, and ELB
  • NAT Gateway deployed one per AZ (not one shared — single NAT is a failure domain)
  • VPC Flow Logs enabled and forwarded to CloudWatch for pod-level connectivity debugging

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use /24 subnets for EKS nodes 254 IPs minus 5 AWS reserved = 249 usable; large clusters exhaust this in one AZ Use /22 (1019 IPs) minimum; /20 for XL clusters Single NAT Gateway for all AZs NAT Gateway AZ outage takes down cross-AZ egress for all nodes Deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ — cost is worth the HA Share VPC CIDR with on-prem without secondary CIDR Pod IPs overlap with corporate RFC1918 — routing breaks via VPN/Direct Connect Add 100.64.0.0/16 secondary CIDR; use ENIConfig to put pods there Use owned tag on shared subnets EKS assumes exclusive ownership and may delete/modify subnet resources on cluster deletion Use shared for subnets used by multiple clusters or other workloads Skip VPC endpoints assuming NAT Gateway is cheaper ECR image pulls generate significant NAT data transfer charges; VPC endpoints eliminate this Interface endpoints cost ~$0.01/hr each; pay for 3 endpoints, save on GB charges for image pulls

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List VPCs and CIDRs aws ec2 describe-vpcs --query 'Vpcs[*].{ID:VpcId,CIDR:CidrBlock}' Add secondary CIDR aws ec2 associate-vpc-cidr-block --vpc-id <id> --cidr-block 100.64.0.0/16 Tag subnet (internal LB) aws ec2 create-tags --resources <subnet-id> --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb,Value=1 Tag subnet (public LB) aws ec2 create-tags --resources <subnet-id> --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/elb,Value=1 Check subnet free IPs aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids <id> --query 'Subnets[0].AvailableIpAddressCount' List VPC endpoints aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --query 'VpcEndpoints[*].{Service:ServiceName,State:State}' Create S3 gateway endpoint aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id <id> --service-name com.amazonaws.<region>.s3 --route-table-ids <rtb> Enable flow logs aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type VPC --resource-ids <vpc> --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type cloud-watch-logs --log-group-name /vpc/flows Check ENIConfig kubectl get eniconfig View NACL rules aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filter "Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc>" Create private EKS cluster aws eks create-cluster ... --resources-vpc-config "endpointPrivateAccess=true,endpointPublicAccess=false"

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Design Decision Recommendation VPC CIDR /16 primary (65k IPs); add 100.64.0.0/16 secondary for pods at scale Private subnet size /22 per AZ (1019 usable IPs) minimum; /20 for large clusters Public subnet size /24 per AZ — NLBs and NAT Gateways only Subnet tags kubernetes.io/role/elb=1 (public), internal-elb=1 (private) — required for LB provisioning NAT Gateway One per AZ — never share across AZs VPC endpoints ECR (api+dkr), S3 (gateway), STS, EC2, ELB — required for private clusters Security Groups Cluster SG + Node SG (auto-created); Pod SG for sensitive workloads Traffic visibility VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch — essential for pod-level debugging

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does the EKS documentation recommend at least /22 subnets per AZ for production clusters, and how does the IP planning formula account for pod IPs?
Answer The VPC CNI assigns one real VPC IP per pod (not just per node), so a typical medium cluster with 10 nodes × 29 pods each in one AZ already needs 290 pod IPs plus 10 node IPs plus buffer. A /24 subnet provides only 251 usable IPs (259 minus 5 AWS-reserved), which is exhausted quickly. A /22 provides 1,019 usable IPs. The planning formula is: (nodes_per_AZ × 1) + (pods_per_node × nodes_per_AZ) + (LBs × 1) + 20% buffer — always round up to the next power-of-two subnet that accommodates the result.
  1. [Scenario question] A new LoadBalancer Service is stuck in <pending> on EKS even though the VPC and subnets exist. The AWS Load Balancer Controller logs show "No subnets found." What subnet tag is most likely missing?
Answer The subnet is missing the EKS discovery tag. For internal NLBs the required tag is `kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1`; for internet-facing NLBs the tag is `kubernetes.io/role/elb=1`. Both internal and external subnets also need `kubernetes.io/cluster/=shared` (or `owned`). Without these tags the AWS Load Balancer Controller cannot discover which subnets to place the load balancer in. Add the tags with `aws ec2 create-tags --resources --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb,Value=1`.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check how many IP addresses are still available in a specific EKS subnet?
Answer 
aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids <subnet-id> \
  --query 'Subnets[0].AvailableIpAddressCount'
If this number is below 20% of the subnet's total capacity (for example, below 200 for a /22), plan to expand the subnet or add a secondary CIDR (such as `100.64.0.0/16`) before the cluster runs out of IPs and node groups fail to launch.

docs.title: Lesson 31 — AWS Load Balancer Controller Deep Dive
docs.text:
Track: AWS Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 20 — Cloud Load Balancers, Lesson 29 — EKS Networking Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Configure AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision ALBs via Ingress and NLBs via Service, using IRSA, IngressGroups, weighted canary routing, and WAFv2 integration.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get deployment -n kube-system aws-load-balancer-controller 2>/dev/null || \
  echo "AWS LBC not installed — see section 2 for installation"
kubectl get ingressclass
kubectl get targetgroupbindings -A 2>/dev/null

# Terminal 2 — Mac (aws CLI)
aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers \
  --query 'LoadBalancers[*].[LoadBalancerName,Type,State.Code]' \
  --output table 2>/dev/null || echo "Configure AWS CLI first"

docs.title: 1. AWS LBC vs In-Tree CCM
docs.text: Feature In-tree CCM (legacy) AWS Load Balancer Controller NLB type Classic LB or NLB NLB (Network Load Balancer) ALB No Yes (via Ingress) Target type Instance only Instance or IP (pod-level) Annotations Limited 50+ annotations IngressGroup No Yes — share one ALB across Ingresses WAFv2 integration No Yes Weighted routing No Yes (canary via ALB listener rules) Maintenance Deprecated Actively developed

docs.title: 2. Controller Architecture
docs.text:
The LBC watches Ingress and Service resources, reconciles against the ELBv2 API, and creates or updates ALB or NLB resources. It authenticates to AWS via IRSA (IAM Role for Service Account) — no EC2 instance profile needed.

flowchart LR
    subgraph K8s["Kubernetes Cluster"]
        IC[Ingress / Service\nresource] -->|watch events| LBC[aws-load-balancer-controller\nkube-system pod]
        SA[ServiceAccount\nIRSA annotation] --> LBC
        TGB[TargetGroupBinding\nCRD] --> LBC
    end
    subgraph AWS["AWS ELBv2 API"]
        LBC -->|CreateLoadBalancer| ALB[Application\nLoad Balancer]
        LBC -->|CreateLoadBalancer| NLB[Network\nLoad Balancer]
        ALB --> TG1[Target Group\ntarget-type=ip]
        NLB --> TG2[Target Group\ntarget-type=instance]
        TG1 -->|direct pod ENI| Pods[EKS Pods]
        TG2 -->|NodePort→kube-proxy| Nodes[EKS Nodes]
    end
    subgraph IAM["IAM / OIDC"]
        SA -->|assume role via OIDC| IRSA[IAM Role\nAWSLoadBalancerControllerPolicy]
        IRSA --> AWS
    end

See also: Lesson 29 — EKS Networking for VPC CNI and ENI assignment that enable ip target type.

docs.title: 3. ALB Provisioning Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API
    participant LBC as aws-load-balancer-controller
    participant AWS as AWS ELBv2 API

    Dev->>K8s: kubectl apply Ingress (ingressClassName: alb)
    K8s->>LBC: Ingress event (informer)
    LBC->>AWS: DescribeLoadBalancers (check existing)
    LBC->>AWS: CreateLoadBalancer (ALB, scheme, subnets)
    LBC->>AWS: CreateTargetGroup (per backend Service)
    LBC->>AWS: RegisterTargets (pod IPs or node IPs)
    LBC->>AWS: CreateListener (HTTP:80, HTTPS:443)
    LBC->>AWS: CreateRule (host/path → target group)
    AWS-->>LBC: LoadBalancer DNS name
    LBC->>K8s: Patch Ingress .status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname
    Dev->>K8s: kubectl get ingress (shows ADDRESS)
    Note over Dev,K8s: Create Route53 CNAME/alias to ALB DNS

docs.title: 4. NLB via Service (type: LoadBalancer)
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    # Required: use external controller, not CCM
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "external"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip"

    # Scheme
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internet-facing"
    # or: "internal" for private NLB

    # Health check
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-protocol: "HTTP"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-path: "/healthz"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-interval: "10"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-healthy-threshold: "2"

    # Cross-zone LB (distributes traffic evenly across AZs)
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"

    # Preserve client IP
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-target-group-attributes: "preserve_client_ip.enabled=true"

    # Static IP via Elastic IP
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-eip-allocations: "eipalloc-xxxxx,eipalloc-yyyyy"

    # TLS
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert: "arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123:certificate/xxx"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports: "443"

    # Access logging
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-access-log-enabled: "true"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-access-log-s3-bucket-name: "my-nlb-logs"
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

docs.title: Instance vs IP Target Type
docs.text:
Instance mode: NLB → NodePort → kube-proxy → pod 

service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "instance"

IP mode: NLB → pod IP directly (requires VPC CNI) 

service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip"
# Lower latency — skips NodePort and kube-proxy
# Client IP preserved natively

docs.title: 5. ALB via Ingress
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip

    # TLS
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123:certificate/xxx
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP":80},{"HTTPS":443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"

    # Health check
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /healthz
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-interval-seconds: "15"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/success-codes: "200-399"

    # Stickiness
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-group-attributes: stickiness.enabled=true,stickiness.lb_cookie.duration_seconds=86400

    # WAF
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/wafv2-acl-arn: arn:aws:wafv2:us-east-1:123:regional/webacl/xxx

    # Access logs
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/load-balancer-attributes: "access_logs.s3.enabled=true,access_logs.s3.bucket=my-alb-logs"

spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - host: web.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 8080
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: frontend
                port:
                  number: 80

docs.title: 6. IngressGroup — Share One ALB Across Ingresses
docs.text:
# Multiple Ingress resources share one ALB (cost saving)
metadata:
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: "production"   # same group = same ALB
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.order: "10"          # rule priority order

# All Ingresses with group.name=production share one ALB
kubectl get ingress -A | grep production
# web-ingress     web.example.com
# api-ingress     api.example.com
# → both served by the same ALB DNS name

docs.title: 7. TargetGroupBinding — Attach External Target Groups
docs.text:
# Register pods directly to an existing Target Group (useful for blue/green)
apiVersion: elbv2.k8s.aws/v1beta1
kind: TargetGroupBinding
metadata:
  name: web-tgb
spec:
  serviceRef:
    name: web
    port: 8080
  targetGroupARN: arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:us-east-1:123:targetgroup/web/xxx
  targetType: ip

docs.title: 8. Weighted Routing for Canary Deployments
docs.text:
# Two services, weighted via annotations
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-canary
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/actions.weighted-routing: |
      {"type":"forward","forwardConfig":{"targetGroups":[
        {"serviceName":"web-v1","servicePort":"80","weight":90},
        {"serviceName":"web-v2","servicePort":"80","weight":10}
      ]}}
spec:
  rules:
    - http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: weighted-routing
                port:
                  name: use-annotation

See also: Lesson 33 — ArgoCD GitOps for Argo Rollouts progressive delivery using ALB weighted target groups.

docs.title: 9. IAM Permissions (IRSA)
docs.text:
The LBC needs IAM permissions to manage ALBs and NLBs:

# Create IAM policy
curl -o iam-policy.json \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-load-balancer-controller/main/docs/install/iam_policy.json

aws iam create-policy \
  --policy-name AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy \
  --policy-document file://iam-policy.json

# Create IRSA service account
eksctl create iamserviceaccount \
  --cluster my-cluster \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --name aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:policy/AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy \
  --override-existing-serviceaccounts \
  --approve

docs.title: NLB Service Annotations
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change aws-load-balancer-type (CCM) Set to external to force LBC ownership Always set when using LBC for NLBs aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type instance ip sends directly to pod ENI Use ip for lower latency + accurate client IP aws-load-balancer-scheme internal internet-facing creates public NLB External-facing services aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled false Evenly distributes across AZs Multi-AZ clusters with uneven node counts aws-load-balancer-eip-allocations (dynamic IPs) Assign static Elastic IPs per AZ IP allowlisting by external partners aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert (none) ACM cert ARN for TLS termination HTTPS/TLS on NLB aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-interval 30 Seconds between health checks Tune for faster failover (10s)

docs.title: ALB Ingress Annotations
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type instance ip routes directly to pod Lower latency; requires VPC CNI alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme internal internet-facing for public ALB Public-facing applications alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name (none) Share one ALB across multiple Ingresses Multiple services to save ALB cost alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.order 0 Priority of rules within the shared ALB Prevent rule conflicts in shared ALB alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/wafv2-acl-arn (none) Attach WAFv2 Web ACL to ALB DDoS and bot protection for public APIs alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect (none) 443 redirects all HTTP to HTTPS Enforce TLS in production alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-interval-seconds 15 Seconds between ALB health checks Tune for fast pod failover vs noise

docs.title: 11. Hands-On Practice
docs.text:
# 1. Verify LBC is running and has IRSA wired up
kubectl get sa aws-load-balancer-controller -n kube-system \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.eks\.amazonaws\.com/role-arn}'
# Expected: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/AWSLoadBalancerControllerRole

# 2. Confirm IngressClass is registered
kubectl get ingressclass alb -o yaml | grep controller
# Expected: controller: ingress.k8s.aws/alb

# 3. Create a minimal ALB Ingress and watch reconciliation
kubectl apply -f web-ingress.yaml
kubectl describe ingress web-ingress | grep -A 20 Events
# Expected: Normal  SuccessfullyReconciled ... Reconciled

# 4. Get the provisioned ALB DNS name
kubectl get ingress web-ingress \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}'
# Expected: k8s-default-webingress-XXXX.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com

# 5. Verify target group health (ip-mode shows pod IPs; instance-mode shows node IPs)
TG_ARN=$(aws elbv2 describe-target-groups \
  --query 'TargetGroups[?contains(TargetGroupName,`k8s`)].TargetGroupArn' \
  --output text | head -1)
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "$TG_ARN" \
  --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[*].[Target.Id,Target.Port,TargetHealth.State]' \
  --output table
# Expected: pod IPs with State=healthy (ip-mode) or node IPs (instance-mode)

# 6. Verify IngressGroup — services in same group share one ALB
kubectl get ingress -A \
  -o custom-columns='NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,GROUP:.metadata.annotations.alb\.ingress\.kubernetes\.io/group\.name,ADDR:.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname'
# Expected: same ADDR for all Ingresses in the same group

# 7. Test weighted canary routing — confirm traffic split
for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s https://web.example.com/ | grep -o "v[12]"; done | sort | uniq -c
# Expected: approximately 18x v1, 2x v2 (90/10 split)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Ingress has no ADDRESS after 2 min LBC not running or wrong IngressClass kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/aws-load-balancer-controller \| tail -30 Verify ingressClassName: alb and LBC pod status AccessDenied in LBC logs Missing IRSA or wrong IAM policy kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/aws-load-balancer-controller \| grep AccessDenied Recreate IRSA with eksctl create iamserviceaccount No subnets found in LBC logs Subnets missing ELB role tags aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=tag-key,Values=kubernetes.io/role/elb Tag public subnets kubernetes.io/role/elb=1, private: kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1 Target group health check failing Wrong health check path, port, or pods not ready aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn> Set alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path and verify pod readiness Two ALBs created for same IngressGroup Different group.name spelling or case kubectl get ingress -A -o jsonpath='{..annotations}' Ensure exact same group.name value across all Ingresses 502 Bad Gateway from ALB Pod not ready or wrong targetPort kubectl get endpoints <service> Verify pod readiness and Service targetPort matches container port Certificate error on HTTPS ACM cert in wrong AWS region aws acm describe-certificate --certificate-arn <arn> Use cert ARN from same region as EKS cluster WAF blocking legitimate traffic Overly strict WAF rules Check WAF sampled requests in AWS Console Add IP set allow-rule or adjust managed rule group sensitivity

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Subnet tags set: kubernetes.io/role/elb=1 (public subnets) and kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1 (private subnets)
  • IRSA configured — LBC ServiceAccount has eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation, no EC2 instance profile
  • ALB access logs enabled, shipped to versioned S3 bucket with 90-day lifecycle policy
  • WAFv2 ACL attached to all internet-facing ALBs via wafv2-acl-arn annotation
  • ssl-redirect: "443" enforces HTTPS; HTTP listener only redirects, never serves content
  • IngressGroup used to minimize ALB count across namespaces (ALB limit: 50 per region by default)
  • target-type: ip used with VPC CNI for direct pod routing and accurate client IP logging

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use legacy CCM annotation (aws-load-balancer-type: nlb) Creates classic NLB via old in-tree controller, misses LBC features like IP mode and WAF Add external value and use full LBC annotation set One Ingress per service with no group.name Each Ingress creates a separate ALB — costly and exhausts the 50 ALB regional limit quickly Group with alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name to share one ALB target-type: instance for latency-sensitive workloads Adds NodePort hop and kube-proxy latency; source IP is node IP, losing client identity Use target-type: ip with VPC CNI for direct pod routing Hard-code ALB DNS name in app config or external DNS ALB DNS changes on delete and recreate, breaking connectivity Create Route53 alias or CNAME record pointing to the ALB DNS name No WAF on internet-facing ALBs Exposes APIs to bots, scrapers, and common OWASP exploits without filtering Attach WAFv2 ACL via alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/wafv2-acl-arn annotation

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command Check LBC is running kubectl get deploy -n kube-system aws-load-balancer-controller Get ALB DNS for Ingress kubectl get ingress <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}' Watch LBC reconciliation logs kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/aws-load-balancer-controller -f List all TargetGroupBindings kubectl get targetgroupbindings -A List ALBs in account aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --query 'LoadBalancers[?Type==\application`].[LoadBalancerName,State.Code]' --output table` Check target group health aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn> View IngressGroup members kubectl get ingress -A -l alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name=<group> Check required subnet tags aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=tag-key,Values=kubernetes.io/role/elb --query 'Subnets[*].[SubnetId,Tags]' Force LBC to re-reconcile Ingress kubectl annotate ingress <name> reconcile="$(date +%s)" --overwrite Get IRSA role on LBC ServiceAccount kubectl get sa aws-load-balancer-controller -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.eks\.amazonaws\.com/role-arn}' Describe IngressClass kubectl describe ingressclass alb Watch Ingress events kubectl get events -n <ns> --field-selector involvedObject.name=<ingress-name> -w

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Resource AWS Component Use Case Service (ip target) NLB → pods directly TCP/UDP, low latency Service (instance target) NLB → NodePort Simple setup Ingress ALB → pods HTTP/S, path routing, WAF IngressGroup Shared ALB Multiple services, one LB TargetGroupBinding Existing TG Blue/green, external traffic

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is the difference between target-type: instance and target-type: ip for the AWS Load Balancer Controller, and when would you choose each?
Answer With `target-type: instance`, the ALB or NLB sends traffic to each node's NodePort; kube-proxy on that node then performs a second hop (DNAT) to route the packet to the actual pod, which may be on a different node. With `target-type: ip`, the load balancer registers pod ENI IPs directly as targets and routes traffic in a single hop to the pod without going through kube-proxy. Choose `instance` when pods are using host-network or when you have strict compatibility requirements with older kube-proxy; choose `ip` for lower latency, correct client IP preservation, and direct pod health checks.
  1. [Scenario question] Two teams each defined an Ingress with ingressClassName: alb for different paths on the same domain. The controller provisioned two separate ALBs, doubling cost. What annotation would consolidate them into one ALB?
Answer Add the `alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name` annotation with the same value on both Ingress resources, for example `alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: "shared-prod"`. The AWS Load Balancer Controller merges all Ingress resources that share a group name into a single ALB, combining their listener rules. Each Ingress still manages its own rules independently — deleting one Ingress removes only its rules, not the shared ALB.
  1. [Practical question] What AWS CLI command would you run to check the health of targets registered behind a specific ALB target group, to see which pods are healthy vs. draining vs. unhealthy?
Answer 
aws elbv2 describe-target-health \
  --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:<region>:<account>:targetgroup/<name>/<id>
The output lists each target (IP or instance ID) with its `TargetHealth.State` (`healthy`, `unhealthy`, `draining`, `unused`) and a `TargetHealth.Reason` explaining any failure. Unhealthy targets are typically caused by security group rules blocking the health-check port or the pod not yet passing its readiness probe.

docs.title: Lesson 32 — AWS Hybrid and Multi-Cluster Networking
docs.text:
Track: AWS Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 22 — Multi-Cluster Networking, Lesson 30 — AWS VPC Design Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Connect multiple EKS clusters and on-premises workloads using VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, Direct Connect, and VPC Lattice, with cross-cluster DNS discovery and GitOps delivery.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl multi-context)
kubectl config get-contexts
aws eks list-clusters --output table 2>/dev/null || echo "Configure AWS CLI first"

# Terminal 2 — Mac (aws CLI — inspect Transit Gateway if present)
aws ec2 describe-transit-gateways \
  --query 'TransitGateways[*].[TransitGatewayId,State,Description]' \
  --output table 2>/dev/null || echo "No Transit Gateways or AWS CLI not configured"

docs.title: 1. Connectivity Options at a Glance
docs.text: Solution Routing Transitive Latency Cost Best for VPC Peering Direct VPC-to-VPC No Lowest Very low 2–3 clusters, no overlap Transit Gateway Hub-and-spoke Yes Low Medium 3+ clusters or on-prem hybrid VPC Lattice DNS/L7 service mesh N/A Low Per-request Service-to-service, no IP routing Direct Connect Dedicated fiber Via TGW Very low High (port fee) Production on-prem hybrid Site-to-Site VPN IPsec over internet Via TGW Medium Low Dev/backup on-prem EKS Anywhere On-prem EKS N/A Bare-metal Infra cost On-prem with EKS API

docs.title: 2. VPC Peering (simplest, same region or cross-region)
docs.text:
# Create VPC peering between cluster A VPC and cluster B VPC
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection \
  --vpc-id vpc-cluster-a \
  --peer-vpc-id vpc-cluster-b \
  --peer-region us-west-2   # omit for same region

# Accept the peering request
aws ec2 accept-vpc-peering-connection \
  --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-xxxxx

# Update route tables in both VPCs
aws ec2 create-route \
  --route-table-id rtb-cluster-a \
  --destination-cidr-block 10.1.0.0/16 \     # cluster B VPC CIDR
  --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-xxxxx

aws ec2 create-route \
  --route-table-id rtb-cluster-b \
  --destination-cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 \     # cluster A VPC CIDR
  --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-xxxxx

Pod CIDRs must not overlap. With VPC peering + VPC CNI, pods can reach each other directly by IP.

Limitations: no transitive routing (A↔B, B↔C, but not A↔C via B). N VPCs require N×(N-1)/2 peering connections (10 VPCs = 45 connections).

docs.title: 3. Transit Gateway (hub-and-spoke, recommended for 3+ VPCs)
docs.text:
# Create Transit Gateway
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway \
  --description "EKS multi-cluster TGW" \
  --options DefaultRouteTableAssociation=enable,DefaultRouteTablePropagation=enable

# Attach VPCs to TGW
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment \
  --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxxxx \
  --vpc-id vpc-cluster-a \
  --subnet-ids subnet-a1 subnet-a2

aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment \
  --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxxxx \
  --vpc-id vpc-cluster-b \
  --subnet-ids subnet-b1 subnet-b2

# Add routes in each VPC pointing to TGW for other clusters
aws ec2 create-route \
  --route-table-id rtb-cluster-a-private \
  --destination-cidr-block 10.1.0.0/16 \
  --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxxxx

TGW supports transitive routing: A↔B, B↔C, A↔C all work. Scales to 5,000 attachments.

flowchart LR
    subgraph TGW["Transit Gateway (hub)"]
        RT[Route Table\n10.0.0.0/8 → all attachments]
    end
    EKS1[EKS Cluster-1\n10.0.0.0/16] -->|attachment| RT
    EKS2[EKS Cluster-2\n10.1.0.0/16] -->|attachment| RT
    EKS3[EKS Cluster-3\n10.2.0.0/16] -->|attachment| RT
    OnPrem[On-Premises\n192.168.0.0/16\nvia Direct Connect] -->|attachment| RT
    RT -->|routes| EKS1
    RT -->|routes| EKS2
    RT -->|routes| EKS3
    RT -->|routes| OnPrem

docs.title: 4. Multi-Cluster Connectivity Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Region["AWS Region us-east-1"]
        subgraph ClusterA["EKS Cluster A — 10.0.0.0/16"]
            PodA[Pod\n10.0.1.5]
        end
        subgraph ClusterB["EKS Cluster B — 10.1.0.0/16"]
            PodB[Pod\n10.1.2.8]
        end
        TGW[Transit Gateway]
        Lattice[VPC Lattice\nService Network]
        ClusterA -->|TGW attachment| TGW
        ClusterB -->|TGW attachment| TGW
        ClusterA -->|service registration| Lattice
        ClusterB -->|service registration| Lattice
    end
    subgraph OnPrem["On-Premises Data Center"]
        DC[Servers\n192.168.0.0/16]
    end
    DX[AWS Direct Connect\nLocation] -->|dedicated fiber| TGW
    DC --> DX

See also: Lesson 22 — Multi-Cluster Networking for Cilium Cluster Mesh and Submariner details.

docs.title: 5. Cross-Cluster Pod Communication Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PodA as Pod (EKS-A: 10.0.1.5)
    participant NodeA as Node ENI (EKS-A)
    participant TGW as Transit Gateway
    participant NodeB as Node ENI (EKS-B)
    participant PodB as Pod (EKS-B: 10.1.2.8)

    Note over PodA,PodB: Pre-condition: VPC CIDRs do not overlap
    PodA->>NodeA: packet dst=10.1.2.8
    NodeA->>NodeA: route lookup: 10.1.0.0/16 via tgw-xxxxx
    NodeA->>TGW: forward packet
    TGW->>TGW: route table lookup: 10.1.0.0/16 → EKS-B attachment
    TGW->>NodeB: deliver to EKS-B subnet
    NodeB->>PodB: direct to pod ENI (VPC CNI ip-mode)
    PodB-->>PodA: response (symmetric return path)

docs.title: 6. Cross-Cluster Service Discovery
docs.text: After VPC peering or TGW, pods can reach each other by IP. But DNS discovery still needs work.

docs.title: Option A: Shared CoreDNS (stub zones)
docs.text:
# In cluster A's CoreDNS, forward cluster-b.local queries to cluster B's DNS
kubectl edit cm -n kube-system coredns

cluster-b.local:53 {
    forward . 172.30.0.10   # cluster B's kube-dns ClusterIP
    cache 30
}

# For this to work, cluster A nodes must be able to reach cluster B's kube-dns
# → ensure security groups allow UDP/TCP 53 between clusters

docs.title: Option B: ExternalDNS + Route53
docs.text:
# Install ExternalDNS in both clusters
# It creates Route53 records for Services and Ingresses

helm install external-dns bitnami/external-dns \
  --set provider=aws \
  --set aws.region=us-east-1 \
  --set domainFilters[0]=cluster-a.example.com \
  --set policy=sync

# Services with annotation get DNS records:
kubectl annotate svc web \
  external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname=web.cluster-a.example.com

docs.title: Option C: AWS VPC Lattice (new, managed service mesh)
docs.text:
# VPC Lattice provides service-to-service connectivity without VPC peering
# Install AWS Gateway API Controller
helm install aws-gateway-controller \
  oci://public.ecr.aws/aws-samples/aws-gateway-api-controller \
  -n aws-application-networking-system

# Create a ServiceNetwork (spans VPCs/clusters)
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: application-networking.k8s.aws/v1beta1
kind: VpcLatticeServiceNetwork
metadata:
  name: my-service-network
EOF

# Services registered in the network are reachable cross-cluster

docs.title: AWS Direct Connect
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    DC[On-Premises\nData Center] -->|dedicated fiber\n1-100 Gbps| DXLoc[Direct Connect\nLocation / PoP]
    DXLoc --> DXGW[Direct Connect\nGateway]
    DXGW -->|Transit VIF\nBGP session| TGW[Transit\nGateway]
    TGW --> EKS[EKS VPC\n10.0.0.0/16]
# Create a Transit Virtual Interface
aws directconnect create-transit-virtual-interface \
  --connection-id dxcon-xxxxx \
  --new-transit-virtual-interface \
    virtualInterfaceName=to-tgw,\
    vlan=100,\
    asn=65000,\
    mtu=9001,\
    transitGatewayId=tgw-xxxxx

# BGP peers automatically for route exchange
# On-prem router advertises: 192.168.0.0/16 (on-prem CIDR)
# AWS TGW advertises: 10.0.0.0/8 (VPC CIDRs)

docs.title: Site-to-Site VPN (simpler, over internet)
docs.text:
# Create Customer Gateway (your on-prem router)
aws ec2 create-customer-gateway \
  --type ipsec.1 \
  --public-ip 203.0.113.1 \  # on-prem public IP
  --bgp-asn 65001

# Create VPN Gateway and attach to VPC
aws ec2 create-vpn-gateway --type ipsec.1
aws ec2 attach-vpn-gateway \
  --vpn-gateway-id vgw-xxxxx \
  --vpc-id vpc-eks

# Create VPN connection
aws ec2 create-vpn-connection \
  --type ipsec.1 \
  --customer-gateway-id cgw-xxxxx \
  --vpn-gateway-id vgw-xxxxx \
  --options StaticRoutesOnly=false   # use BGP

# Download VPN config for your on-prem router
aws ec2 describe-vpn-connections \
  --vpn-connection-ids vpn-xxxxx \
  --query 'VpnConnections[0].CustomerGatewayConfiguration'

docs.title: 8. EKS Anywhere (On-Premises EKS)
docs.text:
EKS Anywhere brings EKS to your data center with the same tooling.

# Install eksctl-anywhere plugin
brew install aws/tap/eks-anywhere

# Create a cluster spec
eksctl anywhere generate clusterconfig my-cluster \
  --provider vsphere > cluster.yaml  # or: baremetal, docker, nutanix

# Review and deploy
eksctl anywhere create cluster -f cluster.yaml

# Networking with EKS Anywhere:
# - Uses Cilium as default CNI
# - Full BGP support for bare-metal
# - Same kubectl/eksctl experience as cloud EKS

docs.title: 9. Cilium Cluster Mesh on EKS
docs.text:
# Enable Cluster Mesh on EKS clusters
# (after replacing VPC CNI with Cilium)
cilium clustermesh enable \
  --service-type LoadBalancer \
  --context eks-cluster-a

cilium clustermesh enable \
  --service-type LoadBalancer \
  --context eks-cluster-b

# Connect the clusters
cilium clustermesh connect \
  --source-context eks-cluster-a \
  --destination-context eks-cluster-b

# Verify
cilium clustermesh status --context eks-cluster-a

docs.title: 10. Cross-Account EKS Access
docs.text:
# Share Transit Gateway across accounts
aws ram create-resource-share \
  --name tgw-share \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:ACCOUNT-A:transit-gateway/tgw-xxxxx \
  --principals ACCOUNT-B-ID

# In account B, accept the share
aws ram accept-resource-share-invitation \
  --resource-share-invitation-arn arn:aws:ram:...

# Attach account B's VPC to the shared TGW
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment \
  --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxxxx \  # from account A
  --vpc-id vpc-cluster-b-accountB \
  --subnet-ids subnet-xxxxx

docs.title: VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway Parameters
docs.text: Parameter VPC Peering Transit Gateway Max connections N×(N-1)/2 — unlimited but unmanageable 5,000 attachments Transitive routing No Yes (via TGW route tables) Cross-account Yes (requires accept in peer account) Yes (via AWS RAM sharing) Cross-region Yes (inter-region peering) Yes (TGW peering between regions) Bandwidth limit None (limited by NIC) 50 Gbps per attachment burst Cost No hourly fee; data transfer charged $0.05/hr per attachment + data transfer

docs.title: Direct Connect Virtual Interface Types
docs.text: VIF Type Connects To Use Case When to change Private VIF VGW (single VPC) Simple single-VPC connectivity Upgrade to Transit VIF for multi-VPC Public VIF AWS public endpoints Access S3, DynamoDB over DX Avoid unless specifically needed Transit VIF Direct Connect Gateway → TGW Multi-VPC, multi-account hybrid Default choice for EKS hybrid Hosted VIF Partner-managed Smaller bandwidth increments When <1 Gbps is sufficient

docs.title: 12. Hands-On Practice
docs.text:
# 1. Check existing VPC peering connections
aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections \
  --query 'VpcPeeringConnections[*].[VpcPeeringConnectionId,Status.Code,RequesterVpcInfo.VpcId,AccepterVpcInfo.VpcId]' \
  --output table

# 2. Verify TGW attachments and their state
aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-vpc-attachments \
  --query 'TransitGatewayVpcAttachments[*].[TransitGatewayAttachmentId,VpcId,State]' \
  --output table

# 3. Inspect TGW route tables
TGW_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-transit-gateways \
  --query 'TransitGateways[0].TransitGatewayId' --output text)
aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-route-tables \
  --filters Name=transit-gateway-id,Values=$TGW_ID

# 4. Cross-cluster pod reachability test
kubectl run -it --rm test-connectivity \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot --context eks-cluster-a -- \
  ping -c 3 10.1.2.8   # pod IP in cluster B
# Expected: 3 packets transmitted, 3 received

# 5. Verify CoreDNS stub zone resolves cross-cluster
kubectl run -it --rm dns-test \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot --context eks-cluster-a -- \
  dig +short web.cluster-b.local
# Expected: ClusterIP of service in cluster B

# 6. Check BGP session status (Direct Connect)
aws directconnect describe-virtual-interfaces \
  --query 'virtualInterfaces[*].[virtualInterfaceName,virtualInterfaceState,bgpPeers[0].bgpStatus]' \
  --output table
# Expected: bgpStatus=up for healthy session

# 7. VPN tunnel status
aws ec2 describe-vpn-connections \
  --query 'VpnConnections[*].VgwTelemetry[*].[OutsideIpAddress,Status,StatusMessage]' \
  --output table
# Expected: Status=UP for both tunnels (redundant pair)

See also: Lesson 29 — EKS Networking for VPC CNI behavior and pod CIDR assignments that must not overlap across peered clusters.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Pods cannot ping across clusters Missing routes in VPC route tables aws ec2 describe-route-tables --route-table-ids <rtb-id> Add route to peer VPC CIDR via pcx- or tgw- TGW attachment in failed state Subnet not in correct AZ or quota exceeded aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-vpc-attachments --filters Name=state,Values=failed Check TGW subnet requirements; request quota increase DNS not resolving cross-cluster CoreDNS stub zone missing or wrong IP kubectl exec -n kube-system deploy/coredns -- nslookup web.cluster-b.local Add stub zone to CoreDNS ConfigMap pointing to cluster B kube-dns VPC peering traffic rejected CIDR overlap between VPCs aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /aws/vpc/flowlogs --filter-pattern "[...,action=REJECT]" CIDRs must be non-overlapping; delete peering and re-plan CIDRs Direct Connect BGP not establishing Wrong ASN or MTU mismatch aws directconnect describe-virtual-interfaces Verify ASN matches on-prem router; set MTU=9001 for jumbo frames VPN tunnel DOWN On-prem IP change or IKE mismatch aws ec2 describe-vpn-connections --query 'VpnConnections[0].VgwTelemetry' Re-download VPN config and reconfigure on-prem device Cross-account TGW attachment pending RAM share not accepted aws ram get-resource-share-invitations Accept invitation in account B with aws ram accept-resource-share-invitation

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• All VPC CIDRs (including pod CIDRs) are non-overlapping before any peering or TGW attachment
  • Transit Gateway used for 3+ VPCs — VPC peering mesh avoided past 3 connections
  • TGW route tables segment traffic (e.g., dev clusters cannot route to prod clusters)
  • Direct Connect has two redundant connections at different PoPs for HA
  • Security groups explicitly allow required ports between cluster security groups (not just route-level)
  • VPC Flow Logs enabled on all cluster VPCs for connectivity audit
  • EKS cluster kubeconfigs for all clusters stored in a secrets manager, not local files

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Full-mesh VPC peering for 5+ clusters 10 clusters = 45 peering connections; no transitive routing, complex route management Use Transit Gateway for hub-and-spoke at 3+ VPCs Overlapping pod CIDRs across clusters Peered VPCs with overlapping pod CIDRs cause routing ambiguity Plan CIDR allocations before cluster creation; use IP Address Manager (IPAM) Single Direct Connect connection Physical fiber failure takes down all hybrid connectivity Provision two DX connections at different PoPs + VPN as fallback Security group "allow all" between clusters Effectively no network isolation between clusters Use specific port/protocol rules per service; use VPC Lattice for service-level access control DNS discovery via /etc/hosts Does not scale and breaks on pod restart Use CoreDNS stub zones or ExternalDNS + Route53 for dynamic DNS

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List EKS clusters aws eks list-clusters --output table Show kubectl contexts kubectl config get-contexts Switch cluster context kubectl config use-context <context-name> List TGW attachments aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-vpc-attachments --output table Check TGW route tables aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-route-tables View VPC peering connections aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --output table Check DX virtual interfaces aws directconnect describe-virtual-interfaces Check VPN tunnel status aws ec2 describe-vpn-connections --query 'VpnConnections[0].VgwTelemetry' Cross-cluster pod ping test kubectl run -it --rm t --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- ping -c3 <pod-ip> View VPC Flow Logs (rejected) aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /aws/vpc/flowlogs --filter-pattern "[...,action=REJECT]" Cilium cluster mesh status cilium clustermesh status --context <ctx> List RAM resource shares aws ram list-resources --resource-owner SELF --output table

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Solution Use Case Routing VPC Peering 2–3 clusters, same/cross region Direct, no transit Transit Gateway 3+ clusters, hub-and-spoke Transitive VPC Lattice Service mesh across VPCs/accounts Managed, L7-aware Direct Connect On-prem to AWS, production BGP, dedicated VPN On-prem to AWS, dev/backup BGP or static, over internet EKS Anywhere On-prem EKS Same as bare-metal (Lesson 07)

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does VPC Peering become unmanageable for 10 or more VPCs, and what AWS service solves this at scale?
Answer VPC Peering is non-transitive: each pair of VPCs requires a separate peering connection and route table entry in both VPCs. For N VPCs the number of connections grows as N×(N-1)/2 — a full mesh of 10 VPCs requires 45 peering connections, and 20 VPCs requires 190. Transit Gateway replaces this with a hub-and-spoke model: each VPC attaches to the Transit Gateway once, and the TGW routes between all attachments. Route tables on the TGW can also isolate environments (dev/prod) without separate peering connections.
  1. [Scenario question] Cross-cluster pod-to-pod traffic fails even though VPC routes and security groups are correctly configured. Pods on the same node can communicate, but traffic destined for another node's pod is dropped. What AWS EC2-level setting is likely missing?
Answer Source/destination checking is enabled on the EC2 instance's ENI by default. This check causes the hypervisor to drop any packet where the source or destination IP is not one of the ENI's own IPs — but pod IPs are secondary IPs or prefix-delegated CIDRs, not the primary ENI IP. For nodes that act as routers (self-managed Kubernetes without VPC CNI), you must disable source/destination checking on each node's primary ENI: `aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id --no-source-dest-check`. EKS with VPC CNI handles this automatically.
  1. [Practical question] What AWS CLI command would you run to list all Transit Gateway VPC attachments and their current states to verify that all expected VPCs are attached and active?
Answer 
aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-vpc-attachments --output table
Look for `State: available` on each attachment. A state of `pending` means the attachment was just created and the TGW route table may not yet have a route to that VPC; a state of `failed` indicates a permissions or subnet issue.

docs.title: Lesson 33 — ArgoCD and GitOps for Network Configuration
docs.text:
Track: GitOps & Delivery Prerequisites: Lesson 22 — Multi-Cluster Networking, Lesson 16 — Network Policies Duration: ~2 hours

Goal: Use ArgoCD to manage NetworkPolicies, CoreDNS configs, and Ingress rules as code — with sync waves for ordered delivery, ApplicationSets for multi-cluster rollout, and drift auto-remediation.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — check ArgoCD is running
kubectl get pods -n argocd
kubectl get applications -n argocd

# Terminal 2 — watch sync events
kubectl logs -n argocd -l app.kubernetes.io/name=argocd-application-controller -f

docs.title: 1. ArgoCD Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Git["Git Repository"]
        NP[network-policies/]
        IC[ingress/]
        CNI[cni-configs/]
    end
    subgraph ArgoCD["ArgoCD (argocd namespace)"]
        RS[repo-server\nclones repo\nrenders Helm/Kustomize] --> Redis[(Redis\ncache)]
        AC[application-controller\nwatches Application CRDs\ncompares live vs desired] --> AC
        SRV[argocd-server\nREST API + Web UI + CLI]
        DEX[Dex\nOIDC/SSO\noptional]
    end
    subgraph Clusters["Target Clusters"]
        K1[Cluster 1\nNetworkPolicy, Ingress, ...]
        K2[Cluster 2\nNetworkPolicy, Ingress, ...]
    end
    Git -->|pull every 3 min\nor webhook push| RS
    RS --> AC
    AC -->|kubectl apply| K1
    AC -->|kubectl apply| K2
    SRV --> AC
# Install ArgoCD
kubectl create namespace argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Wait for all pods
kubectl wait --for=condition=available deployment -l app.kubernetes.io/name=argocd-server -n argocd --timeout=120s

# Get initial admin password
argocd admin initial-password -n argocd

# Port-forward the UI (or expose via Ingress/LoadBalancer)
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443

docs.title: 2. GitOps Sync Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Network Engineer
    participant Git as Git Repository
    participant Webhook as GitHub Webhook
    participant ArgoCD as ArgoCD\napplication-controller
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API

    Dev->>Git: git push (new NetworkPolicy or Ingress change)
    Git->>Webhook: POST /api/webhook (if webhook configured)
    Webhook->>ArgoCD: trigger immediate sync
    ArgoCD->>Git: clone / fetch latest revision
    ArgoCD->>K8s: GET live manifests (compare)
    Note over ArgoCD,K8s: Diff: live != desired (OutOfSync)
    ArgoCD->>K8s: kubectl apply (sync waves order)
    K8s-->>ArgoCD: resource events (applied/failed)
    ArgoCD->>ArgoCD: health check (Healthy / Degraded)
    Note over Dev,ArgoCD: selfHeal=true: reverts manual changes automatically
    Dev->>ArgoCD: argocd app get (verify Synced + Healthy)

docs.title: Application — single cluster, single source
docs.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: network-policies
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/your-org/k8s-network-config
    targetRevision: main
    path: network-policies/production
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: default
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true        # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true     # re-apply if someone edits by hand
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

# CLI equivalent
argocd app create network-policies \
  --repo https://github.com/your-org/k8s-network-config \
  --path network-policies/production \
  --dest-server https://kubernetes.default.svc \
  --dest-namespace default \
  --sync-policy automated \
  --auto-prune \
  --self-heal

# Check sync status
argocd app get network-policies
argocd app diff network-policies   # show what would change
argocd app sync network-policies   # force immediate sync

docs.title: Deploying CoreDNS config from Git
docs.text:
# In Git: coredns/configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: coredns
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  Corefile: |
    .:53 {
        errors
        health
        kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
          pods insecure
          fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
        }
        hosts /etc/coredns/NodeHosts {
          ttl 60
          fallthrough
        }
        prometheus :9153
        forward . /etc/resolv.conf
        cache 30
        loop
        reload
        loadbalance
    }
    # Custom stub zone for internal services
    internal.corp:53 {
        forward . 10.100.0.53
    }

ArgoCD will detect drift the moment someone edits this ConfigMap manually.

docs.title: 4. Sync Waves for Network-Dependent Resources
docs.text:
Network resources must deploy in a specific order. A NetworkPolicy that blocks traffic must exist before the app starts, not after.

Sync Wave Order:

Wave -1: CRDs (Gateway API CRDs, Calico CRDs, cert-manager CRDs)
           │
Wave  0: CNI configuration (IPPool, BGPConfiguration, Cilium ConfigMap)
           │
Wave  1: NetworkPolicy (default-deny + allow rules)
           │
Wave  2: Application workloads (Deployments, StatefulSets)
           │
Wave  3: Ingress / Route / HTTPRoute (external access last)
           │
Wave  4: Monitoring (ServiceMonitor — after service exists)

# Wave -1: CRDs first
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"

---
# Wave 0: CNI IP pool
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: IPPool
metadata:
  name: production-pool
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
spec:
  cidr: 10.244.0.0/16
  ipipMode: Never
  natOutgoing: true

---
# Wave 1: NetworkPolicy before the app
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: frontend

---
# Wave 2: Application
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: backend
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "2"

---
# Wave 3: Ingress (only after pods are ready)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: backend-ingress
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "3"

# Watch sync waves progress in real time
argocd app get network-stack --watch

# See which wave each resource is in
argocd app resources network-stack

docs.title: 5. Multi-Cluster Deployment with ApplicationSet
docs.text:
Deploy the same NetworkPolicy baseline to every cluster from a single Application definition.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: network-baseline
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - clusters:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            environment: production   # only prod clusters
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "network-baseline-{{name}}"   # name = cluster name
    spec:
      project: network-team
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/your-org/k8s-network-config
        targetRevision: main
        path: network-baseline/
        helm:
          values: |
            clusterName: "{{name}}"
            clusterCIDR: "{{metadata.annotations.podCIDR}}"
      destination:
        server: "{{server}}"   # cluster API server URL
        namespace: kube-system
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          selfHeal: true

# Register clusters with ArgoCD
argocd cluster add production-eu-west-1 --name eu-west-1
argocd cluster add production-us-east-1 --name us-east-1
argocd cluster add production-ap-southeast-1 --name ap-southeast-1

# Label clusters to match the ApplicationSet generator
kubectl label secret -n argocd eu-west-1 environment=production
kubectl label secret -n argocd us-east-1 environment=production

# ApplicationSet creates one Application per cluster automatically
kubectl get applications -n argocd | grep network-baseline

# Check sync status across all clusters
argocd app list | grep network-baseline

docs.title: 6. Health Checks for Network Resources
docs.text:
ArgoCD has built-in health checks for core Kubernetes resources. Network resources vary:

Resource ArgoCD Health Behavior Service (ClusterIP) Healthy immediately Service (LoadBalancer) Healthy when .status.loadBalancer.ingress is populated Ingress Healthy when .status.loadBalancer.ingress is populated NetworkPolicy Always Healthy — ArgoCD cannot verify enforcement Gateway (Gateway API) Healthy when .status.conditions[Ready]=True HTTPRoute Healthy when parent Gateway accepts it Certificate (cert-manager) Healthy when .status.conditions[Ready]=True

NetworkPolicy is a critical gap — ArgoCD marks it healthy the moment it's applied, but cannot know if the CNI is actually enforcing it.

docs.title: Custom Lua health check for NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
-- In argocd-cm ConfigMap, resource.customizations section:
-- resource.customizations.health.networking.k8s.io_NetworkPolicy: |
hs = {}
if obj.metadata.creationTimestamp == nil then
  hs.status = "Progressing"
  hs.message = "NetworkPolicy not yet created"
  return hs
end
-- Check for a custom annotation set by a policy verification job
if obj.metadata.annotations ~= nil then
  if obj.metadata.annotations["network-policy/verified"] == "true" then
    hs.status = "Healthy"
    hs.message = "Policy applied and verified"
    return hs
  end
end
hs.status = "Degraded"
hs.message = "Policy applied but not verified — run policy conformance test"
return hs

# In argocd-cm ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  resource.customizations.health.networking.k8s.io_NetworkPolicy: |
    hs = {}
    hs.status = "Healthy"
    hs.message = "Applied (enforcement depends on CNI)"
    return hs

docs.title: 7. Detecting Network Policy Drift
docs.text:
selfHeal: true means ArgoCD detects and reverses any out-of-band change within seconds.

# Scenario: network engineer manually tightens a firewall rule
kubectl patch networkpolicy allow-frontend-to-backend -n production \
  --type='json' -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/ingress/0/ports"}]'

# ArgoCD detects the diff within ~3 minutes (or immediately via webhook)
argocd app get network-policies
# STATUS: OutOfSync
# MESSAGE: NetworkPolicy production/allow-frontend-to-backend
#          spec.ingress[0].ports: missing (live) vs [{port:8080}] (desired)

# With selfHeal=true: ArgoCD automatically reverts it
# Without selfHeal: notify and wait for manual sync

# To allow intentional overrides, use ignoreDifferences:
spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: networking.k8s.io
      kind: NetworkPolicy
      jsonPointers:
        - /metadata/annotations/kubectl.kubernetes.io~1last-applied-configuration

# Webhook setup (GitHub): push-triggered sync instead of poll
argocd app set network-policies --sync-policy automated
# Configure webhook in GitHub repo settings:
# URL: https://argocd.your-domain.com/api/webhook
# Secret: $(kubectl get secret argocd-secret -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.data.webhook\.github\.secret}' | base64 -d)

docs.title: 8. Argo Rollouts: Progressive Delivery with Network Integration
docs.text:
Argo Rollouts enables canary and blue-green deployments with network-layer traffic splitting.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: backend
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: backend-canary   # separate Service for canary pods
      stableService: backend-stable   # Service for stable pods
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService:
            name: backend-vsvc
            routes:
              - primary
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10    # 10% traffic to canary
        - pause: {duration: 5m}
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: success-rate
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 5m}
        - setWeight: 100

The VirtualService is updated automatically by the Rollout controller:

# ArgoCD syncs this; Rollouts controller modifies weights during deployment
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: backend-vsvc
spec:
  http:
    - name: primary
      route:
        - destination:
            host: backend-stable
          weight: 90      # Rollout controller updates this
        - destination:
            host: backend-canary
          weight: 10

See also: Lesson 31 — AWS Load Balancer Controller for weighted ALB target groups as an alternative to Istio for canary traffic splitting.

Git repository structure
docs.text:
k8s-network-config/
├── network-baseline/
│   ├── default-deny.yaml         # wave 0: deny-all NetworkPolicy
│   ├── allow-dns.yaml            # wave 0: allow CoreDNS egress

docs.title: Default-deny as wave 0 (foundation of zero-trust)
docs.text:
# network-baseline/default-deny.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
---
# Always allow DNS (without this, pods can't resolve service names)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - ports:
        - port: 53
          protocol: UDP
        - port: 53
          protocol: TCP

docs.title: ApplicationSet deploying the full stack
docs.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: zero-trust-stack
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - cluster: production-eu
            url: https://eks-eu.example.com
          - cluster: production-us
            url: https://eks-us.example.com
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "zero-trust-{{cluster}}"
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/your-org/k8s-network-config
        path: .
        targetRevision: main
      destination:
        server: "{{url}}"
        namespace: production
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
        syncOptions:
          - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true
          - ServerSideApply=true

docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change syncPolicy.automated.prune false Delete resources removed from Git Enable in production — prevents ghost resources syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal false Revert manual out-of-band changes Enable for security-sensitive resources (NetworkPolicy) syncPolicy.syncOptions.CreateNamespace false Create namespace if missing Enable for autonomous app deployment syncPolicy.syncOptions.ServerSideApply false Use server-side apply (better conflict handling) Enable when multiple controllers manage same resource argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave "0" Integer controlling sync order (-1 to N) Use -1 for CRDs, 0 for CNI, 1 for NetworkPolicy, 2+ for apps timeout.reconciliation (argocd-cm) 180s How often ArgoCD polls Git Reduce to 30s or use webhooks for fast drift detection resource.exclusions (argocd-cm) (none) Exclude resources from management Use for high-churn resources like Jobs ArgoCD shouldn't sync

docs.title: 11. Hands-On Practice
docs.text:
# 1. Check ArgoCD application health and sync status
argocd app list
# EXPECTED: NAME=network-policies, STATUS=Synced, HEALTH=Healthy

# 2. See current diff between Git and live cluster
argocd app diff network-policies
# EXPECTED: no output (synced) or +/- lines showing drift

# 3. Simulate drift — manually edit a NetworkPolicy
kubectl patch networkpolicy allow-frontend-to-backend -n production \
  --type='json' -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/ingress/0/ports/0","value":{"port":9999}}]'

# 4. Observe ArgoCD detects OutOfSync within 3 min (or faster with webhook)
argocd app get network-policies
# EXPECTED: STATUS=OutOfSync, details show the spurious port 9999

# 5. Force a dry-run sync to preview changes
argocd app sync network-policies --dry-run
# EXPECTED: shows kubectl apply operations that would run

# 6. Trigger real sync to revert the drift
argocd app sync network-policies
# EXPECTED: Synced, NetworkPolicy restored to Git state

# 7. Watch waves progress in an ApplicationSet sync
argocd app sync zero-trust-production-eu
argocd app get zero-trust-production-eu --watch
# EXPECTED: resources sync in wave order -1, 0, 1, 2, 3

# 8. Verify ArgoCD can manage NetworkPolicies (RBAC check)
kubectl auth can-i create networkpolicies \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-application-controller -n production
# EXPECTED: yes

See also: Lesson 16 — Network Policies for NetworkPolicy syntax and default-deny patterns used in wave 0.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• ArgoCD namespace has wave -1 NetworkPolicy allowing egress to all cluster API servers
  • selfHeal: true enabled on all NetworkPolicy and security-critical Applications
  • prune: true enabled — ghost resources from deleted Git entries are removed
  • AppProject RBAC configured — teams can only sync to their own namespace
  • Webhook configured for sub-minute drift detection (not relying on 3-minute poll)
  • timeout.reconciliation tuned or webhooks used for security-sensitive applications
  • All cluster secrets in ArgoCD are labeled correctly for ApplicationSet generators

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Deploy default-deny without wave -1 ArgoCD allow policy ArgoCD loses access to its own cluster mid-sync Always put ArgoCD self-allow NetworkPolicy at wave -1 selfHeal: false on NetworkPolicies Manual edits (even accidental kubectl apply) persist undetected Enable selfHeal: true for all security-enforcing resources No sync waves — all resources at wave 0 Ingress created before Deployment, NetworkPolicy after app traffic starts Annotate with sync-wave: CRDs first, policies before apps, Ingress last One Application per namespace with no AppProject No team isolation — any ArgoCD user can deploy to any cluster Create AppProject per team with destinations and sourceRepos restricted Managing coredns ConfigMap manually alongside ArgoCD ArgoCD reverts manual DNS changes immediately with selfHeal Commit all CoreDNS changes to Git; use kubectl edit only in ArgoCD-managed PRs
